name: Entelligence AI
what_it_does: AI production-reliability / engineering-intelligence platform for software teams. Its agent "Ellie" reviews every pull request against the team's past incident history (citing the specific prior incident as precedent), watches production telemetry live (spans, logs, metrics), spawns parallel sub-agents to root-cause incidents, ships and verifies fixes, then writes the root cause back into a learning graph. Product surfaces: Code Review, Incident/production loop, Model Router (routes each coding request across Claude Opus/Sonnet, GPT-5.5 Codex, Gemini, GLM, DeepSeek for cost/quality), Ask Ellie (codebase Q&A), Team Insights (engineering metrics), Agent Insights (beta - visibility into every agent run), a CLI, and auto-generated documentation. Headline marketing claims: #1 on their code-review benchmark at 47.2% F1, 43% of incidents auto-resolved, SOC 2 Type II. Their research pitch: across 1M+ PRs and 2,400+ orgs, only $0.18 of every AI-coding dollar reaches production. Integrations span GitHub/GitLab, Jira/Linear/Asana, Datadog/Sentry/New Relic/PagerDuty/CloudWatch, Slack/Discord, Notion/Confluence/Google Docs, Cursor/Copilot/Windsurf/Claude.
category: dev tools / AI code review + engineering intelligence (AI-native)
stage: seed (self-reported $5M raised; round name not stated)
funding: $5M - homepage banner reads "We raised $5M to run your Engineering team on Autopilot". Investor names not disclosed on the site; no Crunchbase/press confirmation obtained (web search budget exhausted this session).
headcount_estimate: 11-50 (LinkedIn company page band); likely at the low end of that band
yc_or_accelerator: unknown - no YC or accelerator affiliation found on their site, GitHub org, or LinkedIn page
founded_year: 2024 (LinkedIn company page)
sells_to: B2B - engineering leaders (CTO/VP Eng/EM) at startups through mid-size engineering orgs; developers are the daily users. Custom/quote-based pricing, "start free" self-serve entry, SOC 2 Type II for larger buyers. Named/logo customers on their own site include MindsDB (CEO Jorge Torres testimonial), SeekOut, Composio, Standard Metrics, Pylon, Docket, Smallest, Bespoke, Allocore, Upscale - and, notably, Corgi and Eragon (the other two companies in this batch).
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the product, not a feature. Ellie is an autonomous agent that (1) reviews each diff against every past incident, (2) monitors production signals and triages before the pager fires, (3) fans out parallel sub-agents for root-cause analysis, ships the fix and verifies it in prod. The Model Router is agent infrastructure - it routes coding-agent requests across frontier and cheap models per task. Agent Insights instruments other teams' agent runs. Their GitHub org (github.com/entelligence-ai) ships an "entelligence-claude-code" PR-review agent and Claude Code Agent Skills.
why_they_need_memory: Their entire architecture is an org memory claim: a "Production Intelligence World Model" - one living graph joining codebase, observability, production incidents, PRs and agent sessions, so "a memory that compounds with every incident." Incidents become searchable precedent recalled by future reviews ("checked against 1,247 incidents"). That memory must also span Slack, Discord, Notion, Confluence, Jira and Google Docs, i.e. exactly the cross-tool retrieval layer a company-brain vendor sells. Corroborating signal: their GitHub org has forked Memori, "SQL Native Memory Layer for LLMs, AI Agents & Multi-Agent Systems." A buyer like this either builds memory itself or rents the retrieval/ingestion layer - which is what Hyperspell's logo-wall placement implies.

name: Corgi (Corgi Insurance)
what_it_does: AI-native, full-stack insurance carrier for technology companies and small businesses. Unlike a broker or MGA, Corgi underwrites and issues its own policies - a federally chartered Risk Retention Group (TRRG) for primary coverage plus A-rated admitted-carrier partnerships where states require it (CA producer license #6012791). Pitch is quote in under 10 minutes and same-day binding versus weeks of broker back-and-forth. Products: General Liability, Tech E&O, Cyber, D&O, EPLI, Fiduciary, Media Liability, Hired & Non-Owned Auto, an AI Liability product, plus SMB verticals (trucking/auto liability, cargo, liquor liability for clubs and lodges). Segmented by startup stage (pre-seed/seed, Series A, growth, custom) and industry (SaaS, AI, fintech, crypto, marketplace, health-tech, sports). Company has expanded well past insurance into brand/consumer surfaces - Corgi Cafe (24h coffee shops in SF and NY), Corgi Bus, and Corgi ETFs (corgifunds.com) - and now positions itself as "the first AI financial infrastructure company," tagline "Insurance at the speed of compute."
category: insurtech / AI-native financial infrastructure (vertical AI, regulated)
stage: Series B (post-unicorn)
funding: $108M combined Seed + Series A at a $630M valuation, announced coming out of stealth (YC dates this Jan 8, 2026); investors named on their site: Y Combinator, Kindred Ventures, Oliver Jung, Leblon Capital, Contrary, Glade Brook Capital Partners. Then a $160M Series B at a $1.3B valuation, which is the figure currently on corgi.insure. UNVERIFIED: the YC company page's news feed also carries a headline "Doubles Valuation To $2.6 Billion" dated May 28, 2026 - I could not confirm the underlying round or article, and their own site has not been updated past $1.3B, so treat $2.6B as unconfirmed.
headcount_estimate: ~250 (YC directory "Team Size: 250"); LinkedIn shows the 51-200 band but ~354 associated employee profiles; 60 open roles listed on their careers page across SF, Boston, Dallas, London and remote. Best estimate 250-350 and growing fast - unusually large for a 2024-founded company because carrier operations (underwriting, claims, actuarial, BDR) are headcount-heavy.
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Summer 2024 batch (primary YC partner Jared Friedman)
sells_to: B2B SMB, self-serve-leaning. Primary ICP is venture-backed startups (pre-seed through growth) buying D&O/GL/Tech E&O/Cyber; expanding into non-tech SMB verticals (trucking, clubs and lodges) and offering a broker/partner program. Buyer is typically the founder, COO or finance lead - "built for founders by founders."
how_they_use_agents: Two places. (1) In the product: AI underwriting and quoting - instant quote generation, same-day bind, automated risk pricing that a full-stack carrier can do because it owns underwriting end to end. (2) In internal operations: Corgi's CEO Nico Laqua is the lead testimonial on Eragon's website and describes agents running "from onboarding, to insurance underwriting, to internal operations." Corgi is also a logo customer on Entelligence's homepage, implying agentic code review / production reliability on the engineering side. So agents touch underwriting, customer onboarding, back-office ops and engineering.
why_they_need_memory: A carrier's agents must reason over sprawling, long-lived, regulated state - submissions, policy documents, underwriting guidelines and appetite rules, claims history, billing, CRM - across many systems, and be consistent months later at renewal or claim time. Laqua's own words to Eragon are essentially a company-brain requirement: one system spanning onboarding, underwriting and internal ops. Add fast headcount growth (250+ across four-plus offices) and heavy regulatory audit pressure, and shared institutional memory becomes the bottleneck. This is the archetypal non-AI-infra buyer of the category: an AI-native operator with real operational sprawl, cash from a $160M round, and a bias to buy from other SF seed-stage AI startups.

name: Eragon
what_it_does: Self-described "Applied AI Lab for Operational Intelligence" selling an "AI Operating System for your company" - a reasoning engine that connects a company's tools, data and channels (explicitly no rip-and-replace), trains company-specific models on that proprietary data, and evaluates agent output against business outcomes. The stated stack: multi-model orchestration, persistent memory, composable skills, agent isolation, automation triggers, voice interaction and enterprise security, all with "your data stays in your environment and your weights stay in your hands." Their thesis is explicitly anti-frontier-rental: "Every company building on frontier models today is renting intelligence from someone else." Delivery model is forward-deployed engineering (stated in their schema.org description). NOTE: this makes Eragon a direct category adjacency to - arguably a competitor of - company-brain/agent-memory vendors like Hyperspell.
category: company brain / AI operating system / applied AI lab (agent + memory infrastructure itself)
stage: seed
funding: $12M seed round (site-wide banner: "Announcing our $12 million seed funding round"). Backers named on their About page: Arielle Zuckerberg, Cyan Banister, Lee Jacobs, SOMA (SOMA Capital) and Axiom. Lead investor and exact date not disclosed on the site.
headcount_estimate: 11-50 (LinkedIn band); 4 open roles listed (Member of Technical Staff, ML Engineer, Applied Research Engineer, Applied AI Intern), all San Francisco. Realistically a small single-digit-to-low-teens team given a 2025 founding and a $12M seed.
yc_or_accelerator: unknown - no YC or accelerator affiliation found; investors are angels plus SOMA and Axiom
founded_year: 2025 (schema.org foundingDate on eragon.ai; founder listed as Josh Sirota)
sells_to: B2B - "AI Native Companies", i.e. venture-backed startups and scaleups in the SF network, sold top-down to founders and heads of ops/finance. Named customer testimonials on their site: Nico Laqua (CEO & Founder, Corgi), Victor Cardenas Codriansky (CEO & Co-Founder, Slash), Nicky He (Head of Operations, Staff & Finance, Labs), Michael Kim (Co-Founder), Sid Rajaram (Co-Founder). Sales motion is high-touch ("Book a call" only, no self-serve, no public pricing) with forward-deployed engineers.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the product. They run across a customer's connected systems (product data, billing, revenue, CRM, underwriting, onboarding) as read-and-write operators rather than chat toys, and Eragon benchmarks each agent on accuracy, speed and value delivered against business outcomes. Customers describe replacing multi-tool lookups with a single chat query for decision-making. "Agent isolation" and "automation triggers" are named stack components, so agents run unattended, not just on demand.
why_they_need_memory: Persistent memory is an explicitly listed layer of their own stack, so the need is structural: an AI OS that answers cross-system business questions is a retrieval-and-memory product first. Their customers' quotes are memory complaints verbatim - Slash's CEO on business data scattered across product, billing, revenue and CRM and wanting "one place where we can read and write to all those systems." IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON DIRECTION: the relationship with Hyperspell appears reciprocal and possibly inverted. Eragon founder Josh Sirota's "51 weeks, 51 customers" LinkedIn series features Hyperspell, with Hyperspell's Conor Brennan-Burke saying Eragon made a difference to their journey - i.e. Hyperspell as Eragon's customer. Hyperspell's unlabeled homepage marquee is the only evidence in the other direction. Most likely reading: mutual customers, or a partnership/investor-network relationship rendered as a logo. Either way, Eragon is a poor archetype for "who buys agent memory" - it is closer to a peer building the same thing.

name: Snorkel AI
what_it_does: Frontier-AI data lab spun out of the Stanford AI Lab in 2019 (from the Snorkel weak-supervision research project). Originally sold Snorkel Flow, a programmatic/weak-supervision data labeling platform for enterprise ML; has since repositioned as 'expert data development for frontier AI.' Three current lines per their own site: (1) Data Development — expert-curated post-training datasets, expert demonstrations, reasoning traces, preference labels and rubrics for cases where 'off-the-shelf coverage runs out'; (2) Specialized Agents — custom agents built on specialized data and scored against task-specific pass/fail criteria on real workflows; (3) Benchmarks & Research — Terminal-Bench 4.0, Senior SWE-bench (with Princeton and UW-Madison, July 2026), OSWorld 2.0, plus domain benchmarks in legal, scientific and insurance work, and a $3M Open Benchmarks Grants program. Customers/partners named or implied include frontier labs (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft), large enterprises, and US defense (Army xTech AI Grand Challenge winner Aug 2025; completed a DIU challenge Dec 2025).
category: AI training data / evaluation infrastructure (data labeling → frontier-AI data + RL environments + agent benchmarks)
stage: Late-stage private (Series C+); strategic corporate investment from Accenture in Aug 2025
funding: $35M Series B (April 2021, per TechCrunch) and an $85M Series C (2021) are the rounds I could confirm; Accenture made a strategic investment on 2025-08-06 with no disclosed amount. Total disclosed is roughly $135M+ across all rounds but I could not verify a precise cumulative figure, and I could NOT confirm any valuation or any Series D — treat both as unknown. Investors listed on snorkel.ai itself: Greylock, GV, Lightspeed (LSVP), In-Q-Tel (IQT), Addition, BlackRock, SV Angel, Walden Catalyst.
headcount_estimate: 201-500 (LinkedIn company page band); no exact figure published
yc_or_accelerator: None — Stanford AI Lab spinout, not an accelerator company
sells_to: B2B enterprise, plus frontier AI labs and US government/defense — the largest and most upmarket buyer of the three by a wide margin
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the subject of the product, not just a feature. Snorkel builds the evaluation environments and training data that agents are measured and trained on — coding-agent benchmarks (Senior SWE-bench), terminal-agent benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 4.0), computer-use benchmarks (OSWorld 2.0), and RL environments. They also ship 'Specialized Agents': custom domain agents (legal, insurance, financial services) built on client-specific expert data and graded on real workflows rather than generic copilot demos. Internally the delivery model is FDE/solutions-engineering-heavy — bespoke data projects per enterprise client.
why_they_need_memory: IMPORTANT CAVEAT — Snorkel is NOT a confirmed customer of Hyper. Hyper's own site says it is 'scoping paid design pilots with co's like Razorpay and Snorkel AI' (prospective, not closed), and Hyper co-founder Kanyes Thaker is a Snorkel alum ('prev youngest FDE at Snorkel AI'), with the FAQ saying the founders 'felt the same pain firsthand at Matic Robots and Snorkel AI.' Snorkel has made no public statement about using Hyper. So Snorkel appears on that site primarily as a founder's former employer / warm-network prospect. The plausible underlying need, if a pilot happens: a 200-500 person org running bespoke per-client data engagements accumulates enormous tacit project context (rubric decisions, annotation guidelines, client edge cases) across FDEs, which is exactly the 'company brain' pain — but this is inference, not an advertised use case.
confidence: high on the company facts (site, LinkedIn, TechCrunch, own press page); LOW on the customer relationship — it is a scoping-stage pilot mediated by a founder-alumni tie, not an advertised closed customer

name: Composio
what_it_does: Tool-calling and integration infrastructure for AI agents. The platform gives agents authenticated access to 1,500+ third-party app integrations with 'just-in-time tool calls, secure delegated auth, sandboxed environments, and parallel execution.' Key pieces: managed OAuth that triggers inline when an agent needs a credential; a Tool Router (beta, Oct 2025) that selects tools from agent intent instead of static configuration; remote sandboxes where tools execute as code; support for Claude, Gemini and other model providers. Freemium — '100k free tool calls/mo, no credit card required.' Logos on the homepage include Glean, Zoom, AWS, Google, Wix, Hostinger and Arizona State University. Strategic direction stated in their funding post is agent memory-adjacent: 'a shared learning infrastructure where every interaction makes the entire ecosystem smarter' — capturing tacit knowledge from millions of interactions and turning edge cases into agent intuition (the 'fleet of Waymos' analogy). As of May 2026 agents can sign themselves up for Composio accounts.
category: Agent infrastructure / developer tools — the tool-calling, auth and execution layer for AI agents
stage: Series A
funding: $29M Series A announced 2025-07-22 by co-founder Soham Ganatra ('We raised $29M to build skills that evolve with your agents'). Note a discrepancy: the post's metadata/headline references $25M while the body says $29M. The company's own announcement names NO investors, and I could not confirm a lead investor or valuation from any other source — treat lead investor and valuation as unknown. Do not assume a specific VC.
headcount_estimate: 11-50 (LinkedIn band); likely toward the upper half of that range given a Series A and shipping cadence, but no exact number published
yc_or_accelerator: Unknown / not confirmed — ycombinator.com/companies/composio returns 404 and neither the site nor the blog claims an accelerator. Do not state Composio is YC without better evidence.
sells_to: Developers first (self-serve freemium, SDK, GitHub), expanding to enterprise — logo wall shows both AI-native companies (Glean) and large orgs (AWS, Google, Zoom, ASU)
how_they_use_agents: Composio IS agent infrastructure — its entire product is the action/tool layer agents call to do work in external SaaS. Agents are the users of the product (they even self-register as of May 2026). Internally, the team is a small AI-native engineering org building distributed self-improving systems, and the stated roadmap ('skills that evolve with your agents') is itself an agent-memory/learning play — notable because it means an agent-memory-adjacent vendor is buying a company-brain tool for its own internal knowledge work.
why_they_need_memory: This is the strongest, most concrete signal of the three. The Glen testimonial is from a named employee — 'KJ, MTS at Composio' — and describes a real onboarding/context-recovery moment: 'Yesterday I got Posthog access and was trying to understand some stuff, glen surfaced Sarah's context and was very very very helpful, would recommend.' The buying trigger is a fast-growing small eng team where knowledge lives scattered across Slack, GitHub, PostHog and agent sessions, and a new MTS cannot reconstruct why a teammate did something. Composio also appears in Glen's 'Powering knowledge work at' logo wall, so it is an advertised customer, not just a quote. Two things worth flagging to the buyer-persona analysis: (a) founder Nikos Dritsakos of Glen is ex-Head of Special Projects (MTS) at Composio, so this is also a warm founder-network account, though unlike Snorkel there is a named current-employee usage quote; (b) Composio published two security incident reports (2026-02-13 covering a Feb 9 incident, and 2026-05-21 covering a May 2026 incident affecting internal systems), which is context for how such companies think about piping internal knowledge into third-party tools.
confidence: high — company facts confirmed from homepage, blog, LinkedIn; customer relationship confirmed by a named-employee testimonial plus logo wall on tryglen.com. Funding amount confirmed from the company's own post; lead investor and headcount precision remain unknown.

name: Final Round AI
what_it_does: Consumer/prosumer AI interview-prep company. Flagship product is "Interview CoPilot" — a desktop app that listens to a live video interview (Zoom, Meet, Teams, Webex, HackerRank, CoderPad, phone screens) and pushes real-time suggested answers into a private overlay window, with a "Stealth Mode" that hides the overlay from screen shares and recordings. Around it sits a Prepare / Perform / Review loop: AI-run mock interviews, auto-capture-and-solve for coding and system-design problems on screen, automatic post-interview debriefs, a resume/LinkedIn optimizer, and "AI Job Hunter," an automated job-application agent. Homepage claims 10M+ job seekers and 80+ countries; the About page claims 1M+ users across 100+ countries (the two numbers do not reconcile — treat marketing metrics with caution). A Final Round AI employee's public LinkedIn bio claims "millions of users and 10M ARR" (unverified). Founders Michael Guan (CEO, Yale) and Jay Ma (CTO) are also publicly building a follow-on product, Work Trial AI / "Hellyeah AI" (assess candidates through real work rather than interviews). Pricing: free tier plus Pro from ~$25/mo (a review site lists $59). NOTE ON THE CITATION: Hyperspell's homepage does list "FinalRoundAI" in an unlabeled logo marquee — I independently confirmed the logo strip exists. But there is no testimonial, quote, case study, or usage detail attached to it, and both Final Round AI and Hyperspell appear in the portfolio of the same investor, Mento VC. The logo may reflect an investor-network relationship rather than a mature paying deployment.
category: AI interview copilot / career-tech (B2C job seekers)
stage: Seed
funding: $6.88M seed led by Uncork Capital, announced 30 Jan 2025 (PR Newswire, described as oversubscribed). The company's own media kit says "$8M in funding from top Silicon Valley investors" — likely seed plus pre-seed/angel. Crunchbase lists 13 investors including Level One Partners and Sky9 Capital; Soma Capital and Mento VC also appear in third-party investor lists. No Series A found.
headcount_estimate: ~10-50 — sources conflict and none is authoritative. Final Round AI's own LinkedIn company page self-reports "2-10 employees" (almost certainly stale/understated). Ritual Capital's job board lists "11-50 employees." One aggregator (Startup Intros) says 201-500, which I regard as unreliable. LinkedIn following is ~4.9K.
yc_or_accelerator: None found — not a YC company and no accelerator identified.
sells_to: Prosumer / B2C — individual job seekers on self-serve subscriptions, not companies. (The Work Trial AI spinout would be the first B2B motion.)
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the entire product surface, in two modes. (1) Real-time assistive agent: an always-listening agent transcribes the live interview, understands the question in context, and generates an answer in seconds into a private window; a vision component auto-captures coding/system-design problems on screen and solves them. (2) Autonomous agent: "AI Job Hunter" searches, matches, and auto-submits job applications on the user's behalf, tailoring materials per role. AI also runs mock interviews and produces structured debriefs. Every one of these needs deep per-user state — resume, target roles, company research, what the candidate said in the last three interviews.
why_they_need_memory: The product's core loop is explicitly longitudinal — Prepare, Perform, Review, repeat, across many interviews for many roles for the same user — so per-user long-term memory (resume facts, target companies, past answers, feedback from prior debriefs) is a product requirement, not a nice-to-have; a copilot that forgets last week's mock interview cannot personalize this week's live one. The AI Job Hunter agent additionally needs persistent state on which jobs were applied to, what was said, and what worked. Separately, Hyperspell markets itself as an internal "company brain" / agentic memory network connecting a company's own tools, so the use may equally be internal ops (a small team with a large support and content surface) rather than in-product. I could not determine which. Caveat: no public statement from Final Round AI about Hyperspell exists.

name: Madhavan (Maddy) Malolan — INDIVIDUAL, not a company (co-founder/CEO, Reclaim Protocol; angel investor in Memory Store)
what_it_does: IMPORTANT — READ BEFORE COUNTING THIS AS A CUSTOMER. This is a named individual, not a company account, and I resolved the ambiguity the original note flagged. Two things are now confirmed from independent sources: (1) Malolan's own personal website lists his angel investments and includes, verbatim, "[AI] Memory Store (YCx26, investment before they entered YC)" — so he is an ANGEL INVESTOR in Memory Store who invested before the company entered YC. (2) The vendor testimonial itself is corroborated: Google's index of Memory Store's LinkedIn company page and of co-founder Ishita Jindal's post both surface the same text describing him as "one of the most honest, no-BS users we have," matching the partial render originally captured. So the quote is real and the person is correctly identified. His day job: co-founder and CEO of Reclaim Protocol (YC W21), an AI-fraud-resistant identity/credential verification stack using zkTLS — lets a user prove facts about themselves from any website (education, employment, loyalty status, financial data) without the site's cooperation. Founded 2021 by Sriharsha Karamchati, Subhash Karri and Madhavan Malolan; 17 employees, Hyderabad, India per YC. He previously founded Questbook / CreatorOS Inc and Socionity. THE ANALYTICAL POINT: this is NOT arms-length demand. An angel investor in the company using the product daily is a friendly design partner, not a market signal. It should be excluded from, or heavily discounted in, any count of who independently buys agent-memory. The vendor's own post frames him as a skeptic-turned-daily-user, which is a credible product signal but a weak commercial one. No employer is named in the vendor's post, and Memory Store never publicly tied him to Reclaim Protocol — that link comes from his own site and LinkedIn, not from the vendor.

how_they_use_agents: Not disclosed. The vendor post describes personal daily use of a "company brain" — persistent shared memory across his own work — rather than any agent embedded in a product. Reclaim Protocol's own product line is zkTLS verification with an anti-AI-fraud framing (deepfake/synthetic-document resistance), which is AI-adjacent but is not an agent product. There is no evidence of Memory Store being wired into Reclaim Protocol's product or company workflows.
why_they_need_memory: The stated need is personal, not organizational: per the vendor's post he initially found limited value, then reported using it daily and being unable to work without it — the classic pattern of a founder wanting continuity of context across scattered tools and sessions. As a serial founder running one company while angel-investing across five startups, the pull is plausibly cross-context recall (threads, deals, portfolio, product decisions) rather than any agent-memory API need. Treat as an unconfirmed-revenue, investor-aligned power user.

name: Razorpay
what_it_does: India's largest full-stack payments and business-banking platform — a fintech unicorn, and by far the largest and least AI-native name in this cohort. Six business lines: (1) Accept Payments — payment gateway, links, pages, buttons, POS, subscriptions, smart collect, QR, Optimizer, international payments; (2) RazorpayX payouts — API and bulk payouts, source-to-pay, tax payments; (3) RazorpayX business banking — current accounts, escrow, forex, corporate credit cards; (4) payroll automation; (5) credit and instant settlements; (6) a new "AI Native Products" line. Claims 150,000+ Indian businesses including Swiggy, Zomato, BookMyShow, Zepto and Lenskart. Eight acquisitions to date (Ezetap POS, BillMe, PoshVine, IZealiant, Curlec and others). Reportedly preparing a mid-2026 IPO of roughly Rs 4,500 crore, with Axis Capital, Kotak, J.P. Morgan and Citi India appointed. MAJOR CAVEAT ON THE CITATION — this is the weakest customer claim of the three. The only evidence is a single line Hyper wrote about itself on its own YC company page: "scoping paid design pilots with co's like Razorpay and Snorkel AI." I verified that text is live on Hyper's YC profile. But "scoping" means a pilot under negotiation, not a signed or paying customer, and "co's like" makes the list illustrative rather than exhaustive. Razorpay has made no public statement about Hyper, and I found none. This should be logged as an unconverted prospect, not a customer.
category: Payments / fintech infrastructure — with a newly launched agentic-AI product line
stage: Late-stage private (Series F), pre-IPO
funding: $741.5M total across Series A through F per Razorpay's own YC profile (Tracxn: ~$742M over 11 rounds). Last valuation $7.5B at Series F. Investors include Lone Pine Capital, Alkeon Capital, TCV, GIC, Tiger Global, Sequoia Capital India, Ribbit Capital, Matrix Partners, Salesforce Ventures, Mastercard and Y Combinator. (One aggregator, Parsers VC, claims $3.61B raised — I regard that as wrong and am not using it.)
headcount_estimate: ~3,000-4,700; sources disagree. LinkedIn company page states 1,001-5,000. Revelio Labs reports 4,665 for 2026 (up from 4,567 in 2025). LeadIQ says ~4,100 as of July 2026. Tracxn says 3,028 as of Aug 2025. AmbitionBox says 3,900+ in India. Best single estimate: roughly 4,000+.
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator Winter 2015 — the second Indian company ever to go through YC.
founded_year: 2014 (Harshil Mathur, CEO; Shashank Kumar, MD)
sells_to: B2B, both SMB and enterprise — 150,000+ Indian businesses spanning kirana shops on POS through large consumer internet companies (Swiggy, Zomato, Zepto). Also increasingly sells to developers and AI builders via "Payments for AI Builders."
how_they_use_agents: Substantial and recent. Razorpay launched Agent Studio (blog dated 12 Mar 2026; showcased at Razorpay Sprint/FTX 2026 alongside 100+ launches), built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK. It ships prebuilt autonomous agents for payment and revenue operations — Dispute Responder (auto-assembles chargeback evidence to maximize win rates), Subscription Recovery (analyzes failed payments, smarter retry logic, targeted nudges), Abandoned Cart Conversion (WhatsApp/email re-engagement with personalized offers), RTO Shield (flags high-risk COD orders via address validation before dispatch), Settlement Insights (daily payout summaries over WhatsApp), and Cashflow Forecaster (3-7 day cash position with payroll alerts) — plus custom agent building in beta and an AI-partner program. Adjacent lines: Agentic Payments ("turn every chat into a checkout"), Agentic Business Banking, and Payments for AI Builders. The CEO has publicly promoted an AI "co-founder" service launched in April.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. Externally, Razorpay is now shipping long-running autonomous agents against merchant money — disputes, retries, forecasting — where an agent must carry merchant-specific history (which evidence won past chargebacks, which retry windows work for this merchant's customers, this business's cash rhythm) across weeks; that is a durable-memory problem, and it is why an agent-memory vendor would target them. Internally, a ~4,000-person organization rolling out agents across dozens of product lines needs shared org context so each agent team is not rebuilding the same knowledge. Hyper's pitch — "company brain that powers your AI employees" — maps to the internal case, and the wording ("paid design pilots") suggests an internal/design engagement rather than embedding memory in Razorpay's shipped product. Note the more likely read: a large enterprise doing a small paid pilot with a 12-day-old YC startup is a logo-and-learning exercise for both sides, not evidence of category budget.

name: Litmus
what_it_does: Technical hiring assessment platform; tagline "Evals for humans." Litmus "turns your repos, tickets, and job descriptions into real hiring signal" — it auto-generates async, real-world coding assessments from a customer's own codebase, issue tickets, and JDs, scoped so the task resembles work the candidate would actually ship. Candidates complete the task in their native dev environment and are explicitly encouraged to use AI tools; Litmus instruments the whole session, capturing prompts, file iteration, commit history, and decision-making (the site shows examples of candidates driving "claude · Sonnet 4.6" and "codex · GPT-5.2"). Grading is two-layer: submissions run against deterministic harnesses in live sandboxes for correctness, plus "configurable LLM graders evaluate qualitative dimensions like process and architecture." Candidates also record walkthroughs explaining their choices. Integrates with Ashby, Greenhouse, and Lever, or Litmus runs the loop end-to-end. Pricing is custom by hiring volume. Named customers on the site: Neo Scholars, Mercor, Composio, Astranis, Wispr Flow, August, Spur, Autumn AI, Pine Labs, Sleuth, Series, Laurence, Dryft. LinkedIn frames the longer ambition as "the most accurate framework for evaluating and benchmarking human capability, starting with technical hiring." DISAMBIGUATION CONFIRMED: this is Litmus the hiring startup, NOT litmus.com the email-testing company — matching the SVG-embedded provenance comment in Glen's logo asset.

stage: seed / accelerator (YC S26); no priced round disclosed

how_they_use_agents: Agents appear on both sides of the product. (1) Generation: the platform ingests a customer's repos, tickets, and JDs and synthesizes a scoped, buildable assessment from them — a codebase-comprehension task. (2) Grading: configurable LLM graders score qualitative dimensions (process, architecture) alongside deterministic sandbox test harnesses. (3) Measurement: Litmus treats candidate AI-tool usage as signal rather than cheating, recording and analyzing how candidates prompt and refine with coding agents. Internally it is a ~4-person team, so day-to-day engineering is almost certainly agent-driven.
why_they_need_memory: INFERRED — evidence is logo-wall-only. Litmus appears in Glen's "Powering knowledge work at" wall with no testimonial, so the wall header implies usage but Glen never labels these as paying customers. The plausible fit: Litmus's core product requires deep, repeated machine comprehension of many different customers' codebases, and its own tiny team ships that with coding agents — exactly the pattern where per-repo context has to be rebuilt every session. Glen's agent-memory and skills-distillation pitch (inject prior work into prompts, cut repeat token cost, retain the reasoning behind a change) targets that. Also notable: Litmus and Glen share a customer, Composio, which appears on both companies' walls — suggesting the same small YC-adjacent network rather than an independent enterprise sales motion.

name: Corgi Insurance

Unlike a broker or MGA, Corgi does underwriting, policy design, servicing, and claims administration in-house — coverage is written through Technology Risk Retention Group (TRRG), a federally chartered risk retention group, with A-/better AM Best partner carriers for state-admitted policies (CA license #6012791). Products are packaged by funding stage: Pre-Seed/Seed gets GL, D&O, Tech E&O, Cyber (~$2,000-$5,000/yr); Series A adds Media Liability and EPLI (~$5,000-$15,000/yr); Growth adds Fiduciary. Additional lines: Umbrella, Workers' Comp, Professional E&O, Crime, K&R, Hired/Non-Owned Auto, Reps & Warranties. Target verticals: SaaS, AI, fintech, crypto, marketplaces, health-tech, trucking. The blog claims quotes in under 10 minutes and same-day binding. The company also runs adjacent ventures — Corgi Funds/ETFs (corgifunds.com), Corgi Cafe (SF and NY), Corgi Bus — and self-describes as "building the first AI financial infrastructure company" aiming to "rebuild the $1T+ insurance industry from the ground up." corgi.com 301-redirects to corgi.insure. This is Corgi (YC S24, corgi.insure), NOT the unrelated YC company Corgi Labs (payments).

Corgi describes itself as "the first full-stack AI insurance carrier": AI drives underwriting and quoting (sub-10-minute quotes, same-day binding, no broker in the loop) and is paired with human claims expertise ("60+ years of claims experience") for end-to-end claim ownership. name: AgentMail
what_it_does: API-first email provider that gives AI agents their own inboxes — "Gmail, but for agents." Programmatic inbox creation, send/receive with threading, webhooks + WebSockets for real-time events, IMAP, custom domains with DKIM/SPF/DMARC, semantic "Agent Search" over an inbox, LLM-driven auto-labeling and structured extraction, multi-tenant "Pods" for platform builders, and "Outposts" BYOC deployment. Python/TypeScript SDKs plus an MCP server. Positions the inbox as an agent's identity and persistent record. Their own published customers include AISDR, Balance, Lanesurf, Locus, Pancake, Cofounder, DoAnything, Eragon, Junior, Browser Use, AgentCard and Dossium; distribution/integration partners include Vercel, Telnyx, Clay, LiveKit, LangChain, Google ADK and OpenClaw. Pricing is usage-based and self-serve: Free ($0, 3 inboxes / 3k emails per month), Developer ($20/mo), Startup ($200/mo), Enterprise custom — explicitly no per-seat charges on API access.
category: AI agent infrastructure / email API (dev tools)
stage: Seed
funding: $6M seed announced 2026-03-10, led by General Catalyst, with Y Combinator and Phosphor Capital participating; angels include Paul Graham, Dharmesh Shah (HubSpot), Paul Copplestone (Supabase), Karim Atiyeh (Ramp) and Taro Fukuyama
headcount_estimate: ~10-11 (YC directory lists team size 10; LinkedIn structured data reports 11, band "2-10 employees")
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Summer 2025 batch (group partner Ankit Gupta); LinkedIn name is literally "AgentMail (YC S25)"
sells_to: developers — AI agent startups and platform teams building autonomous agents; self-serve PLG bottom tier with an enterprise/BYOC tier on top
how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product's end user: AgentMail sells inboxes that autonomous agents own and operate — signing up for services, receiving confirmations, authenticating, and running email threads with no human in the loop (their AISDR case study cites thousands of emails/week fully unattended). Internally, per Adi Singh's testimonial, they run Hyperspell's "company brain" as a shared source of truth across the human team and their internal agents, which they say lets them automate most internal operations, customer support especially.
why_they_need_memory: Small (~10 person) dev-tools team fielding high-volume developer support across docs, Discord, email and a large SEO blog surface; support answers must be grounded in constantly-shipping product docs. They wanted one retrieval layer both humans and their internal support agents query rather than building ingestion/search themselves. Thematically aligned too — they publish content arguing email is itself agent memory and identity ("email as memory for AI agents", "the next trillion users need an identity"), so a persistent-context vendor is an adjacent, well-understood purchase rather than a leap.

name: Hobbes
what_it_does: AI sales agent that lives on a company's website and replaces the "Book a Demo" button. It runs live, multilingual, 24/7 product demos inside a sandbox of the actual product, researches the visitor's company in real time to surface relevant use cases, enriches contacts and scores them against the ICP, then either offers checkout or books a meeting with a human rep when intent appears. It learns continuously from docs, help-center content and recorded sales calls, and feeds back transcripts plus "product heatmaps" showing where buyers hesitate or object. CRM integrations with Salesforce, HubSpot and Attio; SOC 2 Type 2 and SSO via SAML/OIDC. A public API shipped around August 2026. Claimed results: +53% human booking volume, +30% qualified leads. Named customers: Digit, SalonScale, Entelligence, Fundable, Canary, Haulvana — plus Hyperspell itself ("How Hyperspell 2x'd their revenue with Hobbes"), making the Hyperspell relationship reciprocal. Pricing is tiered by leads/month: Starter (250, SMB), Growth (650, mid-market), Scale (2,000, enterprise) and Custom (SSO/SAML, security review, SLA, dedicated SE).
category: AI SDR / AI sales agent (GTM software)
stage: Seed
funding: $6M seed, announced ~May 2026, led by Steve Vassallo at Foundation Capital, with support from Ramy Adeeb (1984 Ventures), Gaurav Jain and Joseph Cardini (Afore Capital), plus investors from Emergence Capital. The $6M figure is also stated on their own homepage.
headcount_estimate: ~9 (LinkedIn reports 9 employees, band "2-10"); careers page says "a small team" that "changes every month"
yc_or_accelerator: none found — no YC or accelerator affiliation surfaced on their site, careers page or LinkedIn
sells_to: B2B, SMB through enterprise — sales/GTM and demand-gen teams at software companies; self-serve-ish tiers at the bottom, security-reviewed enterprise contracts at the top
how_they_use_agents: The agent is the entire product — a conversational sales rep that autonomously drives a live product walkthrough, qualifies, and closes or books. Publicly described as powered by Claude, with buyer memory carried across sessions and self-improvement loops; the founders say agent-to-agent sales, world-models and self-improving product feedback loops are next on the roadmap.
why_they_need_memory: The agent has to be grounded in a customer's whole knowledge surface — product docs, help center, recorded sales calls — and stay current as that surface changes, per customer, across every tenant. Arjun Athreya's testimonial is explicit that reliable ingestion, search, monitoring and tuning would have taken a nine-person team months to assemble, so they bought it out of the box instead. Memory is not a convenience here, it is the substrate of the demo agent's competence, and the buyer-memory/world-model roadmap deepens that dependency.

name: Scale Agentic (ScaleAgentic, Inc.)
what_it_does: Sells "Scout," marketed as an AI GTM Engineer: you give it a business goal and it researches, strategizes, executes and self-optimizes the go-to-market motion. Four-phase playbook — instant campaign strategy, real-time cross-channel listening, hyper-personalized engagement, optimized pattern recognition. Identifies decision-makers matching the ICP, monitors LinkedIn, X, Reddit, Discord, Slack, Meta and Notion for buying-intent signals, generates and queues personalized outreach, and reports into real-time GTM dashboards with custom KPIs. Company framing is explicitly memory-shaped: an "Agentic GTM Brain," a company-specific "GTM World Model" (a living representation of market, buyers, positioning, workflows, tools, signals and outcome history) that serves as the reasoning layer for which motion to run next, plus "Helix-Max," a live GTM command center where every customer interaction becomes learning for the brain. name: SuperMe (SuperMe Network, Inc.)
what_it_does: An AI-native professional network — self-described as 'a hybrid AI-powered search engine and social network' whose mission is 'to index collective human knowledge.' Each professional builds a 'SuperMe' profile trained on their own real work: writing, talks, meeting notes, docs. Others can then (a) query a specific person's profile directly, (b) let their own SuperMe agent search the network, find the right experts, collect their perspectives and return a synthesized answer, or (c) open a Group Chat where multiple people's SuperMe profiles discuss a question in real time, watchable live or as a summary. 'Work Groups' are curated panels of founders and executives. An 'Insights Agent' connects to Google Drive, Notion, Gmail and Granola and turns real work output into the profile, deciding what is worth surfacing versus keeping private. Granular per-item privacy: public / private / team-only / let-SuperMe-decide, plus incognito mode. A SuperMe MCP server exposes the whole network inside Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor and Codex. Explicit anti-hallucination stance: if a profile doesn't know how that person thinks on a topic, it says so. The public sitemap lists roughly 4,000 profiles, including Lenny Rachitsky, Reid Hoffman, Ben Casnocha, Kyle Poyar and Casey Winters. Free to sign up; there is an app as well as the web product. Not a classic B2B seat sale; the closest thing to a B2B surface is team-scoped content sharing and Work Groups. Monetization is not disclosed publicly (the /pricing route renders nothing).
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the entire product surface. Every user has a personal agent (their 'SuperMe') that is trained only on that person's own material. When you ask a question, your agent searches the network, selects the right experts, queries their SuperMe profiles, and returns a synthesized multi-perspective answer. Group Chat orchestrates several people's agents debating a question against each other in real time. A separate 'Insights Agent' does the ingestion side — connecting to Drive, Notion, Gmail and Granola and deciding what to index, what to surface and what to discard. And they ship an MCP server so the network is callable as a tool from Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor and Codex.
why_they_need_memory: Of the three, this is the purest fit — the product IS agent memory, sold as a network. Their core technical problem is exactly what a company-brain vendor sells: ingest heterogeneous personal work corpora (Drive, Notion, Gmail, Granola meeting notes, talks, posts), synthesize them into a queryable representation of how a specific person thinks, keep it fresh as new work happens, enforce per-document privacy scoping at retrieval time (public / team / private / incognito), and ground every answer hard enough that the agent can say 'I don't know' rather than hallucinate a fake opinion attributed to a real named person. That last constraint is unusually severe — putting words in Reid Hoffman's mouth is a reputational failure, not a bad completion — so ingestion quality, provenance and retrieval precision are existential rather than nice-to-have. Doing that for ~4,000 profiles with a team of roughly a dozen is exactly the 'would have taken months to build ourselves' pitch in Hyperspell's own testimonials.

(2) Internally, which is the relevant part: Nedap's engineering team first built a DIY ChatGPT-over-Slite-docs integration, which hallucinated confidently about company policy. They replaced it with Slite Agent connected to eight systems — Slack, GitHub, Confluence, Notion, Jira, HubSpot, SharePoint plus custom internal systems — and then built role-specific agents on top: a customer-success agent wired to HubSpot, and an on-call engineering agent drawing on incident history and troubleshooting docs. They also run a daily digest. Multilingual retrieval matters (teams work in Dutch, Spanish, Polish and Ukrainian) — queries in one language, sources in another.
why_they_need_memory: Classic 'scaled past the wiki' buyer. Headcount roughly tripled in one division (150 to ~400) while documentation accumulated inconsistent naming conventions and taxonomies across a decade of Slite use (customer since 2019) plus seven other systems. CTO Andre Foeken's framing: people were 'planning their mornings just to try and catch up, and it didn't work anymore.' Critically, they already tried to build this themselves and failed on grounding — the purchase decision hinged on abstention, not recall: 'the biggest change was when it said I don't know. Previous solutions always knew something. They were never right, but they were fully convinced.' For a regulated healthcare vendor, a confidently wrong answer about policy is a liability, so calibrated refusal and source citation are the actual product requirements. Add multilingual staff and 8+ source systems and a single retrieval layer with per-role agents becomes the only tractable shape.

The agent usage is entirely internal/support-facing: a Slite Agent button embedded inside Intercom so support reps get sourced answers in the ticket; a separate assistant scoped for white-labeled end-user support; an internal assistant that drafts help-center guides for new features ('in 30 seconds I can create a guide for any new feature'); and a Zapier workflow that pipes feature requests into the knowledge base. Their CTO Nick had been building a DIY Slack bot at night wiring Google Drive to the help center — Mark Weisberg's line is that Slite Agent 'was what Nick was trying to build, but already done and on steroids.'
why_they_need_memory: A 91-person, fully remote, 27-country company supporting 4,000+ creators and 15M end users cannot route every question to a human. Knowledge sat in silos — Intercom, GitHub, Linear, Google Drive, help center — and subject-matter experts were spending roughly half their day answering questions instead of shipping. They are a serial churner in this category, which makes them a revealing datapoint on what fails: Guru was dropped after a year because its verification workflow generated notification overload (maintenance tax too high); Intercom Fin/Copilot was beta-tested but priced per-resolution in a way that blocked company-wide rollout (pricing model mismatch for a low-ACV support org); and the DIY route was a CTO moonlighting on a Slack bot. Reported outcome: 97-98% CSAT held while handle times dropped, and they retired a standalone support-QA tool. The buying trigger is documentation freshness plus cost-per-ticket, not knowledge nostalgia.

It has a command surface that does tasks on request ("Draft email to John", "Summarize unread investor emails") with human accept/reject on sensitive sends. It generates small internal apps from a prompt. And via Micro Blocks it exposes MCP/API so other agents (Claude, Codex, Cursor) can build on the workspace. It also publishes downloadable "Agentic Fundraising / Sales / Hiring / Content / Investing" skill packs for use in third-party AI tools.
why_they_need_memory: This is the clearest fit of the three, and the reciprocity confirms it. Micro's entire value proposition is cross-source context: it has a dedicated homepage section titled "Micro knows you better than anyone else — Micro remembers everything from your work and conversations. It dreams and takes notes to keep everything fresh," showing memory buckets for Priorities, Work, Network, Memory, My Company, Meetings and Preferences, and a section on being "Powered by you and your team's personal context graph." To deliver that with a 2-10 person team they would otherwise have to build and maintain 1000+ OAuth connectors, permission inheritance, incremental sync, freshness, a context/entity graph across email + messages + calendar + CRM + docs, and per-user preference memory — precisely the ETL-forever problem Hyperspell's pitch targets. They are also the ideal buyer profile: AI-native, tiny team, memory is a core surface rather than a nice-to-have, and they still need it to be permission-aware for the Enterprise tier.

name: Smallest.ai

On top sits Voice Agents — conversational agents that "keep the conversation going. Any language. Any channel" — configurable no-code in a playground or via API, with on-premise deployment offered. Vertical landing pages for healthcare, banking, real estate, travel, automobiles and e-commerce. Press kit claims the platform processes millions of call minutes per month. Compliance: SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, GDPR, HIPAA. The differentiating thesis is small, fast, domain-specific models rather than general-purpose LLMs.
category: voice AI infrastructure + voice agents (TTS/STT/S2S models and an agent platform)
stage: Series A

Both amounts are corroborated by multiple independent outlets (Inc42, DealStreetAsia, Tracxn, Value Add VC).

how_they_use_agents: Voice agents are the shipped product. Customers build agents that place and receive real-time phone calls — support, collections, lead qualification, appointment setting, feedback calls — across 38-70+ languages and multiple channels. The agent loop runs on their own models: Pulse transcribes, Electron/an LLM reasons, Lightning v3.1 synthesizes, and Hydra collapses that into one full-duplex speech-to-speech model. Agents are configured no-code in a playground or wired up via API/SDK, and can be deployed on-premise inside a customer's environment.
why_they_need_memory: Two plausible reasons, and I could not confirm which applies. (1) In-product: real-time voice agents have the tightest possible context budget — sub-100ms — and yet need to know who is calling, what happened on the last three calls, what the CRM says about the account, and what was promised. Retrieval that takes seconds is unusable, so a pre-synthesized, always-fresh context layer is far more valuable to a voice vendor than a generic RAG pipeline. Enterprise voice deployments in banking/healthcare additionally need permission-aware context, which is exactly what Hyperspell markets. (2) Internal: at 51-200 people with enterprise customers, a "company brain" over Slack/Gmail/Notion/CRM for support and internal ops matches the use case in Hyperspell's own testimonials. Caveat: Hyperspell's logo strip is unlabeled and unlinked, so the nature and depth of the relationship is unverified — it could be a design-partner or pilot logo rather than a production dependency.

how_they_use_agents: AI appears as features inside their own martech product, not as agent infrastructure: (1) Forms AI, which generates signup forms from a natural-language description; (2) Audience Insights, which analyzes the customer list and auto-builds segments; (3) an AI-powered marketing assistant that surfaces insights on email/SMS campaign performance. There is no evidence of autonomous multi-step agents, an agent platform, or agent memory in the product. This is a conventional SaaS bolting generative features onto an existing workflow.
why_they_need_memory: The buying trigger was human onboarding pain, not agent memory. Engineering went from ~15 to 80-90 people in three to six months (VP Eng Tomas Kazragis: "there was a lot of pain"), while the company scaled to 250+ across three countries. Confluence was locked to Engineering and integrated with JIRA, so it never reached the rest of the company; everything else lived in scattered ad-hoc Google Docs. They needed one cross-functional knowledge base new hires and non-technical managers would actually adopt — they built "Omnipedia" in Slite with general, departmental and private leadership channels. The explicit selection criterion was low activation cost: Slite's "entry point was the easiest" versus tools requiring complex linking. Read as a buyer signal: the pain is fast headcount growth destroying institutional context in a NON-AI-native company, and the buyer is a VP Engineering purchasing for the whole org.

Founded 2019 in Córdoba, Argentina by Mariano Lisiotti (ex-VP Projects South America at NERA), Juan Alvarez, Juanjo Ferrero and Federico Garcia Dura. sells_to: B2B enterprise — telecom operators and their deployment contractors (Telefónica, Claro, Ericsson/OFG, IHS), plus energy and construction firms. Sold top-down into operations leadership, not self-serve.
how_they_use_agents: Genuinely agentic, and unusually well-matched to the memory pitch. (1) Trigger-based agents: "set triggers and let Sytex agents act — assign, notify, advance and sync across any platform the moment conditions are met," wired through REST APIs, webhooks, scripting and CLI. (2) AI quality control that validates completeness and consistency of field-captured evidence at the moment of capture, to prevent revisits. (3) Alfred, a natural-language assistant that generates dashboards and operational insight from field data with "no SQL and no analyst queue." All of it runs on accumulated field state — work orders, task logs, photos, readings, signatures — which means their own product thesis IS a knowledge base that agents read from. They are the closest of the three to being a peer/prospect for agent-memory infrastructure rather than just a wiki buyer.
why_they_need_memory: Internal trigger: post-COVID remote-first work fragmented a distributed back-office + field-team org. CEO Mariano Lisiotti: "Teams became very segmented. No one knew what was happening in other departments, and everyone had their own way of documenting things." They ran on Discord for chat and scattered Google Docs, and tested and abandoned GitHub, local platforms and Notion (explicitly evaluated and rejected Notion — they wanted something focused: "primarily a knowledge base and a place to share work asynchronously," not another all-in-one). Kept Linear for project management. Strategic angle: as a YC company already shipping AI agents on top of operational data, they understand the "one living knowledge base feeding agents" argument natively — a warm audience for the category framed as agent context rather than as a wiki.

name: Zima Labs (legal entity: Zima Chat Inc.)
what_it_does: Confidential-computing AI inference gateway. Two surfaces: (1) an OpenAI-compatible API — swap base URL + API key, no code changes — routing to 100+ foundation models (Qwen3, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Llama, Mistral, plus proxied GPT/Claude/Gemini) at per-token pay-as-you-go rates; (2) Zima Chat (zima.chat), a consumer/prosumer chat UI with a free tier and paid monthly plans. The differentiator is that open-source model inference runs inside hardware-secured enclaves (Intel TDX + NVIDIA Confidential Computing), with cryptographic attestation verifying the execution path before processing, and zero data retention — prompts, outputs and metadata are never logged or persisted; requests 'exist only for the duration of execution inside the enclave.' For centralized/frontier models they proxy without logging (noting upstream providers keep their own infra). Enterprise tier starts at $10k/month and adds fine-tuning, dedicated infrastructure, 24/7 support, custom rate limits, analytics and SSO. Positioned for three use cases: everyday personal questions, sensitive work (legal/health/finance), and developers building applications.

This is inferred from Glen's product description, not from anything Zima has said.
why_they_need_memory: Inferred, not stated. A 2-10 person infra startup shipping fast across NYC and SF: context lives in agent sessions, GitHub and Slack rather than in written docs, and there is no one to maintain a wiki. Glen's 'company brain' pitch (auto-capture, context injection, skills) targets exactly that shape. sells_to: n/a as a vendor — YC invests in founders. As a buyer in this context it is an institution with a very large relationship/entity graph to track.
how_they_use_agents: Per gbrain's own materials: Garry Tan runs OpenClaw and Hermes agent deployments on top of gbrain as the persistent memory layer, at a stated scale of 155,795 pages, 24,589 people, 5,340 companies, and 66 cron jobs running autonomously. gbrain itself is a hybrid-search-plus-synthesis knowledge system with a self-wiring knowledge graph that creates typed entity relationships automatically, returning synthesized cited answers and flagging knowledge gaps; the hosted product runs as a continuous cloud assistant with 20+ prebuilt skills (team syncs, research briefs, inbox management, fact-checking, transcript generation). The described workflows are personal executive ones — founder notes, meeting prep, press mentions — not an org-wide YC rollout.
why_they_need_memory: The stated need is entity-scale continuity: thousands of founders and portfolio companies to keep straight across years of notes, meetings and press, where a chat tool that forgets between sessions is useless. The pull quote used on the page is 'The future belongs to individuals who build compounding AI systems, not to individuals who use corporate-owned centralized AI tools' (Garry Tan, April 2026) — i.e. the argument is for owning your own compounding memory substrate.
confidence: high on the underlying facts, but this should be treated as a DISQUALIFIED customer datapoint for buyer-persona analysis. CONFIRMED SELF-REFERENTIAL: gbrain.io's own about page lists three co-founders — Brad Gessler (CEO, co-founder), Garry Tan (co-founder), and Jamison Mercurio (co-founder) — who met working on Garry's List, with Garry having built the first version for personal use and open-sourced it on GitHub (MIT, ~29.7k stars, 4.4k forks). gbrain is backed by Y Combinator, Initialized Capital and Transpose Platform. So the 'Y Combinator runs on gbrain' story is the vendor's own co-founder using his own product, and YC is additionally an investor in the vendor. Two further caveats: (a) it is ambiguous whether 'Y Combinator' denotes an institutional deployment or one executive's personal brain — every described workflow is personal; (b) the same first-party claim appears in the repo README and docs tutorial, so the repetition across sources is not independent corroboration.

name: Forest Admin (now operating as "Forest")
what_it_does: MAJOR FINDING: forestadmin.com now 301-redirects to forest.app. The company has pivoted and rebranded. ORIGINALLY (2016-~2024): a low-code developer tool that auto-generated internal admin panels / back-office CRUD UIs on top of a company's existing database (Postgres, MongoDB, MySQL) — Slite's case study describes it as 'instant admin panels for 1000+ companies'. TODAY (2026): repositioned as 'the ops infrastructure that regulated companies grow on' — a control plane for compliance-heavy operational workflows at fintechs. It connects directly (read/write, no data copying) to Postgres, MongoDB, BigQuery and Snowflake plus third-party compliance APIs, and runs unified workflows for KYC/KYB onboarding, sanctions screening, transaction monitoring, AML and dispute handling, with record-level audit logging and RBAC. Target verticals named on site: neobanks and BaaS providers, crypto platforms, lending/BNPL, payment processors, wealth management, insurtech. Headline claims: '3x productivity gain in case management', '50% reduction in lead time on complex cases', '100% compliant KYB process', '50-75% manual review rate reduction'. SOC 2 Type II attested. Public pricing: Sandbox free (2 users, 2 datasources, 500 audit events/mo), Starter $499/mo (7 users, +$60/user), Professional $2,199/mo (25 users, +$70/user), Enterprise $5,999/mo (60+ users).
category: ops infrastructure / agent governance for regulated fintech (formerly low-code internal-tools / admin panels; dev tools)
stage: Series A (2021); no publicly announced round since. Now effectively a post-pivot Series A company.
funding: Total in the $10M-$50M range per Dealroom — exact total NOT confirmed, do not treat as precise. Seed from Hexa (eFounders) startup studio; Series A investors listed by Dealroom as Connect Ventures, Runa Capital, Notion Capital, Xavier Niel, Taavet Hinrikus (TransferWise co-founder) and Eduardo Ronzano. I could not confirm the Series A dollar amount from a primary source and am not going to guess it.
headcount_estimate: ~34 (the number Slite's own case study states, likely 2023-2024 vintage). Dealroom lists '<100' with team distribution France 93.8%, Belgium 3.1%, US 3.1%. Current 2026 headcount unconfirmed — LinkedIn company page was not fetchable. Best estimate: 30-70.
yc_or_accelerator: Not YC. Built by Hexa (formerly eFounders), the Paris startup studio — the same studio that built Slite, the vendor citing them. This is a studio-sibling relationship, NOT an arm's-length purchase, which materially discounts the testimonial as evidence of category demand.
sells_to: B2B — mid-market to enterprise regulated financial services (fintech). Originally sold to developers/eng teams building internal tools; now sells to Head of Ops, Head of Onboarding, Compliance and Risk leaders. Entry price of $499/mo and a $2,199/mo recommended tier signals mid-market, not SMB self-serve.
how_they_use_agents: Forest is now an agent-governance/agent-ops company, which makes it the most interesting of the three for this category. Concretely: (1) it ships an MCP server so external AI agents can act inside Forest's control plane; (2) it advertises '16 vertical AI agents built for regulated financial operations'; (3) its pricing page treats 'humans, AI agents and external users' identically — 'one rate per identity', i.e. an AI agent literally consumes a paid seat; (4) it logs 'prompt, tool calls, result, reasoning trace' for any authorized runtime (it names Claude, open-source and custom agents) and applies the same RBAC to agents as to humans; (5) its blog covers partnerships where third-party agents run compliance workflows under Forest governance — Sphinx (compliance agents), Diligent (AML/financial-crime detection, '99.9% precision' claim), and Dust (an AI agent platform) for KYB review, plus a guide on 'deploying agentic operations in fintech' for 2026. Separately and much more mundanely, as a Slite CUSTOMER they use Slite's AI search over internal docs for onboarding and department playbooks.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct and non-overlapping reasons, worth keeping separate. (a) As a Slite customer, the stated need was ordinary internal-wiki knowledge management: a 34-person team wanting onboarding, HR processes, CS/sales/product playbooks and product specs findable in one place — the quoted use case is a new Head of Customer Success self-serving her own onboarding. That is documentation, not agent memory. (b) As a product company, Forest has an acute and genuine agent-memory/context problem it is monetizing: agents executing KYC/KYB and AML decisions in a regulated environment must carry case history, prior decisions and policy context across sessions, and every step must be reconstructable for an auditor. Their entire pitch — audit every agent action at record level, scope agents with RBAC, keep the reasoning trace portable across runtimes — is the durable-memory-plus-provenance problem stated in compliance language. If you sell agent memory, Forest is simultaneously a plausible buyer of the persistence/context layer AND a potential competitor on the governance layer.

This is generative content assist over event recordings and transcripts — not autonomous agents, no agent framework, no MCP or tool-calling story that I could find. As a Slite CUSTOMER (implemented May 2020, so pre-AI-era) their agent exposure is likewise just Slite's AI search over their internal docs.
why_they_need_memory: The stated pain is knowledge loss in a globally distributed, fast-scaling startup, and the failure of the incumbent tool. Nitin Pratap (Director of Operations) says flatly 'It's impossible to find a document in Google Drive' — Google Drive was the thing being replaced. They then imposed a hard cultural rule that makes documentation the definition of done: 'If there is no Slite doc, that job is not done. A task with the customer is not completed unless you create a Slite document for it' — explicitly so reps summarize and reflect on customer calls. Deployed across engineering, success, service, support, product and sales, i.e. company-wide, not one team. The underlying need is capturing customer-interaction context that otherwise lives only in an individual's head across timezones, plus onboarding continuity during headcount growth. IMPLICATION FOR THE CATEGORY: this is the 'distributed remote-first venture-backed startup, ops-leader champion, single source of truth' buyer — and note the purchase is from 2020, so it is evidence for wiki demand, not for 2026 agent-memory demand. Also note the honest caveat that this logo may be stale as a reference account.
