name: PVcase
what_it_does: End-to-end software platform for solar project development, spanning four modules: PVcase Prospect (cloud GIS site selection / early-stage feasibility and interconnection screening, from the acquired Anderson Optimization), PVcase Ground Mount (AutoCAD plugin that auto-generates construction-ready utility-scale layouts on real terrain, including terrain-following trackers and ground grading), PVcase Roof Mount (C&I rooftop design), and PVcase Yield (energy modeling / yield assessment, benchmarked against PVsyst). Recently extended the Prospect siting engine into data-center site selection ('power-first' siting). Homepage claims 1,900+ customers in 88+ countries and 4+ TW designed annually; named customers include AES, RWE, Iberdrola, Voltalia, New Leaf Energy, Valmont Solar, Radiance Solar. Sold as licensed CAD/GIS engineering software with published pricing tiers and a demo-request motion.
category: vertical SaaS — renewable-energy (solar) engineering, design and siting software; CAD + geospatial, not AI
stage: Series B / growth-stage private
funding: ~$123M+ total per company statement. €20M Series A announced 2021-10-05 (Elephant, Practica Capital, Contrarian Ventures) — described as the largest European solar-software round at the time, on 4x ARR growth. $100M announced 2023-07-18, co-led by Highland Europe and Energize Ventures with existing investor Elephant; the release notes the company had grown mostly on revenue and held the cash partly for further M&A. Acquired Anderson Optimization (US solar siting software) 2023-06-06, terms undisclosed. No round found after 2023.
headcount_estimate: ~250-350. LinkedIn lists company size 201-500 with ~334 employees; the careers page states '250+ employees' across '14+ countries' and '24+ languages', with offices in Vilnius (HQ, Bokstas Square), Kaunas, and Barcelona.
yc_or_accelerator: None found — no YC or accelerator affiliation; funded directly by European/US VCs (Practica Capital and Contrarian Ventures are Lithuanian/Baltic funds).
founded_year: 2017 per LinkedIn; the Ground Mount product launched ~2018 (Series A post says 'three years ago' in Oct 2021) and the About page describes 'eight years of continuous growth' as of 2026, so 2017-2018.
sells_to: B2B mid-market and enterprise — solar developers, IPPs, EPCs, engineering consultancies and utilities, plus a growing data-center siting segment. Buyer personas on their own site are design engineers, EPC managers, and consultants.
how_they_use_agents: Essentially none. This is the weakest AI story of the three. Every product claim on the site is deterministic automation, not agents: parametric CAD layout generation on AutoCAD, terrain/grading algorithms, geospatial layer analysis, and physics-based yield simulation. A full-text scan of the homepage found 22 automation-ish mentions but zero references to an AI copilot, assistant, or agent in any product; 'AI' appears only in thought-leadership content (a blog post on AI and climate, and webinar chapters on 'using AI and automation to improve design workflows'). The one live AI artifact is a third-party marketing widget (app.getshowme.ai) embedded on the homepage. Treat PVcase as a non-AI incumbent buying knowledge tooling, not an agent builder.
why_they_need_memory: Their stated pain is internal support knowledge, not product memory. The Slite testimonial comes from a Product Manager and is explicitly about reducing escalation times — i.e. front-line CS answering technical questions about a four-module, AutoCAD-dependent product without escalating to engineering. The structural drivers: 250+ people across 14+ countries and 24+ languages in 3+ offices; a product suite assembled partly by acquisition (Anderson Optimization) so knowledge lives in two merged orgs; 1,900 customers in 88 countries on version-sensitive software (AutoCAD 2025/2026 compatibility, PVsyst benchmarking) where documentation goes stale fast. That last point is the real 'company brain' hook — docs that silently rot as the CAD host version changes. Buys the knowledge-base/self-updating-docs value prop, not agent memory.

name: Meero (now rebranded as Diffusely)
url: https://www.meero.com — DEAD. The domain now serves an Apache2 Ubuntu default page. Live successor: https://diffuse.ly, which 301s to https://www.carcutter.com
what_it_does: Historically (2016-2022): an on-demand photography marketplace — businesses booked a shoot, Meero dispatched one of ~100k freelance photographers, and computer-vision models did the post-production/retouching automatically, delivering in under 24h. Verticals were real estate, food, e-commerce, retail, corporate, hospitality, automotive. By 2024 it had pivoted away from the marketplace into AI visual-enhancement SaaS with four brands: ProperShot (real estate photo app), CarCutter (automotive dealer imagery), AutoRetouch (fashion e-commerce retouching), and Meero Studios (fashion/luxury content factory). In 2025 the Meero brand was retired: meero.com redirected to diffuse.ly, and the LinkedIn page now reads 'This company page is no longer active. We have rebranded. Please follow our new official page: Diffusely.' ProperShot was sold to Nodalview in 2024. Today the surviving public surface is CarCutter — 360° spins, AI backgrounding, virtual showrooms and guided capture for ~4,000 dealership groups (AutoNation, Koons, Flow) — operated by DIFFUSELY Austria GmbH.
category: AI media / computer-vision image enhancement (originally a photography services marketplace); now automotive and fashion visual-commerce tooling
stage: Formerly a Series C unicorn; now post-restructuring and recapitalized under a new brand. Effectively a down-round turnaround, not a growth-stage company.
funding: ~$275M+ raised historically. $45M Series B, July 2018, co-led by Alven Capital and Idinvest. $230M Series C, June 2019 — made Meero France's newest unicorn (>$1B valuation); press coverage of both rounds is indexed on Meero's own archived newsroom. Subsequently, as Diffusely, an €11M round led by Alven, Eurazeo and Prime Ventures (per the Diffusely LinkedIn page) — the same investor set at a far smaller size, consistent with a recapitalization. Do not treat the $230M figure as reflecting current scale.
headcount_estimate: Peak ~700 (2019-2020); 600 employees and 49 nationalities per the 2022-2023 About page. Now roughly 90-100: the Diffusely LinkedIn page shows size 51-200 with ~91 employees listed. The old Meero LinkedIn page is inactive.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. French VC-backed (Alven, Idinvest/Eurazeo, Prime Ventures, Aglaé Ventures era); no accelerator.
founded_year: 2016, by Thomas Rebaud (CEO), Paris, France
sells_to: B2B. Originally SMB-to-enterprise across real estate agencies, restaurants, e-commerce and hospitality; today enterprise/mid-market automotive (dealership groups and car marketplaces) and fashion brands. Never sold to developers.
how_they_use_agents: Computer vision, not agents. Their AI is a batch image-processing pipeline: automated retouching and color/exposure correction, background removal and 'AI backgrounding' into virtual showrooms, 360° spin generation from as few as 4 photos, and automated quality checking. AutoRetouch is explicitly a 'hybrid model' — AI algorithms plus human retouchers in the loop. Diffusely describes itself as processing 2M+ images weekly. There is no LLM, chat assistant, or autonomous agent anywhere in the product. AI-native in the deep-learning sense, but not an agent company.
why_they_need_memory: The cited testimonial is a scaling artifact, not an agent-memory need — and it is old. The quote ('grown from 250 people to over 700 in the last year, across different offices') pins it to the 2019-2020 post-Series-C hypergrowth, when a Head of Customer Service needed a structured place to route incoming questions across a rapidly expanding, multi-office, multi-country org staffed largely with non-technical ops and CS people. Classic onboarding-and-routing knowledge management. Worth flagging for the buyer-profile exercise: this logo is a cautionary data point, not a live customer — the company that wrote it has since shed ~85% of its headcount, retired the brand, and the URL on the vendor's page resolves to a default web-server page. Logo walls citing Meero are stale.

name: GrandPad
what_it_does: A purpose-built tablet-plus-phone and secure cloud service for adults aged 75+. The device ships with built-in 4G LTE (no wifi setup), oversized icons, a private contact network that blocks spam and scam calls, and 24/7 human customer care; features include video calls, photo sharing, streaming music (7digital), radio, multiplayer games, and a free family Companion App with 600k+ downloads. Hardware has been co-designed with Acer. Two distinct channels: (1) consumer/family — direct e-commerce, Amazon, and carrier bundles (Consumer Cellular in the US, Swisscom, Orange Belgium/Ericsson, TechSilver in UK/IE); (2) healthcare/enterprise via grandpad.biz 'Enterprise Edition' — telehealth and remote patient engagement, preferred telehealth provider for the National PACE Association, partnerships with Home Instead and Prospero Health, HITRUST certified and HIPAA-oriented, with connected-device/remote-monitoring capability and multi-party video that puts family and a patient's care team in one call. Reports 1.6M users (seniors, family members, caregivers) across 110+ countries and ~40 languages.
category: agetech — senior-focused consumer hardware + subscription SaaS, with a healthcare/virtual-care enterprise line
stage: Late-stage private, angel- and VC-backed; no publicly disclosed round since 2020. Board-governed with outside stockholders (an Aug 2026 release quotes a board member and refers to 'long-term value for our stockholders').
funding: ~$26-27M disclosed via SEC Form D filings (GrandPAD Inc., CIK 0001624554, Delaware): $985,067 sold in 2014; $673,670 in 2015; $8,000,000 in 2016; a $15M offering with $6M sold as of the 2017 filing, amended to $14,000,000 sold in the Jan 2019 D/A; and $3,000,000 of a $4M offering in March 2020. No Form D filed after 2020, so any later financing is either unreported here or has not occurred. Named one of the Most Innovative Companies by the Angel Capital Association in 2019, consistent with heavy angel-syndicate rather than large-fund backing. No Crunchbase/PitchBook figure was reachable — treat ~$27M as the floor of disclosed capital, not a verified total.
headcount_estimate: 51-200 per LinkedIn. No more precise public figure found.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not a YC company; Angel Capital Association recognition (2019) suggests angel-network rather than accelerator financing.
founded_year: 2014 (LinkedIn founded date; SEC Form D year-of-incorporation is also 2014). A Jan 2025 release describes the company 'celebrating its 10-year anniversary.'
sells_to: Dual-motion and unusual: prosumer/consumer (adult children and caregivers buying for a parent or grandparent, plus carrier retail bundles) AND B2B healthcare enterprise (health plans, PACE programs, home-care agencies, virtual-care providers). Not developer-facing.
how_they_use_agents: Real and strategically central, unlike the other two. GrandPad launched 'Grandie,' an AI-enabled virtual companion for seniors, in Feb 2024, expanded it in June 2024, and shipped 'Grandie Chat' — a voice-first generative-AI assistant — announced Jan 2025. The design is deliberately agent-shaped for a non-typing user: voice-first with pre-programmed prompts, so an 80- or 90-year-old can speak and listen rather than type. They report their users adopt generative AI at three times the rate of others in their age group, and cite a legally-blind former physician who now researches his interests entirely by voice. The AI is co-designed with 'Grand Advisors,' a panel of users aged 80+. Co-founder Isaac Lien's title is Chief AI & Product Officer — an unusually senior AI mandate for a hardware company this size. A spin-off consumer app, Grandie Games, passed 10,000 downloads in three months (2025).
why_they_need_memory: Two independent reasons, which makes GrandPad the most interesting of the three for this category. (1) Internal, which is what the cited testimonial is about: the quote is from an Operations Lead and stresses that the tool 'is not intimidating to use so even non-technical team members can dive in' — and GrandPad appears across the IT & Operations, HR, Customer Support and Sales solution pages, i.e. company-wide adoption rather than one team. They run 24/7 live human support for a population that calls for help with everything, in ~40 languages across 110+ countries, plus a volunteer companionship program (GrandPad Connections); that is enormous, constantly-changing procedural knowledge held by non-technical staff, and hardware/carrier variants multiply the surface area. Low-friction authoring matters more to them than power features. (2) Product-side, which is the stronger agent-memory thesis: Grandie is a long-lived companion for a single elderly user, so per-user persistent memory — who their family is, what they like, their routines and health context — is the actual product, and it has to work under HITRUST/HIPAA constraints alongside care-team data. If you are selling agent memory rather than a wiki, GrandPad is the profile that buys the real thing.
sources: https://www.grandpad.net/about-us/press-releases (SPA; content extracted from the site's JS bundles, incl. the Jan 2025 'Grandie Chat', Feb/Jun 2024 'Grandie', Mar 2025 'Grandie Games' and Aug 2026 CEO-appointment releases)

name: Pumpkin
what_it_does: DEFUNCT. Pumpkin was a French consumer fintech: a peer-to-peer money-transfer app (a French Venmo) that let users split bills, add notes to transfers, and collect money for groups, with a strong beachhead in student associations (2,000+ associations across ~400 French campuses). After being acquired it pivoted into a neobank for 18-28 year-olds. Metrics before acquisition: 100k users end-2016 growing to 250k by mid-2017, EUR 3M/month transaction volume late 2016 rising to EUR 5M+/month by July 2017. IMPORTANT: the company no longer exists — Credit Mutuel Arkea wound it down in 2022, and www.pumpkin.fr today resolves to a domain-for-sale listing operated by the French auction house Boischaut, with no product on it. The Slite testimonial is a legacy quote from roughly the 2017-2020 period and should not be treated as a live customer reference. Note also a title discrepancy: Slite credits Hugo Salle de Chou as 'Co-Founder & CTO', but French press consistently lists Victor Lennel as CTO and Salle de Chou as a co-founder on the business/product side.
category: Consumer fintech - P2P payments / neobank (defunct)
stage: Acquired (July 2017, 80% by Credit Mutuel Arkea); wound down 2022
funding: EUR 600k in 2015, then ~EUR 2M seed from Kima Ventures, Jacques-Antoine Granjon and Damien Guermonprez. Acquired July 2017 by Credit Mutuel Arkea, which took 80% of the capital (price undisclosed) and committed to invest EUR 15M+ over three years. No further outside rounds.
headcount_estimate: unknown (0 today - company ceased operations in 2022; no reliable headcount figure found for its peak)
yc_or_accelerator: unknown (no accelerator affiliation found; earliest institutional backer was Kima Ventures, Xavier Niel's seed fund)
sells_to: B2C consumer (French 18-30 year-olds, students and young professionals) - not a B2B buyer at all
how_they_use_agents: None. Pumpkin predates the agent era entirely (founded 2014, dead by 2022) and there is no evidence it ever shipped or used AI agents. It is a pure pre-AI knowledge-management buyer.
why_they_need_memory: Per the testimonial itself, the pain was classic startup knowledge fragmentation rather than anything agent-related: work context was scattered across Google Docs where 'no one came to check what work others were up to', and insights were being lost in Slack history. The buyer was a ~30-person venture-backed startup CTO consolidating scattered docs into one searchable place - the pre-AI 'single source of truth' motive, not an agent-context motive.
sources: https://www.pumpkin.fr (now a Boischaut domain-sale page, confirming the product is gone)
https://www.maddyness.com/2023/03/13/pumpkin-rachat-credit-mutuel-arkea/ (post-mortem: founders, 2014 founding, EUR 600k + EUR 2M funding, 2022 shutdown)
https://www.maddyness.com/2017/07/13/fintech-pumpkin-credit-mutuel-arkea-neobanque/ (acquisition terms, 80% stake, EUR 15M investment, user and volume metrics)

name: Shippeo
what_it_does: Real-time multimodal transportation visibility platform (RTTVP) for large enterprise shippers and logistics providers. Shippeo ingests telematics, TMS and ELD feeds to track shipments across road (FTL/LTL), rail, ocean, air, parcel and last mile, and layers on ML-based predictive ETAs (claimed up to ~90% accuracy), carrier performance analytics, and workflow tooling. Adjacent modules cover eCMR digital transport documents, carbon visibility, and detention & demurrage. Scale: ~90-100M shipments tracked per year across 150+ countries, 228,000+ carriers and 1,100+ TMS/telematics integrations. Named a Leader in the 2025 Gartner Magic Quadrant for RTTVPs. Customers include Coca-Cola HBC, Carrefour, Renault Group, L'Oreal, LVMH, Leroy Merlin, Amazon, Fujifilm, Philip Morris International and Yamaha Motor North America. Acquired Logward in May 2026 to push from visibility into AI-powered supply chain execution.
category: Supply chain / logistics SaaS - real-time transportation visibility (enterprise vertical SaaS)
stage: Late-stage growth (7 rounds since 2014; the Jan 2025 $30M was framed as strategic rather than a lettered round)
funding: ~$140M raised in total since founding (per FreightWaves, Jan 2025). Most recent: $30M announced 15 Jan 2025, led by Woven Capital (Toyota's growth fund), with participation from Battery Ventures, Partech, NGP Capital, Bpifrance Digital Venture, LFX Venture Partners, Shift4Good and Yamaha Motor Ventures. Shippeo's own about page also lists ERB Partners and FRST among investors.
headcount_estimate: ~236 employees (LinkedIn; 201-500 band). Shippeo's about page says 'over 200 Shippians' from 30 countries. Likely higher post-Logward acquisition (May 2026).
yc_or_accelerator: none found (French Tech badge holder and Bpifrance-backed, but no YC or accelerator affiliation)
sells_to: B2B enterprise (large multinational shippers, manufacturers, retailers and 3PLs; long sales cycles, SAP Store endorsed app, Gartner-influenced buying)
how_they_use_agents: Shippeo shipped 'Shippeo AI' on 6 Nov 2025 - an agent layer embedded across the platform with a growing 'Agent Library' of task-specific agents covering data-quality remediation, carrier ETA analysis, telematics health checks, carrier performance analysis, shipment status lookup, and port congestion analysis. Two surfaces: 'Sidekick', a fast conversational interface for urgent in-workflow questions (e.g. 'why don't I have an ETA?'), and 'Workspace' for deeper root-cause and performance analysis. Agents run continuously to proactively flag issues; the stated roadmap is agents that autonomously execute recommended actions. The May 2026 Logward acquisition was explicitly positioned as turning visibility into 'AI-powered supply chain execution'. Their public framing is that agents run on SLA-backed, verified visibility data - the differentiator is data trustworthiness rather than an external memory layer.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. (1) The Slite testimonial is about internal knowledge, not agents: a 200+ person, 30-nationality, multi-office company where the VP Operations wanted 'a place of focus and clarity' for operational runbooks and process docs. (2) Strategically, they are now building an in-product agent fleet on top of enterprise logistics data, which creates real demand for durable context - carrier-specific quirks, customer-specific escalation rules, past root causes - that persists across sessions and users. Note they currently solve the agent-context problem with their own proprietary data platform, so they are a plausible buyer of internal-knowledge tooling but a likely build-not-buy for agent memory itself.
sources: https://www.shippeo.com/company/about-us (2014 founding, five co-founders incl. Thibaut Morlot as VP Operations, 200+ staff, investor list)

name: Remote Sensei
url: https://remotesensei.org (remotesensei.io now 301-redirects here; the .io HTTPS endpoint is dead)
what_it_does: A small Warsaw-based consultancy, not a software product company. Remote Sensei implements Asana for remote and hybrid mid-market and enterprise teams, selling a 'Reliability Protocol' methodology plus Asana licences, workflow design, delegation systems, training and change management. Positioning is that adoption comes from habit-building and management practice, not tool configuration; marketing claims include '19 out of 20 teams' still using the systems a year later, up to 90% less ad-hoc work and 30% fewer project delays. Credentials: first Asana Certified Pro in Europe (2018) and first Asana Gold Solutions Partner in Poland (2022). Case studies name Go2Market, Grecos and Angelus24. Caveat worth flagging: the .io domain in the Slite citation no longer serves HTTPS and only forwards to the .org, and remotesensei.com is parked for sale on Atom - so their web presence is somewhat degraded, though the LinkedIn page and Asana partner listing are live.
category: Work-management consultancy / Asana implementation partner (professional services, not a software vendor)
stage: Bootstrapped services business (no venture funding found)
funding: unknown - no funding rounds, investors or accelerator backing found anywhere. Almost certainly self-funded consulting revenue.
headcount_estimate: ~12 employees (LinkedIn; 11-50 band)
yc_or_accelerator: none found
sells_to: B2B SMB / mid-market (they say mid-market and enterprise teams, but at ~12 people the realistic deal size is SMB-to-mid-market services engagements)
how_they_use_agents: Second-hand rather than first-party. Their Asana partner-directory listing says they are 'AI certified' and build Asana 'AI Teammates (agents)' into client workflows alongside their Reliability Protocol - i.e. they are an implementation channel that configures someone else's agents for clients, not a company shipping its own agent product. Their own .org marketing site makes no AI claims at all, so the AI positioning appears recent and confined to the partner listing.
why_they_need_memory: The Slite testimonial is the weakest of the three as evidence of the category: it is a customer-support compliment ('very swift response from the support team with the fix exactly as requested'), not a statement about consolidating company knowledge. The underlying need is the ordinary one for a consultancy: reusable methodology playbooks, client-engagement notes and onboarding material for a dozen consultants who need the same implementation framework applied repeatably across clients. If they ever needed agent memory it would be for client-specific context in the Asana AI Teammates they configure - but that context lives in Asana, not in their own stack.

https://asana.com/partners/channel/directory (Gold Solutions Partner listing, AI Teammates/agents mention)

name: HKUST KnowComp (Knowledge Computation Group, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)
what_it_does: An academic research lab, not a company. KnowComp is the Knowledge Computation Group in HKUST's Department of Computer Science and Engineering, directed by Associate Professor Yangqiu Song (PhD Tsinghua 2009; previously Amazon A9, UIUC, MSRA, IBM Research China; co-directs the HKUST-WeBank Joint Lab). Its stated mission is building 'intelligent agents to help with knowledge-intensive works,' with an emphasis on trustworthiness (privacy, security, fairness). Horizontal research: system optimization of agentic workflows, regulatory compliance, neural-symbolic structures. Vertical research: enterprise data agents for automated knowledge discovery, query answering, and database interaction. The GitHub org has ~196 repositories and ~276 followers, and ships well-known open-source KG/agent projects including AutoSchemaKG (automatic knowledge-graph construction), NewtonBench (scientific-law discovery for LLM agents, ICLR 2026), AutoGraph-R1 (ACL 2026), and OmniCompliance-100K (ACL 2026 Findings).
category: Academic research lab — knowledge graphs, neural-symbolic reasoning, and LLM agents (NOT a commercial buyer)
stage: Not applicable — university research group, no commercial stage
funding: No venture funding. Research grants only: HK-UGC, HK-RGC, HK-ITC, China NSFC, plus industry/institutional support from Tencent AI Lab, Hong Kong Mediation and Arbitration Centre (HKMAAC), and California University School of Business Law & Technology.
headcount_estimate: ~35-50 researchers (3 postdocs, ~30 PhD students, plus multiple MPhil students, per the group's own page); not employees in a commercial sense
yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: unknown (group formed around Yangqiu Song's HKUST faculty appointment; no founding date published)
sells_to: Nobody — does not sell a product. Outputs are peer-reviewed papers and MIT-licensed open-source repos consumed by researchers and agent developers.
how_they_use_agents: They build agents as research artifacts. The specific Graphify tie is DeepRefine-Skill (https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/DeepRefine-Skill, ~92 stars, 7 forks, MIT, v0.2.0): an agent skill that installs into Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Google Gemini CLI, Codex, and OpenCode. On a single /deeprefine command it imports queries from Graphify memory logs, analyzes pending/unanswered questions against the existing knowledge graph (stored as graph.json by Graphify's 'LLM-Wiki' engine), proposes node insertions and edge modifications labeled HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW by evidence confidence, and applies approved changes while keeping graph backups. It is test-time knowledge-base evolution intended to improve future retrieval and Q&A. Backed by an accompanying paper.
why_they_need_memory: They do not 'need' it as buyers — they research it. Agent memory and self-evolving knowledge bases ARE their research object (AutoSchemaKG, DeepRefine, enterprise data agents). Graphify's open-source graph.json engine is a convenient experimental substrate on which to publish a refinement method. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for buyer-persona analysis: this is an academic lab building on top of an open-source engine, not a paying or enterprise customer, and there is no revenue signal here. Its presence on a vendor logo wall reflects open-source ecosystem credibility, not commercial demand.

'Feynman-2' was their AI tutoring engine — an in-workspace tutor agent that explained concepts, generated interactive diagrams, edited the student's writing, referenced both the student's own notes and the web, ran background tasks, and gave feedback mid-session. Mem0 sat inside Feynman-2 to drive per-student 'learner profiles' spanning the whole platform and all its tools, so the tutor could open with things like 'You highlighted the chain rule diagram yesterday — want to apply it to this example?' or 'You stopped at Newton's Second Law. Would you like a quick recap before moving to momentum?'
why_they_need_memory: Three stated drivers, all classic for this category. (1) Session fragmentation: the tutor could not recall a student's prior questions, struggles or learning path, so every session restarted cold — fatal for a tutoring product whose value proposition is continuity. (2) Token cost/latency: they were stuffing full interaction histories into prompts; Mem0 cut token usage per prompt by 40%. (3) Build-vs-buy on a 3-person team: they estimated 3-4 weeks to build memory infrastructure in-house and integrated Mem0 in 2 days with no changes to core infrastructure. This is the archetypal buyer for agent-memory: a tiny AI-native team whose product is a long-lived personalized agent, where memory is core UX but not core IP, and engineer-weeks are the scarcest resource.

name: PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers)
what_it_does: REAL COMPANY, BUT THE CUSTOMER CLAIM IS UNVERIFIED — see why_they_need_memory. PwC is one of the Big Four global professional-services networks: financial audit and assurance, tax and legal, and management/technology consulting and risk advisory. It is not a single company but a network of legally separate member firms coordinated by PricewaterhouseCoopers International Limited, a UK private company limited by guarantee; the US and UK firms are LLPs. Clients are multinational corporations, financial institutions and governments.
category: Professional services / management consulting and audit (Big Four). Not a software vendor in the usual sense, though it now ships productized AI platforms to clients.
stage: Not applicable — private partnership network, ~1849/1854 predecessor firms, current form since the 1998 Price Waterhouse / Coopers & Lybrand merger. Never venture-funded; no stage, no investors.
funding: N/A — partner-owned, no external funding. Revenue rather than funding is the relevant scale figure: US$56.9bn globally in FY2025.
headcount_estimate: ~364,000 globally (364,782 stated in the FY2025 Global Annual Review; ~370,000 in FY2024). This is the whole network across all member firms, not an AI or engineering org.
yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: 1998 (current merged form); predecessor firms trace to 1849 (Price Waterhouse) and 1854 (Cooper Brothers)
sells_to: B2B enterprise and government — the largest companies in the world, plus public sector. Buying centers are partners and CIO/CTO offices, with long procurement cycles, not self-serve developer signup.
how_they_use_agents: Agents appear in two places. (1) Productized for clients: 'Agent OS' is a real PwC offering and won a 2026 CIO 100 Award for tech innovation — PwC frames it as putting agentic technology to work 'at scale'; 'Eclipse', under the PwC One platform, streamlines workflows, connects prior insights and embeds expert review at decision points; PwC publicly collaborates with Anthropic on agentic workflows across core business functions, and cites client outcomes such as a 75% reduction in time-to-fill on a Chipotle hiring engagement. PwC One is pitched as combining PwC expertise, client data and AI in one connected experience that 'builds on prior work and interactions, refining insights over time' — i.e. it has its own memory ambitions. (2) Internal adoption: PwC became ChatGPT Enterprise's largest customer in May 2024 and resells it to other large businesses. PwC does not publish agent-deployment counts or internal adoption metrics.
why_they_need_memory: TREAT AS AMBIGUOUS — this is a logo-wall name, not a documented account. The evidence is a single logo in the Framer marquee on the Mem0 homepage, under a section headed 'Used by 100k+ Developers from:' with adjacent copy reading '150,000+ Developers build with Mem0' (the 150k developer claim is confirmed live on mem0.ai today). The claim being made is that developers FROM these companies use Mem0 — not that PwC is a contracted account. There is no testimonial, no case study, no named person, and no PwC URL anywhere in Mem0's sitemap (I checked: zero URLs containing 'pwc'). The image alt text is literally 'pwc client logo', the only logo whose alt says 'client', which is suggestive but is alt text, not a contract. The plausible reality is bottom-up: individual PwC engineers pip-installing the Mem0 open-source library on a client or internal project. If PwC ever did buy this category at the firm level the rationale would be persistent context across long-running client engagements and audit workflows — but that is my inference, not something either party has stated. For a 'who buys this category' analysis, I would not count PwC as a validated enterprise buyer without independent confirmation.

name: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
what_it_does: REAL, BUT MISCLASSIFIED AS A CUSTOMER — AWS is a Mem0 PARTNER and, in the memory layer specifically, a direct COMPETITOR. AWS is Amazon's cloud subsidiary, selling on-demand compute, storage, networking, databases, analytics, ML and IoT — 200+ services on metered pay-as-you-go pricing — to individuals, enterprises and governments. 2025 revenue US$128.7bn. Customers include Netflix, NASA, the CIA, US Navy and US Air Force.
category: Cloud infrastructure / developer platform. In this context: an agent-platform vendor that ships its own competing agent-memory service.
stage: Not applicable — wholly owned subsidiary of Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN), a public mega-cap. No stage, no investors.
funding: N/A — not independently funded. Revenue is the meaningful figure: US$128.7bn in 2025.
headcount_estimate: unknown — Amazon does not break out AWS headcount separately, and I found no reliable disclosed figure. Amazon overall is well over a million employees, but attributing any slice of that to AWS would be fabrication.
yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: 2006 (cloud computing launch; earlier web services from July 2002)
sells_to: Developers first, then B2B enterprise and government — the widest possible base, from a solo developer on a free tier to Fortune 500 and defense procurement.
how_they_use_agents: AWS sells the agent stack rather than consuming one. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is its production agent platform — 'Any framework. Any model. Secure at scale.' — supporting LangChain, the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Claude Agent SDK and custom frameworks, with identity/authorization across tool calls, observability and tracing, and connections to MCP servers, knowledge bases, internal APIs and Lambda. Strands Agents is its lightweight open-source agent framework with multi-agent support, deployable to Lambda, Fargate and EC2. Amazon Nova is its own foundation-model family for agentic applications.
why_they_need_memory: THEY DON'T BUY IT — THEY SHIP IT. AWS offers AgentCore Memory, a fully managed agent-memory service with short-term memory (turn-by-turn context within a session) and long-term memory (automatic extraction of user preferences, key facts and session summaries across sessions), pitched with exactly the same framing Mem0 uses: solve agent statelessness, deliver personalized experiences, 'offload the undifferentiated heavy lifting'. That is a head-on competitor to Mem0's core product. The actual AWS-Mem0 relationship is a partnership on the Strands side: Mem0's own post is titled 'AWS and Mem0 partner to bring persistent memory to next-gen AI agents with Strands' and opens 'We're excited to announce a strategic partnership between AWS and Mem0'; the post frames Mem0 as an optional add-on integrated 'in just a few lines of code', and quotes no AWS employee. Mem0's Series A page makes the stronger claim that 'AWS selected us as the exclusive memory provider for their new Agent SDK', which is a distribution/OEM arrangement, not a purchase. AWS Bedrock is separately listed on mem0.ai/integrations as a technical integration. RECOMMENDATION: exclude AWS from any 'who buys agent memory' analysis — including it inflates the enterprise-buyer picture with what is really co-marketing, and the same logo-marquee caveat as PwC applies (the marquee says developers FROM these companies, and '150,000+ Developers build with Mem0').

funding: N/A — publicly traded since 1962. ~$36.29B revenue (FY2024). No venture funding.

founded_year: 1926 (as Electric Prospecting Company, Paris)
sells_to: B2B enterprise — national and international oil companies, energy operators, industrial and new-energy customers. Multi-year, procurement-heavy contracts.
how_they_use_agents: SLB ships agents as product, not just uses them internally. Tela is marketed as an 'agentic-AI assistant catalog' — a library of domain agents a petrotechnical professional invokes by discipline and task (data discovery, subsurface interpretation, drilling optimization, production, sustainability reporting), running on the Lumi data and AI platform and hosted inside Delfi applications. Internally, an org of ~111k also has an unknown number of individual developers experimenting with agent frameworks, which is the more likely explanation for a logo on a developer marquee.

The plausible fit: Tela agents operate over long-running, multi-session engineering workflows on a single asset or well, where a petrotechnical expert's preferences, prior interpretations, unit conventions and rejected hypotheses need to persist across sessions and across the several agents in the catalog. Persistent per-user and per-asset context is exactly what a catalog-of-agents architecture makes expensive to rebuild each time. But note the direction of the business: SLB is more likely to build or buy this at enterprise-procurement scale than to be a self-serve Mem0 account, and there is no evidence of a commercial relationship.

founded_year: unknown (site copyright 2026; press coverage of the Fred24 launch dates to July 2026, suggesting the AI-twins product launched 2025-2026)
sells_to: Two motions: prosumer/creator (coaches, consultants, sales trainers, well-known founders monetizing an audience) for the AI-twin platform; B2B SMB and French mid-market/enterprise (retail, real estate, education franchises) for the training and custom-build consultancy.
how_they_use_agents: The agent IS the product on the platform side: each AI twin is a persona agent grounded in one expert's entire published corpus (books, courses, podcasts, video transcripts, social posts), serving paying subscribers over chat and voice around the clock and reproducing that person's reasoning and opinions rather than generic LLM answers. On the services side they build "domain agents" for clients — e.g. the Wall Street English conversational agent that greets every site visitor, answers in the visitor's language, qualifies the project and hands off to a human advisor at the right moment.
why_they_need_memory: Textbook fit for agent memory. Every twin needs a durable, per-expert knowledge store ingesting heterogeneous long-form media (video, audio, PDF, posts) and retrieving from it with high fidelity — a twin that misquotes its human is a product defect and a personal-brand risk. They run ~30 separate twins, so they need multi-tenant, strictly isolated memory namespaces rather than one index. Because twins are sold as recurring subscriptions, conversations are long-running and repeat: retaining what a given subscriber already asked, their business context and prior advice is what makes a $29/mo subscription feel like coaching instead of a stateless chatbot. Their explicit pitch ("never repeat yourself again," the twin handles the questions you've answered a hundred times) is a memory pitch. Ingestion is also continuous — experts keep publishing, and the twin must absorb new content without a rebuild. Buying Supermemory rather than building retrieval is the obvious call for a 2-10 person team running both a platform and a consultancy.

name: Mosaic (Mosaic AI Labs, Inc.)
what_it_does: San Francisco company building agentic video editing — it calls itself "The AI Video Editing Company." Core product is Canvas, a node-based canvas (not a chat copilot bolted onto a timeline) where users compose and run video editing agents: rough cuts, clip extraction, AI reframe, montage, motion graphics, cinematic captions, color correction, audio sync, background removal, AI avatars, transcoding. Workflows are reusable and built for high-volume automation, with brand-style/format rules, custom nodes, and triggers from Google Drive, Dropbox, S3 and YouTube. It integrates with professional media stacks — sources assets from MAMs like Mimir and Iconik, exports editable timelines back to Premiere, Final Cut and DaVinci Resolve, and posts status to Slack. There is also an API/webhook layer and, notably, packaged Agent Skills for OpenClaw and Claude Code so an external coding agent can drive video edits (`openclaw skills install mosaic-video-editor`). Newest product is Motion, "a video agent for tasteful motion design" (early access), plus a Motion Studio service making launch videos for startups (customers include several YC W26 companies). Users can also A/B test multiple cut variants from the same raw footage. Pricing is credit-based and self-serve: Creator $40/mo (2,500 credits), Pro $125/mo (10,000 credits), Enterprise custom with SOC 2 Type 2 and GDPR, RBAC, audit logs and founder-led onboarding. Claims 1,000+ marketers, agencies and creators.
category: AI video editing / agentic creative tooling (media production automation)
stage: Seed
funding: $3.8M seed, announced April 7, 2026. Investors named in their own announcement: Y Combinator, Mayfield Fund, Elevation Capital, Pioneer Fund, Transpose Platform, TwentyTwo Ventures, Script Capital, Phosphor Capital, Amino Capital, Olive Technology Ventures, Fog Ventures, DCG, plus angels from YC, OpenAI and Google DeepMind. No lead investor is explicitly named in the post.

yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Winter 2025 batch. Also 1st place SaaStr AI Competition (May 2025) and 1st place Google Gemini Long Context Kaggle competition (Nov 2024); featured Google/Gemini and Veo 3 launch partner.
sells_to: Broad: prosumer/creator self-serve ($40-125/mo — podcasters, founders, solo creators), B2B SMB (agencies, small media brands), developers (API + agent skills, e.g. EasySlice built its clipping product on Mosaic as a backend), and enterprise media. Named enterprise partnerships: TubeScience (Meta's largest ad creative partner, 8K videos/month, 100M views/day) and News Corp / News UK (The Sun, talkSPORT, WSJ, The Times, HarperCollins) — talkSPORT tripled vertical video output.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the product. Users create and run multimodal video editing agents on a node canvas; the agent watches footage, decides cuts, reframes, places captions and motion graphics, and produces near-final edits (their pitch: gets you 80-90% of the way there before human polish). Explicitly orchestration-first — they argue the UI melts away and the orchestration layer that turns creative intent into a finished video is the real product, addressable by CLI, chat, canvas or voice. They also support agent-to-agent invocation: Claude Code and OpenClaw can install a Mosaic skill and drive full editing workflows, and any workflow can be triggered by API or file-drop events. Heavy multimodal model use (Gemini 2.0 Flash, Veo 3 partner).
why_they_need_memory: Their agents run long, high-volume, repeated jobs over huge multimodal inputs — up to 300-minute/20GB uploads per video, thousands of videos a month for a single customer — so raw context windows cannot hold the working state. The specific memory needs: persistent per-customer brand kits, style rules, guidelines and format preferences that must apply consistently across every future run (Enterprise explicitly sells "custom brand kits"); recall of what a workflow produced last time so reusable workflows and A/B variant tests stay coherent batch to batch; and durable indexing of footage libraries and transcripts pulled from MAMs, Drive and S3 so an agent can find the right moment without re-ingesting terabytes. Agent-to-agent invocation from Claude Code/OpenClaw adds a cross-session state problem — the external agent needs Mosaic-side memory of the project rather than re-briefing every call. Buying a memory layer is cheap relative to their multimodal compute spend.

name: Vela
what_it_does: AI scheduling coordinator sold to professional services firms — executive search and recruiting, law, consulting, and business development teams. Vela is an agent you CC on an email (vela@yourdomain.com) or text directly; it reads the thread's context, pulls availability from your calendar and from all participants, does the timezone math, proposes real options in each person's local time, follows up with non-responders, books the meeting, sends confirmations and reminders, and re-coordinates automatically when someone needs to reschedule. Explicit design goal is zero workflow change: it works over channels people already use — email (Gmail/Outlook), SMS, WhatsApp, Slack, Teams and phone — rather than asking anyone to adopt a booking link or new app. The site includes an ROI calculator by persona (associate, lawyer, business development, partner/director) showing roughly 13 hours/month saved at 15 meetings/week, and says Vela schedules thousands of meetings each week. Sales motion is demo-only — no public pricing, no self-serve signup. Contact is a Michigan (248) phone number with an SF HQ address.
category: AI scheduling/coordination agent for professional services (recruiting and executive search primary wedge)
stage: Pre-seed / seed (YC W26 — very early)
funding: Amount not disclosed anywhere I could verify. Backers named on their own site: Y Combinator, Pareto Holdings, Z Fellows, and angel Cory Levy. Presumably includes the standard YC deal, but no dollar figure is published — do not assume one. No Crunchbase/TechCrunch round record found.
headcount_estimate: Small, likely 2-15, with a conflict in the sources: the YC directory profile lists team size 2 (the two cofounders), while the LinkedIn company page shows an 11-50 band with about 15 people listed. Given a Winter 2026 batch, the true full-time count is probably in the low single digits to low teens; treat 15 as an upper bound.
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Winter 2026 batch. Also Z Fellows and Pareto Holdings.
founded_year: 2026 (per YC profile; company is brand new)
sells_to: B2B, professional services firms — executive recruiters and search firms first, plus law firms, consultancies (LinkedIn copy references people at McKinsey and BCG) and BD teams. SMB-to-mid-market services firms rather than pure enterprise; the site name-drops end clients its customers work with (Netflix, LinkedIn, SanDisk, AWS).
how_they_use_agents: Vela is a single autonomous agent that owns the whole scheduling loop with no human in it: parse intent from a natural-language email or text, identify participants, read calendar state, negotiate across parties over separate channels (one participant on email, another on WhatsApp), propose and hold slots, book, confirm, remind, and re-run the entire negotiation on a cancellation. Multi-attendee and international-timezone coordination are called out as first-class cases, as are per-user meeting-type preferences.
why_they_need_memory: Scheduling is the canonical stateful agent problem, and Vela's architecture makes it acute. A single meeting negotiation spans days, multiple channels (email plus SMS plus WhatsApp) and multiple humans, so the agent must carry one coherent thread of state across sessions and mediums — no context window survives that. It also needs durable per-principal preference memory: meeting-type defaults, buffer rules, which days a partner protects, who is a VIP worth double-booking around, how a given candidate or client prefers to be contacted, and the outcome of past coordination with that same person. In executive recruiting the same candidates and hiring managers recur across searches, so remembering prior interactions is what separates it from a booking link. Rescheduling explicitly requires recalling the original negotiation. And with a two-to-fifteen person team in their first year, buying a memory layer instead of building durable cross-channel agent state is the fastest path to shipping.

headcount_estimate: ~44 (LinkedIn company page lists 44 employees, 11-50 band). Company site's own timeline says 10+ employees end-2024 and 'nearly 20' in spring 2025, so LinkedIn's 44 likely includes alumni/loosely-affiliated profiles; real headcount is plausibly 20-45.

how_they_use_agents: AI agents are the newer half of the product, not the origin. 'AI Agents' autonomously answer repetitive inbound customer inquiries across WhatsApp, email, chat and social in multiple languages 24/7; an AI Voice Assistant handles inbound phone support; a WhatsApp AI chatbot handles instant replies; a workflow builder lets brands script agent-driven support processes (WISMO/order status, returns, cancellations/refunds, invoice requests, product advice). The agent has to answer as the brand, using that brand's catalogue, shipping policy, order data and past conversation with that specific shopper.
why_they_need_memory: Their agent's context problem was latency and token cost, not storage. Every reply ran a full RAG pipeline — embed the query, hit a vector store, assemble context, then generate — which pushed average AI response time to ~40s, unacceptable in a live WhatsApp thread where the shopper is waiting. They replaced RAG entirely with Supermemory's memory layer plus near-realtime web search for volatile data (stock, order status, pricing), cutting response time to ~12s, reducing tokens 40-50%, and eliminating RAG infra maintenance for a ~20-person bootstrapped team with no infra headcount to spare. The durable need is per-shopper and per-brand conversational memory that persists across long-running WhatsApp threads and across channels (chat, email, voice) in one omnichannel inbox.

name: Scira AI
what_it_does: Open-source agentic research/search platform, positioned as a Perplexity alternative — 'Research at the speed of thought… plans, retrieves, and cites'. Formerly MiniPerplx. A query is decomposed into sub-questions, run in parallel across live sources, cross-checked, and returned as a grounded answer with inline clickable citations and a visible trace of every step. 17-18 search modes (Web, Chat, X, Stocks, Code, Academic, Extreme/deep research, Reddit, GitHub, Crypto, Prediction markets, YouTube, Spotify, Connectors, Memory, Voice, XQL) and 28 tools. AGPL-3.0, self-hostable, bring-your-own-models. Built on Next.js + Vercel AI SDK over xAI Grok, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others; retrieval via Exa, Firecrawl, Tavily, Parallel and Context.dev; Upstash Redis, Cloudflare R2, Daytona sandbox, Better Auth, Drizzle. Site claims 5M+ searches answered, 100K+ people researching, 100+ connected apps; GitHub 11.9k stars / 1.5k forks, repo created Aug 2024.
category: AI search & research (consumer/prosumer answer engine, open source)
stage: indie / bootstrapped solo-founder project — no institutional round found
funding: unknown, most likely none institutional. No Crunchbase/PitchBook/TechCrunch record found. Revenue is direct subscription: Free (3 searches/day), Pro $15/mo (₹1,390 in India), Max $60/mo (₹5,990) — the pricing page also displayed a $9 Pro figure, likely promotional/regional. Billing runs through Polar and DodoPayments, an indie-developer payment stack rather than an enterprise billing vendor. Non-dilutive support only: Vercel OSS Program badge, plus partner/sponsor placements from Context.dev, Exa AI and Upstash.
headcount_estimate: 1 (solo founder) plus open-source contributors. No LinkedIn company page and no named team found; terms and support both route to zaid@scira.ai, and the GitHub owner's bio reads 'founder @ scira.ai'. No formal legal entity is named anywhere — the terms say only 'the laws of the jurisdiction in which Scira AI operates'.
yc_or_accelerator: none found — no YC page (ycombinator.com/companies/scira and /scira-ai both 404). Vercel's OSS Program is a sponsorship, not an accelerator.
founded_year: 2024 (GitHub repo created 2024-08-07 as MiniPerplx; rebranded to Scira)
sells_to: prosumer / individual — researchers, students, developers and analysts on $15-60/mo self-serve subscriptions; secondarily developers, since the whole stack is AGPL and self-hostable
how_they_use_agents: The agent IS the product. 'Agentic planning' breaks a question into sub-tasks, picks a model and source per sub-task, and executes multi-step workflows end to end. 'Extreme search' is an LLM-driven deep-research agent with multi-step planning, code execution and artifact storage in R2. 'Lookouts' are scheduled recurring research agents that monitor a topic, track changes and email updates. Plus 'Scouts', a 'Scira Agent' in limited preview on the Max tier, and 100+ MCP-connected apps the agent can call.
why_they_need_memory: Two jobs. First, continuity: research is multi-session, so the agent must carry what a user already asked, found and rejected across sessions — Memory is a paid Pro mode ('your personal memory companion'). Second, personal corpus: Connectors let the agent search the user's own Google Drive, Notion and OneDrive alongside the live web, so the memory layer doubles as the ingestion/index path for user documents. Mem0 failed on both — high retrieval latency, indexing that silently dropped items ('every time it was indexing something, it wouldn't add it to the memories'), weak recall as user data grew, poor scaling, and no connectors. Moving to Supermemory cut mean retrieval latency 37.4%, drove ~32% usage growth after memory launched, and directly converted 10 pro subscribers who signed up for memory alone. For a one-person company, buying memory rather than operating a vector stack is the only viable option.

name: Google (Alphabet Inc.)
what_it_does: Google is the internet-services subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL): search, online advertising (~73% of revenue), YouTube, Android, Chrome, Google Workspace, Maps, Pixel hardware, and Google Cloud. AI product lines include Gemini, Imagen, Veo, NotebookLM, AI Overviews in Search, and Google DeepMind research. Sibling Alphabet bets include Waymo, Verily, Calico, Isomorphic Labs, X, GV/CapitalG.
category: Mega-cap technology platform — search/advertising, consumer software, cloud infrastructure, frontier AI. NOT a startup and NOT an agent-memory buyer profile.
stage: Public mega-cap (Alphabet Inc., NASDAQ: GOOGL). Not venture-stage.
funding: Public company. Alphabet 2025 revenue ~US$403B. Historical VC funding is irrelevant/immaterial at this scale. No agent-memory-related funding event found.
headcount_estimate: ~198,933 (Alphabet, as of June 2026). The Google segment alone was ~187,000 in 2022; a current Google-only figure was not confirmed.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Google was founded in 1998, pre-dating YC; Alphabet operates its own accelerators (Google for Startups) rather than being an alumnus of one.
founded_year: 1998 (Google, Menlo Park, CA). Alphabet holding structure created 2015.
sells_to: All of the above and none cleanly: consumers (Search, Android, YouTube), advertisers (SMB through enterprise), enterprise IT (Google Cloud, Workspace, Gemini Enterprise), and developers (Cloud APIs, ADK, Gemini API). Google is a horizontal platform, not a segment-specific vendor.
how_they_use_agents: Google BUILDS and SELLS the agent stack rather than buying it. Confirmed first-party: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI Agent Engine) ships a managed 'Memory Bank' that stores and retrieves long-term user preferences and facts across sessions, with memory generation from events, memory profiles, revision tracking, and Agent Development Kit (ADK) integration — verified live in Google Cloud docs (last updated 2026-09-02). Google also ships Agentspace/Gemini Enterprise for internal-knowledge agents, plus consumer agent memory in Gemini. In other words, Google is a direct COMPETITOR to Supermemory, Cognee, Honcho and Memvid in this exact category.
why_they_need_memory: They do not need to buy it — they sell it. Treat this logo as a category red flag, not an ICP signal. The evidence supports at most individual-engineer adoption: on Supermemory the wordmark sits inside a use-case card headlined 'Internal Use — Used by engineers from the best teams,' and on Cognee's homepage the marquee is explicitly headlined 'Trusted by engineers from' (Google appears alongside Apple, AWS, Microsoft, IBM, Adobe, Samsung, Uber, ByteDance, Baidu and ~10 more — a list whose shape strongly suggests it is derived from self-reported user email domains or GitHub stargazers, not contracts). No logo link, no quote, no case study, no press release, no procurement trace was found for any of the four vendors. A Googler running an open-source memory library on a side project is not Google as a customer. Any real motivation would be the same one every large org has — long-horizon context over internal docs, wikis and institutional knowledge — but Google's answer to that is its own internal infrastructure.

how_they_use_agents: Verified and specific. Bayer R&D used Cognee to move 'from an AI chatbot to agentic research memory': roughly 10,000 scientific papers (preclinical literature) were converted into an agentic research memory combining graph-based and vector-based reasoning, supporting hypothesis generation — reported as 'hypothesis generation in hours, not months.' The agent is a research/discovery agent operating over an internal scientific corpus, not a customer-facing or sales agent. Named sponsor: Nikola Milosevic, Technical Ecosystem Owner, Bayer R&D — a credible attribution, as the Nikola Milosevic associated with Bayer is a biomedical text-mining/NLP researcher (University of Manchester PhD, published on information extraction from tables in biomedical literature). Note: an arXiv author page for a 'Nikola Milosevic' returned a different researcher working on reinforcement learning and active inference — a name collision, not the same person, so do not cite those papers as Bayer work.
why_they_need_memory: This is the archetype for the category, and the only one of the three with real evidence. The stated buying criteria in the customer's own quote are precise: 'combining graph and vector reasoning over our preclinical literature, with the explainability our scientists need to trust the output.' Three forces make it a real purchase: (1) scale and heterogeneity of unstructured scientific literature that no single scientist can hold in context; (2) a regulated, evidence-chain environment where a black-box RAG answer is unusable — explainability and provenance are procurement requirements, not nice-to-haves, which is exactly what a knowledge-graph-plus-vector memory sells against plain embeddings; (3) an economic prize large enough to justify enterprise spend, since compressing hypothesis generation from months to hours moves preclinical cycle time. Corroboration is strong for a logo-wall claim: a full linked case study at /case-study/bayer, a named individual with title, a direct quote, presence on Cognee's /product/enterprise page, and inclusion in the homepage marquee. One honest caveat — the homepage marquee Bayer also appears in is headlined 'Trusted by engineers from', the same weak framing used for Google and Apple; the case study, not the marquee, is what makes this credible. Deal size, contract status and go-live date remain undisclosed.

name: Moonage, Inc.

The loop is five steps: name an Outcome, Assemble the right humans and agents, Carry the work across company tools, route consequential Judgment to a human, and Learn from the result. Product surfaces: Agents (persistent members, each with a name, @handle, an email address at agents.moonage.ai, a role, a persistent computer, declared skills, a model, a budget, scoped access, an autonomy setting, and an audit record); Spaces (durable work containers per project/team/outcome, holding channels, threads, tasks, members, and a budget); Inbox (approvals, questions, exceptions, proposals, receipts — a paused action arrives with the exact command and spend-to-date, and you approve/edit/steer/reject); Memory; Integrations; and Models (model-agnostic — "The model is replaceable. name: Jinso Labs (Jinso Inc.)
what_it_does: Jinso sells "AI Infrastructure for Institutional Learning" — a single platform replacing what it counts as seven disconnected systems (LMS, assessment platform, content library, WhatsApp/messaging, teacher dashboard, SIS, reporting/analytics). Homepage hero: "Stop adding tools. Start improving your students' outcomes." The architectural centerpiece is the "Jinso Context Engine": raw institutional data (LMS, SIS, ERP, courses, content, learner profiles, policies) is normalized into a "Jinso Ontology" unified context layer, which then powers three consumers — an AI Agent for learners, an AI Copilot for teachers, and outcome dashboards for administrators. Components: a 24/7 adaptive AI tutor via chat, web, and WhatsApp; automated placement/formative/summative assessments that are AI-graded and auto-posted to the LMS; a fully hosted and managed Canvas LMS (Jinso runs hosting, config, maintenance) with rostering, lesson deployment, and campus coordination; an Institutional Copilot with role-based dashboards, real-time engagement flags, and predictive at-risk alerts; subject-specific content packs (employability, medicine, tourism, sciences); unlimited teacher training; white-labeling (logo, colors, domain); and automated lesson deployment at scale. Teacher autonomy over the AI is configurable from "Fully Autonomous" to "Teacher Guided." Named customer logos on the homepage include Arizona State University, Temple University, MESCYT (Dominican Republic Ministry of Higher Education), Ministerio de Educación Pública Costa Rica, Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, and a set of Latin American binational centers (ICPNA, ICANA, IBEU, Centro Boliviano Americano, Instituto Cultural Brasil, IHCI, ICDA, IMNRC, Pernambuco). (2) Agents as the thing being secured: a full AI-security line — AI Asset Management (auto-discovers models, agents, MCP servers, shadow AI, with data lineage across 2,900+ apps), Secure Access to AI / AI Gateway (inline DLP and zero trust on every model, agent and API call; governs agent-to-agent traffic), AI red-teaming (5,000+ attack scenarios, mapped to MITRE ATLAS/NIST/EU AI Act), and previewed AI Broker (MCP and agent-to-agent brokering with fine-grained policy), AI Access Graph (visibility into how agents use data and identities) and Endpoint AI Security. Add HIPAA/SOC 2 scope and a governed, auditable memory store with provenance beats rolling their own vector-store hack.

Separately, the company has long marketed 'machine learning' for talent mapping in its core search platform, and a VP of Product & AI (Stephen/Steve Corby) plus a VP of AI (James Kirk) appear on the team.
why_they_need_memory: Three reinforcing reasons. (1) Per-user agent fleet: because each employee and each chat room gets its own agent instance, they need per-agent persistent state managed centrally rather than one stateless bot — this is exactly the quoted pain, 'deploy and manage a huge fleet of agents with a single API endpoint... we didn't want to have to build our own tooling to manage agents.' (2) Consistency as a business asset: recruiting quality depends on every recruiter evaluating candidates the same way, and their VP of AI framed memory as behavioral consistency — improving Hunter once improves the process across all teams. (3) The underlying data is a long-lived relationship graph (7M+ candidates, expert referrers, prior searches) where context about a candidate, a client, and a search accumulates over months; a stateless chat assistant would re-derive it every session.

That accumulated semantic layer is the moat, and it is exactly what an agent-memory substrate stores. Note the buying pattern: Kognitos is a sophisticated AI-native vendor that still chose to buy the memory/agent-runtime layer rather than build it, because prototyping speed and agent observability mattered more than owning that stack.

Founded 2022 in Bengaluru (HSR Layout), by Anand Krishna (CEO) and Ranvir Singh (CTO). yc_or_accelerator: NOT a YC company — correction to the source note. I downloaded the full Y Combinator company dataset (yc-oss API, 6,203 companies, batches through Summer 2026/Winter 2027) and found no 'Inkle' entry by name or website. The 'YC company' impression almost certainly comes from Inkle's own marketing line that 'over 5% of YC companies' USE Inkle — they sell to YC startups rather than being one. Backers Saison Capital, Picus Capital and Force Ventures are traditional VCs, not accelerators.

Buyer is the founder or a lean one-person finance function, not a CFO org. Price points ($30-$99/mo) confirm the low end of the market.
how_they_use_agents: Weak and mostly cosmetic. Inkle's product uses AI as feature-level assistance inside a human-in-the-loop service: AI-suggested transaction categorization, AI-enabled receipt matching, 'Smart Reconcile' AI matching for Stripe, and a mentioned 'LLM integration.' Licensed human CPAs still do the actual tax work, and their own case-study pages contain no mention of AI agents at all. There is no evidence Inkle runs an autonomous agent fleet or builds agentic products. Their appearance in this dataset is as a CUSTOMER of Poth Labs — an AI customer-intelligence tool that finds gaps in a company's customer evidence and runs adaptive AI surveys to fill them, storing responses back against customer accounts. So Inkle is a buyer of an agent-flavored SaaS tool for go-to-market/customer research, not a builder of agents.
why_they_need_memory: Weaker case than the other two, and worth flagging to the parent as a likely false positive for the 'agent memory buyer' thesis. The plausible pull is customer-account knowledge accumulation: Inkle serves 500+ small startups over multi-year compliance relationships where entity structure, filing history, jurisdictions and founder residency status must persist and compound — and Poth Labs' pitch is precisely an evolving per-account knowledge base assembled from evidence plus survey responses. But this is a GTM/customer-research use case, not core-product agent memory. Note also the citation quality: this is a logo-wall placement only — no quote, no case study, not listed as an integration — so it is unverified whether Inkle is a paying customer, a design partner, or a friendly logo (both are early-stage companies and Composio, another Poth logo, is also India-linked, suggesting a shared network rather than an enterprise sales motion).

name: Bilt (Bilt Rewards)

category: Consumer fintech — loyalty, payments and local commerce (a non-AI-native scaled startup buying agent infrastructure, not an AI startup)

funding: Multiple large rounds; reporting only rounds I could verify rather than a fabricated total. $150M Series B (2022, led by Left Lane Capital, $1.5B valuation); $200M Series C (Jan 2024, led by General Catalyst, $3.1B valuation); Aug 2024 investment involving Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan at $3.25B; $250M (July 2025, co-led by General Catalyst and GID) at a $10.75B valuation — the $10.75B figure and the $250M round also appear on Bilt's own careers page. Careers page lists 20+ open roles across engineering, product, marketing, finance, enterprise sales and CX. Real number is plausibly at or above the top of that band given the valuation.
yc_or_accelerator: none — not a YC company; venture/growth-equity funded from the start
founded_year: 2019 per Wikipedia (product publicly launched 2021); Bilt's own careers page says 'founded in 2020' — note the discrepancy. Founder and CEO: Ankur Jain.
sells_to: Primarily B2C (renters and homeowners), acquired through B2B2C channels — property managers/landlords (Greystar and others), mortgage servicers, and card issuers — plus a B2B merchant side (local businesses and national brands buying into the rewards/offers network).
how_they_use_agents: The clearest large-scale agent-memory deployment of the three. Per Letta's case study: Bilt runs a memory-augmented agent architecture for personalized local-merchant and neighborhood-benefit recommendations. Architecture: unstructured transaction data is processed asynchronously in BATCH MODE with a strong model (Anthropic batch mode) to write shared Letta memory blocks; a cheaper, faster model then does real-time inference against those blocks — sophistication without frontier-model latency/cost per request. They first tried fine-tuning and rejected it ('The fine tuned model was very matter-of-fact and lost its creativity' — Kosta Krauth, CTO). Scale: over 1 million agents in production, scaling from one agent per benefit per user toward tens of millions across the user base; 'All the latency in the end-to-end system is 99+ percent just inference time' and 'Scaling from the perspective of agents is no longer a concern' (Andrew Fitz, lead engineer on the AI personalization project). Notably non-technical: PMs, team leads, GMs and the CEO all worked inside Letta's Agent Development Environment editing prompts and agent behavior. Case study first archived July 2025.
why_they_need_memory: Per-user persistent state at consumer scale. Their recommendation problem is not retrieval over documents — it is remembering an individual's evolving behavior (Letta's example: recognizing timing-dependent patterns, not just static preferences) across millions of members, with an explanation attached. Fine-tuning collapsed the nuance; RAG alone doesn't hold user state. Memory blocks let them (a) separate expensive memory-writing from cheap real-time reads, (b) keep a durable per-user profile that improves without retraining, and (c) expose that state as human-editable text business staff can inspect and steer. This is the archetypal buyer for the category: a large non-AI-native consumer company with millions of users, high per-request cost sensitivity, and a personalization problem.

The pipeline is Identify (filter signals across 50+ data sources) -> Research (enrich with company news, tech stack, competitive intel) -> Personalize (per-prospect messaging, no templates) -> Engage (multi-channel with contextual continuity). No later round found. MATERIAL CONTEXT for anyone treating them as a reference account: TechCrunch reported in March 2025 that 11x displayed logos of customers that were not active (one threatened legal action), alongside reporting on churn and product problems; founder-CEO Hasan Sukkar stepped down in May 2025 to become non-executive chairman, with then-CTO Prabhav Jain (ex-Brex, three-time founder) taking over as CEO. Prabhav Jain is quoted as 'CTO' in the Letta case study, dating that story to on/before that transition.
headcount_estimate: ~100 employees (LinkedIn shows 100 associated profiles; company size band 51-200; 29,793 followers). Two offices, SF and London.
yc_or_accelerator: none — not a YC company (absent from YC's public directory). Backed directly by Benchmark then a16z.
founded_year: 2022 — founded by Hasan Sukkar in London; 11X LIMITED (company no. 14393667) incorporated at Companies House on 3 October 2022, and 11x.ai first archived February 2023.
sells_to: B2B — sales, marketing/demand-gen, growth and RevOps teams, from high-growth startups up to large enterprises (Xerox, UST, Sage). Mid-market-to-enterprise motion with AEs and sales engineers demoing (their own quotes reference 'our Account Executives and Sales Engineers are demoing it').
how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product — Alice and Julian are the deliverable, not an internal tool. Their agent-memory purchase was for a specific feature: the Alice Deep Research Agent, built on Letta in about 72 hours. It queries their Pinecone knowledge base and shows visible step-by-step reasoning at each hop, so customers can see what the agent used. Adoption of that feature went from 3 to 85 customers 'overnight' after launch, with reported lifts in reply rates. Quotes: Keith Fearon (Head of Growth) — 'Letta is so easy to understand. Anyone can do it. The Agent Development Environment is the Cursor of agent building'; Satwik Singh (engineer) — 'When we're building agents there's often this whole time period of making sure the graph's connected... With Letta, there's none of that'; Prabhav Jain (CTO, now CEO) — 'Imagine we have a large customer that adds 200 offers to our platform. That's when your context limit completely blows up.' They said they were then exploring stateful agents that learn which messaging works over time, plus call-recording analysis and deeper CRM integration.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct drivers. (1) Immediate: context-window blowout. Enterprise customers load hundreds of products/offers into the platform and it will not fit in a prompt; naive RAG solved the size problem but destroyed trust because customers could not see what the agent drew on. They needed an agent that could hold and reason over a large per-customer body of knowledge with visible reasoning. (2) Strategic: an SDR agent is worthless if it forgets the prospect. Multi-channel sequences (email -> LinkedIn -> phone -> WhatsApp) need contextual continuity across channels and weeks, per-account and per-prospect, and they explicitly want agents that learn message effectiveness over time. That is state, not retrieval. Also notable as a buyer profile: the value they emphasize is speed of iteration and non-ML-engineer accessibility (the ADE), not model quality — they bought a build-velocity tool as much as a memory layer.

Three layers to the business: (1) Wetlab — proprietary chemistry, BIRT + PERD for RNA sequencing (claimed ~10x cheaper and requiring ~10x less sample) and MARE for DNA-based newborn screening covering 5,000+ inherited diseases; (2) Diagnostics — an MS blood panel with three clinical uses (MS vs. NMO differential, 91.3% AUC; MS subtyping, 78.8% AUC; early MS screening, 74.2% AUC), plus N-Act AI which turns biological signal into clinician-facing insight; (3) AI — foundation models for molecular medicine, and K-Dense, a multi-agent "AI scientist" that runs autonomous scientific analysis and produces publication-ready manuscripts, launched in beta Sept 2025 with validation work alongside Harvard Medical School on aging research, and written up as "K-Dense Analyst" on arXiv. K-Dense has since been spun out into a separate company, K-Dense Inc. Subsidiary Bayosthiti partnered with Narayana Health (Oct 2025) to build an India-specific cardiac AI dataset across 12,000 patients. HQ in Houston, TX, with subsidiaries/offices in Palo Alto, Shanghai, Wuhan, Bengaluru and Riyadh, and 20+ institutional collaborations.

why_they_need_memory: This is the SME end of the agent-memory market and the reason is exception density, not scale. 150,000 documents a year across thousands of suppliers means the same supplier's idiosyncratic order-confirmation layout, the same recurring partial-delivery or price-discrepancy case, and the same 'which cost center does this go to' judgment recur constantly — and the answers currently live with a handful of long-serving back-office staff, not in the ERP. Hard-coded parsers per supplier are exactly the 'legacy systems that only do one specific thing' the company says it wants to retire. A memory/precedent layer lets the system learn a supplier's format and a clerk's routing decision once and reapply it, which is the only economical path for a company this size that cannot staff an ML team. Retiring three legacy tools also means the institutional knowledge encoded in those tools' rules has to go somewhere — a context graph is that somewhere.

The upstream note flagged comdirect as logo-only — no case study, no testimonial, no mention on Interloom's press page — and that remains true: I could not find comdirect (or any logo wall) anywhere on interloom.com as of Sept 2026, and Interloom's press page names only Zurich Insurance, Fiege and Volkswagen Group Services. However, the Wayback archive of interloom.com shows dedicated single-tenant deployments at comdirect.interloom.com AND commerzbank.interloom.com, each with the same full supporting stack Interloom provisions per customer — langfuse (LLM observability), unleash (feature flags) and zitadel (identity) — captured Jan–Mar 2025. Two separate tenants for the parent bank and its retail brand is what you would expect from a real engagement inside Commerzbank, not from a partner or prospect listing. So the most defensible reading is: a genuine deployment or funded PoC that has not been turned into a public reference, most likely because a regulated German bank will not sign off on a named case study. On the workload: Interloom's own Banking solution page describes exactly this shape — KYC reviews, wire approvals and fraud alerts, with a screening agent running sanctions checks and packaging evidence, core-banking integration validating account status and limits, and a compliance analyst signing off with an audit trail attached. For comdirect specifically the natural back-office surfaces are securities-account onboarding/KYC, transfer-of-custody (Depotübertrag) cases, corporate-action and tax-document queries, and customer complaint handling — all high-volume, exception-heavy, and email/ticket-shaped.
why_they_need_memory: A regulated retail bank is the highest-value buyer for agent memory and the hardest to sell. Case handling is dominated by precedent: the correct answer to a custody-transfer exception or a tax-treatment question is whatever compliance decided last time, and that decision must be reproducible and auditable. Volume is large and seasonal (tax season, corporate actions, market volatility spikes), the knowledge is scattered across a core banking system, a ticketing tool, shared inboxes and policy PDFs, and staff turnover in service operations is high. Any agent acting here must cite the specific policy object and prior case it relied on — which is precisely the pitch of Interloom's Context Graph and MemoryRank (route by what actually resolved similar work before, cheap automation on clear matches, human sign-off where policy demands it). The single-tenant, self-hosted deployment pattern visible in the archive (own identity server, own observability) is itself evidence of the data-residency and auditability constraints this buyer imposes.

category: BFSI / distressed-debt asset reconstruction (buyer of the agent-memory product, not a vendor)
stage: unknown
funding: unknown
headcount_estimate: unknown

founded_year: unknown
sells_to: B2B enterprise — not a software company. Buys NPA portfolios from banks/NBFCs and monetises recovery; its 'customers' are selling banks and its counterparties are borrowers, DRTs and investors.
how_they_use_agents: Colrows describes a three-layer system it built for this customer: (1) an ML layer for bulk scoring of loan accounts, behavioural classification, payment-anomaly detection and collateral timeline estimation; (2) a semantic graph with RBI SARFAESI provisions, DRT procedures and RBI circulars modelled into it, used for edge-case interpretation, legal-enforceability assessment and auditable reasoning trails; (3) an AI agent that ingests a portfolio, segments it against the graph, samples and deep-analyses accounts, and synthesises a valuation. Inputs are loan files, KYC documents, payment history, borrower behavioural data and historical portfolio outcomes. The valuable asset is not the LLM but the durable, versioned context: regulatory rules (SARFAESI, DRT, RBI circulars), enforcement precedent, and per-account history that must be reused across every bid and reconstructed later under audit. Colrows' pitch is that the reasoning must be point-in-time reproducible because an investment committee and a regulator will both ask how the number was reached — the anonymous quote used is 'The investment committee didn't ask us to justify the number. For the first time, the number came with its own justification - traceable to regulation, to precedent, to the account itself.' Their prior state — four expert disciplines working apart, with knowledge locked in individual analysts — is exactly the institutional-memory gap this category sells against.
