sells_to: B2B enterprise. Multi-unit and multi-brand hospitality operators, from single locations up to 500+ unit portfolios, sold to restaurant execs, franchisees and hotel/grocery/care groups. The buyer is an operations or HR leader, not a developer.
how_they_use_agents: Harri ships "Salli," marketed as "hospitality's first and only end-to-end agentic AI platform" and explicitly positioned against the category norm — the homepage says "It's not a chatbot. It's not a copilot. It's a suite of autonomous AI agents that serves as a system of action." Salli is the single manager-facing assistant that orchestrates specialized background agents and "returns one clean response." Concrete agent behaviors advertised: Talent Gap Alert (detects understaffing and recommends pre-screened candidates), Compliance Warning (flags break violations and minor-hour-limit risk before penalties accrue), Overtime Cost Alert (projects labor cost in real time and proposes scheduling moves), Scheduling Optimization (one-click conflict resolution with consent/premium logging), Labor Insight (surfaces Fair Workweek rules at the point of scheduling), and Recognition Alert. Status is pre-GA — the Agentic AI page has a "Join The Waitlist" CTA and links a post titled "Harri Announces The Launch Of Its Agentic AI Open Beta." A customer quote from Kevin Brennan (Owner/Director of Operations, JMB Foods) describes it blocking non-compliant schedule posts and using historical sales data to optimize labor targets. Separately, Harri is itself a buyer: Coworker names it as a production OM2 customer, but gives no detail on whether OM2 sits inside Harri's product or is used internally.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pressures. (1) Product-side: their agents have to reason over deeply fragmented per-location operational state — schedules, time cards, sales forecasts, employee availability and history, and compliance rules that differ by state, city and jurisdiction — across 55-60K locations and millions of users. That is exactly the multi-hop, permission-scoped retrieval problem an organizational-memory layer claims to solve, and it is why an agent that starts cold each session is useless to a restaurant GM. (2) Internal: Harri is a ~15-year-old company running four offices across four time zones (New York, London, Ramallah, Hyderabad) with engineering separated from GTM by 7+ hours, so institutional context is scattered across Slack, CRM and docs. Coworker's OM2 post does not say which of these two the deployment serves, so the specific internal use case is unverified.
confidence: high on identity, product and the agentic-AI positioning (all read directly off harri.com); medium on funding and headcount (single-source, no cross-check possible with web search exhausted)

name: Column (Column Software, PBC)
what_it_does:
Public-notice software and marketplace. Column connects the parties legally required to publish public notices — law firms, local and state governments, businesses, estate administrators, storage-lien operators and individuals — with the local newspapers that must carry them, and automates the whole workflow: finding a compliant publication, submitting the notice, coordinating publication deadlines, prepaying the newspaper, collecting proofs, generating court-ready affidavits (1-2 business days), consolidating billing into monthly statements, and storing everything for compliance. Submission is via self-serve web, email automation, or API. Self-reported scale: ~1,700 notices processed daily, 25,000+ affidavits per month, 1,600+ newspapers across all 50 states, 30,000+ government/law-firm/business customers, 98% self-serve rate, 98% CSAT, and "#1 processor of public notice." Legal entity confirmed as "Column Software, PBC" in its own terms and privacy policy — a public benefit corporation, consistent with its local-journalism-support mission framing.

IDENTITY RESOLUTION (the vendor gave no outbound link): I downloaded Coworker's logo file at coworker.ai/images/logos/column.png (395x82 PNG, rendered at 118x24) and compared it against all three plausible candidates' own wordmarks. Coworker's file is a dark-navy SERIF "Column" wordmark. Column Software PBC's own site logo (framerusercontent.com/images/OnSJFKQqLi0Ys1V2v8M4ZMvgzA.png, 1001x172, alt="Column logo") is the identical navy serif "Column" wordmark, paired with a blue classical-pillar icon that Coworker cropped off. The two rivals do not match: Column N.A. (column.com, the nationally chartered bank founded by William Hockey) uses a LOWERCASE SANS-SERIF "column" in navy, and Column Tax (columntax.com) uses a sans-serif wordmark with a cyan bar-glyph mark. The serif face, weight and navy color are a direct match to column.us only.
category: Legal tech / govtech workflow automation + a two-sided media marketplace (notice placers on one side, 1,600+ local newspapers on the other). Adjacent to compliance and local-journalism infrastructure.
stage: Unknown. Private, venture-backed public benefit corporation. Could not confirm a round or stage — column.us has no about, company, team, careers, press or investor page (/about-us and /careers return 404; /team, /press, /company and /newsroom fall through to a JavaScript app shell), its blog covers only state notice-law changes and customer case studies, no Crunchbase or CB Insights profile was reachable, and no Greenhouse/Lever/Ashby board exists under any 'column' slug I tried (the jobs.ashbyhq.com/Column board belongs to the bank, not this company).
funding: unknown — no figure, round or investor could be confirmed from any reachable source. Do not treat any number as established. Note the company operates as a PBC, so mission-aligned or philanthropic capital alongside venture money is plausible but unverified.
headcount_estimate: unknown. No careers page, no job board, no fetchable LinkedIn or TheOrg profile for this specific entity (TheOrg's /org/column is an unrelated 1-10 person Australian brand studio; /org/column-2 is Column N.A., the bank). The operating scale it advertises — order management staff handling intake for high-volume publishers, 1,700 notices a day — implies a meaningful ops team, but I have no basis for a number.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. No YC page exists under a 'column' slug I could reach, and there is no accelerator badge on the site.
founded_year: 2019 — the homepage states the company has operated "since 2019." No independent confirmation obtained.
sells_to: B2B, spanning a wide size range. Enterprise and public sector on one side (state and local governments, large law firms, newspaper publisher groups, legal-services vendors), long-tail SMB on the other (small firms, community newspapers, estate administrators, self-storage operators placing lien notices). Verticalized landing pages exist for newspapers, government, law firms, legal services, estates and storage.
how_they_use_agents: No product-facing AI agents. This is the notable finding: I read the homepage and the dedicated /automation page in full and there is zero mention of AI, ML, LLMs or agents anywhere. What Column calls "Automated Placement" is deterministic workflow orchestration — newspaper routing and selection, deadline coordination, prepayment, proof and affidavit collection, compliance tracking, consolidated billing — reached by email automation or API, not by a model. A customer quote frames the win as "the manual labor has been reduced to a single button click." So Column's presence on Coworker's wall is almost certainly internal adoption (an ops/knowledge tool for its own team) rather than agent infrastructure embedded in its product. Coworker's OM2 post names it only in a list — "runs in production with customers including Harness, RapidSOS, Harri, and Column" — with no quote, named person, use case or link.
why_they_need_memory: Column runs a jurisdiction-knowledge business, which is the archetypal org-memory problem. Notice requirements differ by state and often by county, and they change constantly — Column's own blog is dominated by posts tracking statute changes in Missouri, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Arizona and Florida. On top of that sits per-newspaper tribal knowledge: which paper is a jurisdiction's paper of record, its deadlines, rate card, proof format and affidavit requirements, multiplied across 1,600+ publishers. That knowledge lives in ops team heads, email threads and support tickets, and it decays. An organizational-memory layer that keeps answers current across Slack, docs and CRM is a direct fit for a support and ops org fielding compliance questions all day. Secondary driver: a document-heavy compliance workflow (25,000+ affidavits/month) generates a large searchable corpus that no single employee can hold.
confidence: medium — identity is well-evidenced by the exact wordmark match and by ruling out both rivals, but it rests on visual comparison rather than a vendor link or a public statement from Column itself. Product description is high confidence (read directly off the site). Funding, headcount and stage are unknown, not estimated.

name: Ecom Nation

category: Marketing services — ecommerce/DTC performance marketing agency. A services business, not a software company. This is the outlier in the set: the other two Coworker logos are venture-scale software companies.
stage: Bootstrapped, owner-operated agency. Not venture-backed; no funding stage applies.
funding: None / not applicable. No evidence of outside investment, and none would be expected for a boutique agency of this shape.
headcount_estimate: unknown, but small — likely under 20. Three people are named on the site: Mal Chia (Founder & Managing Director), Paul Waddy (Founder) and Casey Huth (Performance Director). The Coworker case study says the team spent 15-20 hours a week in client and internal meetings and saved "2-3 hours per week per team member," which implies a team measured in single or low double digits, not hundreds. The site's "senior strategist on every account, no juniors" model structurally caps headcount.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Not applicable to a services agency.
founded_year: 2021 — the homepage carries an "EST. 2021" marker.
sells_to: B2B SMB / lower mid-market. Australian and international DTC ecommerce brands doing 7+ figures in revenue; the buyer is a founder or head of growth at a consumer brand. Selling retainer services, not software.
how_they_use_agents: Pure buyer, not builder — no AI in what they sell. They use Coworker as a meeting-intelligence and organizational-search layer: meetings are transcribed and summarized automatically, then the content is contextualized and connected to their other business tools, with unified search, custom reports and topic tracking on top. They replaced Fireflies with it. Mal Chia's quote makes the distinction the vendor wants: "Coworker isn't just a transcription tool — it's fundamentally changed the way we operate. Before, we'd spend hours digging through disjointed meeting notes trying to piece together client conversations. Now that information is automatically captured, contextualized and connected to everything else." Reported results: 30-40% reduction in time spent searching for information, 2-3 hours/week saved per team member, and roughly 30-40% of previously wasted time redeployed into client work.
why_they_need_memory: This is the clearest and most honest buyer profile in the set, and it is the classic small-services-firm case: billable strategist time is literally the product, so any hour spent reconstructing what a client said is margin destroyed. A senior strategist juggling many concurrent accounts has to recall months-old context per client on demand, and that context lives scattered across meeting notes, Slack and ad platforms. Chia frames it as a competitive argument rather than a productivity one: "The difference between average agencies and exceptional ones isn't just talent — it's how effectively you deploy that talent." He also notes the counterintuitive outcome — "by focusing less on documenting meetings and more on acting on them, our client communication has actually improved." Notably, the pain here is meeting-and-client memory, a narrower and more concrete need than the enterprise-wide knowledge-graph pitch Coworker makes to Harri, Harness and RapidSOS — which suggests the category is selling to two quite different buyers under one story.
confidence: high — the site was read in full, the founder's name and title match the testimonial exactly, and the agency's self-description matches Coworker's "retail marketing agency" framing. Headcount is honestly unknown; no funding exists to get wrong.

The buying trigger is scale-driven fragmentation — ~3,000 venues in ~40 countries, ~49k staff, dozens of markets running campaigns simultaneously — where every business question crossed team and tool boundaries and no consistent metric definition survived. Per https://colrows.com/use_cases/cipla.html, Colrows deployed a semantic execution layer over a Trino federated query engine spanning Cirrius CRM (prescription data), Oracle (campaign performance), the ERP (inventory and batch) and scattered field-activity platforms — no data movement, no new warehouse. On top sits a knowledge graph in which doctors, brands, campaigns and regions resolve to consistent business entities, plus a reasoning layer that compiles NL or SQL questions into a cross-source execution plan. The worked example is diagnostic rather than retrieval: 'Why did prescription volume drop for Brand X in the West region this month?' resolved in under 4 minutes (previously 2-3 days across 3 teams), returning three corroborated causal drivers (high-value prescriber visits down 31%, West-territory campaign spend 22% below plan, competitor share-of-voice up 18 points) with a reasoning trail and a recommended action. Colrows separately markets 'analytics and reporting agents' for this account and lists Cipla as its lead homepage logo. Claimed results: 8x data-adoption increase, >90% reduction in decision latency, 80% drop in IT report requests, 1000x faster campaign diagnosis, 18-24% sales productivity uplift, 30% reduction in stockouts.
why_they_need_memory: The stated problem is a meaning problem, not a storage problem — Cipla had already invested in data infrastructure; the gap was knowing what data meant in business context and how metrics related across systems. Case-study framing: 'The organisation could see what was happening, but not why', and 'every new dashboard introduced another version of the truth'. That is exactly the agent-memory value proposition in enterprise clothing: a durable, governed semantic graph that persists entity definitions and relationships so an agent can reason across CRM, ERP and Oracle instead of re-deriving context per query. Regulated-industry constraints add the governance half of the pitch — Colrows enforces RBAC/ABAC and row/column security at compile time, before SQL executes, with full audit trails, which is what makes a pharma commercial team willing to let an agent touch prescriber data at all.

name: Nous Research
what_it_does: Open-source AI research lab and product company. Two main lines: (1) the Hermes family of open-weight, "human-aligned" general-purpose LLMs (Hermes 4 is current), plus distributed-training research (DisTrO, Psyche) for coordinating decentralized model training; (2) Hermes Agent, an open-source, self-improving agent harness that is now its flagship product. Hermes Agent runs from a CLI or as a gateway across Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal and email, executes in sandboxes (Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Vercel Sandbox), delegates to parallel subagents, schedules work via built-in cron, and reaches 300+ models through Nous Portal. Other surfaces: Nous Chat, Nous Portal (inference API/router), and sims.nousresearch.com. Self-describes as "a frontier open source AI company" and "a leader in the American open source AI movement," fully remote with an NYC office; LinkedIn lists HQ as Austin, TX. Commercially it sells a hosted Hermes Cloud on Free/Plus/Super/Ultra tiers (roughly $20–$200/month per TechCrunch).
category: AI research lab + open-source agent harness / consumer-and-developer AI agent (frontier AI lab adjacent)
stage: Series B-ish / late growth-stage private. TechCrunch (July 13, 2026) reported it was in talks to raise at least $75M at a $1.5B valuation, led by Robot Ventures with significant participation from USV.
funding: ~$70M raised prior to the mid-2026 round, from Paradigm, Robot Ventures, North Island Ventures, Delphi Ventures, OSS Capital and Balaji Srinivasan (per TechCrunch, July 2026). A new round of at least $75M at a $1.5B valuation was reported as in talks as of July 2026 — treat the new round as reported-but-unconfirmed, not closed. Exact per-round breakdown (seed vs. Series A amounts) not confirmed from primary sources in this pass.
headcount_estimate: 11-50 (LinkedIn company page). Careers page lists ~10 open roles (Forward Deployed Engineer, ML Engineer Evals, Product Analytics, Security, several Software Engineer roles incl. Hermes Cloud and Mobile, UI/UX, NYC Office Manager), so headcount is likely growing past 50.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not a YC company; began as an open-source/Discord research collective in 2023 and was funded directly by crypto-adjacent and open-source VCs (Paradigm, Robot Ventures, Delphi, OSS Capital).
sells_to: Developers primarily, plus prosumer — open-source agent harness (MIT-licensed) with a paid hosted cloud tier at $20–$200/month, and open-weight models consumed by the broader AI developer community. Not an enterprise-seat B2B motion.
how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product. Hermes Agent is an autonomous agent harness with an explicit closed learning loop: it creates skills from experience and improves them during use, nudges itself to persist knowledge, searches its own past conversations (FTS5 full-text search with LLM summarization for cross-session recall), and "builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions." It runs long-lived across chat platforms with a unified context, spawns parallel subagents, and executes in isolated sandboxes. The GitHub README explicitly names Honcho for dialectic user modeling — i.e., Honcho is wired in as a memory/user-model backend so the agent can understand user patterns over time. Honcho's own homepage advertises this back: "Hermes Agent — Autonomous agent with built-in Honcho memory."
why_they_need_memory: Structurally the most memory-dependent buyer profile in this category. Hermes Agent's core differentiation is persistence — same agent, same user, across Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp/CLI, over months. That requires cross-surface identity, a durable user model, and cross-session recall that a context window cannot provide, so a user-modeling layer is a first-class dependency rather than a nice-to-have. Note the relationship is as much partnership/integration as pure purchase: Nous ships Honcho as a bundled memory backend inside an MIT-licensed open-source product, which is distribution for Honcho and a build-vs-buy shortcut for Nous. That mutual interest should be discounted when reading it as a customer proof point — though it is still the strongest-evidenced name on the list, corroborated in three independent places (Honcho homepage integration copy, Honcho's blog, and the Hermes Agent README itself).

name: Cisco Systems

Sells networking hardware and software (switching, routing, Silicon One ASICs, wireless), cybersecurity (Splunk, AI Defense, Secure Access), collaboration (Webex), observability (AppDynamics/ThousandEyes), and increasingly AI data-center infrastructure — the company frames itself around "networking, cybersecurity and AI." FY2025 revenue $56.65B; ~$9.3B in AI-infrastructure orders and ~$4B in AI infrastructure revenue reported in FY2026.
category: Enterprise networking / cybersecurity / infrastructure incumbent (not an agent-memory-native buyer)
stage: Public company (NASDAQ: CSCO), founded 1984, IPO 1990
funding: Not applicable — publicly traded. FY2025 revenue $56.65B.
yc_or_accelerator: Not applicable
sells_to: B2B enterprise (plus service providers, public sector, and commercial/mid-market through channel partners)
how_they_use_agents: Agentic AI is a stated product direction, not the core business. Cisco's AI solutions page markets: Cisco AI Assistant (generative assistant across Cisco's operational domains), AI Canvas (a generative UI unifying cross-domain telemetry with AI-powered execution), and Cisco Cloud Control under the "AgenticOps" banner — explicitly "trusted, policy-bound AI agents to operate at machine scale — automating decisions, executing workflows, and resolving issues responsibly." But Cisco is overwhelmingly likely to build that internally or buy from an enterprise-grade vendor with procurement, SOC2/FedRAMP and vendor-risk clearance, not adopt a seed-stage memory API as a company standard.

Umbrella for CNCF (Kubernetes), PyTorch Foundation, OpenSSF, LF AI & Data, and — since December 2025 — the Agentic AI Foundation. Funded by member dues (platinum members reportedly ~$500K/year) rather than product revenue; over 1,000 corporate members. Headquartered in San Francisco (registered in Delaware).
category: Open-source nonprofit foundation / standards and governance body (not a product company)
stage: Nonprofit, not venture-backed
funding: Not applicable — member-dues funded 501(c)(6). Wikipedia cites at least ~$14.94M in annual fees as of June 2024; that figure looks like a partial/dues-only measure rather than total revenue, so treat overall revenue as unknown.
headcount_estimate: LinkedIn lists 201-500 as the size band with 1,042 profiles associating themselves with the org (that larger number likely includes project contributors and community members, not payroll). Wikipedia says 150 employees, which appears stale. Best read: a few hundred staff.
yc_or_accelerator: Not applicable
founded_year: 2007 (merger of Open Source Development Labs and the Free Standards Group)
sells_to: Not a commercial seller — corporate members and individual supporters fund it; its "users" are open-source developers and member companies.
how_they_use_agents: The Linux Foundation is the governance host for much of the open agent stack rather than an agent operator. It launched the Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025 with contributions including Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose and AGENTS.md; the foundation added 97 new members (Feb 2026), 43 more (May 2026) and 57 more (Aug 2026, incl. financial services and APAC). Related projects: Agentgateway (Aug 2025), DNS-AID for decentralized agent discovery (May 2026), and an announced Agent Name Service for trusted agent identity (June 2026). It also runs AGNTCon + MCPCon events. So agents appear as hosted standards and infrastructure projects, not as an internal product.
why_they_need_memory: Essentially no organizational buying need. An individual LF-affiliated developer experimenting with a memory API is plausible — which is all a "used by developers at" logo claims — but the Foundation has no product that would run stateful user-facing agents, and it deliberately stays vendor-neutral, which cuts against endorsing a commercial memory vendor. Its relevance to this category is as a standards venue (MCP, agent identity/discovery) that a memory vendor would want to be visible in, not as a customer.

category: Out-of-home / connected-TV media and adtech (FAST streaming for businesses). Not an AI company.

founded_year: 2019 (spun out of Chive Media Group; LinkedIn lists Founded 2019, and a Mar 2023 release described it as being in its "fifth year of operation")
sells_to: B2B, two-sided. Supply side is SMB and multi-location chain venue operators (restaurants, bars, gyms, clinics, laundromats, airports) who get the service free; the revenue side is enterprise/national brand advertisers and agencies buying DOOH CTV inventory, plus SMBs buying local self-serve ads and digital signage.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents in the customer-facing product — the only "agent" on product surfaces is a human support agent in the Business Manager app. AI shows up as an internal-productivity program: Atmosphere published a blog in early 2025 describing a company-wide AI integration strategy kicked off with a 24-hour AI-driven hackathon, using Augment Code for coding (claimed ~5x dev speed), a "snarky AI judge," and "an entire suite of LLMs" as engineering rubber ducks, with an explicit taxonomy of adoption styles ("the Consultant, the Intern, the Overlord") and guidance on giving assistants codebase context. That declared top-down AI push is the plausible buying trigger for Coworker. The Coworker citation is logo-wall only — no quote, named user, or case study — so the specific internal workflow is unverified.
why_they_need_memory: A sales-led media business where context is scattered: ~60,000 venue accounts, 60+ channels, dozens of content/sports partnership deals, and a field ad-sales org spread across a dozen-plus US metros plus London. Who is on which plan, which advertiser ran which creative in which venue class, which partner deal covers which channel — that lives across CRM, ad ops, support and Slack rather than in any one system. An organizational-memory layer is what makes agents usable for GTM and revenue ops at that spread. They also already committed publicly to company-wide AI adoption in 2025, so they were shopping.
confidence: high (existence, product, funding and scale all confirmed from first-party press releases and LinkedIn; the specific Coworker use case is inferred, since the citation is a logo only)

HQ Los Angeles; operations in the US, Canada, UK, Australia, India (Ahmedabad) and Latin America; London office in the West End.
category: Vertical SaaS + two-sided marketplace for entertainment casting and crew hiring (HR-tech/recruiting adjacent). Not AI-native.
stage: Private-equity majority-owned, not venture-staged. Mature, acquisitive platform company.
funding: No disclosed VC rounds. RedBird Capital Partners, together with StepStone Group (Nasdaq: STEP), announced a definitive agreement to acquire a majority stake in July 2022 — financial terms not disclosed. Prior backer Caltius Equity Partners stayed on as a minority investor; co-CEOs Rafi Gordon and Alex Amin retained significant equity. William Blair advised Talent Systems on the deal. Growth has been M&A-driven: Casting Networks and Cast It Systems (2017), then Casting Frontier, Spotlight, eTribez Casting Platform and Staff Me Up (June 2022), and Tagmin (May 2023). No dollar figures are public — do not quote one.
headcount_estimate: ~1,221 LinkedIn-associated employee profiles, though the company self-reports the 201-500 band on LinkedIn — the gap likely reflects alumni across the many acquired brands. Substantial engineering/ops presence in Ahmedabad, India, plus London and Los Angeles. Actual headcount unknown; several hundred is the defensible read. Careers run on HiBob (talentsystems.careers.hibob.com).
yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: Talent Systems as a platform dates to 2017, when Alex Amin and Rafi Gordon acquired Casting Networks and Cast It Systems. Its oldest brand, Spotlight, was founded in 1927.
sells_to: Mixed. B2B enterprise (major film/TV studios, networks, production companies buying Cast It and Cast It Reach), B2B SMB (casting offices, talent and creative agencies), and prosumer subscriptions (actors, performers, and freelance production crew paying for profiles and submissions).
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents visible anywhere in the customer-facing products — Casting Networks, Spotlight and the Talent Systems corporate site carry zero AI messaging as of Sept 2026, and a full-text scan of the corporate site returned no AI or agent content. What is visible is a technology-modernization arc: Sathish Pottavathini hired as CTO in Dec 2024 (ex-LinkedIn and other large-scale engineering orgs), and Justin Kramer named CEO effective March 2, 2026, replacing the founding co-CEOs, with an explicit brief around "investing in people and technology" and customer-driven improvement. Coworker appears as a logo-wall citation only, so the deployment is unattributed; the realistic use is internal — support, ops and engineering knowledge work across the brand portfolio — not embedded product AI.
why_they_need_memory: This is the classic roll-up memory problem. Eight acquired brands, each with its own codebase, product vocabulary, support queue, pricing and contracts, operated across five-plus countries and time zones (LA, London, Ahmedabad, Toronto, Sydney). Nobody holds the whole map. Answering "how does self-tape submission work in Spotlight versus Casting Networks," routing a studio escalation, or onboarding staff after two CEO transitions and repeated M&A integrations all require institutional context that no single system holds. A knowledge-graph layer spanning those tools is the wedge; a plain chatbot without cross-brand memory would be useless here.
confidence: high on existence, ownership, brands and scale (all first-party press releases plus LinkedIn); medium on the agent-usage rationale, which is inference — there is no case study, no AI in the product, and the Coworker citation is a logo only

name: SafetyWing (legal entity: Safety Nest, Inc.)

category: Insurtech / global health and benefits for remote work and digital nomads
stage: Venture-backed private. YC W18 seed confirmed; later round stage not confirmable from accessible sources.
funding: unknown. Confirmed: went through Y Combinator's W18 batch and raised a seed at that time (per SafetyWing's own timeline). No dollar figure should be quoted for this company without a fresh check.

yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Winter 2018 batch
founded_year: 2018 (YC W18). Founders: Sondre Rasch (CEO; previously a policy advisor to the Norwegian government on the social safety net, and a founder of Superside/YC W16), Sarah Sandnes (CTO), Hans Nyvold Kjellby (COO). Norwegian founding team, US-incorporated.
sells_to: Dual motion. Prosumer/direct-to-individual (digital nomads, freelancers and remote workers buying Nomad Insurance or Nomad Citizen with a card) plus B2B SMB and mid-market (remote-first companies buying Remote Health to cover employees and contractors worldwide), with a third embedded/partnership channel selling through platforms and marketplaces.
how_they_use_agents: The strongest and best-corroborated agent buyer of the three. Two hard signals: (1) SafetyWing is named in text on Coworker's own homepage customer list — not only in the logo marquee — alongside Scale AI, Harri, RapidSOS, Cortex, Harness, Truecaller and Huuuge Games; (2) SafetyWing's public team page lists a Chief AI Officer, Jarle Sandnes (an early backend/data engineer who joined full-time when the company entered YC), based in Prague. A C-level AI mandate at a ~150-person insurer is unusual and indicates a budgeted, top-down agent program rather than a departmental pilot. The operational surface that fits Coworker's "Organizational Memory" pitch is claims and member support: the team includes a Claims Experience Team Lead plus claims-experience specialists, billing specialists, compliance and technical-operations staff running a fully digital, 24/7 claims process across 175+ countries. No public case study or quote exists yet, so the exact workflows are unconfirmed.
why_they_need_memory: Claims and coverage decisions are memory-bound work: every answer depends on policy wording, country-specific coverage and provider rules across 175+ countries, regulatory and compliance constraints, and precedent from prior cases. That knowledge is too large to hold in one head and, in a fully async company with no office and staff in 60+ countries, there is no hallway to absorb it in. New support and claims hires have no colocated senior to ask. A memory layer that spans policy documents, the claims system, Slack and support history is the difference between an agent that invents a coverage answer — a real liability in insurance — and one that can safely act. Layer on the Chief AI Officer mandate and a distributed workforce with meaningful turnover, and SafetyWing is close to the archetype buyer for a "company brain."
confidence: high on existence, product, YC batch, founders, team profile and the Coworker relationship (SafetyWing is named in text on coworker.ai, not just a logo); low specifically on funding, which could not be verified from any accessible source

name: LoadShare Networks

LoadShare runs a shared, asset-light fleet of gig delivery riders that a single rider pool serves across four demand verticals simultaneously: ecommerce forward/reverse logistics (19,000+ PIN codes), quick commerce (sub-30-min dark-store delivery), food delivery, and two-wheeler passenger mobility. Marketing site claims 1M+ deliveries/day and 21,000+ active riders across 215+ cities; the About page gives more conservative FY26 figures of ~Rs 800 Cr revenue and ~550K deliveries/day with a 20,000+ rider network. Enterprise customers named on-site: Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto, Blinkit, Instamart, Flipkart, Amazon, Tata 1mg, Meesho, Uber, Rapido. Second business line: licensing its in-house logistics tech stack (dispatch engine, rider management, payments/settlement, tracking, analytics) to other operators — they claim the licensed platform moves another ~2M orders/day. Founded Jan 2017 in Bengaluru (Koramangala) by Raghuram Talluri (CEO, ex-Myntra/McKinsey), Pramod Nair (CTO, ex-FreeCharge/Snapdeal), Rakib Ahmed (Ops).
category: last-mile logistics / supply-chain infrastructure (traditional tech company, not AI-native)

yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not a YC company; VC-backed through the standard Indian venture route (Stellaris, Matrix, Tiger Global, BII, Beenext).
sells_to: B2B enterprise — India's largest consumer internet and commerce platforms (quick commerce, food delivery, marketplaces, pharma delivery, ride-hailing). Secondary two-sided audience: gig riders recruited as independent delivery partners. Also B2B tech licensing to other logistics operators.
how_they_use_agents: No LLM-agent claims anywhere on the site. Their /technology page describes classical ML/optimization inside the dispatch stack: demand forecasting by zone/vertical/time window, dynamic real-time dispatch across a cross-vertical rider pool, rider earnings optimization, fraud and acceptance-gaming anomaly detection, multi-stop route optimization, and SLA-compliance prediction. Stack is Go/Python backend services with real-time event processing and rider mobile apps. So: heavy ML in production, zero evidence of agentic/LLM workloads or of an agent that would need conversational memory.
why_they_need_memory: Weak/indirect fit, and the vendor link is thin. LoadShare appears only in Colrows' homepage 'Trusted by' logo marquee (assets/images/clients/loadshare.png) and is NOT among the five companies named in Colrows' 'Trusted by engineering teams at Pfizer, Cipla, BTS Group, Flobiz, and Brexa' sentence — no case study, no testimonial, no named person. The plausible use case is not agent memory at all but Colrows' actual product: a governed semantic layer over their warehouse so ops/commercial teams (and any internal text-to-SQL assistant) can ask questions across dispatch, rider payout, and SLA data without hand-written SQL. Ops-analytics buyer, not an agent-product buyer.

Autonomy is graduated: assist, then co-do, then propose automation. why_they_need_memory: By far the strongest fit of the three, and also the most likely to be a competitor rather than a customer. Wordware's stated product thesis is literally 'an AI assistant built for compounding context' that 'learns your taste, detects hidden patterns, augments your brain context' — persistent per-user memory of style, priorities and boundaries across email, docs and meetings is the entire moat, not a feature. A Honcho logo here most plausibly reflects either evaluation/experimentation, or usage during the V1 IDE era before the pivot, rather than production dependence today. Worth noting as a category signal though: the profile of company that ends up on these logo walls is 'small, well-funded, agent-native, building a personal assistant' — Wordware is the archetype.

how_they_use_agents: Agents ARE the product. Voice agents conduct autonomous patient phone calls at scale, backed by a proprietary "constellation architecture" — Polaris, a suite of ~22 LLMs (reported 4.2T parameters in v3.0, 5.0T+ in later versions) with specialized safety/support models supervising a primary conversational model. Integrated with 50+ EMR systems including Epic. 0.5-1% of live calls sampled for safety monitoring; agents validated across 775,000+ test calls with 7,700+ licensed U.S. clinicians. The Aug 2026 "Orchestrators" release moves from single-task agents to multi-agent workflows chasing clinical outcomes.
why_they_need_memory: Strongest and most legible need of the three. Their agents hold repeated longitudinal relationships with the same patient — a chronic-care or medication-adherence agent calls the same person weekly for months. Without persistent user-level memory the agent re-asks answered questions, loses stated preferences (best time to call, language, caregiver present, prior side effects, why the patient skipped a dose), and breaks the trust the whole clinical-safety pitch depends on. EMR data covers clinical facts but not conversational/relational context. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: PHI under HIPAA makes a third-party memory vendor a hard procurement path, and their proprietary-model, in-house posture suggests they build this internally — which makes the Honcho logo more likely a developer/experiment than a production contract.

name: Polymarket
what_it_does: Prediction market / event-derivatives exchange. Users buy and sell binary outcome shares on future events (elections, Fed rate decisions, sports, crypto, AI model rankings, world events); prices function as crowd-sourced probabilities. Selected by MeitY in April 2025 to build an indigenous foundation model under the IndiaAI Mission (with government-allocated GPU compute); partnered with UIDAI on AI voice interactions for Aadhaar. sells_to: Developers, overwhelmingly. Free/open-source distribution with an undefined enterprise motion. Their libraries are embedded by large companies (AWS, Shopify, Nvidia, GitHub are cited as users of the libs), but that is OSS adoption, not a sales relationship. Effectively prosumer/developer, not enterprise B2B.
how_they_use_agents: Genuinely agent-building, and recently so. Crush is a terminal-native agentic coding assistant ("Glamourous agentic coding for all") that plugs into the user's LLM of choice — announced July 30, 2025 and now their flagship app. Underneath it they built and open-sourced Fantasy ("Build AI agents with Go. Multiple providers, multiple models, one API") — a Go agent framework with tool-calling and a provider abstraction over OpenRouter, Azure, Bedrock, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints — and Catwalk, a registry of LLM inference providers and models. Mods gained MCP server support in July 2025; Crush gained Docker MCP integration in March 2026. So they ship an agent product, an agent framework, and agent infrastructure.
why_they_need_memory: Clear and specific. Crush is precisely the use case Honcho advertises under "Coding Agents: permanent first days — solved" — learning team conventions and architecture philosophy so generated code matches the user's style across sessions. Charm also ships Fantasy, an agent framework whose users would need a pluggable memory backend, making Charm a potential distribution channel for a memory vendor, not just an end user. CAVEAT: evidence is only a logo in Honcho's ticker with no quote or case study, and Charm's own OSS ethos plus its habit of building its own primitives (Fantasy, Catwalk, Skate — which is itself a key-value store) means they may well roll their own rather than buy.
sources: https://charm.land/ and https://charm.land/blog/ (products, Crush announcement, roadmap)
https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/charm-1814 (founders Christian Rocha, Toby Padilla; aka Charmbracelet)

name: OrbStack (Orbital Labs, LLC)
what_it_does: A native macOS app for running Docker containers, Kubernetes, and Linux VMs — positioned explicitly as a drop-in replacement for Docker Desktop. Written in Swift, optimized for Apple Silicon. Selling points are all performance and resource efficiency: <0.1% background CPU on Apple Silicon, <10 MB initial disk, fast VirtioFS file sharing, Rosetta x86 emulation, zero-config HTTPS and local domain names for containers, 16 Linux distros, USB passthrough, SSH agent forwarding, remote VS Code editing, and "isolated sandboxes for untrusted code." Headline benchmark on the homepage: provisioning a dev environment in 17 min vs Docker Desktop's 45 min (as of Aug 2023). Pricing: $0 free tier for personal/non-commercial use; Pro at $8/user/month ($96/yr); Enterprise custom with SAML SSO and invoice/PO billing.
category: Developer infrastructure / local dev tooling — container and VM runtime for macOS. NOT an AI company.
stage: Bootstrapped (apparent)
funding: unknown — and most likely none. I found no funding round, investor, or press release for OrbStack or Orbital Labs, LLC in any source. A Crunchbase profile exists but surfaced no funding data. Note the LLC (not Inc./C-corp) structure, which is atypical for a VC-backed startup. Treat as bootstrapped/revenue-funded, but this is inference, not a confirmed fact — do not report a number.
headcount_estimate: unknown — very likely 1-5. No LinkedIn company page exists at /orbstack or /orbital-labs. Every blog post is authored by Danny Lin. The "We're hiring!" link in the site footer points to the founder's personal Twitter status (twitter.com/kdrag0n/status/1750965469518176438, Jan 2024) rather than a careers page or job board, which is a strong signal of a one- or two-person company.
yc_or_accelerator: None found.
founded_year: ~2022 (development/beta); OrbStack 1.0 shipped Sep 21, 2023. Founded by Danny Lin (GitHub: kdrag0n, bio "stacking orbs @OrbStack"), previously known for Android systems work.
sells_to: Developers and small teams — bottom-up, self-serve, seat-based at $8/user/month, with an Enterprise tier bolted on for SSO and PO billing. Prosumer/developer with a light B2B SMB motion.
how_they_use_agents: None that I could find. There is zero mention of AI, LLMs, or agents anywhere on the homepage, pricing page, docs site, or blog (latest post Aug 2024). The only adjacency is architectural rather than marketed: OrbStack advertises "isolated sandboxes for untrusted code" and fast container provisioning, which is exactly the substrate people use to run coding agents locally — but OrbStack does not position itself that way and ships no agent of its own.
why_they_need_memory: No credible product-level need. This is the weakest of the three by a wide margin and I would flag it as a likely false positive for the category. OrbStack has no agent product, no LLM surface, and no user-state problem that a memory layer solves. The Honcho logo is almost certainly a single developer at OrbStack trying the tool on a side project — consistent with the parent finding that this is a developer-level claim in a "Used by developers at" ticker with no quote or case study. ADDITIONAL CAVEAT: when I loaded honcho.dev directly, the "Used by developers at" region rendered empty (no img/svg/background-image nodes in the DOM), so I could not independently re-verify which logos actually appear there.
sources: https://orbstack.dev (product, positioning, testimonials, footer '© 2026 Orbital Labs, LLC', 'We're hiring!' link to founder's personal Twitter)
https://orbstack.dev/pricing (free / $8 per user per month Pro / Enterprise)
https://docs.orbstack.dev/ (docs; Orbital Labs, LLC copyright; no AI content)
https://orbstack.dev/blog (all posts authored by Danny Lin; latest Aug 22, 2024)

name: Qualcomm (Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.)
what_it_does: Fabless semiconductor and wireless-technology giant. Designs Snapdragon SoCs (CPU/GPU/NPU/modem) for smartphones, PCs, XR, wearables and automotive; Dragonwing for industrial/IoT edge; Dragonfly for data-center AI inference. Two revenue engines: QCT, the chip business (~80% of revenue), and QTL, the CDMA/3G/4G/5G patent-licensing business (~19%). Founded July 1, 1985 in San Diego by Irwin Jacobs, Andrew Viterbi, Franklin Antonio and four others. FY2025 revenue $44.28B, operating income $12.36B, ~$180B market cap (NASDAQ: QCOM). Recent AI-driven M&A: Alphawave IP ($2.4B, June 2025), Arduino (Oct 2025), Modular ($3.9B, 2026).
category: semiconductors / edge AI silicon — NOT an agent-memory buyer; this is a platform/silicon partnership
stage: Public company (NASDAQ: QCOM), IPO December 1991
funding: N/A — public since 1991. FY2025 revenue $44.28B, net income $5.54B, market cap ~$180B
headcount_estimate: ~52,000 (2025); 170 offices in 30+ countries
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2B enterprise — device OEMs, automakers, carriers, industrial/IoT customers; plus developers via Qualcomm AI Hub
how_they_use_agents: Qualcomm sells the substrate agents run on, rather than running agents as its own product. Qualcomm AI Hub offers hundreds of pre-optimized ML models, SLMs and LLMs for on-device deployment, with tooling (AIMET quantization, ONNX Runtime, ExecuTorch, LiteRT) to profile/test/deploy across 60+ cloud-hosted device targets. Marketing explicitly foregrounds 'agentic AI': agentic IT ticket automation, multi-device orchestration, voice interfaces, web-research workflows. Copilot+ PCs on Snapdragon X-series, and the Snapdragon X2 Elite, are positioned as agentic-AI hosts. The 2026 Modular acquisition ($3.9B) buys edge-to-cloud AI infrastructure. Qualcomm sized edge gen-AI at a $900B TAM by 2030.
why_they_need_memory: They do not buy agent memory — they want it as a workload. The Memories.ai relationship is inverted relative to a customer relationship: Memories.ai announced it will 'run natively on Qualcomm processors starting in 2026,' i.e. Memories.ai is porting to Qualcomm silicon, and Qualcomm's Vinesh Sukumar (VP Product Management, Head of Gen AI/ML) gave a supporting quote about combining Qualcomm edge computing with the Large Visual Memory Model. Confirmed independently: memories.ai's 'Project LUCI' post (June 1, 2026) names the Qualcomm X2 Elite as the desktop compute platform and Snapdragon AR Glasses as the wearable capture device, running a 3B-parameter embedding model 100% on-device via Windows ML. Qualcomm's strategic interest is that persistent on-device visual memory is a heavy, sticky NPU workload that justifies premium silicon and differentiates edge inference against cloud. Treat Qualcomm as an ecosystem enabler / co-marketing partner, not as a buyer of the category.

name: Ring (Amazon)
what_it_does: Consumer and small-business home-security hardware plus subscription software, owned by Amazon. Product lines: video doorbells (wired, battery, 4K Pro), outdoor cameras (Floodlight Cam Plus, Spotlight Cam 2K, Outdoor Cam Plus), indoor cameras (Pan-Tilt), alarm kits and contact sensors, chimes and accessories, and professional installation from $129.99. Revenue mix is hardware plus Ring Protect subscription plans (up to 180-day video history, AI Video Descriptions, Familiar Faces, 24/7 professional monitoring). Also operates the Neighbors community-safety app. Founded November 15, 2013 by Jamie Siminoff as 'Doorbot,' renamed Ring September 26, 2014; acquired by Amazon April 12, 2018 for roughly $839M–$1.15B depending on source. HQ Santa Monica, California.
category: consumer IoT / smart home security — NOT a customer; Ring is the app-store platform Memories.ai distributes on
stage: Wholly-owned Amazon subsidiary since April 2018 (previously VC-backed)
funding: Acquired by Amazon April 12, 2018 for ~$839M (some sources say ~$1.15B). Pre-acquisition VC rounds existed but I could not verify totals this session — treat as unknown.
headcount_estimate: ~1,300 as of 2018; current headcount unknown — Amazon does not break Ring out separately
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: Consumer / prosumer households, plus B2B SMB via Ring for Business; and now third-party developers via the Ring Appstore
how_they_use_agents: Ring ships first-party AI directly in the product: 'Video Descriptions' generate text explanations of what triggered a motion alert; 'Familiar Faces' (launched Sept 2025) does opt-in face recognition to suppress noise notifications; 'Search Party' (Oct 2025) uses object recognition across the Neighbors network to find lost pets; 'Active Warnings' produce automatic spoken alerts. Strategically more important: Ring has opened a developer platform — the Ring Appstore, live at ring.com/appstore in limited availability, framed as turning 'Ring data into actionable intelligence,' with launch categories for business intelligence and operations, home analytics, elderly care monitoring, and pet wellness. That is Ring exposing its camera fleet as a substrate for third-party AI apps.
why_they_need_memory: IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE PREMISE: Ring is not buying agent memory from Memories.ai — the direction is the reverse. Memories.ai's own post states 'Memories.ai is now available in the Ring Appstore, bringing our visual memory technology to Ring cameras used in homes and businesses around the world' (authored by Shawn Shen, Memories.ai co-founder/CEO). There are no quotes from any Ring or Amazon employee in that post, and memories.ai is not named on the public Ring Appstore page. Memories.ai's homepage stat '100M+ cameras powered by partner integrations' is derived from Ring's installed base, not from a Ring purchase order. TechCrunch coverage of the Ring app-store launch listed memories.ai as one launch app, a risk/security detection app for fires, smoke, falls and leaks. Ring does have the exact problem the category solves — continuous video that must become searchable, persistent, pattern-aware memory rather than raw clips — but it builds that in-house (Video Descriptions, Familiar Faces) and lets third parties fill gaps through the app store. As a go-to-market signal, Ring is a distribution channel, not an ICP.

name: Vivo (vivo Mobile Communication Co., Ltd.)
what_it_does: Chinese smartphone OEM, consistently a top-5 global handset maker with roughly 10% worldwide share and 400M+ users across 60+ countries. Founded May 22, 2009 by Shen Wei and Duan Yongping; headquartered in Dongguan, Guangdong (with major Shenzhen operations). Formerly under BBK Electronics (2009–2023); Shen Wei became owner in 2023. Flagship lines X300 Ultra / X300 Pro (ZEISS co-engineered imaging), V-series, Y-series budget devices, plus the iQOO performance sub-brand. Software: OriginOS in mainland China, Funtouch OS internationally, plus BlueOS, an open-source distributed OS announced November 2023, and the Jovi AI assistant. Roughly 10 R&D centers including Shenzhen, Beijing and San Diego. Private and founder-owned — no venture funding.
category: consumer smartphone OEM / device manufacturer — relationship to the agent-memory vendor is unverified and weakly evidenced
stage: Private, founder-owned (no external venture funding); formerly a BBK Electronics affiliate
funding: unknown — privately held and never venture-funded; no disclosed raise. Do not attribute a funding number to this company.
headcount_estimate: ~40,000 (2022 figure); current headcount unknown
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: Consumer (B2C) — smartphone buyers in China, India, Southeast Asia and other emerging markets; secondarily developers via BlueOS
how_they_use_agents: Vivo's agent surface is on-device assistant tech shipped inside its own handsets: the Jovi AI assistant, the BlueLM family of in-house large models, and BlueOS as a distributed OS layer intended to carry AI across phone, wearable and IoT. Note that vivo's own English-language homepage and About page foreground ZEISS imaging and OriginOS smoothness, not AI agents — I could not confirm any specific agent-memory feature from vivo's own English site this session. Like other Chinese OEMs, vivo is a large Qualcomm Snapdragon customer, which is the most plausible mechanical link to the Memories.ai/Qualcomm edge-AI story.
why_they_need_memory: LOWEST-CONFIDENCE OF THE THREE. Vivo appears in exactly one prose sentence on memories.ai/about — 'Three years later we are deployed across physical AI, media, security, and consumer devices, with partners that include NVIDIA, Lenovo, Samsung, Vivo, Ring, and Comcast' — with no logo, no case study, no quote and no named contact. I independently confirmed the memories.ai homepage logo wall contains Microsoft, NVIDIA, Samsung, Lenovo, Qualcomm and Ring, and does NOT contain Vivo, so this name exists only in that one About sentence. The word 'partners' sits inside a 'we are deployed across...' clause, so it is genuinely unclear whether vivo is a paying customer, a device OEM integration target, or an aspirational name-drop. A secondary ambiguity: 'Vivo' is also the consumer brand of Telefônica Brasil; the surrounding company list (Samsung, Lenovo, consumer devices) makes the smartphone OEM far more likely, but the vendor never disambiguates. The generic thesis for why a handset OEM would want visual memory — on-device photo/video recall, an assistant that remembers what the camera saw, differentiating a flagship against Apple and Samsung — is plausible but is my inference, not anything either company has stated. The company is unquestionably real; the buyer relationship is not established.

name: Zillow Group
what_it_does: The largest US residential real-estate marketplace. Zillow operates a consumer search platform (web + the most-visited US real estate app) covering a database of ~173M homes with ~239M average monthly unique users in Q2 2026, plus the Zestimate automated valuation model. Revenue comes from selling leads, software and advertising to real-estate professionals (Premier Agent), rentals marketplace listings for landlords/property managers, Zillow Home Loans (mortgage origination), and Zillow Showcase listing products. Brand portfolio includes Zillow, Trulia, StreetEasy, HotPads, Zillow Rentals and Zillow Home Loans. Notably, it is NOT an AI vendor — it is a large distributed tech enterprise that bought Glean as an internal knowledge/agent platform.
category: Real estate marketplace / proptech (buyer of enterprise AI search + agent platform, not a vendor of one)
stage: Public. Nasdaq: Z (Class C) and ZG (Class A); IPO July 2011; Russell 1000 component.
funding: Not applicable as a startup — public company. Venture-backed before its 2011 IPO (Benchmark and TCV among early investors); exact pre-IPO totals not verified in this research. Financials: FY2024 revenue $2.24B; Q2 2026 revenue $772M (company IR page).
headcount_estimate: ~7,200 (Zillow investor relations, Q2 2026). Corroborating points: 6,856 employees reported for 2024; the Glean case study cites '7,000 employees.' LinkedIn was not fetchable in this session.
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: Hybrid: B2C marketplace for home buyers/sellers/renters, monetized B2B SMB — individual real estate agents, brokerages, loan officers, landlords and property managers buy leads, advertising and software. Not an enterprise-sales motion.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers. (1) INTERNAL — this is what Glean sells: employees have built 3,400+ agents on Glean (500 in the first six weeks), on top of 30+ connected data sources and 138M indexed documents, with 80% adoption across ~7,000 employees and a claimed 1.5+ hours/week saved per user. Named agent workloads: Slack-based HR support agents wired to Databricks Genie; an 'Ask Z' agent that democratizes UX research findings; platform-support Q&A agents living in Slack channels; self-review and peer-feedback agents that drove a 7% increase in performance-review participation; an incident-timeline documentation agent for postmortems. Engineering pulls the same index into coding tools via Glean MCP with Cursor and Claude Code. Anne Wingate (Sr PM, Enterprise Technology) frames adoption as peer-driven: employees learn AI by sharing and experimenting rather than by mandate. (2) PRODUCT — AI-powered natural-language home search, AI virtual tours and interactive 3D floor plans, the Zestimate valuation model, and a First Street climate-risk score. The Glean deployment is internal-productivity, not embedded in the consumer product.
why_they_need_memory: Classic distributed-enterprise knowledge-fragmentation case. Zillow went remote-first after the pandemic; institutional knowledge scattered across 30+ SaaS systems and 138M documents with no single retrieval surface. Toby Roberts (SVP Engineering) explicitly frames the value as 'uniting a distributed workforce' and going 'beyond just enterprise search' to leverage all their data through current AI models. An engineer's line is the sharpest statement of the memory thesis: Glean 'is like the teammate that's been at the company for many years.' The buying trigger is org memory for onboarding, incident history, UX research reuse and HR/platform self-service — plus a self-serve agent-builder so 7,000 non-engineers can encode their own workflows without central IT building each one.

name: TIME (Time USA, LLC)
what_it_does: One of the best-known US news brands — the TIME weekly/biweekly newsmagazine founded in 1923, plus time.com, TIME100 and TIME100 AI franchises, TIME Studios (film/TV), TIME for Kids, conferences/events, and branded-content and licensing businesses. Revenue is subscriptions plus advertising, sponsorship and events sold by a B2B ad-sales team. Its distinguishing asset for this analysis is a 100+ year proprietary editorial archive.
category: Media / news publishing (mid-size private media company; buyer of enterprise AI search, not a vendor)
stage: Private. Acquired by Marc and Lynne Benioff from Meredith Corporation in October 2018 for $190M; operated as Time USA, LLC. NOT venture-funded.
funding: Not venture-funded. Ownership transaction: $190M acquisition by the Benioffs (Oct 2018), preceded by Meredith's Nov 2017 purchase of Time Inc. CAVEAT: I recall press reporting of a subsequent ownership change involving Greek media group Antenna Group, but I could NOT verify it with the tools available in this session — treat as unconfirmed and re-check before using.
headcount_estimate: unknown — could not verify. LinkedIn was not fetchable and no headcount appears on time.com or in the Glean case study. TIME is a mid-size media organization (order of hundreds, not thousands), but I am not putting a number on it without a source.
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: Hybrid: B2C subscriptions to readers, and B2B enterprise advertising/sponsorship/branded-content sold to brands and agencies. The Glean use case is aimed at both the internal sales org and the newsroom.
how_they_use_agents: Internal knowledge retrieval, not a product feature. TIME indexed 100+ years of historical articles into Glean and connected core systems including Google Workspace and Salesforce. Two use cases: (1) editorial research — reporters searching the century-deep archive to develop stories faster; (2) sales enablement — the ad-sales team pulling historical data and past coverage to prep pitches and shorten deal cycles. Deployment speed is the headline stat: live in 2-3 weeks, with full integration into core systems taking about five months. CIO Sharon Milz: 'We're up and running in three weeks. I don't think I've ever been able to integrate something quicker and faster than that.' Separately (not part of the Glean deployment), TIME runs the TIME100 AI editorial franchise and a dedicated AI news vertical — brand-level AI presence, not AI infrastructure.
why_they_need_memory: The purest 'company brain' case of the three: TIME's core commercial asset IS its archive, and it was effectively unsearchable — a century of articles plus scattered historical sales and business records. The buyer motivation is unlocking a proprietary corpus that no general model has good access to, for two revenue-adjacent workflows (faster stories, faster pitches). Note the buying profile: a small IT org with no capacity to build retrieval infrastructure, which is why three-week time-to-value was the quoted proof point rather than agent volume or governance. This is the 'lean team, deep archive' segment of the category.

name: Ericsson
what_it_does: Swedish multinational telecom network infrastructure and software company — one of the two or three dominant global suppliers of mobile network equipment. Sells 4G/5G radio access networks, cloud RAN, IP transport, core networks, OSS/BSS, enterprise wireless, and managed services/consulting to telecom operators in ~180 countries. Business areas: Networks, Cloud Software and Services, Managed Services, and Enterprise. Reports 27,739 R&D staff. Founded 1876 in Stockholm; HQ in Kista.
category: Telecom network infrastructure and software (very large B2B enterprise; buyer of enterprise AI search + agent platform)
stage: Public. Nasdaq Stockholm (ERIC A, ERIC B) and Nasdaq US (ERIC). 150-year-old incumbent.
funding: Not applicable — long-public incumbent, no venture funding. FY2025 revenue SEK 236.681B (~$22-25B depending on FX).
headcount_estimate: ~89,000 (2025). Company site separately reports 27,739 R&D experts. LinkedIn was not fetchable in this session.
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: B2B enterprise at the largest scale — telecom carriers/CSPs, governments, and large enterprises, across ~180 countries. Long, regulated, multi-year procurement cycles.
how_they_use_agents: Two layers again. (1) INTERNAL, via Glean: employees have created roughly 3,000 agents covering network operations, customer support, service-delivery optimization, HR support and engineering troubleshooting. The distinguishing feature is the enablement and governance program around it — an 'AI driver's license' program plus critical-skills paths that trained 20,000+ employees, and a TIERED agent-governance model where individual contributors may build and run personal agents freely, while departmental or enterprise-scope agents require moderation and approval through the owning business unit. Global CDO Joel Nygards named the two blocking problems as raising AI competency across tens of thousands of heterogeneous employees, and putting governance in place that permits enterprise data access without slowing innovation. They are now shifting measurement from task-level time savings to whole-workflow outcomes. (2) PRODUCT, unrelated to Glean: Ericsson sells agentic AI in its own network stack — AI agents replacing rule-based algorithms across baseband, RAN Compute and cloud/ops layers for dynamic resource allocation, traffic prediction and anomaly detection; claimed results include 10% spectrum-efficiency gain from AI-native link adaptation, 25% better 5G coverage, and 33% radio energy savings; and it positions 6G as AI-native from day one.
why_they_need_memory: Scale, heterogeneity and compliance. ~89,000 employees across ~180 countries means the retrieval problem is multilingual by necessity, and regional data-residency and data-protection rules make an ungoverned index a non-starter — the case study lists data protection, regional compliance, multilingual support and use-case flexibility as the hard platform requirements. Equally important is the governance surface: at this scale the risk is not too few agents but ungoverned proliferation, so the tiered personal-vs-departmental-vs-enterprise approval model is the actual product requirement. This is the segment that buys 'company brain' for permission-aware institutional memory plus an agent control plane, not for search quality alone.

name: Caleb Picker Consulting
what_it_does: Could not confirm this exists as a company. The PERSON is real and verifiable: Caleb J. Picker (GitHub @calebjpicker) — MA in Cognitive Psychology, partial PhD in Quantitative Psychology, then ~4 years as a data analyst with the stated career goal of becoming a data scientist. His public repos are R/Quarto/Python data-science work (BoardGameGeek data analysis, an applicant-tracking-system notebook, a CV and blog built in Quarto, a tabletop-gaming project). His conference decks (Picker & Parks, WPA 2015; UNLV Research Forum 2013) are academic psychology research. He is verifiably a Basic Memory user: he has starred basicmachines-co/basic-memory and gannonh/memento-mcp (another agent-memory MCP project), and has filed six substantive issues on basic-memory between 2025-06 and 2026-08. But the BUSINESS ENTITY 'Caleb Picker Consulting' has no confirmable footprint: calebpicker.com and calebpickerconsulting.com both return 'No match' in WHOIS (they are not registered at all), no website is linked by the vendor, and web search surfaces nothing. A separate site, pickerconsulting.com, exists — a nationwide remote bookkeeping/payroll/financial-consulting practice for 1–20-employee small businesses, domain created 2026-03-11 via Squarespace with registrant redacted — but it never names Caleb anywhere on the page and the name does not match. I flag it as an unverified lead, not a match. Treat this entry as an individual power user who described himself with a personal-brand consulting label, not as a confirmed company customer.
category: Unconfirmed solo consultancy; the individual profiles as data science / quantitative analytics (possibly small-business financial consulting if the pickerconsulting.com lead is real, which I could not verify)
stage: unknown
funding: unknown
headcount_estimate: unknown (if real, almost certainly 1 — a solo practice)
yc_or_accelerator: none found
founded_year: unknown
sells_to: unknown (if the pickerconsulting.com lead were confirmed, B2B SMB — but unverified)
how_they_use_agents: Uses Basic Memory as persistent memory for Claude and Claude Code — the testimonial is about chatbot experience ('the missing wow factor in AI chatbots'), i.e. personal assistant use, not an agent embedded in a product. His GitHub issues show unusually deep hands-on use of the retrieval layer: he asked for a 'retrieval inspector / chunk viewer' exposing chunking, vector retrieval, FTS, hybrid fusion, thresholding and reranker scores; for mutation event envelopes from the write path enabling live tail, revert and per-agent trust; for a default_search_type config; and for section/observation anchor wikilinks. He also filed bugs that full-text search indexes only the first ~5,600 chars of a note and that assistant-authored suggestions render without accept/reject controls. That issue set implies he runs multiple agents writing into a shared memory store and wants provenance and trust controls over what they write.
why_they_need_memory: Individual knowledge-worker continuity across chat sessions rather than an enterprise or product need. His own framing is that Basic Memory is what makes Claude/Claude Code usable at all. The deeper signal in his issues is multi-agent write provenance — he wants to see which agent wrote what, revert it, and assign per-agent trust — which is a real requirement but one coming from a sophisticated solo practitioner, not a buying organization.

name: @groksrc (Drew Cain) — NOT a customer; he is a co-founder of the vendor
what_it_does: This is not a customer and not a company. @groksrc is Drew Cain, a software engineer and founder in Austin, TX — and his own website states plainly: 'I'm building Basic Memory — a local-first AI memory platform,' with a career timeline entry reading 'Now — Co-Founder, Basic Memory.' Three independent confirmations: (1) he is one of only two public members of the basicmachines-co GitHub org (the other is phernandez, the project lead); (2) he is the #2 contributor to basicmachines-co/basic-memory with 127 commits versus phernandez's 1,192, committing continuously from at least 2025-10 through 2026-09-06; (3) groksrc.com lists Basic Memory first under 'What I'm Building' with the tag 'Co-founder. Open source.' So the README testimonial attributed to '@groksrc, Developer' is a vendor-authored quote, not a third-party customer reference. This materially changes how the Basic Memory testimonial wall should be read: of the small set of named references, at least one is the vendor's own co-founder, presented only as 'Developer.' Separately, Drew's actual day job is Principal Engineer at Olea Edge Analytics (edge computing/analytics for water utilities), and he sells unbranded solo consulting from his site — AI/MCP integration, infrastructure and DevOps, fractional CTO, and small-business AI automation. He also builds Hexnut, an AI phone receptionist for home-services trades (plumbers, HVAC) that answers 24/7, qualifies leads and books appointments. Prior roles: SVP of Technology at vCreative (2022), Senior Engineer to Senior DevOps at Simpli.fi (2015–21, adtech at billions of requests), and earlier Six Flags, ClickMotive, D.R. Horton, Improving.
category: AI memory / MCP infrastructure vendor (this is the supply side, not the demand side); secondarily solo AI consulting and an AI voice-agent product for home services
stage: Basic Machines / Basic Memory appears bootstrapped and open-source-led — no funding round found. The commercial product is Basic Memory Cloud at $15/seat/month with credit-based pricing for agent fleets; the OSS repo has ~3,870 stars, 275 forks, AGPL-3.0, created 2024-12-02.
funding: unknown (no round found for Basic Machines; no funding disclosed on basicmemory.com or in any source I could reach)

name: Booking.com
what_it_does: The world's largest online travel agency and accommodation marketplace, founded in Amsterdam in 1996 and now the flagship brand of Booking Holdings (Nasdaq: BKNG). It aggregates and sells accommodation, flights, car rentals, taxis, attractions and vacation packages. Scale per its own about page: more than 28 million reported accommodation listings including over 6.6 million homes, apartments and unique stays; over 70 million verified guest reviews; hundreds of thousands of transactions daily; 198 offices in over 70 countries. It is a two-sided marketplace — consumers on the demand side, accommodation and travel suppliers ('partners') on the supply side. This is the only genuine enterprise customer in this batch, and it is the archetype of the enterprise 'company brain' buyer: tens of thousands of employees, hundreds of internal SaaS systems, strict GDPR obligations, and a stale-information problem that search alone did not solve.
category: Online travel agency / consumer travel marketplace — a large non-AI-native enterprise buying an internal AI work assistant and agent platform
stage: Public company. Booking.com is a wholly owned brand of Booking Holdings Inc. (Nasdaq: BKNG), headquartered in Norwalk, Connecticut, with Booking.com itself based in Amsterdam.
funding: Not venture funded — publicly traded. Booking Holdings reported revenue of US$26.9B and net income of US$5.40B for 2025.
headcount_estimate: Booking Holdings: 24,300 employees as of 2025 (all brands). Glean was deployed to 14,000 Booking.com employees specifically, per Glean's own case study — that 14,000 figure is the deployed seat count, not necessarily total Booking.com headcount.
yc_or_accelerator: none — founded 1996, long predates the accelerator era
sells_to: Primarily B2C — travelers booking accommodation and travel. Also B2B on the supply side: accommodation partners, property managers and travel suppliers who list inventory. Not a developer-facing company.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers. INTERNALLY (this is the Glean purchase): Glean was rolled out to 14,000 employees as Booking.com's first enterprise-wide AI platform, spanning Glean Assistant and Glean Agents. Named use cases from the case study: a 'Research Craft Insights Bot' agent giving curated access to customer insights, with planned expansion to consolidate insights across multiple sources and index over 500,000 monthly survey responses; promotional video script creation for partner content, which cut production time from 8 weeks to 2 weeks while raising output from 2 to 5 videos per month; and IT ticket resolution via natural-language queries, eliminating up to 10 minutes of searching per ticket. The quoted buyer-side voice is Tadeu Faedrich, Senior Engineer Manager, whose framing is cultural adoption — getting the organization comfortable with AI — plus the line Glean features on the story: Glean 'helps you get work done, rather than just find information.' EXTERNALLY, in the product: Booking.com began testing a ChatGPT-based AI Trip Planner in summer 2023 with a limited US userbase, to help travelers choose a destination, plan a route, or ask questions. Note that the external trip-planning agents are a separate initiative from the Glean deployment — the Glean purchase is an internal-productivity and enterprise-knowledge buy, not a customer-facing agent buy.
why_they_need_memory: Classic enterprise 'company brain' drivers, stated in the case study: inefficient information access and stale data spread across a large number of workplace applications, under strict GDPR security requirements. At 14,000 seats and 198 offices in 70+ countries, institutional knowledge is fragmented across tools and geographies, and the failure mode is employees re-deriving answers that already exist somewhere. The agent-memory need is organizational context — grounding assistants and agents in company-specific knowledge (customer research, IT runbooks, brand and partner content) so an agent can execute work rather than return links. The 500,000-survey-responses-per-month indexing plan is the clearest memory-scale signal: they want a durable, queryable corpus of customer voice that agents can reason over, not a one-off search index.

founded_year: Unclear — approximately 2018-2019 as the Storable brand, formed by combining several self-storage software and marketplace businesses. Its oldest component product, SiteLink, dates to 1996. I could not confirm an official founding year on the company site; treat this as low-confidence.
sells_to: B2B, spanning SMB to enterprise. Buyers range from single-facility owner-operators (Storable Easy) to large multi-facility REIT-scale portfolios (Storable Edge). Predominantly non-technical operators, not developers.
how_they_use_agents: Both sides, and this is the most agent-heavy of the three. IN PRODUCT: an Agent Assist chatbot that converts website traffic into tenants, AI-driven collections and delinquency workflows, sentiment analysis and decision support, and AI positioned as platform-wide automation that 'executes real work inside existing workflows.' INTERNALLY (the Glean deployment): Storable uses Glean as an enterprise context layer unifying Jira, Salesforce, Confluence, Google Drive, Gong and Slack, and has built a real agent portfolio on top — a CSM Account Audit Agent (3-4 hours down to 10 minutes, 96% faster), a Self-Storage Implementation Agent for onboarding prep (90% less prep time, pulling from Gong, Salesforce and email), a company-wide Wrap-Up Agent compiling daily activity and to-dos from Gmail and Slack, and a Governed Salesforce Agent enabling role-based Salesforce writes with controlled access. Engineering wires Glean MCP into Claude Code for debugging. Reported outcomes: ~125,000 hours saved/month, ~60,000 Assistant interactions/month, 90%+ adoption, 99% employee satisfaction.
why_they_need_memory: The clearest illustration of the category's actual buying trigger. Storable is a rollup — a company assembled from multiple acquired products — so its institutional knowledge is structurally fragmented across six-plus SaaS systems that were never designed to talk to each other. Their agents are cross-system by nature: an account audit agent has to reconcile Salesforce records against Gong calls against Jira tickets, and an implementation agent has to reconstruct what was promised on a sales call months earlier. That requires durable, permissions-aware context spanning tools, which is precisely the 'company brain' pitch. The Governed Salesforce Agent also shows the second driver: once agents start writing rather than just reading, role-based guardrails become the purchase requirement, echoed in their quote about 'the right guardrails.'

how_they_use_agents: Overwhelmingly INTERNAL. LegalZoom replaced an outdated intranet with Glean as its enterprise search layer and assistant platform, then built agents on top: a People Team Agent living in Slack that handles T&E, stock administration and HR questions (thousands of runs from hundreds of users within months, consolidating fragmented tier-one support), and a Performance Review Agent that compiles an employee's annual activity and drafts a self-review — reportedly their most-used agent. Also slide-deck generation, MCP connections and coding workflows. Because Glean is native and the data is already indexed and loaded, the value is immediate.' That is a direct argument that pre-indexed persistent context beats stuffing a context window — the exact wedge agent-memory vendors sell. The operational driver underneath is HR/IT support deflection at ~1,200 employees with a dead intranet: knowledge existed but was unreachable, so it generated tickets. A company trading at a fraction of its IPO price also has a sharp cost-reduction incentive behind every hour saved.

Their /ai-strategy page sells a "GTM AI Charter" that "identifies where AI belongs across pipeline, process, data, and execution," mapped to their four phases: AI distills customer interviews and call data to surface revenue-loss patterns (Stabilization), standardizes documentation and playbooks (Foundation), scores calls and enriches account data (Repeatability), prioritizes and predicts (Scalability). Dale's operator page describes "AI-augmented execution patterns that compound revenue without bloating headcount," and he publicly claims he builds the AI himself rather than just having opinions about it. Their /how-to-ai guide is essentially a memory manifesto: it tells leaders to stop using one-off chats because "the model has zero context," and instead build persistent AI workspaces loaded once with ICP, positioning, metrics, sales process, decks, playbooks, call notes and board updates. Explicit stance is "AI adoption follows discipline, not hype" and "we fix the system before we scale it" — no autonomous agent product, no AI SDR army.
why_they_need_memory: Their unit of work is the stakeholder interview. Dale's Papr testimonial says client engagements start with "dozens of stakeholder interviews — each one full of context that needs to be categorized, organized, and analyzed" and that the sorting was entirely manual. That is a classic unstructured-corpus-to-insight problem: many transcripts per engagement, many engagements in parallel, patterns that only appear across interviews, and a 4-week sprint clock that makes manual synthesis the binding constraint on margin. A 2-10 person firm cannot add analysts, so the memory/knowledge layer is the leverage. Note the product fit: they bought Papr Work (the app/workspace surface), not the memory API — they are a no-code buyer who wants an ingest-organize-surface system, not a retrieval SDK. Their own /how-to-ai advice (persistent project context beats one-off prompts) is the buying thesis stated in their own words.
