In-product, they ship an AI marketing/loyalty layer to merchants: "AI agents that write campaigns, optimize timing, and learn what messaging drives your specific customers to visit"; "Our AI agents create personalized offers that drive 41x ROI"; "AI agents working 24/7 to engage customers with personalized offers," pitched as "Your Dedicated AI Marketing Team" and "Your 24/7 Marketing Team." The system analyzes purchase history, visit frequency, favorite drinks and time of day to generate personalized offers, writes push notifications and emails, optimizes send times, and cross-learns across 500+ shops so what works at one shop improves recommendations for all — they call this "collective intelligence" / "shared intelligence." Second, every page of the site runs an "AI agent" support chat with a human fallback. Internally, per Augusto Schiavi's Papr testimonial, agents are used "across the business" beyond marketing. Notably, the public marketing site never mentions Papr, memory, or a context layer — the AI story is told entirely as merchant-facing outcomes.
why_they_need_memory: This is the single most on-thesis reference in the set — the only Papr customer quote that is about the memory/context product rather than the Papr Work app. Schiavi frames it precisely: "the challenge was whether it could retrieve the right context from the right source at the right time. Papr gives us a smarter context layer, helping our agents work with better information while reducing the cost and friction of using AI across the business." Naive RAG over that fails on source selection, and stuffing context is expensive — hence the explicit cost-and-friction framing. A small engineering team (a principal engineer who built the team from scratch, a handful of engineers) with SMB-margin economics cannot build and maintain a bespoke retrieval/memory stack, so they buy one. Buyer persona is the engineer, entry via the API, and the purchase driver is inference cost plus retrieval precision — not knowledge-worker productivity.

name: Pivotvia (Pivotvia LLC)
what_it_does: A one-person fractional-CRO and growth-advisory practice run by Corey Badcock, based in Halifax, Nova Scotia. Target customer is established / growth-stage tech SMBs whose growth has stalled; his framing concept is "momentum debt" — what happens when product, pricing and go-to-market drift out of sync. Three productized offers with public pricing: a 7-Day Growth Sprint diagnostic at $3,000 (core-constraint diagnosis, top 3 growth levers, 30-day plan, GTM reality-check report; creditable toward a fractional engagement); Fractional CRO embedded leadership starting at $10,000/month with a 3-month minimum (uses the Functional Marketing framework); and Advisor / decision support starting at $3,000/month with a 3-month minimum. Lead magnets are a free Profit & Growth Assessment and a pricing calculator (Typeform + Calendly + a Zyro/Hostinger site — a lightweight solo stack). Positioning line: "No hacks. No hype. Just clarity and operating rigor." Background: former Amazon operator (helped lead Kindle through a reinvention) and BlackBerry.
category: Solo fractional-CRO / growth consultancy for growth-stage tech SMBs
stage: Bootstrapped solo practice (single-member LLC). Very new — the pivotvia.com domain was registered 2025-09-14, so the business is roughly a year old as of Sept 2026.
funding: None — bootstrapped, self-funded solo consultancy. No funding of any kind found or expected.
headcount_estimate: 1 (solo). The entire site is written in the first person singular — "I don't outsource judgment," "That inflection point is where I step in" — and the Papr launch post describes him as a "solo consultant." No employees, no partners listed.
yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: 2025 (domain registered 2025-09-14; site copyright "© 2026 Pivotvia LLC")
sells_to: B2B SMB — founders and CEOs of growth-stage tech companies. Prosumer-scale buyer economics: he is the sole decision-maker and payer, buying on a personal credit card, not through procurement.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are internal leverage for a one-person business, and there is zero AI in his own marketing — no AI, agent, or automation copy anywhere on pivotvia.com. His use is documented instead in the Papr testimonial and in a March 2026 blog post about his first week with Open Claw. The testimonial: "I had ChatGPT, Notion, automation tools, and several GTM subscriptions, but I was still the one holding the workflow together. With Papr Work, I started with apps for the jobs I needed done and adapted them to how I operate. Meeting preparation, notes, CRM updates, and follow-up now happen through one system instead of several disconnected tools." So the jobs are: meeting prep, note capture, CRM updates, follow-up. The Open Claw post is a sharp critique of the agent category from an operator's seat — he found the personal-agent surface compelling (Gmail scanning, voice input, pre-built skills, a named persistent agent) but concluded the value was destroyed by having to stand up a VPS, manage Docker, debug in a terminal, and absorb token-cost surprises: "The promise of agents is leverage. The reality is labor, just in a new place... Work is not removed. Work is relocated." His diagnosis is that agent tools are built from a developer lens and hand the user infrastructure, flexibility without constraints, and — critically — "Context is your responsibility. The system does not 'know your world.' You have to build that knowledge layer yourself."
why_they_need_memory: He is the entire company, so every disconnected tool is a tax paid by the only person who can do billable work. He was the integration layer between ChatGPT, Notion, automation tools and several GTM subscriptions — memory in his head, context re-typed into every prompt. What he explicitly demands from the category maps one-for-one onto agent memory: "Built-in context" (tools connected, workflows recognized, history accessible — "not empty boxes"), "Opinionated defaults" including memory structure chosen for him, and "Compounding output" — a system that improves with use "not because you keep tuning it" but because it learns. That is a company-brain spec written by a buyer. He is the clearest instance of the solo-operator persona for this category: he will pay for a hosted memory layer precisely because he refuses to build or operate one, and he bought Papr Work (the app surface, adapting pre-built apps to how he operates) rather than the memory API. Caveat for segmentation: he is a very small ACV buyer with no team seats to expand into, and he is publicly skeptical of the category, so he is a design partner and credibility reference more than a revenue account.

how_they_use_agents: Two places. (1) In the product they sell: Zapier Agents are AI teammates that run "on command and while you sleep," take real actions across 9,000+ apps, are grounded in company knowledge (FAQs, docs, public links, connected app data), can browse the web autonomously, are built with Zapier Copilot, and carry version control plus a full task-history activity dashboard. The pain they describe is literally a memory/context pain, not a search pain: building a customer brief meant manually re-assembling context from product usage, Slack threads and account notes every single time. Add 700+ customer stories, a high-volume internal helpdesk, and remote async work where org knowledge lives in Slack rather than docs. Second-order: they also *ship* agents, so durable memory is both an internal need and a competitive product gap — their own agents are stateless between runs.

On Glean they indexed 13 years of SharePoint plus 100+ data sources, deployed to ~1,500 staff across 14 divisions, and built custom agents for: calendar management and meeting optimization; consolidating travel policy across multiple systems; legislative bill analysis and tracking; drafting HR performance evaluations; and marketing invoice review and annotation. Deployment leaned on Glean Protect+ for governance with human oversight, single-tenant private-by-design architecture that mirrored their existing role-based security model, automated sensitive-content remediation for PII, plus native connectors and MCP. Reported results: 4-6 hours saved per employee per week, 1.5+ hours/week of search time saved, 100+ hours saved collectively per RFP review cycle.
why_they_need_memory: The CTO's own framing is a memory thesis, not a search thesis: "The enduring value of AI isn't making information easier to find, but making organizational wisdom easier to access. Good decisions are rarely limited by intelligence, they are limited by context." Concretely: 13 years of accumulated SharePoint sediment, 100+ fragmented data sources, a heavily regulated environment where policy, legislative and eligibility precedent must be recalled accurately, PII everywhere so memory must inherit role-based permissions rather than flatten them, and long-cycle repeated processes (RFP reviews, bill tracking, annual open-enrollment cadence) where the same context is reassembled from scratch each time. Public-sector staff turnover makes institutional recall an explicit continuity problem.

name: Mediafly
what_it_does: Revenue enablement platform for enterprise sales orgs, built by roll-up. Three product lines: Engagement (AI-powered sales content management, delivery and compliance tracking), Value (interactive value-selling tools — ROI calculators, TCO estimators, business-case builders, from the Alinean acquisition), and Learning & Coaching (Salesforce-native LMS via Appinium). Sits on top of "Command Center," described as an AI engine that automates routine work, surfaces insights and enforces enterprise governance. Positions itself as "the only sales enablement platform with value selling tools built in." HQ Chicago; distributed team with hubs in Chicago, Boston, California, Toronto, UK, Germany and Poland; customers on six continents. Named customers include Nestlé, ADP, Honeywell, TransUnion, Heineken, Adobe, PepsiCo, Databricks, Sealed Air and Moen.
category: Sales / revenue enablement SaaS (GTM software) — enterprise B2B
stage: Late-stage private, growth-equity / PE-backed. Serial acquirer: seven acquisitions in seven years.
funding: $80M growth round announced Aug 29, 2023, led by BIP Ventures with participation from existing investor Boathouse Capital and Mediafly insiders. Total funding to date not disclosed. Company stated its customer base grew 164% over the preceding 18 months; no ARR or revenue figure disclosed. Acquisitions: Alinean (2018, value/ROI selling), Presentify (2020), InsightSquared (2021, revenue intelligence — its largest), Aptology (2022, behavioral talent intelligence), ExecVision (2022, call recording/coaching), Dooly (2024, deal rooms), Appinium (2025, Salesforce-native LMS; closed April 2025, announced June 2, 2025, terms undisclosed).
headcount_estimate: 201-500 (LinkedIn company page band). No precise number disclosed; midpoint estimate ~300-400.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 2006, well before the modern accelerator path; funded by growth equity (Boathouse Capital, BIP Ventures).
sells_to: B2B enterprise — large sales organizations in Manufacturing, CPG, Life Sciences and Technology. Buyer is typically the CRO/VP Sales Enablement/RevOps, with an enterprise procurement and Salesforce-integration motion. Not SMB, not self-serve, not developer-sold.
how_they_use_agents: Both product and internal ops. In the product: Command Center is the AI engine, and the Appinium acquisition was explicitly framed as a move to "autonomous performance enablement" — agents that analyze content engagement to recommend training, surface next-best actions for reps, predict and drive behavior using consumption plus CRM outcome data, automate contextual knowledge delivery, and recommend upskilling paths. CEO Bill Walsh: the deal "accelerates our path to autonomous workflows by providing the fuel (data) and context (CRM-native workflows) for agents to act intelligently." Internally as a Glean buyer: 9 MCP servers connected and workflow-specific agents including a CX Contact Role Identifier (auto-populates Salesforce contact roles), an outbound email/prospecting agent (researches prospects and drafts personalized outreach), a Rep Estimator (updates prospect rep counts in Salesforce), and Support Ticket Triage. Reported results: 90% company-wide adoption, 50% weekly time savings across IT, 20-minute turnarounds on PR code reviews. Roadmap is to chain sales calls + Salesforce + automated follow-up into one agent-driven process.
why_they_need_memory: Mediafly is a roll-up — seven acquisitions in seven years — and the case study names the exact consequence: post-acquisition information fragmentation across many systems, employees defaulting to Slack to ask humans (burning SME time), and an internal directory that decayed into outdated and overlapping content. That is an org-memory failure, not a search-index failure. Their CPO's framing is telling: Glean became "a strategic operating layer... not just a search tool," letting him "spend more time on judgment instead of hunting for information." Second-order, they are also building agentic features into their own product and need durable per-account and per-rep context (content consumption + CRM history) for agents to make next-best-action calls — so they are simultaneously a buyer of memory infrastructure and a builder of memory-dependent features, which makes them an unusually warm ICP.

name: Nextdoor
what_it_does: Nextdoor is the neighborhood social network — a verified-identity local platform where neighbors get community news, real-time public-safety alerts, neighbor recommendations, a For Sale & Free marketplace, events and groups. Confirmed scale from its own site and IR pages: 110M+ verified neighbors across ~350,000 neighborhoods in 11 countries, '1 in 3 U.S. households,' 5M+ claimed business pages, 6,000+ public agencies, and news from 3,500-4,000+ local publications. It monetizes almost entirely through advertising in three tiers: local SMB self-serve ads, enterprise brand campaigns, and public-agency partnerships. Reported metrics: 22.9M weekly active users (Q2 2026 average), 22.3M WAU and $62M revenue in Q1 2026; FY2023 revenue $218M against a $148M net loss. In July 2025 it shipped a full platform redesign around a News section, Alerts and Faves. IMPORTANT FRAMING NOTE: Nextdoor is not an agent startup — it is a 2008-vintage consumer marketplace/social company that bought Glean as an internal employee-productivity tool.
category: Consumer social network / local marketplace and advertising platform (B2C product, B2B ad sales). NOT an AI or dev-tools company. As a buyer of the agent-memory category it is 'large-ish public consumer tech company running an internal AI enablement program.'
stage: Public company. Went public November 2021 via reverse merger with a SPAC (Khosla Ventures Acquisition Co. II) at a $4.3B valuation; trades on the NYSE under NXDR (previously KIND).
funding: Pre-IPO it raised roughly $470M in venture funding (Benchmark, Greylock, Kleiner Perkins, Tiger Global, Riverwood and others) — treat that figure as approximate, from general knowledge rather than a source I fetched. The confirmed, sourced facts are: SPAC merger November 2021 valuing the company at $4.3B, and current public-market financials of $62M revenue in Q1 2026 and $218M revenue in FY2023 with a $148M net loss. It is now funded by public markets and its balance sheet, not by rounds.
headcount_estimate: 594 employees as of 2023 (the most recent figure I could confirm, via Wikipedia citing company filings). Current headcount is unknown — the company has been through cost-cutting and a CEO change since, so I would guess it is flat-to-lower, in the 500-700 band, but I could not confirm a 2025 or 2026 number and will not invent one.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Nextdoor was incubated inside Benchmark Capital rather than an accelerator; it was never a YC company.
sells_to: Two-sided: the neighbor-facing product is free B2C at consumer scale, and revenue comes from B2B advertising split across SMB self-serve (local businesses), enterprise brand advertisers, and public-sector agencies. So the revenue motion is B2B SMB plus B2B enterprise, layered on a consumer network. It does not sell to developers.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places, and the Glean relationship is entirely the second one. (1) In the product: an AI-powered 'Ask' feature that generates neighbor recommendations, plus AI curation/summarization behind the News and Alerts surfaces from the 2025 redesign. (2) Internally, which is what Glean sells against: Nextdoor rolled Glean Work AI out to five teams and let them build their own agents. People Ops built 'Finn,' a benefits-enrollment guide that cut repeat HR tickets. Sales built an instant client-intelligence agent for AEs. Business Operations built Trust & Safety tooling for fraud review. Product/Engineering deployed a technical reference agent credited with a 2-3x productivity boost. Revenue Operations automated address enrichment, cutting 1-2 hours per 50 accounts down to 5-6 minutes. The champion is Shweta Puri, Marketing Technology and AI Operations Lead — a marketing-ops title, not an engineering one, which is a strong signal about who actually buys this category.
why_they_need_memory: The Nextdoor case study is unusually explicit that the hard part is organizational memory, not model quality. Puri's line — 'Work AI doesn't stick because of models and features. It sticks when people see value in their workflows and then share them' — is a description of a memory problem. Nextdoor's answer was to build a deliberate 'learning loop': a Slack support channel for peer tips and wins, weekly-then-monthly office hours, company bulletins, and gamification recognizing top agent builders. That scaffolding exists precisely because agents built by one team had no persistent, shareable substrate — the org was manually doing what an agent-memory layer is supposed to do automatically. The concrete workloads reinforce it: the RevOps address-enrichment agent and the sales client-intelligence agent are only valuable if account context persists and is reused across reps; the technical reference agent's 2-3x claim depends on durable indexed engineering knowledge rather than per-session retrieval. Nextdoor also has genuine governance pressure — Trust & Safety fraud review touches sensitive user data — so any memory layer must be permission-aware.
