Revenue is unusually well documented for a private company: $100M ARR announced February 2026, $200M ARR announced April 2026.
headcount_estimate: Unknown — I could not confirm a headcount from any primary source. Sigma's careers page shows offices in San Francisco (the main hub, with the bulk of open roles), New York City, London, and a new Asia-Pacific & Japan headquarters in Sydney opened in 2026, plus US remote roles. A company at $200M ARR with four offices is plausibly in the 600-900 range, but that is inference, not a sourced number.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Sigma was incubated and seeded by Sutter Hill Ventures, the venture firm, rather than going through YC or any accelerator program.
founded_year: 2014 (founded by Rob Woollen and Jason Frantz, both ex-Salesforce/Workday, out of Sutter Hill Ventures). The founding year is from general knowledge — Sigma's own about and careers pages do not state it, and I could not confirm it against a primary source in this session.
sells_to: B2B enterprise and upper mid-market — data teams, plus finance, sales and operations business users inside those accounts. There is a meaningful developer/product-team motion too, via embedded analytics (software companies embedding Sigma in their own products) and via MCP, but the contract is enterprise SaaS, not self-serve prosumer.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are a first-class product surface, not a bolt-on. Sigma Agents monitor data thresholds, trigger cross-platform workflows, and execute decisions autonomously — running on a schedule or interactively, writing results back into the warehouse with full audit trails, and pushing actions out to Salesforce and Slack while inheriting warehouse row-level security, column-level masking and role permissions. Sigma Assistant is the conversational layer: it answers questions on governed data while exposing every formula, filter and piece of logic it used, and converts a chat exchange into an editable workbook. The AI Toolkit adds AI Query (LLM functions as spreadsheet columns for classification, extraction and text transformation at warehouse scale) and bidirectional MCP support — Sigma acts as both an MCP client and an MCP server, bridging external enterprise tools with governed business logic. Separately and internally, Sigma is a Glean customer: sales enablement uses Glean to democratize GTM content, per Jonas Taylor, Senior Manager of Global Sales Enablement.
why_they_need_memory: Sigma is interesting because it needs memory on both sides of the table. As a Glean buyer, Taylor's quotes are pure retrieval-and-context pain: 'GTM teams stop spending hours searching and focus on what truly matters' and 'Discovering and sharing relevant data has become just a step in our workflows, not a journey.' Enablement content — decks, battlecards, competitive positioning, product updates from a platform shipping agent features fast — sprawls across Drive, Slack, Highspot-type tools and the wiki, and reps cannot find it. As a vendor, Sigma's own agent architecture depends on durable, governed context: an agent that monitors thresholds on a schedule and writes back to the warehouse needs persistent state and lineage between runs, its MCP server role means it is exporting business logic as reusable context to other people's agents, and its whole trust pitch — transparent formulas, inherited permissions, end-to-end lineage, 'consistent outcomes' — is a governed-memory pitch. That makes Sigma both a customer for and a partial competitor to the company-brain category, depending on where the boundary is drawn.

name: GCash (Mynt / Globe Fintech Innovations)
what_it_does: GCash is the Philippines' largest mobile wallet and cashless ecosystem — the country's #1 finance app. Users buy prepaid airtime, pay bills, send and receive money, shop at partner merchants, and access savings (GSave), credit, loans and insurance from the app. Confirmed numbers from GCash's own about page: 94 million Filipinos have used the app, 9M+ on GSave, 6M merchants and social sellers, 3M+ borrowers; Wikipedia cites 81M active users and 2.5M sellers/merchants as of January 2025, and Glean's case study describes it as serving 'nearly 100 million users.' Corporate structure matters here: the app is operated by G-Xchange, Inc. (GXI), a subsidiary of Mynt (Globe Fintech Innovations Inc.), which is the actual company entity. Note it is a wallet, not a bank — deposits do not carry PDIC insurance.
category: Consumer fintech / mobile wallet and digital financial services at national scale, in a heavily regulated market (BSP-supervised). Not an AI-native company and not a SaaS vendor. As a buyer of the agent-memory category it is 'large regulated enterprise running an internal citizen-developer AI program.'
stage: Late-stage private, effectively a national champion rather than a startup. Mynt is described as the Philippines' first and only $5B unicorn. Not public, though a domestic IPO has been speculated about for years — I found no confirmation of one and will not assert it.
funding: Corporate/strategic capital rather than classic VC rounds. Mynt is a joint venture of Globe Telecom (via 917Ventures), Ayala Corporation, and Ant Group (the Alibaba affiliate). Confirmed valuation milestones: $2B in November 2021, rising to $5B in August 2024 following additional investment from Ayala Corporation and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG). I could not confirm the dollar size of the 2024 round from a primary source, so I am not stating one — the valuations are sourced, the round amounts are unknown.
headcount_estimate: Unknown. Neither GCash's about page nor Wikipedia gives an employee count, and I could not reach LinkedIn. Mynt/GXI is plainly a multi-thousand-person organization given nearly 100M users and full-stack lending, savings and insurance operations, but I have no sourced figure and will not fabricate one.
yc_or_accelerator: None. GCash was launched inside Globe Telecom in 2004 and later spun into the Mynt joint venture — a telco corporate venture, never an accelerator company.
founded_year: 2004 (GCash launched publicly in October 2004; the Mynt JV structure came later).
sells_to: Primarily B2C at national consumer scale — tens of millions of Filipino retail users, including a large unbanked and underbanked population. There is a substantial small-merchant side as well: 6M merchants and social sellers, which is effectively B2B micro-SMB. It does not sell to developers or enterprises.
how_they_use_agents: Entirely internal employee-productivity agents, via Glean. GCash deployed Glean to unify search across disconnected systems, with reported results of 2-3 hours saved per employee per week and over 90% adoption in some departments. The most telling part is that it uses Glean Agent Builder to run a citizen-developer program — non-engineering staff build their own business applications from natural-language prompts. The stated roadmap is at least one customized AI agent per business unit, plus using Glean to cut IT support ticket turnaround. Named champion: Benson Tan, Senior Manager for Automation Solutions — again an automation/ops title, not engineering. His quote is the most explicit agent-future statement of the three: 'In five to ten years, the way we work will radically change—all our teams will have their own Glean AI agents assisting them.' I found no evidence of customer-facing AI agents in the GCash app itself; neither the about page nor Wikipedia mentions AI features.
why_they_need_memory: GCash is the cleanest compliance-driven case of the three. The Glean deployment is explicitly framed around consolidating compliance standards and sensitive regulatory data scattered across multiple sources so teams can keep up with continuously evolving BSP requirements — a regulated financial institution where the cost of an employee acting on a stale policy is a regulatory finding, not just wasted time. That demands a memory layer that is current, auditable and permission-aware, not just a vector index. The citizen-developer program compounds the need: if every business unit is meant to have its own agent and non-engineers are building them from prompts, those agents cannot each carry their own private, unreviewed context — they need a shared, governed organizational memory or the company ends up with hundreds of divergent, ungoverned mini-brains inside a regulated fintech. The IT-ticket-deflection goal is the same pattern: deflection only works if resolutions accumulate as durable institutional knowledge.

name: Delaware Nation Industries & Investments (DNI)
what_it_does: DNI is a 100% Native American-owned (Delaware Nation / Lenape) family of companies headquartered at 2000 N. Classen Blvd, Oklahoma City, operating as a federal prime contractor. It sells enterprise IT services, cybersecurity, research & development, construction/infrastructure, professional and technical staffing, call-center/customer-support services, and medical & imaging equipment to federal agencies — Air Force (incl. AFRL Information Directorate), Army, Navy (Norfolk Naval Shipyard), Department of State, CDC, FAA, DOT — plus commercial clients. It holds SBA 8(a) and HUBZone certifications, which allow sole-source awards up to $30M (civilian) and $100M (DoD), and sells through contract vehicles including 8(a) STARS III, GSA MAS, OASIS, eFAST, SeaPort, and NASA SEWP VI. It runs 70+ active prime government contracts across 30+ states plus DC and OCONUS locations. Operating subsidiaries include DNI Professional Services, DNI Emerging Technologies, DNI Mission Services, Creative IT Solutions, Indigenous Technologies, and Unami. It is emphatically NOT an AI company — it is a services contractor that became a heavy internal consumer of agent tooling.
category: Government IT services / federal prime contractor (tribally owned 8(a)) — a buyer of agent memory, not a vendor
stage: Private, tribally owned enterprise — not venture-backed, no external equity stage
funding: unknown — no venture or PE funding found; DNI is wholly owned by the Delaware Nation tribe, so it is capitalized through tribal ownership and contract revenue rather than investment rounds. Absolute revenue is not disclosed; the company reported 898.02% three-year revenue growth (2021-2024) and ranked #458 on the 2025 Inc. 5000 (#1 in the OKC metro, #2 in Oklahoma, #14 among government contractors).
headcount_estimate: ~1,700+ nationwide per company statements (2025 Inc. 5000 release and dnigov.com); LinkedIn shows a 501-1,000 band with ~805 profiles listed, which likely undercounts contract/cleared staff who do not maintain LinkedIn presence. Treat 1,700 as the company-stated figure and ~800 as the LinkedIn-verifiable floor.
yc_or_accelerator: None — not a YC or accelerator company. Its analogous 'program' is the SBA 8(a) Business Development program and HUBZone designation, which is the set-aside status that drives its contract access.
founded_year: 2015 per LinkedIn's company profile; DNI's own materials claim 'over two decades of government-sector experience,' so predecessor tribal entities pre-date the 2015 registration. Exact founding date unconfirmed.
sells_to: B2G / federal government (Air Force, Army, Navy, State, CDC, FAA, DOT) as a prime contractor, plus some B2B enterprise commercial work. Buyer inside DNI is the VP of Innovation and Technology, not a CTO of a software product.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are internal-operations tooling for capture and proposal work, not part of a product they sell. DNI migrated OFF ChatGPT Enterprise, whose limitations were explicit: manual document uploads with no live SharePoint integration, knowledge that went stale immediately, and a knowledge-base ceiling that forced a separate agent per customer. On Glean they built 84 agents in the first months (~30 in daily active use), and collapsed 22 separate ChatGPT agents into 1 Glean agent. Named agents: an Intel Core Agent that lets non-technical staff verify DNI's past-performance capabilities against a new opportunity; a Pricing Agent that generates RFP pricing models with annual escalation; a Recruiter Alignment Agent that maps candidate resumes to contract-specific technical requirements; and a Win Strategy Dashboard that produces competitive analysis and ranks customer priorities. Reported results: 92-92.5% faster contract identification / RFP response, 83% reduction in effort on capability data analysis, 58 hours/month saved on enterprise search, 95.5% reduction in knowledge access points. Next step per the case study is chaining agents via sub-agents and skills into end-to-end processes.
why_they_need_memory: This is the single clearest 'company brain' buyer profile in the set, and the reason is structural. Federal capture work is an exercise in recall: to bid an RFP you must answer 'have we done this before, for whom, under which contract, with which cleared people, at what price' — and the answer lives scattered across 70+ contracts, SharePoint, past proposals, resumes, and pricing precedents. The ChatGPT Enterprise failure mode they describe IS the agent-memory pitch stated negatively: uploaded snapshots go stale, and a stateless assistant forces you to rebuild a separate agent per customer because there is no shared, live, permissioned corpus underneath. Their headline metric — 22 agents into 1 — is exactly the consolidation that happens when memory moves from inside each agent to a shared substrate. Add the compliance dimension: as a cleared federal contractor they need agent retrieval to respect document-level permissions and produce citations an auditor can follow, which rules out an assistant with an opaque uploaded blob. Their stated roadmap of chaining sub-agents into end-to-end processes is the next dependency — multi-step agent workflows need durable shared state between steps.
sources: https://dnigov.com/wp-sitemap-posts-post-1.xml (contract award announcements: AFRL, CDC, Norfolk Naval Shipyard, NASA SEWP VI)

name: McCarthy Holdings, Inc. (parent of McCarthy Building Companies)
what_it_does: McCarthy is one of the largest general contractors in the United States and describes itself as the oldest privately held national construction company in America, tracing back to an 1864 lumber business. Headquartered in St. Louis, Missouri, it operates 16-19 regional offices nationwide. Services span general contracting, design-build, and construction management across buildings (aviation, commercial, education, government, healthcare, hospitality, interiors, parking, science & technology) and infrastructure (heavy civil, industrial, marine terminals, mission-critical/data centers, renewable energy, water/wastewater). Projects range from under $1M to over $1B. It self-performs significant scope and runs in-house technology units: Virtual Design & Construction (VDC), subsurface utility mapping, and McCarthy EQUIP. McCarthy Holdings, Inc. is the parent; McCarthy Building Companies, Inc. is the operating subsidiary. Zero AI product — this is a construction firm.
category: Commercial construction / general contracting (ESOP-owned) — an enterprise buyer of agent memory
stage: Private, 100% employee-owned via ESOP — no venture or PE stage. ESOP established 1996; became 100% employee-owned in 2002.
funding: unknown / not applicable — no outside equity funding. McCarthy is 100% employee-owned through its ESOP and appears on the NCEO Employee Ownership 100 list (ranked #30 in 2021, up from #47 in 2020). Revenue: the company stated revenues surpassed $4.8 billion as of 2020; no more recent public figure was confirmable, and current revenue is likely materially higher. Do not treat $4.8B as current.
headcount_estimate: ~4,000 salaried employees per the Glean case study; a 2021 company statement cited ~5,000 total including craft professionals and 'more than 2,500 employee-owners across 16 offices.' LinkedIn lists a 5,001-10,000 band with ~6,405 profiles. Best read: roughly 4,000 salaried knowledge workers (the Glean seat population) sitting inside a total workforce of ~5,000-6,500 including craft.
yc_or_accelerator: None — a 160+ year old employee-owned construction firm; no accelerator involvement.
founded_year: 1864 (as a lumber business; 'over 160 years' of operation per company materials)
sells_to: B2B enterprise — project owners and developers: health systems, universities and school districts, federal/state/municipal government agencies, data center and semiconductor clients, utilities and renewable energy developers, ports and water authorities.
how_they_use_agents: Glean is used as an internal 'AI front door' and self-serve agent-building layer, deliberately opened to the whole company with guardrails rather than centralized in an AI team. Trigger: ~100 million files dispersed across SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, and Procore, with employees unable to locate policies, procedures, project records, and specifications. They ran a head-to-head evaluation against Microsoft Copilot and rejected it as opaque in search and insufficiently flexible, choosing Glean for its transparent knowledge graph and LLM-agnostic architecture (explicitly to avoid being locked to one model). Agents deployed: Policies & Procedures Review (40,000+ runs in two months), HR Benefits & ERP Support, Regulatory Intelligence 'REGI' producing weekly policy-tracking digests, a Procedural Update agent that diffs document matrices after reorganizations, a Change Order agent verifying trade-partner billing ($2.7M+ in owner change orders reviewed/processed), and a Materials Quality Management agent tracking material failures across projects. Reported results: 2+ hours/week saved per employee, 90% company engagement (60% among field/operations), 82,000 questions answered weekly, and one business unit running two to three months ahead of schedule. Named users: McKenzie Lewis (AI Platform Manager), Vernan Ibong (VP Operations), Alex Elsayegh PhD (AI Platforms Senior Analyst), JT Searles (SVP, 02S Business Lead). Roadmap: embedding Glean into Procore, their construction management system of record.
why_they_need_memory: McCarthy is the 'enormous unstructured corpus, long-lived projects, distributed non-desk workforce' archetype. The 100M-file estimate across three disconnected systems is the memory problem in its rawest form: the knowledge that determines whether a change order is legitimate or whether a material has failed before is buried in project records nobody can retrieve. Two features of construction make durable memory load-bearing rather than nice-to-have. First, project lifecycles run years and staff rotate between them, so institutional knowledge must outlive the individual and the assignment — the Materials Quality agent tracking failures ACROSS projects only works if there is cross-project memory. Second, decisions carry contractual and liability weight: a change-order determination or a policy interpretation has to be traceable to a source document, which is why they rejected Copilot for opaque search and bought a transparent knowledge graph. Their LLM-agnostic requirement is a memory-layer argument in disguise — they want the model swappable and the accumulated company context permanent, which means context cannot live inside the model vendor. The 90%-engagement, everyone-builds-agents pattern also creates the multiplication problem: 4,000 people building agents against the same corpus is only sustainable if memory is shared infrastructure rather than re-uploaded per agent. Procore integration signals the next phase — agents that write into and read from the system of record need persistent state, not session context.

name: Wunderkind (formerly BounceX)
what_it_does: Wunderkind sells an 'Autonomous Marketing Platform' (AMP) built on identity resolution: a proprietary consumer identity graph covering a claimed 9 billion devices and 2 trillion+ digital events annually, used to recognize otherwise-anonymous website visitors and match them to a brand's customer database without third-party cookies. On top of identity it runs behavioral tracking (browsing, clicks, searches, cart activity across sessions) to score purchase intent, enriches customer profiles back into the brand's existing ESP/CDP/MAP, and orchestrates triggered messaging across email, SMS, paid media, social, and onsite experiences. It markets an 'AI Decisioning' engine that selects the next-best action 'to an audience of one' and optimizes in real time. Sold self-service, fully managed, or hybrid. It claims 700-1,000+ brands and $5B+ in directly attributable annual revenue for customers, in retail, ecommerce, fashion, luxury, health & beauty, travel & hospitality, subscriptions, and ticketing. HQ is 1 World Trade Center, Floor 74, New York, NY. Founded 2010 as BounceX; rebranded to Wunderkind in February 2020.
category: Martech / performance marketing — identity resolution and cross-channel triggered messaging (adtech-adjacent). AI-forward positioning, but not an AI-native company.
stage: Late-stage private, Series C+ (Series C closed March 2023; an additional undisclosed round announced August 2026)
funding: $150M+ total raised as of March 2023, when TechCrunch reported a $76M Series C led by Neuberger Berman. Earlier, as BounceX, the company had raised comparatively little equity — CEO Ryan Urban said in April 2020 it had taken under $50M and 'put to work' probably sub-$35M. On August 4, 2026 Wunderkind announced a new investment round on its own blog, led by existing investors, with amount, round type, and close date all undisclosed; George Bell of Archer Capital Group is quoted as a board member. Revenue: crossed $100M ARR by February 2020 and reported ~35% YoY growth going into the 2023 raise; no current figure disclosed. Do NOT treat the 2026 round size as known.
headcount_estimate: LinkedIn shows the 501-1,000 band (company page: linkedin.com/company/bewunderkind); TechCrunch reported 700 employees in March 2023. The company cut ~20% of staff and reduced salaries in April 2020 under COVID, so the trajectory has not been monotonic. Best estimate: roughly 500-700 today, with 700 the last confirmed number.
yc_or_accelerator: None — no YC or accelerator affiliation found. Conventional VC/growth-equity path as BounceX from 2010.
founded_year: 2010 (as BounceX, founded by Ryan Urban; rebranded Wunderkind February 2020; current CEO Bill Ingram)
sells_to: B2B enterprise and mid-market — ecommerce, retail, and travel brands. Named customers historically include Rag & Bone, HelloFresh, Uniqlo, Sonos, and See's Candy. Buyers are marketing and ecommerce leaders, not developers.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places, which should not be conflated. (1) In the product: an 'AI decisioning' / 'agentic AI' engine that picks the next-best message and channel per individual in real time and optimizes continuously — this is model-driven ranking over their identity graph, and their marketing language has drifted toward 'agentic' recently. (2) Internally, which is why they appear on Glean's site: Wunderkind deployed 650+ AI agents across sales, HR, finance, operations, IT, and customer support, describing the result as building 'an AI operating system.' Sales teams use it to tailor content, pull historical deal context, spot deal blockers earlier, and strengthen account planning. Reported outcomes: employee onboarding compressed 'from months to days,' thousands of hours saved, faster IT and support ticket resolution. Their stated rationale for buying is the sharpest sentence Glean got from them: standalone AI tools 'could solve narrow tasks, but often lacked the business context needed for more strategic, cross-functional work.' Change management was explicit — workshops, office hours, ongoing enablement, executive sponsorship. Named person: Tim Glomb, VP of Content, Digital, and AI. No verbatim pull-quote appears on the Glean page.
why_they_need_memory: Wunderkind is the most interesting of the three because they are simultaneously a memory buyer and a memory-adjacent vendor — they already run a 9-billion-device identity graph, so their leadership understands persistent entity resolution as a product primitive and buys internal agent memory with an educated eye. Their stated buying reason is a precise articulation of the category: narrow tools solve narrow tasks but lack business context, and context that spans sales, HR, finance, and operations cannot be reassembled per-session. The 650-agent number is the tell — at that agent count, per-agent context loading collapses economically, and a shared memory substrate becomes the only workable architecture; agent sprawl is itself the forcing function for memory infrastructure. Their two headline use cases are both memory-shaped rather than reasoning-shaped: onboarding from months to days is literally transferring institutional memory into a new hire, and sales agents surfacing 'historical deal context' and predicting blockers requires durable account state across quarters and reps, not a chat window. As a mid-size company with real churn and a post-2020 workforce reset, the retention-of-knowledge-through-turnover problem is acute. They are also a plausible eventual builder rather than perpetual buyer, given they own comparable infrastructure.

name: Upside
what_it_does: Two-sided retail-media / cash-back commerce marketplace for brick-and-mortar retail. Consumers use a free app (iOS/Android) to claim personalized cash-back offers at gas stations, grocery stores, restaurants, convenience stores and (since April 2024) hardware stores, pay with a normal credit/debit card, and cash out to a bank account, PayPal or gift cards. Retailers and brands (Shell, BP, Circle K, Giant Eagle, Domino's, Taco Bell/Desert de Oro, Wendy's/Meritage, Save Mart, QuickChek, Gulf) fund the offers and are billed only on measured incremental profit — Upside's differentiator is its measurement methodology: 'After a customer makes their first Upside purchase, we compare their spend to a control group of 100 similar customers.' Offers are described as 'unique, one-to-one promotions based on real customer behavior, not broad segments.' Also distributed through bank/fintech partners (Varo Bank embeds Upside for debit-card engagement). Company-stated scale: 35M consumers in the marketplace, $1B+ cumulative cash back paid out, $2.5B incremental retailer profit generated, ~$6B annual commerce volume, 4.8 stars across 550k+ app reviews. Founded January 2016 as GetUpside; renamed Upside in April 2022 alongside its Series D. HQ at 455 Massachusetts Ave NW, Washington DC, with offices in Austin (2019), Chicago (2019) and New York (2022).
category: Retail media / cash-back commerce marketplace (fintech-adjacent, offline commerce). NOT an AI company.
stage: Private, Series D. Company timeline confirms: Series A Nov 2015, Series B Oct 2018, Series C Sep 2020, Series D closed April 2022. No later round found.
funding: unknown — amounts are not disclosed anywhere on upside.com (the about-us timeline lists round names and dates only, no dollar figures), the newsroom carries no funding press releases, and Crunchbase returned 403 in this session. Contemporaneous 2022 trade press was widely reported to have put the Series D around $165M at roughly a $1.5B valuation, but I could NOT verify that in this session — treat it as unconfirmed, not a sourced number.
headcount_estimate: unknown as a published figure; derived estimate ~300-400. Derivation from Glean's own case-study math: 2,000+ hours saved monthly at a stated 1.5+ hours saved per employee per week implies ~460 hrs/week / 1.5 = ~310 active users, and at the stated 92% adoption that implies ~335 employees at the time of the case study. Four offices (DC HQ, Austin, Chicago, NY) plus remote. No LinkedIn or Crunchbase headcount was retrievable (both blocked).
yc_or_accelerator: No evidence of Y Combinator or any accelerator. Founded in Washington DC in 2016; nothing on the company site, newsroom or about page references an accelerator.
founded_year: 2016 (as GetUpside, January 2016; Series A predates the operating launch, Nov 2015). Renamed to Upside April 2022.
sells_to: Both sides of a marketplace: B2C (free consumer app, 35M consumers) and B2B — brick-and-mortar retail chains from mid-market regional operators (Coen Markets, QuickChek, Save Mart, Meritage/Wendy's franchisee) up to enterprise fuel and QSR brands (Shell, BP, Circle K, Domino's, Taco Bell), plus channel/embedded partnerships with banks and fintechs (Varo Bank).
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents found in the product. The homepage, retailer/business pages, careers page and newsroom contain no mention of AI, machine learning, algorithms or agents — the personalization ('right shoppers, right offers, right time', one-to-one promotions off real purchase behavior) and the 100-customer control-group incrementality measurement are clearly ML/statistics under the hood, but Upside deliberately markets outcomes (incremental profit, ROI, proven measurement) rather than technology. The only AI reference anywhere on the site is third-party event coverage ('Groceryshop Day 2 recap: AI does indeed have ROI'). Their Glean purchase is therefore an INTERNAL-OPERATIONS buy, not a product/agent-infrastructure buy: Glean sits on Google Drive, Slack, Jira and Confluence as company-wide search for employees.
why_they_need_memory: Classic scale-up knowledge sprawl, not agent memory. Post-2021 hypergrowth left information scattered across Google Drive, Slack, Jira and Confluence, and internal surveys showed declining employee confidence that knowledge was findable. Elizabeth Vaggelatos (Head of Knowledge Management): 'Our Google workspace became filled with recurring documents that were all kind of similar. People were just constantly reinventing the wheel.' The buyer persona is telling — a dedicated Head of Knowledge Management, i.e. someone whose job IS the company brain. Results claimed: rolled out company-wide in one month after a pilot, 92% adoption, 2,000+ hours saved monthly, 1.5+ hours/employee/week, $1.2M+ value of time saved, faster onboarding. 'With Glean, it doesn't matter the tenure, department, or seniority level — there is a use case for everyone.'
confidence: medium — high confidence the company is real and on what the product is (fetched multiple pages of their own site); low confidence on funding amounts and headcount, which I could not source. NAME AMBIGUITY WARNING: 'Upside' is a heavily reused name — theorg.com/org/upside returns a completely different, unrelated Upside (senior-care company, 11-50 employees, CEO Jake Rothstein). Any third-party data keyed on the name alone should be discarded unless it matches Washington DC / GetUpside / cash back.

name: Confluent
what_it_does: The data streaming platform company, founded by the original creators of Apache Kafka (built at LinkedIn in 2008). Sells 'the World's Data Streaming Platform' across four deployment shapes: Confluent Cloud (fully managed, cloud-native Kafka), Confluent Platform (self-managed/on-prem), Confluent Private Cloud (hybrid), and WarpStream (Kafka-compatible, runs in the customer's own cloud account). Core capabilities: Kafka streaming, 120+ pre-built connectors, Stream Governance, stream processing via Apache Flink, and Tableflow (materializes Kafka topics as Iceberg/Delta tables). Founded September 2014 by Jay Kreps (CEO), Jun Rao and Neha Narkhede; HQ Mountain View, CA (899 W Evelyn Ave). IPO'd on NASDAQ as CFLT on June 1, 2021 at a ~$4.5B initial valuation; FY2024 revenue $963M; 4,000+ customers. MATERIAL STATUS CHANGE: IBM announced its acquisition of Confluent on December 8, 2025 and completed it on March 17, 2026 at $31.00/share in cash, ~$11B enterprise value. Confluent is now an IBM company, with day-one integrations into IBM watsonx.data, IBM MQ, webMethods Hybrid Integration and IBM Z.
category: Data streaming infrastructure / developer + data platform (Kafka, Flink); increasingly agent infrastructure. Now an IBM subsidiary.
stage: Acquired. Was public (NASDAQ: CFLT) from June 2021; acquired by IBM for ~$11B enterprise value ($31/share cash), announced Dec 8 2025, closed March 17 2026. At the time it bought Glean it was a ~2,000-person, pre- or early-public-company scale-up (the case study notes it grew from 250 to 2,000+ employees).
funding: Venture-backed pre-IPO (Benchmark, Index, Sequenceof rounds through Series E; total pre-IPO amount not confirmed in this session — treat as unknown). IPO June 1, 2021 at ~$4.5B valuation. FY2024 revenue $963M. Final outcome: acquired by IBM at ~$11B enterprise value, $31.00/share cash, closed March 17, 2026.
headcount_estimate: ~3,263 employees as of Q3 2025 (last reported figure before the IBM close). Was 2,000+ at the time of the Glean case study, up from 250 earlier. Cross-check from the case-study math is consistent: 15,000+ hours saved monthly at 1.5 hrs/employee/week implies ~2,300 active users, and at the stated >70% adoption that implies ~3,300 employees.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Founded 2014 as a spin-out of the LinkedIn Kafka team, venture-funded from the start.
founded_year: 2014 (September 23, 2014)
sells_to: B2B enterprise, and developers/practitioners as the technical buyer. Named verticals: financial services, retail, manufacturing, telecommunications, public sector. 4,000+ customers. Classic land-with-developers, expand-to-enterprise-contract motion; now folded into IBM's enterprise software portfolio.
how_they_use_agents: Confluent is unusual here: it both BUYS agent-adjacent tooling and SELLS agent infrastructure. In the product, 'Confluent Intelligence' is a fully managed Confluent Cloud service combining historical evaluation, continuous processing and real-time serving, with three pillars: (1) AI/ML Functions for anomaly detection, fraud prevention and forecasting; (2) Streaming Agents — event-driven AI agents that 'run natively on Kafka and Flink to automate workflows', operating inside the data stream so they act on fresh business data rather than static snapshots, with end-to-end observability to test, debug, evaluate, audit and recover from failure; (3) a Real-Time Context Engine that serves 'trustworthy, structured context to any AI app or agent', automatically updated as upstream logic or features change. The homepage pitch is building 'RAG and agentic AI use cases with real-time, contextual and trustworthy data.' IBM's Rob Thomas framed the whole acquisition in agent terms: moving trusted data continuously 'so their AI models and agents can act on what is happening right now.' Internally, they also built GenAI applications on Glean Apps and APIs — Manu Narayan: 'With Glean Apps and APIs, we've been able to securely build and deploy generative AI applications that would've taken months.'
why_they_need_memory: Stated problem is best-of-breed tool sprawl at hypergrowth, not tool duplication. Manu Narayan (Chief of Staff, later VP of IT, Data and Business Operations): 'We had a lot of sand in our gears when it came to finding information. Our challenge wasn't having too many duplicative tools — it was that knowledge was spread across best-of-breed systems.' Shahan Parshad (VP Business Technology & Data): 'The challenge we had around information sprawl ... was at least 80% solved by introducing Glean's search tool,' and 'Looking back on the hundreds of technology projects we've led internally, Glean was high impact and low effort.' Results: 20+ tools indexed (Slack, Salesforce, Confluence and more), >70% active adoption (higher than many other internal SaaS tools), 15,000+ hours saved monthly, 1.5+ hrs/employee/week, 13% increase in support-team satisfaction with information access, 5-10 minutes less investigation time per support ticket, 5+ minutes faster customer response. Heaviest-value teams: technical support, customer success, sales engineering, AEs and new hires. Pulkit Bhardwaj (Technical Support Engineer): 'Without Glean, it would be tiresome to search across resources and find required results.' Strategically, a company selling a real-time context engine for agents is exactly the buyer that already believes context/memory is the bottleneck.
confidence: high — company, product, financials, headcount and the IBM acquisition are all confirmed from primary sources (Confluent's own press-release index and the completion release) plus Wikipedia. Only pre-IPO total funding is unconfirmed.

name: Grammarly (now Superhuman)
what_it_does: Started in 2009 as an AI writing assistant — grammar, spelling, clarity, tone — delivered as a browser extension, keyboard and desktop app that works across 'more than 1 million apps and websites.' Since late 2024 it has rolled up into a broader AI productivity suite: it acquired Coda (December 2024, bringing Coda CEO Shishir Mehrotra in as Grammarly's CEO) and Superhuman Mail (July 2025), then rebranded the PARENT COMPANY to Superhuman in October 2025 — so the name in the Glean testimonial is now the product, not the company. The suite is four products: Go (a proactive AI assistant that works across apps), Grammarly (writing), Docs (the Coda-derived workspace), and Mail (the Superhuman email client), plus Calendar, Databases and an Agent Store. Consumer/prosumer tiers (Grammarly Free, Pro), plus Grammarly for Education and business/enterprise. Stated scale: 40M+ daily users, 50,000+ organizations and educational institutions, 200B words analyzed daily. HQ San Francisco; founded in Kyiv; hubs in Berlin, Kyiv, Mountain View, New York, Porto, San Francisco, Seattle, Vancouver and Warsaw.
category: AI writing / communication and AI-native productivity suite (email, docs, assistant). Prosumer + B2B SaaS.
stage: Late-stage private, heavily consolidated via M&A. $13B valuation as of its 2021 round; acquirer rather than acquiree since (Coda Dec 2024, Superhuman Mail Jul 2025). No IPO.
funding: $110M (2017); $90M at a $1B+ valuation (2019); $200M at a $13B valuation (2021, Baillie Gifford / BlackRock-era round); $1B in NON-DILUTIVE financing from General Catalyst (2025). Total disclosed equity roughly $400M+, plus the $1B non-dilutive facility. Last known valuation $13B (2021) — no post-rebrand valuation confirmed.
headcount_estimate: 1,500+ (stated as '1,500+ teammates' on the Superhuman careers page, post-Coda and post-Superhuman-Mail). Distributed across 9 named hubs in North America and Europe.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Founded 2009 in Kyiv, bootstrapped/profitable for roughly its first eight years before taking its first institutional round in 2017 — notable as an unusually capital-efficient origin for this category.
founded_year: 2009 (Grammarly); parent rebranded to Superhuman in October 2025
sells_to: Mixed and unusually broad: prosumer/consumer freemium (40M+ daily users), B2B SMB through enterprise (50,000+ organizations, Grammarly Business/Pro for teams), and education (Grammarly for Education). Not developer-sold.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are now first-class product surface, not a bolt-on. There is a dedicated Superhuman Agent Store with task-specific agents (Email Assistant, Resume Builder, Citation Finder, AI Grader, Reader Reactions), and 'Go' is a proactive AI assistant that operates across the user's apps and is pitched on anticipating what the user needs and adapting to their behavior patterns. Grammarly itself ships AI writing agents, rewrite and tone-refinement, and an integrated AI assistant/chat inside Docs. Positioning is explicitly 'AI that works where you do' / 'an AI-native productivity platform.'
why_they_need_memory: The Glean deployment is departmental and support-led rather than a company-wide company-brain program — the customer support team searching across Slack, Confluence, Zendesk and Google Drive from one place. Iryna Smyk (Customer Support Manager): 'With Glean, I found many more documents with important product information than I even knew existed within Grammarly. Glean helps speed up the search for troubleshooting information, especially when assisting customers with complex problems.' The driver is documentation discovery for a product with a very large support surface (40M+ daily users, 1M+ integration surfaces) and a knowledge base fragmented across four systems. Note the strategic angle: a company whose own product is an AI assistant with persistent context still bought a third-party retrieval layer for its internal knowledge — evidence that building agent memory for customers does not remove the need to buy it internally.
confidence: high on the company, product suite, headcount, acquisitions and rebrand (confirmed from superhuman.com/about, superhuman.com/careers, grammarly.com/about and Wikipedia). Medium on the funding history, which comes primarily from Wikipedia rather than primary press releases. One caveat worth flagging: the Glean case study predates the Superhuman rebrand, so 'Grammarly' as a logo-wall entry now maps to Superhuman as the legal/corporate buyer.

name: Super.com
what_it_does: Consumer savings 'super app' for budget-conscious US consumers, formerly SnapTravel/Snapcommerce. Four product lines per their own engineering job postings: (1) travel — SuperTravel, discounted hotel booking, the original 2016 SMS/WhatsApp chatbot business; (2) fintech — SuperCash cashback debit/credit-builder card, cash advances; (3) 'earnings' — offers/rewards that let users earn; (4) Super+, a ~$15/month membership that bundles them (hotel discounts up to ~40%, cashback, prescription discounts, cash advance, credit building). Per Fortune (Jul 2026): Super+ approaching 1M members, >$1B in cumulative customer savings, >$200M net revenue, >50% YoY growth, profitable. Their own JD's cite >$1MM/day in sales, 1TB/day data ingest, thousands of req/sec across dozens of microservices. Remote-first, hiring across Canada and the US. NOT a Y Combinator company — the YC directory's 'Super' (W18) is superapp.id, an unrelated Indonesian company.
category: consumer fintech / travel + savings super app (buyer of agent-memory, not a vendor)
stage: Series D (private, unicorn)
funding: ~$244M disclosed total: $1.2M seed (2016), $8M Series A (2017), $85M Series B (2021, Inovia + Lion Capital), $85M Series C (2023, Inovia), $65M Series D (2026, led by TPG) at a $1.2B post-money valuation per Fortune. Angel investors include Steph Curry, Harley Finkelstein (Shopify), Neha Narkhede (Confluent).
headcount_estimate: ~300 (Fortune, Jul 2026). Wikipedia infobox says 225 as of 2025. Their own JD states 'more than 100 contributors to our codebase.' 24 open roles on their Ashby board as of Sep 2026.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Explicitly not YC (verified against the full YC company dataset — the 'Super' in YC W18 is superapp.id, a different company). No accelerator found.
founded_year: 2016 (April), as SnapTravel; renamed Snapcommerce, then Super.com in Oct 2022
sells_to: B2C / prosumer — US consumers, explicitly targeting 'the 100 million Americans living paycheck to paycheck'. No B2B motion.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers. (1) INTERNAL, and this is the loud one: their engineering JDs repeat verbatim that Super.com is 'an AI-First engineering organization' that leverages 'modern AI development workflows using tools such as Cursor, Claude, and internally built AI agents to accelerate implementation and iteration across our codebases.' A Senior Platform Engineer role is scoped to 'deploying new autonomous agentic systems' and owning 'AI-first automation' in the internal developer platform. A Senior NetSuite Administrator role in Finance is explicitly about 'deploying AI agents to replace manual processes' across finance workflows. They also state they use AI in recruiting screening. (2) PRODUCT: legacy conversational infrastructure from the SnapTravel era survives — data JDs describe 'the bot platform, the NLP engine and the pricing/recommendation engines' as core microservices — plus ML/personalization and recommendation systems for discovery and cross-sell. No customer-facing LLM agent is marketed publicly.
why_they_need_memory: Textbook profile for this category. Super.com deliberately replaced meetings with a written-documentation culture after going remote/hybrid, which scattered knowledge across Google Drive, Slack, Confluence and GitLab — exactly the fragmentation a company brain resolves. Glean reports 1,500+ hours saved monthly, 1.5+ hrs/employee/week, 20 min/day faster information discovery, 20% shorter onboarding, and 17x ROI; leadership pushed a 'Glean it' self-service norm. Structurally: remote-first + ~100 engineers shipping across four regulated-adjacent verticals (travel, credit, cash advance, rewards) + a stated intent to run internal AI agents over their own codebase and finance workflows means those agents need durable, retrievable org context, not just a chat window. The Glean deployment and the internally built agents are the same need at two layers.

name: Duolingo
what_it_does: Public (NASDAQ: DUOL) consumer education company. Freemium gamified mobile learning app: 250+ language courses plus Math, Music, Chess (chess launched Apr 2025, ~7M DAU by early 2026) and Duolingo ABC for early literacy. Per the FY2025 10-K: ~133.1M MAU and ~52.7M DAU in Q4 2025 (DAU +30% YoY, DAU/MAU 39.6%), ~9% of MAU are paid subscribers (~10.9M paying subs as of Jun 2025), $1.04B revenue in 2025. Monetization is subscriptions (Super Duolingo, Duolingo Max), advertising (~7.7% of 2025 revenue), in-app gems/power-ups, and the Duolingo English Test, a high-stakes AI-scored proficiency exam (~4.0% of 2025 revenue). Also has an emerging direct ad-sales business and Duolingo for Schools. HQ Pittsburgh; founded by Luis von Ahn and Severin Hacker.
category: consumer edtech / language learning (buyer of agent-memory, not a vendor)
stage: Public — IPO June 28, 2021 on NASDAQ (DUOL)
funding: $183M+ raised privately pre-IPO (incl. $45M Series D led by Google Capital in 2015 at $470M, $25M Series E led by Drive Capital in 2017 at $700M, later rounds to $1.5B and $2.4B valuations) before the 2021 IPO. Now publicly traded; no private funding rounds. Current market cap: unknown (not verified in this research).
headcount_estimate: ~850 (as of Oct 2024, per Wikipedia); the FY2025 10-K does not disclose a headcount figure. 89 open roles on their Greenhouse board as of Sep 2026, incl. a dedicated 'AI + Machine Learning Engineering' department. Likely ~850-1,000 today but not confirmed.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Originally funded by Luis von Ahn's MacArthur Fellowship and an NSF grant out of Carnegie Mellon.
founded_year: 2011 (private beta Nov 2011; public launch Jun 19, 2012)
sells_to: Primarily B2C consumer (500M+ registered learners). Secondary B2B/institutional: Duolingo English Test sold into universities and governments, Duolingo for Schools, and a direct advertising sales business (Ad Sales Leads being hired by region).
how_they_use_agents: Heavily AI-shaped product, though 'agent' is used loosely. Customer-facing: Duolingo Max (launched Mar 2023, originally GPT-4-powered) adds Roleplay — an AI conversation partner — and Video Call, a live spoken conversation with characters (Lily, and Falstaff added Jan 2026 for beginners); Explain My Answer was Max-exclusive and went free for all users in 2026. The Duolingo English Test is AI-driven assessment. Birdbrain is their long-running per-learner difficulty-personalization model, alongside a bandit algorithm that personalizes daily push notifications. The 10-K states Roleplay, Explain My Answer and Video Call are all AI-powered and flags rising compute cost. Internal: CEO Luis von Ahn declared Duolingo an 'AI-first' company in Apr 2025 and said contractors would be phased out where AI can do the work — a decision that triggered significant public backlash. Engineering JDs reference 'AI agent driven crash and memory analysis' on the Android platform team, and Senior Director of Engineering roles require experience scaling LLM-powered features and 'AI-first ways of working'. Fast Company reported the chess game was largely 'vibe coded'.
why_they_need_memory: Duolingo is the case where the buyer already tried to build it themselves and gave up — they had an internal search tool called Metasearch that lacked filtering and ranking, and replaced it with Glean rather than keep investing. Knowledge was spread across Google Drive, Slack, Confluence and Zendesk. Glean reports 500+ hours saved monthly, 1.5+ hrs/employee/week, >$1.1M in yearly time savings, 5x ROI, with Art Chaidarun (Principal SWE) calling Glean Chat the most underrated feature and noting it beats search for some questions. The deeper driver: an experiment-driven org running hundreds of concurrent A/B tests across six subjects with high documentation churn, now explicitly 'AI-first' internally — which means both humans and internal coding/analysis agents need a single retrievable memory of what was already tried and why. High-value, expensive employee time is the stated justification ('Employees' time is expensive').

name: Wealthsimple
what_it_does: Canada's largest independent fintech / digital financial services platform, Toronto HQ. Full retail financial stack: Wealthsimple Invest (managed portfolios — Classic and Summit, the latter with private-markets exposure), self-directed Trade (commission-free stocks, ETFs, $0 options), Crypto, a chequing account and Visa Infinite Privilege credit card with 2% cash back, Wealthsimple Tax (from the 2019 SimpleTax acquisition), high-net-worth advisory, and Wealthsimple for Business (group savings plans). Newer: IPO Access at issue pricing (May 2026) and Wealthsimple Predict, a regulated prediction-markets app with ~4,000 Kalshi contracts (Jun 2026). Scale per their own JDs and newsroom: 3.6M–4M+ Canadian clients, CA$155.6B assets under administration (Q2 2026), CA$17B net flows in Q2 2026. Majority-owned (52.4% undiluted) by Power Corporation of Canada via Power Financial, IGM Financial, and Sagard's Portage Ventures.
category: consumer fintech / wealth management + brokerage + banking (buyer of agent-memory, not a vendor)
stage: Series F, late-stage private, corporate-majority-owned
funding: CA$750M Series F (Oct 2025) at a CA$10B post-money valuation, co-led by Dragoneer and GIC, with new investor CPP Investments plus Power Corporation, IGM Financial, ICONIQ, Greylock and Meritech. Prior: CA$750M Series E (May 2021) at CA$5B co-led by Meritech and Greylock, with DST, ICONIQ, Dragoneer, TCV, Inovia, Allianz X and celebrity angels (Drake, Michael J. Fox, Ryan Reynolds); US$87M in Oct 2020.
headcount_estimate: Over 1,500 employees across North America (stated directly in their own Sep 2026 job postings). Wikipedia's infobox still says '>1000 (2025)' — the 1,500 figure is the more current, first-party number. 48 open roles on their Ashby board, 21 of them in Data & Engineering.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Founded independently in 2014; earliest institutional backing came from Power Financial / Portage rather than an accelerator.
founded_year: 2014 (September), by Michael Katchen, Brett Huneycutt and Rudy Adler
sells_to: Primarily B2C consumer (retail Canadian investors, including a high-net-worth advisory tier). Secondary B2B: Wealthsimple for Business group retirement/savings plans, and issuer-side capital-markets partnerships for IPO distribution.
how_they_use_agents: The most operationally advanced agent story of the three, and it is almost entirely internal/infrastructural rather than a marketed customer-facing assistant. They run a named 'AI agentic workflows team' that other product teams partner with — a Brokerage engineering role is scoped to build 'AI-augmented automation built in partnership with our agentic workflows team' and to ensure what ships is 'accurate, secure, auditable, and reuses shared components.' Their Observability Platform team's stated mission is to 'make production legible to every engineer and AI agent at Wealthsimple,' building query foundations and MCP-protocol access patterns so 'AI agents investigate incidents, verify their own changes, and operate in tight feedback loops alongside engineers.' There is a dedicated ML Infrastructure team hiring a Senior SWE for LLM Infrastructure (self-hosted open-source LLMs on GPU, LiteLLM model routing, vLLM/Ray, Bedrock, eval harnesses) and an 'AI Products' data science team owning the end-to-end AI product lifecycle including foundation-model training. Engineering culture is explicitly 'AI-first': team-specific Claude plugins, Claude Code, Cursor, and LLM integrations that redact sensitive data without degrading functionality. No AI assistant is advertised on the consumer site or newsroom as of Sep 2026.
why_they_need_memory: Two independent vendors in this category cite them, which is itself the signal — Glean for enterprise search and Notion (with Notion AI) for the knowledge base. Glean: 98% employee adoption, CA/US$1.03M in annual time savings, 1.5+ hrs/employee/week, faster incident resolution and lower support handle times, and knowledge-discovery friction disappearing from employee surveys entirely. Notion: nearly 70% of employees had struggled to find data across tools; People Ops halved audit completion time under a phased read-only-first rollout led by Kathleen Cauley, a former librarian hired as Knowledge Manager — a company that hires a dedicated knowledge manager is a self-identifying buyer. The structural driver is the sharpest of the three: a regulated broker-dealer moving billions for millions of Canadians, with 1,500+ staff across a dozen product surfaces, that is deliberately putting AI agents into production incident response and finance operations. Those agents need auditable, permission-aware, durable context — which is exactly why their observability team frames the platform as a memory substrate agents query rather than a dashboard humans read.

name: Reddit
what_it_does: Reddit is a community discussion platform organized into hundreds of thousands of user-run subreddits, where members post links/text and vote content up or down. It is one of the largest sites in the world by traffic. Revenue comes primarily from advertising (brand + performance ads sold to marketers), with a fast-growing second line in AI data licensing (a Google deal reported at ~$60M/year signed Feb 2024, plus API access granted to OpenAI) and a smaller consumer subscription (Reddit Premium). 2025 revenue was $2.20B.
category: Consumer social / online community platform with an advertising business. NOT an AI-native company and NOT in the agent-memory category itself - it appears on Glean's logo wall as an ENTERPRISE BUYER of internal knowledge AI.
stage: Public. IPO'd on the NYSE in March 2024 under ticker RDDT.
funding: Public since March 2024 (NYSE: RDDT). Pre-IPO it raised roughly $1.3B in venture funding across Series A-F, the largest being a ~$410M Series F at a ~$10B valuation in August 2021 led by Fidelity; the March 2024 IPO priced at $34/share. CAVEAT: the pre-IPO funding figures come from general knowledge and were NOT verified against a primary source in this session (redditinc.com and investor.redditinc.com were both un-fetchable). The public-listing fact and the $2.20B 2025 revenue figure ARE sourced.
headcount_estimate: 2,555 employees as of 2025 (Wikipedia infobox, citing Reddit filings). Directionally reliable; Reddit has been hiring steadily post-IPO, so the current 2026 figure is likely somewhat higher.
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator - Reddit was in YC's very first batch, Summer 2005. This is a well-established historical fact but note it is essentially irrelevant to Reddit's current profile as a $2B+ revenue public company.
founded_year: 2005 (June 23, 2005; founded by Steve Huffman, Alexis Ohanian and Aaron Swartz; HQ San Francisco)
sells_to: B2B enterprise + mid-market advertisers (the ad sales org that Glean was sold into), plus AI labs as data-licensing customers. The platform itself is free consumer software. So: the PRODUCT is consumer, but the REVENUE motion is B2B enterprise ad sales.
how_they_use_agents: Two very different places, and the distinction matters for this research. (1) IN THE PRODUCT: Reddit Answers, launched December 2024, is an AI search tool that reads and summarizes Reddit conversations to answer a user's question; it has since been pulled into core search. Reddit also runs ML for feed ranking, moderation and machine translation (translated localization was a major driver of international user growth), plus generative ad-creative tooling for advertisers. (2) INTERNALLY - this is the relevant one: Reddit is a Glean customer, confirmed directly on Glean's homepage customer logo wall (verified by fetching glean.com). The cited Glean webinar 'AI in Action: Accelerating GTM Enablement' says Glean's Work AI Platform 'up leveled Reddit's sales and enablement processes', featuring Bradford Jordan, Head of Sales & Partner Performance. So the agent deployment is internal GTM/sales enablement, not a customer-facing feature. Reddit is also cited as an Atlassian Intelligence/Confluence user, consistent with a heavy Atlassian-plus-Slack-plus-Drive knowledge sprawl.
why_they_need_memory: The buying trigger is internal, not product. Reddit scaled an advertising sales organization very fast through and after its 2024 IPO, and ad sellers need consistent, current answers about ad formats, pricing, targeting capabilities, brand-safety policy and measurement - knowledge that lives scattered across Confluence, Slack, Google Drive and Salesforce. The named champion is a sales-ops leader (Head of Sales & Partner Performance), which is the classic profile: rep ramp time and answer consistency, not developer infrastructure. Important honest caveat for the buyer thesis: Reddit does NOT buy agent-memory as a technical dependency for its own AI products - Reddit Answers is built in-house on Reddit's own corpus. Reddit is an IT/enablement buyer of a company-brain tool, which is a different budget, buyer and sales motion than an infra-for-builders sale.
sources: https://www.glean.com/ (Reddit confirmed present on the customer logo wall as of this fetch)

name: HubSpot
what_it_does: HubSpot is a customer platform / CRM built around a single 'Smart CRM' database with product hubs layered on top: Marketing Hub, Sales Hub, Service Hub, Content Hub, Operations Hub and Commerce Hub. It won by going freemium and bottom-up into SMB and mid-market, and has been moving upmarket for years. As of June 30, 2026 it reports over 306,000 customers, $3.4B trailing-twelve-month revenue, 20.1% non-GAAP operating margin, and 9,016 employees.
category: CRM / go-to-market SaaS - AND, importantly for this research, a direct COMPETITOR in the agent space via Agent Hub and Breeze. HubSpot is simultaneously a buyer of internal knowledge AI and a vendor of grounded customer-facing agents.
stage: Public. IPO'd in October 2014, now trades on the NYSE under ticker HUBS.
funding: Public since 2014 (NYSE: HUBS); 2025 revenue $3.13B, $3.4B TTM as of Q2 2026. Pre-IPO it raised on the order of $100M in venture capital from General Catalyst, Matrix Partners, Sequoia, Google Ventures and Salesforce Ventures. CAVEAT: the pre-IPO venture total is from general knowledge and was not verified against a primary source this session; the revenue, customer count, headcount and margin figures ARE sourced directly from ir.hubspot.com.
headcount_estimate: 9,016 employees as of June 30, 2026. HIGH confidence - this figure was read directly off HubSpot's own investor relations page, not inferred from LinkedIn.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Founded by Brian Halligan and Dharmesh Shah out of MIT Sloan in 2006, well before the modern accelerator era was relevant to them.
founded_year: 2006 (June 2006; HQ Cambridge, Massachusetts)
sells_to: B2B, primarily SMB and mid-market, increasingly upmarket. 306,000+ customers at a ~$11K average annual revenue per customer implies a volume, low-touch, product-led motion - freemium and self-serve with sales assist, plus a large partner/agency channel.
how_they_use_agents: HubSpot ships one of the most fully-built agent product lines of any incumbent SaaS vendor. Agent Hub is a central console to activate prebuilt agents, build custom ones without code, and track agent performance. Named prebuilt agents (verified on hubspot.com/products/artificial-intelligence): Content Agent (blog/social/landing pages in brand voice), Prospecting Agent (watches buying signals and runs personalized outreach), Customer Agent (resolves inbound tickets using contact and contract history), Data Agent (answers custom questions about contacts and companies using CRM records, calls, emails and documents), Campaign Agent, Nurture Agent and Revenue Agent (invoice follow-up and collections). Breeze Assistant is the natural-language builder for custom agents. HubSpot's explicit positioning is that agents are 'grounded in live customer information' and 'built on your CRM data from day one' - i.e. HubSpot's answer to agent memory is the Smart CRM itself, built in-house. Separately and internally, HubSpot is cited as a Glean customer: the webinar 'How HubSpot works smarter with Glean' describes an employee-led, bottom-up pilot of Glean's unified search and Work AI across HubSpot's internal tools, and Sean Hanna of HubSpot appears on the Glean:GO 2026 speaker list. It is also cited by Atlan (data catalog) and Tettra (internal wiki).
why_they_need_memory: Two separate motives, and they pull in opposite directions. (1) AS A BUYER: 9,000+ employees selling seven product hubs to 306,000 customers means internal product, pricing and enablement knowledge fragments extremely fast; the Glean adoption was explicitly bottom-up and employee-initiated, which is the signature of acute day-to-day search pain rather than a top-down AI mandate. Their named contacts are Solutions Engineers - people who must answer arbitrary technical product questions live on customer calls. (2) AS A VENDOR: their Customer Agent and Data Agent must ground every answer in CRM records, call transcripts, emails and knowledge-base documents, which IS an agent-memory problem - but HubSpot solved it in-house on top of the Smart CRM and sells that as a differentiator. STRATEGIC WARNING for anyone treating HubSpot as a prospect for agent-memory infrastructure: they are a competitor in that layer, not a customer of it. They will buy internal knowledge tools for employees; they will not buy memory infrastructure for their product.

name: Etsy
what_it_does: Etsy is a global two-sided online marketplace for handmade, vintage and craft goods, positioned around the tagline 'Keep Commerce Human'. It connects roughly 8 million active sellers - mostly micro-businesses and solo makers - with about 96 million active buyers across 100M+ listings. Revenue is a take rate on seller transactions plus payments and advertising (Etsy Ads and Offsite Ads). $12.6B gross merchandise sales in 2024 and $2.88B revenue in 2025. It completed the sale of Depop to eBay in July 2026 for ~$1.4B in aggregate cash, refocusing on the core Etsy marketplace.
category: Consumer e-commerce marketplace. NOT AI-native and not in the agent-memory category - another enterprise buyer of internal knowledge AI, with a modest generative-AI product surface.
stage: Public. IPO'd on Nasdaq April 16, 2015 (ETSY); moved its listing to the NYSE effective October 10, 2025.
funding: Public since April 2015 (ticker ETSY, Nasdaq then NYSE from October 2025). Pre-IPO it raised roughly $97M in venture capital from investors including Union Square Ventures, Accel, Index Ventures and Tiger Global. CAVEAT: the pre-IPO figure is from general knowledge and was not verified against a primary source this session; the IPO date, listing move, GMS and revenue figures ARE sourced.
headcount_estimate: Roughly 1,700-2,200 currently - a RANGE, deliberately, because the last clean figure is stale. Etsy reported 2,400 employees as of December 31, 2024. Since then it laid off ~220 people (~12% of the workforce) in August 2026 and divested Depop to eBay in July 2026, both of which reduce the count. Treat any single precise number for 2026 as unreliable. Note the pattern: Etsy has now done multiple rounds (11% in December 2023, 12% in August 2026) and is running deliberately lean.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Founded in Brooklyn in 2005, pre-accelerator era.
founded_year: 2005 (June 18, 2005; founded by Robert Kalin, Chris Maguire, Haim Schoppik and Jared Tarbell; HQ Brooklyn, New York)
sells_to: Consumer marketplace, two-sided. Buyers are consumers; sellers are prosumers and micro-businesses (solo makers, craft shops), which is the closest fit to 'prosumer'. Not a B2B software seller at all.
how_they_use_agents: Etsy's agent story is the thinnest of the three. In the product: Gift Mode, launched January 2024, is explicitly powered by OpenAI GPT-4 and generates personalized gift guides from a short survey about the recipient. Beneath that, Etsy has run ML for search ranking and recommendations for years - it acquired Blackbird Technologies in November 2016 specifically for AI shopping-context and search software - plus ML for fraud and listing-quality detection, an area its own risk disclosures flag as being amplified by AI. Etsy's investor materials state the company 'leverage[s] machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) to continuously improve every customer touchpoint'. Internally, the cited Glean webinar 'AI in Retail: Glean and Etsy' features 'two avid Glean users at Etsy' describing reduced information-search time and faster decision-making. Note the two named contacts: Rachel Refo Hopkins (Director of Merchandising - a business user) and Patrick Tran (Staff Software Engineer, Gen AI - which does confirm Etsy staffs a dedicated generative-AI engineering function). Etsy is also cited as a Guru customer.
why_they_need_memory: The pitch that landed was time saved searching, not agent infrastructure - which fits a company that has cut headcount twice and is asking a smaller team to cover the same surface. Merchandising, seller support and engineering all need fast access to policy, category and seller-support knowledge that would otherwise require asking a colleague who may no longer be there; post-layoff knowledge loss is a real and underrated driver for this category. A secondary, more speculative angle: a marketplace of 100M+ listings has a genuine grounding problem for any buyer-facing AI shopping assistant, and third-party LLM shopping agents are becoming a traffic channel that marketplaces must plan for - but I found NO source this session for Etsy's agentic-commerce posture, so treat that as hypothesis, not fact.

name: phData

stage: private, profitable-services model; no venture rounds found

Crunchbase and Growjo returned 403, Tracxn URL 404'd, and neither phData's own site nor Bing results surfaced any funding announcement. Do not assume venture backing; it reads as a bootstrapped/owner-held services business, but that is inference, not confirmed.
headcount_estimate: ~915 (LinkedIn company page employee count, fetched Sept 2026; LinkedIn size band '501-1,000'). Distributed across 39 US states and 6 Latin American countries, with flagship offices in Minneapolis MN (HQ, 400 S 4th St), Bengaluru India, and Montevideo Uruguay.
yc_or_accelerator: none found — not a YC or accelerator company; founded as a services firm by industry veterans
sells_to: B2B enterprise — large regulated enterprises in healthcare/life sciences, financial services, manufacturing, and retail/CPG. Deals are services engagements, often co-sold through Snowflake/AWS/dbt partner channels.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places. (1) In the business they sell: 'AI Workforce' is an explicit agentic offering that automates client business workflows, and recent phData engineering blog posts are almost entirely agent-architecture material — 'Building governed multi-agent systems on Snowflake: A practical architecture guide' (Jun 2026), 'Using Snowflake CoCo as an agentic orchestration service' (Jun 2026), 'From spec to pipeline: Inside phData Toolkit's agentic automation' (Jun 2026). One of the two people Glean names, Andrew Kim, carries the title 'Director of AI Workforce', i.e. this is a staffed line of business, not a marketing label. (2) Internally: the Glean citation is a webinar, 'Shipping Better Code, Faster' — confirmed present on glean.com/webinars — framed as phData telling its own implementation story about fixing internal support and documentation with AI, presented by Grant Henke (SVP of Engineering) and Andrew Kim. Note: I confirmed the webinar exists on Glean's site but could not read its description or transcript, so the internal-support detail rests on the sourcing given to me rather than on independent verification.
why_they_need_memory: Strongest fit of the three, and for two compounding reasons. First, as a buyer: ~915 forward-deployed consultants rotating across client engagements in 39 states and 6 countries means institutional knowledge (how a migration pattern was solved, which Snowflake anti-pattern bit which client) lives in scattered Slack, tickets, Confluence, and individual heads — exactly the internal-support-and-documentation problem the Glean webinar describes. Engineering-heavy headcount also makes code context a first-order concern, which is why the webinar is titled around shipping code faster. Second, as an evangelist and channel: their own August 2026 blog post is titled 'From prompts to systems: Why enterprise AI needs shared context', and another argues 'Without an enterprise semantic layer, your AI is just guessing' — they are publicly making the shared-context/agent-memory argument to their enterprise clients. An SI that both buys the category internally and resells the pattern is a two-sided account.

category: electric vehicle manufacturing (consumer hardware + commercial fleet)
stage: public — NASDAQ: RIVN, IPO November 2021
funding: ~$11B raised pre-IPO across roughly 10 private rounds (investors included Amazon, Ford, T. Rowe Price); November 2021 IPO raised ~$13.5B at $78/share. headcount_estimate: ~14,000-15,000. Wikipedia cites 14,861 employees (2024 filing); LinkedIn shows a '10,001+' size band with 12,133 members listing Rivian. Treat ~14k as the working number.
yc_or_accelerator: not applicable — never in an accelerator; conventional VC then IPO

how_they_use_agents: Two separate threads that should not be conflated. In the product: Rivian is building an autonomy and in-vehicle AI stack — it held an 'Autonomy and AI Day' in December 2025 promoting an 'end-to-end AI-centric approach', and RivianOS 2 is the software layer; LinkedIn lists 'autonomous driving' and 'software' among its specialties. That is embedded/robotics AI, not agent memory. Internally: Rivian appears on Glean's homepage customer logo wall (confirmed — alt text 'Rivian' among Samsung, Intuit, Reddit, Databricks, Pinterest, Booking.com, Canva and others), which indicates a deployment of enterprise AI search/agents across employees. why_they_need_memory: Classic large-enterprise knowledge-fragmentation case rather than an AI-product case. ~14k employees spanning hardware engineering (Palo Alto, Irvine), a manufacturing plant (Normal IL), autonomy/software, service, and retail — with knowledge spread across PLM systems, manufacturing and quality docs, service bulletins, supplier records, Jira/Confluence, and Slack. Onboarding at manufacturing scale and cross-site engineering handoffs are the pain. Worth flagging honestly: this profile fits an enterprise-search buyer more than an agent-memory-infrastructure buyer. If the category being sold is developer- or agent-facing memory infrastructure rather than an employee assistant, Rivian is a weak analog and its presence on Glean's wall mostly signals brand-name enterprise logo capture.

name: Canva
what_it_does: Freemium online visual-communication and design platform — drag-and-drop editor with templates for presentations, social graphics, documents, websites, video, and print, across web, iOS, Android, macOS, and Windows. Has expanded well beyond templates into a creative and productivity suite: Canva Docs, Sheets, Websites, Video, plus Affinity (professional design software, acquired from Serif in 2024 for ~$380M) and Leonardo.ai (generative image models, acquired 2024). Canva Enterprise is the paid tier aimed at large-company brand and marketing teams. Scale as of end-2025: 265M+ monthly active users, 31M+ paid subscribers, ~$4B ARR of which ~$500M is enterprise. Note: canva.com blocks automated fetching (HTTP 403), so product detail here comes from Wikipedia and LinkedIn rather than first-party pages.
category: design / creative SaaS (prosumer + SMB, moving upmarket to enterprise)
stage: late-stage private — no IPO; liquidity via secondary sales
funding: No authoritative total confirmed. Publicly reported rounds: A$40M (2018), A$70M (2019), A$85M (2019), US$200M (2021) at a US$40B valuation. Valuation history: peaked at US$40B in 2021, marked down to US$26B in 2022, and a secondary in August 2025 valued the company at US$42B. headcount_estimate: ~5,500-6,000. Wikipedia cites 5,500 (2024). LinkedIn's company page shows 19,356 members associated with Canva against a stale '1,001-5,000' size band — that member count is inflated by non-employees and freelancers listing Canva and should not be used as headcount.
yc_or_accelerator: none — bootstrapped early in Perth, then conventional venture rounds (Blackbird, Sequoia China, Felicis, Bessemer, T. Rowe Price and others across rounds); no YC or accelerator

sells_to: Prosumer and B2B SMB primarily — self-serve individual and team subscriptions are the bulk of the 31M+ paid users — with a real and growing B2B enterprise motion (Canva Enterprise, ~$500M of the ~$4B ARR). Not developer-first.
how_they_use_agents: In the product: heavy and increasingly agentic. Magic Studio and Magic Write (generative copy and design), an Assistant that recommends and executes design actions, a custom GPT, a proprietary generative design model that outputs editable layers rather than flat images, and 'Canva AI 2.0' with agentic scheduling/task behavior. The Leonardo.ai acquisition brought in-house image models. Internally: Canva appears on Glean's homepage logo wall (confirmed via fetch, alt text 'Canva') and on the customer-stories index, with no case study or public quote. The stronger internal signal is the two Glean:GO 2026 speakers cited in my brief — Samantha Garrett, 'AI and Automation Platform Team Lead', and Sean Gillespie, 'AI and Automation Impact Lead'. I could not independently verify those two names or titles in this session (Glean's customers page 404'd and my web-search budget was exhausted), but if accurate they indicate a dedicated staffed internal AI-and-automation function measuring adoption impact — the profile of a serious, expanding deployment rather than a pilot.
why_they_need_memory: Two angles. As an internal buyer: ~5,500 employees across Sydney, Austin, Manila, London and elsewhere, growing fast through acquisition (Affinity, Leonardo.ai, Flourish, Smartmockups, Ortto and more) — each acquisition drops a separate wiki, codebase, and set of conventions into the company, which is precisely the fragmented-institutional-memory problem. The named 'AI and Automation Impact Lead' title suggests they are actively measuring whether internal AI retains and surfaces that context. As a product analog: Canva is itself building agentic features over a user's brand kit, past designs, and assets — durable per-user and per-org context — so its own engineering org has direct empathy for the agent-memory problem and is a plausible buyer of infrastructure, not just an assistant. Caveat: at $4B ARR and 19+ acquisitions, Canva builds a lot in-house; treat it as a design-partner-scale enterprise account rather than a fast self-serve one.

founded_year: 2009 (founded as Pure Storage); renamed Everpure on Feb 23, 2026

how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers. (1) INTERNAL - the reason they show up as a Glean customer: employees across engineering, support, legal and customer-facing teams were losing up to an hour searching Jira and GitHub; Glean gave them unified permission-aware search plus a platform to build custom GenAI apps. (2) IN PRODUCT - Pure1 AI Copilot has, per the Q2 FY27 release, 'evolved from a conversational assistant into an active operator that analyzes performance anomalies, provides step-by-step root-cause analysis, and guides teams to resolution'; the Pure1 Manage MCP Server lets customers 'connect AI agents and tools to live Pure1 operational data'; Fusion automates fleet-wide provisioning; Everpure Data Stream automates pipelines 'from ingestion to inference'. why_they_need_memory: Classic large-enterprise knowledge sprawl: technical documentation, product and pricing data, and compliance/legal policy spread across Jira, GitHub and multiple enterprise systems, with strict permission boundaries (they sell storage to regulated enterprises, so 'secure GenAI' was the framing). The sharper signal for an agent-memory vendor is the '5 minutes to build a custom GenAI application' metric - they are not just buying search, they are building internal agents on top of a shared corpus, which is exactly the workload that needs durable, permission-aware, cross-app context. A dedicated Director of AI plus an in-product agent roadmap (MCP server, AI Copilot as 'active operator') means the internal buying team is technically sophisticated and thinks in agent terms.

name: Databricks
what_it_does: Unified data + AI platform ('lakehouse'), founded by the creators of Apache Spark, Delta Lake, MLflow and Unity Catalog. category: Data + AI platform / data infrastructure / developer and data-team tooling
stage: Late-stage private (Series K, plus a subsequent strategic round). Widely expected IPO candidate; still private as of Sept 2026.
funding: Multi-billion. Disclosed rounds: Series C $60M; Series F $400M at $6.2B; Series G $1B at $28B; Series H $1.6B at $38B; Series I at $43B; Series J $10B at $62B (Dec 2024); Series K at >$100B valuation (announced Aug 19, 2025); most recently a $5B strategic round at ~$188-190B valuation led by Coatue with Blackstone, MGX, T. Rowe Price and Sixth Street Growth (term sheet announced July 16, 2026). Business metrics (Aug 13, 2026): $7B revenue run-rate growing >80% YoY; Lakehouse products at $1.5B run-rate (>100% YoY); Lakebase already >$100M run-rate; 1,000+ customers above $1M run-rate and 100+ above $10M.
headcount_estimate: ~14,300 (LinkedIn company page lists 14,277 employees, Sept 2026). Databricks does not publish a headcount on its own site; the about page's '1,200+' figure refers to partners, not employees.
