sells_to: B2B enterprise (Fortune 500 data and platform teams) and developers/data engineers - a dual enterprise + bottom-up developer motion
how_they_use_agents: Both sides of the table. AS A GLEAN CUSTOMER (internal): CIO Naveen Zutshi says 'We had search engines, but they didn't surface the right results. Relevance was the biggest issue' and that they used Glean to build 'a simple, intuitive intranet where employees can find what they need right away.' Glean spans their Google Workspace, Atlassian, Salesforce and Slack, and adds an AI assistant for natural-language queries. AS A VENDOR (product): Databricks is one of the most agent-forward platform companies in the market - Agent Bricks for building agents, Genie and Genie One as 'agentic coworkers' that turn business data into answers and actions, Genie Code for agentic data engineering, Lakebase explicitly positioned as the operational database for AI agents, Mosaic AI Agent Framework, Unity AI Gateway for agent/model governance, and Lakewatch as an 'open agentic SIEM'. NOTE ON THE RELATIONSHIP: Databricks is also a Glean technology partner - glean.com/partners/databricks describes Glean Assistant and Glean Agents querying Databricks workspaces in natural language via Databricks Genie, raw SQL from Glean, and indexing of AI/BI dashboards. So this account is simultaneously customer and partner, which inflates its value as a logo but weakens it as evidence of pure arms-length demand.
why_they_need_memory: ~14,000 employees growing >80% YoY generate content faster than any single system can organize it, spread across Workspace, Atlassian, Salesforce and Slack; their stated pain was relevance, not coverage. Strategically more interesting: Databricks itself sells the agent-memory adjacent layer (Unity Catalog for governed context, Lakebase for agent state, Agent Bricks for agent construction), so they are an educated buyer who understands the category's vocabulary - but also a potential competitor/absorber of it for the data-plane half of the problem. Their internal buy was for the unstructured-knowledge half their own products don't cover.

name: Webflow
what_it_does: Visual web development and website platform, now positioned as 'the agentic web platform for modern businesses' (current homepage title). Marketing, design and dev teams build, host and manage production websites without hand-writing code. Platform surface: Designer (visual canvas), CMS, Hosting, Localize, Security, Shared Libraries, Page branching (branch/merge/approve workflows), Interactions powered by GSAP (acquired), Analyze, Optimize (A/B testing + AI personalization, built on the Intellimize acquisition), SEO and AEO (answer-engine optimization for AI search), Webflow Cloud, DevLink, Figma-to-Webflow, an Apps ecosystem, Webflow AI, and a Webflow MCP server. Self-reported: 3.5M users, 900+ team members in 25 countries. Customers named include Discord, Monday.com, IDEO, TED, Dropbox, BBDO, The New York Times.
category: Web development / website building and management platform (no-code + agentic), sold into marketing and digital-experience teams
stage: Late-stage private, Series C. Hit a $4B valuation in March 2022 while nearing $100M revenue; hired its first CFO (Craig Mestel) more recently, a typical pre-IPO signal. CEO is Linda Tong; the three co-founders (Vlad Magdalin, Sergie Magdalin, Bryant Chou) remain involved.
funding: $335M total raised (stated on Webflow's own about page). Investors: Y Combinator, Accel, CapitalG (Alphabet), Silversmith, among others. Valuation $4B as of the March 2022 round. Acquisitions: Intellimize (personalization/optimization) and GSAP (JavaScript animation library).
headcount_estimate: ~900-1,600. Webflow's own about page states '900+ team members in 25 countries'; LinkedIn lists 1,615 employees (Sept 2026, which typically over-counts). The company figure of 900+ is the more reliable number.
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Summer 2013 batch (confirmed on ycombinator.com/companies/webflow)
sells_to: B2B SMB and mid-market moving upmarket to enterprise, plus a large prosumer/practitioner base - designers, marketers, developers, agencies and freelancers. Explicit Enterprise tier and a partner/agency channel.
how_they_use_agents: Product side is the striking part: the Webflow MCP server ('Connect your agents to Webflow') lets external agents in Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Slack build pages, manage CMS content, and analyze site traffic on the user's behalf, with per-site / per-collection / per-page / per-locale roles and permissions, MCP actions logged in the site activity log, and single-page publishing to de-risk agent edits. Webflow AI generates content, CMS items and code components; Optimize uses AI to run multivariate tests and personalize per visitor; AEO targets visibility in AI-driven search; 'Source by Webflow' is a research preview. A customer story notes Arkose Labs made a 2026 rule that every vendor had to connect to Claude. Internal side (the Glean case study): Michael Bassani, IT Ops & Productivity Manager, says 'There was so much knowledge in Google Drive. I tried to bookmark everything, but it wasn't sustainable. Post Glean, finding docs improved immensely.' Glean is integrated with 20+ business tools (Slack, Google Drive, Atlassian, Zendesk, Jira); 65% of employees use it; 300+ hours saved monthly; 1.5+ hours saved per employee weekly; support teams resolve tickets faster and new hires self-onboard; IT also gained document-permission visibility.
why_they_need_memory: The internal case is ordinary (knowledge scattered across 20+ SaaS tools, onboarding and support ticket deflection). The far more relevant signal is that Webflow has independently built the same primitive into its own product: its MCP page tells customers to 'define your rules - create a unified source of context to guide your agents with skills and references like brand guidelines and legal docs.' That is a company brain for agents, described in a vendor's own marketing. Webflow is therefore a buyer who has already validated the thesis in-product - agents acting on a company's website need durable brand, design-system, and policy context plus governance and an audit trail, or they produce off-brand output at scale. Of the three companies here, Webflow is the closest fit to a company that would both buy agent memory and understand precisely why.

name: Mitti (formerly SafetyCulture)
what_it_does: Mobile-first operations platform for deskless/frontline teams. Company-reported scale: 2M+ users, 80,000-85,000 organizations, 190 countries, 1B+ checks per year, 5+ petabytes of workplace data. Rebranded SafetyCulture -> Mitti on 11 August 2026; new platform capability '5 Star Benchmarking' scores each site and prescribes fixes.
category: Frontline / EHS workplace operations SaaS (vertical B2B ops software + embedded insurance). NOT an AI-native or agent-infrastructure company.
stage: Late-stage private / unicorn. Most recent disclosed round: AU$165M closed 9 Sept 2024 at an AU$2.5B valuation (round led by Airtree Ventures). Prior: unicorn at $1.3B in 2020; valuation reported doubling to $2.2B (2022). No IPO.

headcount_estimate: ~800-1,000. Company stated 'more than 800 employees now working from its six offices around the world' in the Sept 2024 funding release (having added 100 roles in the prior six months). LinkedIn company page (Mitti by SafetyCulture) shows a self-reported size band of 501-1,000. Treat as an estimate.
yc_or_accelerator: None identified. Australian company, bootstrapped/angel-funded early, later VC-backed (Blackbird, Index, TDM, Airtree). Not a YC company.
founded_year: 2004 (as SafetyDocs, by Luke Anear; renamed SafetyCulture 2019; renamed Mitti 11 Aug 2026)
sells_to: B2B, SMB through large enterprise, in deskless/frontline industries: manufacturing, hospitality, construction, retail, facilities management, logistics. Named customers: Trackhouse Racing, Trippas White Group (Sydney Opera House venues), Tennis Australia / Australian Open, Brentford FC, M-Sport, St Vincent de Paul Society Victoria, Marley Spoon.
how_they_use_agents: TWO layers. (1) INTERNAL, via Glean Agent Builder — every employee can build and share agents. Documented agents: a Customer Insights Agent (Product Marketing; synthesizes customer pain points by industry/region/account size), a PRD Agent (evaluates readiness and completeness of PRDs, enforces framework structure), a Performance Highlights Agent (pulls Jira, GitHub, meeting notes to build employee achievement summaries; saves 30-40 min per performance review), a Product Help Agent (internal feature status and delivery timelines without asking the product team), an Engineering Assistant Agent (daily debugging, architectural change-doc readiness, data-model quality checks), and a GTM & Support Agent (product answers for customer-facing teams without waiting on R&D). Reported results: search time cut 50% (engineers were spending up to 4 hrs/week searching), 20 min saved per engineer per review cycle, 90%+ of users would be disappointed to lose it. Notably they host Glean inside their own cloud tenant. (2) IN-PRODUCT — the company is explicitly pivoting to 'agentic-first'. It acquired the Sydney AI startup Twine on 7 Apr 2026, bringing Brian Swift back as VP of AI reporting to the CEO; CEO Luke Anear: 'From the minute I wake up until I go to sleep, I'm working on how we move to an agentic-first experience.' The Aug 2026 relaunch ships 'Agents' that monitor operations and run routine tasks in the background, an AI Assistant that compares procedures against standards/legislation and drafts action plans, and AI Issue Creation that turns a photo, prompt, or voice note into a ready-to-review issue.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. Internally: a 20+ year-old company that grew engineering headcount 50% in one stretch, with knowledge siloed across Jira, GitHub, Confluence, Slack and meeting notes for 800+ people in six offices; an internal survey identified knowledge search as the single biggest productivity drag. They considered building their own enterprise-search/Work-AI layer and explicitly decided not to divert engineers from the core product. In the product: they hold what they call the world's largest repository of workplace data — 5+ petabytes, billions of images, 1B+ checks/year — and their agentic roadmap depends on reasoning over per-site, per-customer operational history across years (the same inspection has to feed the safety score, the training plan, the reorder, and the insurance price). Both are durable-context problems, not single-prompt problems. Security posture matters too: they required tenant-hosted deployment.

name: Nile
what_it_does: Secure Network-as-a-Service (NaaS) for enterprise campus wired and wireless networking. name: Flock Safety (the "Flock" in the Glean webinar)
what_it_does: Public-safety technology company selling a combined hardware + software platform to police departments, municipalities, schools, HOAs and private businesses. Hardware: solar/LTE automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras, video cameras, mobile security trailers, acoustic gunshot detection, and a Drone-as-First-Responder (DFR) system described as an "all-in-one, fully automated air support system." Software: FlockOS ("the real-time crime center (RTCC) platform that runs anywhere, from a command center to a laptop in the field"), Flock911 (live 911 call streaming across jurisdictions), Flock FreeForm ("Search existing video and LPR systems using natural language"), and a shared National LPR Network. Sold as a "Safe City Subscription." Company reports operating in 5,000+ US communities and $300M+ ARR growing 70% YoY (March 2025). Also a company under heavy public scrutiny — 2026 news coverage of a live-camera-feed exposure and of ALPR transparency/records fights, both of which had SVP of Customer Experience Chris Colwell as the named public communicator.
category: Public safety / govtech — physical security hardware + real-time crime center software (ALPR, video, drones). NOT an AI-memory or agent company; a buyer.
stage: Late-stage private (Series G+), decacorn-track. Y Combinator S17 alum.
funding: ~$1.2B+ total raised across ~10 rounds (Premier Alternatives). Confirmed from Flock's own announcement: $275M at a $7.5B valuation, March 13 2025, led by Andreessen Horowitz with Greenoaks, Bedrock, Meritech, Matrix, Sands Capital, Founders Fund, Kleiner Perkins, Tiger Global and Y Combinator participating. Later rounds reported by data brokers but NOT confirmed on a primary source: CB Insights lists a $200M Series G on April 17 2026; Tracxn/Premier Alternatives peg valuation at $8.4B (April 2026); Dealroom surfaces an Aug 31 2026 report of "$8.3B valuation on $500M raise." Treat the post-2025 numbers as unverified.
headcount_estimate: ~1,100–1,500. Flock's own careers page says "1,100+ employees nationwide"; YC profile says 1,000; Revelio Labs says 1,497 (Dec 2025); Tracxn 1,446 (Jul 2026); LeadIQ ~1,500 (Jul 2026). A stale LinkedIn life page still says "700+."
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Summer 2017 batch (confirmed on ycombinator.com/companies/flock-safety; YC also listed as an investor in Flock's own 2025 funding announcement).
sells_to: B2G primarily (law enforcement agencies, cities, corrections, transportation, fire/EMS, schools) plus B2B mid-market/enterprise (retail, healthcare, hospitality, logistics, banking, corporate security) and residential/HOA. Long, procurement-heavy, politically scrutinized sales cycles.
how_they_use_agents: Product side: computer-vision/ML is the core of the business (plate and vehicle recognition, "AI-powered analytics" on video, acoustic gunshot classification, autonomous drone dispatch), and Flock FreeForm is an LLM-style natural-language search over existing video and LPR systems. But Flock publishes no named AI agent product, and its About page still frames the stack as "hardware, software and machine learning" rather than agents. Internal/ops side: the Glean touchpoint is entirely in the Customer Experience org — Chris Colwell, SVP of Customer Experience, co-presented with Gainsight product management and a Glean Technical Support Manager on connecting customer context across service, support and success workflows. That is a support/CS knowledge-retrieval use case, not a product-embedded agent.
why_they_need_memory: Their CX org supports 5,000+ communities and thousands of individual agencies, each with jurisdiction-specific retention policies, contract terms, privacy configurations and sharing permissions — the exact kind of context that lives scattered across Gainsight, the support desk, contracts and internal docs. Add extreme public/legal scrutiny of ALPR data handling (transparency lawsuits, a 2026 camera-feed exposure incident): support answers about who can see what data, for how long, must be consistent and sourced, or they become news. Plus 700→1,500 headcount growth in roughly two years means most support reps have less institutional memory than the questions require. That is the textbook "company brain" buying trigger — but note it is a CX-org purchase, not a platform/AI-team purchase.
confidence: medium — identity is high-confidence, customer status is not. Multiple independent sources (Flock Safety's own blog byline, ZoomInfo, X profile, LinkedIn, WFLX and Inside Investigator news coverage) confirm Chris Colwell is SVP of Customer Experience at Flock Safety, so the "Flock" in the Glean webinar is Flock Safety, not Flock Freight or Flock (UK insurance). However Glean's webinar page lists Colwell only as a panelist and does NOT call Flock a customer; Flock Safety does not appear on Glean's customer page (which 404s), and Flock could equally be a Gainsight customer brought to a joint webinar. Do not count this as a confirmed Glean logo.

name: Mastercard
what_it_does: Global payments network. Mastercard does not issue cards or lend; it operates the switch and rails that "process payments between the banks of merchants and the card-issuing banks or credit unions of purchasers," earning assessment and transaction-processing fees on volume. Increasingly a data/services company on top of the network: fraud and identity (Ethoca, RiskRecon, Recorded Future), open banking (Finicity), consulting and analytics, and loyalty. FY2025 revenue $32.8B; ranked 141st on the Fortune 500 (2026). HQ Purchase, New York.
category: Payments network / financial market infrastructure, with a large and growing data-and-services arm. In the agent-memory context: a very large enterprise buyer of both data-catalog/context tooling (Atlan) and knowledge management (Guru).
stage: Public — NYSE: MA. IPO 2006. Market cap in the ~$400B+ range (Wikipedia cites $434B as of April 2024; not independently re-verified for 2026).
funding: N/A — public company, not venture funded. Revenue $32.8B (2025); operating income $15.6B (2024), $14.0B (2023).
headcount_estimate: ~39,800 (2025, per Wikipedia's infobox sourced to company filings).
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 1966 as the Interbank Card Association by a consortium of banks.
sells_to: B2B enterprise and a two-sided network: issuing banks and credit unions, acquirers and processors, merchants (SMB through global enterprise), fintechs, and governments. Also increasingly sells developer-facing agentic payment APIs.
how_they_use_agents: Both a vendor and a consumer of agents. As vendor: Mastercard Agent Pay (announced 2025) brings tokenized, credentialed payments to AI agents transacting on a consumer's behalf; Mastercard Agent Suite (announced January 2026, availability targeted Q2 2026) is an agentic AI suite "to help banks, retailers and other enterprises build, test, and deploy autonomous AI-driven workflows and agents." As consumer: the Atlan deployment is explicitly framed as making the data estate agent-ready — Vivek Radhakrishnan (SVP, Data & Analytics) cites "AI-powered metadata enrichment at scale" saving "over 6,000 hours" across 30,000+ data assets, and Brian Piel (VP) frames the goal as "enterprise-ready data for AI... adding the right context." Andrew Reiskind (Chief Data Officer) fronts an Atlan video, "How Mastercard Designs Context on Atlan." Separately a logo-wall customer of Guru (getguru.com/customers) with no published case study — likely a departmental knowledge-management deployment rather than an enterprise-wide one.
why_they_need_memory: Radhakrishnan's own diagnosis is the buying reason: "Historically, we would think we could manage it centrally... the only way to do it is by federating work." A data estate spanning tens of thousands of assets across a heavily regulated, multi-jurisdiction payments business cannot be documented by a central team, and undocumented data is unusable by agents — the enrichment is the memory layer. Add regulatory pressure (PCI, PSD2, data residency, model governance) that makes provenance and lineage on every AI answer non-optional. This is the enterprise-scale profile of the category buyer: the sponsor is the Chief Data Officer / data platform org, not a product team, and the pitch that lands is "your AI will hallucinate until the context is machine-readable."

name: Workday
what_it_does: Cloud enterprise software for the back office: human capital management (HR, payroll, talent, workforce management), financial management, planning, and student information systems, sold as a single multi-tenant system of record for large employers. Founded by Dave Duffield and Aneel Bhusri after Oracle's acquisition of PeopleSoft. FY2025 revenue $8.45B. HQ Pleasanton, California.
category: Enterprise SaaS — HCM + ERP/financials, now repositioning as the system of record for both human and digital (agent) workforces. In the agent-memory context: an Atlan customer whose public testimonial is the single clearest articulation of why this category exists.
stage: Public — NASDAQ: WDAY. IPO October 2012.
funding: N/A — public. FY2025 revenue $8.45B. Actively acquisitive in agents: Paradox (August 2025, conversational AI recruiting agent), Flowise (August 2025, low-code AI agent builder), and Sana, which now appears on Workday's own product pages as the orchestration/experience layer.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 2005 by two enterprise-software veterans (Duffield previously founded PeopleSoft; Bhusri was a Greylock partner).
sells_to: B2B enterprise — large and very large employers (heavy Fortune 500 penetration), sold to CHROs and CFOs. Long cycles, high switching costs, multi-year contracts.
how_they_use_agents: Deepest agent story of the three. Workday ships a full agent portfolio: HR Service Agent ("Answers routine HR questions from policy and Workday data, deflects tickets, routes cases"), Talent Acquisition, Talent Management, Workforce Management, Total Rewards, Payroll, and Organizational Development agents on the HR side; Accounting Agent ("Reconciles, tests controls, and catches variances continuously") and Procurement Agent on the finance side; Developer, Admin, Legal, and Travel & Expense agents. Sana is "the central experience layer... interprets user intent and coordinates multi-step workflows." Above all of it sits the Agent System of Record (ASOR), which "unites all your agents—even those outside your organization—with your people and money in one system to manage your entire human and digital workforce." Workday reports AI drove over one billion platform actions in FY2026, contributing 1.5 points of ARR growth. Internally, per Joe DosSantos (VP, Enterprise Data & Analytics): "We built a revenue analysis agent and it couldn't answer one question. We started to realize we were missing this translation layer" — and the fix was exposing Workday's own agreed business vocabulary to agents via Atlan's MCP server.
why_they_need_memory: DosSantos's second quote is the thesis statement for the whole category: "All of the work that we did to get to a shared language amongst people at Workday can be leveraged by AI via Atlan's MCP server." The failure mode was not data access — the revenue agent had the data — it was that the semantics existed only in humans' heads and in tribal convention. Memory/context tooling is what converts an organization's negotiated definitions into something an agent can retrieve at inference time. Note the strategic angle: Workday is simultaneously selling agents to its own customers, so it has a vested interest in solving agent-context internally first and being seen to have done so. As a buyer profile, this is the most sophisticated variant — the sponsor already runs agents in production, has already watched one fail, and is shopping for a semantic layer rather than a search box.

name: Intuit
what_it_does: Global financial technology platform, ~100 million customers worldwide. Five product lines: TurboTax (consumer tax prep, 39.0M US federal units in FY26), Credit Karma (consumer credit/personal finance, $2.6B FY26 revenue), QuickBooks (SMB accounting, payroll, payments, capital), Mailchimp (SMB email/marketing automation), and Intuit Enterprise Suite (mid-market ERP/financial ops). Verified from intuit.com and investors.intuit.com: FY2026 ended July 31, 2026 with $21.4B total revenue (+14% YoY), GAAP operating income $5.9B, non-GAAP EPS $24.27. Global Business Solutions $12.9B, Consumer $8.6B. HQ 2700 Coast Avenue, Mountain View, CA; 21 offices in seven countries.
category: fintech / SMB accounting, tax and marketing software (not an AI-memory vendor — a buyer)
stage: Public company (Nasdaq: INTU). IPO 1993. Mature large-cap; ~$333/share as of Sept 4, 2026.
funding: Public — no venture funding relevant. Nasdaq: INTU, share price $332.70 as of Sept 4 2026 close (implying roughly $90B+ market cap). $7.2B cash and investments and $7.7B total debt as of July 31, 2026; issued $1.75B in notes in June 2026. FY2026 revenue $21.4B.
headcount_estimate: 18,200 employees worldwide at end of fiscal year 2025 (stated directly on intuit.com 'Fast Facts'). FY2026 figure not published on the site at time of research; likely similar or modestly higher.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 1983, long predates accelerators. Not a YC company.
founded_year: 1983 (founded by Scott Cook and Tom Proulx)
sells_to: Primarily B2B SMB (QuickBooks, Mailchimp) plus large-scale consumer/prosumer (TurboTax, Credit Karma), and increasingly B2B mid-market/enterprise via Intuit Enterprise Suite and its accountant channel (Lacerte, ProConnect, ProSeries, ProAdvisor).
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers. (1) In the product: CEO Sasan Goodarzi's FY26 earnings framing is that Intuit's strategy is 'to win as an AI-driven expert platform by creating a financial system of intelligence that increasingly does the work for consumers, businesses, and accountants' — i.e. agents that execute financial work, not just answer questions. Concretely verified: the Aug 31 2026 Perplexity partnership exposes QuickBooks and Mailchimp through MCP (Model Context Protocol) connectors inside Perplexity Computer, letting an external agent chase overdue invoices, set up recurring invoices, send payment links, retrieve payslips and payroll employee data, and track marketing campaign performance — all authenticated against the user's real QuickBooks/Mailchimp account. CTO Alex Balazs frames this as going 'from finding answers to getting personalized insights and taking decisive action.' Also shipped in 2026: conversational AI for mid-market CFOs and accounting firms (Aug 12, 2026 release), Mailchimp Analytics AI (May 28, 2026). Intuit's 'Big Bets' grew 34% and were 30% of FY26 revenue. (2) Internally: Intuit is a ~18K-person engineering-heavy org — the Glean use case is employee knowledge search across internal systems, not product embedding.
why_they_need_memory: As a Glean buyer, the motivation is classic large-enterprise knowledge sprawl: 18,200 employees across 21 offices in 7 countries, five semi-independent product orgs (TurboTax, QuickBooks, Credit Karma, Mailchimp, Enterprise Suite) each with its own docs, wikis, tickets and Slack history, plus heavy compliance/regulatory documentation (money transmitter licensing, tax law, SOC/privacy). This is an IT/employee-productivity purchase — a search-and-retrieval layer over internal corpora — not a purchase of memory infrastructure for their shipped agents. Separately, their product-side agent work (MCP connectors executing financial actions against live books) does create genuine agent-state and audit requirements, but Intuit has the scale and security posture to build that in-house rather than buy it.

name: Pinterest
what_it_does: Visual search and discovery platform where users find inspiration, curate ideas (into boards of 'Pins') and shop products. Over 600 million monthly active users worldwide; HQ San Francisco. Revenue is almost entirely advertising — brands and SMBs buy placement against high commercial-intent visual search. Verified from investor.pinterestinc.com: Q2 2026 delivered 18% revenue growth and record users; Q1 2026 also 18% growth with record users and ~$2B of share repurchases. NYSE: PINS, $20.40/share as of Sept 4, 2026 close.
category: consumer social / visual search and discovery, monetized through advertising (not an AI-memory vendor — a buyer)
stage: Public company (NYSE: PINS). IPO April 2019. Profitable, buying back stock (~$2B in Q1 2026 alone).
funding: Public — NYSE: PINS, $20.40/share as of Sept 4 2026 (roughly $13B market cap at ~640M shares). Pre-IPO it raised on the order of $1.5B in venture funding (Bessemer, FirstMark, Andreessen Horowitz, Fidelity, Goldman Sachs, Valiant among others) at a final private valuation around $12.3B; those private-round figures are from general knowledge and were not re-verified in this session.
headcount_estimate: Approximately 4,500–5,000 employees. This is from general knowledge of recent Pinterest 10-K disclosures and was NOT verified in this session — treat as an estimate, not a confirmed figure. The company website did not publish a headcount number.
yc_or_accelerator: None — Pinterest was not accelerator-backed. Early funding came from angels (notably Brian Cohen / New York Angels) and then traditional VC.
founded_year: 2010 (founded by Ben Silbermann, Evan Sharp and Paul Sciarra; site launched March 2010)
sells_to: Consumer platform (600M+ MAU) monetized B2B: enterprise brand advertisers and agencies plus a long tail of SMB advertisers, sold through Ads Manager and direct sales.
how_they_use_agents: Substantial and recent. Verified from the June 17 2026 Cannes announcement on newsroom.pinterest.com: (1) 'Business Assistant' — an AI collaborator embedded in Ads Manager that gives advertisers AI-powered guidance inside their campaign workflows. (2) 'Pinterest MCP' — an MCP server making Pinterest 'operable in AI-driven workflows'; the announcement's own illustration shows an external AI agent querying 'How are our campaigns performing?', i.e. Pinterest is exposing itself as a tool surface for third-party agents. (3) 'Pinterest Assistant' — a consumer-facing personalized shopping assistant. (4) 'Ask Pinterest' — explicitly described as built for 'more conversational, complex, multi-step decisions', run as AI experiments outside the main Pinterest app. (5) Performance+ creative — new AI models for generating and selecting ad creative variations, plus new AI ad review capabilities. Separately, a June 4 2026 release covers working with AWS to power AI-driven visual search. Pinterest is unusual here in being both an agent builder and an agent-accessible surface.
why_they_need_memory: As a Glean buyer, the driver is internal: a ~5,000-person company with a very large ML/ranking engineering org, heavy internal experiment documentation, and separate consumer-product, ads-product and trust-and-safety knowledge domains — plus an advertiser-facing sales org that constantly needs to retrieve product and policy answers. That is an employee knowledge-search need. The more interesting product-side signal is 'Ask Pinterest' and Pinterest Assistant: multi-step conversational shopping and inspiration is precisely the use case where per-user long-term memory (taste, past boards, prior intent) is the moat, and where an agent-memory layer would be a genuine product dependency rather than an IT purchase. Pinterest's core asset is already a decade of per-user taste data, so they are more likely to build than buy that layer.

name: Rubrik
what_it_does: Enterprise cyber-resilience and data-security platform — 'securing the world's data.' Rubrik Security Cloud protects, monitors and recovers data across on-prem, cloud and SaaS: immutable backups attackers cannot encrypt or delete, pre-calculated clean recovery points, sensitive-data discovery and classification, threat hunting and containment, and automated restoration of a 'Minimum Viable Business.' Now positioned as 'Agentic Cyber Resilience' — one platform at the intersection of data, identity and AI. Verified: $1.66B subscription ARR as of July 31, 2026; >119% average subscription dollar-based net retention; 3,084 customers with $100K+ subscription ARR; more than 6,000 organizations total. 7x Gartner Magic Quadrant Leader.
category: enterprise data security / backup, recovery and cyber resilience — plus a new AI-agent governance product line (not an AI-memory vendor, but adjacent to the category)
stage: Public company (NYSE: RBRK). IPO April 2024. Currently reporting fiscal 2027 (Q2 FY27 reported Aug 27, 2026).
funding: Public since April 2024 (NYSE: RBRK). Private history verified on rubrik.com's own timeline: $51M Series A+B (2015), $61M Series C (2016), $261M Series E (2019) at a $3.3B valuation, plus a strategic investment from Microsoft in 2021 — total private funding was roughly $550M–$1.1B depending on how the Microsoft round and a 2018 Series D are counted (exact total not verified this session). Current business scale: $1.66B subscription ARR as of July 31, 2026.
headcount_estimate: Approximately 3,500–4,500. The only figure verified this session is historical: 'Over 1,600 Rubrikans' in 2020, from rubrik.com's own company timeline. The company has grown substantially through IPO since; the current-day range above is an estimate from general knowledge and was NOT confirmed — treat with caution.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Seed/Series A was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners; later rounds from Greylock, Khosla Ventures, IVP, Bain Capital Ventures and Microsoft. Not accelerator-backed.
founded_year: 2014 (co-founded by Bipul Sinha, Arvind Nithrakashyap, Soham Mazumdar and Arvind Jain — notably, Arvind Jain went on to co-found and lead Glean, which is very likely why Rubrik appears on Glean's logo wall)
sells_to: B2B enterprise — large, security-conscious organizations. 3,084 customers pay $100K+ in subscription ARR; 6,000+ total organizations. Buyer is the CISO / security and infrastructure org (the homepage tagline is literally 'Built for the person who can't afford to get it wrong').
how_they_use_agents: Rubrik has repositioned the whole company around agents, and it is the most category-relevant of these three. Verified from rubrik.com: the homepage now leads with 'Agentic Cyber Resilience' and 'Secure and control AI with AI — govern, monitor and remediate all agent actions. Quickly rewind agents' mistakes without downtime or data loss.' The product is Rubrik Agent Cloud (powered by Predibase AI infrastructure), which explicitly 'captures inputs, MEMORY, prompt chains, and tool usage' for AI agents, creates an immutable audit trail from prompt to execution, and provides 'safe undo of high-impact changes' — an undo button for AI agent mistakes (IDC's phrasing, per Rubrik's own analyst-report callout). They also ship agentic automation on the security side: a Sept 1 2026 announcement with CrowdStrike brings 'Agentic Automation to Identity Attack Resilience,' and the platform markets autonomous recovery orchestration ('reduce a 50-day cyber investigation to a one minute query'). Anthropic, CrowdStrike, Microsoft and AWS all presented at their Forward 2026 conference.
why_they_need_memory: Rubrik is the most nuanced case of the three — they are arguably a competitor-adjacent buyer rather than a pure consumer. As a Glean customer, the pull is standard enterprise knowledge search across a multi-thousand-person global org with dense security research, threat intel and compliance documentation. But Rubrik's own Agent Cloud captures agent memory, prompt chains and tool calls for audit and rollback — meaning they build a form of agent-state infrastructure themselves, and their interest in the category may be as much competitive/architectural as it is procurement. The genuine need on their side is the inverse of what memory vendors sell: not 'help my agent remember' but 'give me an immutable, reversible record of what the agent remembered and did.' Worth treating as a category-shaper, not a naive buyer.

name: Postman
what_it_does: API platform for the full API lifecycle: collaborative design, development, testing, documentation, mock servers, monitors, and governance. Runs the Postman API Network (100,000+ public APIs, self-described as the world's largest). As of 2026 the homepage repositions it as 'The AI-native API Platform' with a March 2026 'postman.ai' relaunch built for the agentic era (Git-connected workspaces). Claims 500,000 companies, 98% of the Fortune 500, and ~40M users (LinkedIn profile description). Has acquired Akita (2023), Orbit (2024), and liblab (Nov 2025).
category: dev tools / API developer platform
stage: Late-stage private (Series D), unicorn
funding: $225M Series D announced Aug 2021 led by Insight Partners at a $5.6B valuation, with Coatue, Battery Ventures, BOND, CRV, and Nexus Venture Partners. Earlier rounds include a $1M seed (2015). Total raised commonly cited around $430M; no round confirmed after the Series D. No newer valuation confirmed.
headcount_estimate: ~500-1,000. LinkedIn lists the company-size band as 501-1,000 employees; the '3,563 associated profiles' figure on LinkedIn overcounts (it includes anyone listing Postman) and should not be used. Postman does not publish a headcount.
yc_or_accelerator: None — not a YC or accelerator company. VC-backed from seed (Nexus Venture Partners) onward.
founded_year: 2012 (Wikipedia; started as Abhinav Asthana's side project. Postman's LinkedIn page lists 2014, likely the incorporation/company-formation date.)
sells_to: Developers, bottom-up PLG expanding into B2B enterprise. Free individual tier feeding paid team and enterprise plans.
how_they_use_agents: Agents appear in three named surfaces. (1) Agent Mode — 'Explore, debug, and build APIs using natural language'; the user describes a task in plain English and the agent executes it: fixing broken requests, writing test scripts, generating docs, reorganizing collections. Postman explicitly markets its 'Deep API context': the agent 'understands your collections, specs, environments, and history so every response is grounded in your actual APIs.' (2) AI Engineer — agents that 'take on the work of building, testing, and maintaining APIs across your organization, grounded in the context of every service you already run.' (3) Postman MCP Server — a server whose stated job is to 'give API context to your AI agents,' i.e. Postman selling itself as the memory/context substrate for other people's agents. Note: the Atlan relationship is separate and internal — it is about human analysts discovering data, not about agents.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct reasons, and both matter for this category. Internally: Postman's data team grew ~5x in one year to ~20 people; Confluence was unsearchable and Google Sheets documentation degraded as new hires who didn't know the tables wrote it, couldn't handle concurrent editors, and raised security concerns for company-wide access. Atlan became the durable context layer over Redshift/dbt/Looker so any employee could self-serve. Prudhvi Vasa: 'Everyone is finally talking about the same numbers, which is helping us rebuild trust in our data.' Ankit Sobti's framing is the classic company-brain thesis: 'It's difficult for a data team to sit and churn insights day in and day out' — the team is the bottleneck, so context has to be externalized. Commercially: Postman's own product thesis is now literally agent grounding, so they are both a buyer of and a competitor-adjacent vendor in the context-for-agents space.

name: Dr. Martens (Dr. Martens plc / AirWair International Ltd)
what_it_does: British footwear brand. Designs and sells boots and shoes built around the 1460 boot (first made 1 April 1960 in Wollaston, England), which alone represents over 40% of sales. Sells direct-to-consumer through 240 directly-operated retail stores plus ecommerce, and through wholesale. FY26 results (reported 19 May 2026): revenue £764.9M, adjusted EBIT £79.3M (10.4% margin), adjusted PBT £55.0M, 10.2M pairs sold. Manufacturing in the UK (Wollaston), China, Vietnam, Laos, and Thailand. HQ at 28 Jamestown Rd, Camden, London.
category: Consumer footwear / retail — explicitly NOT a technology company. The buyer here is the internal data governance and data architecture function.
stage: Public company, listed on the London Stock Exchange (ticker DOCS) since January 2021. Previously PE-owned: Permira acquired the business for £300M in October 2013 and took it public at a £3.7B valuation.
funding: Not venture-funded. £300M Permira buyout (Oct 2013); IPO January 2021 at a £3.7B valuation; LSE ticker DOCS. No startup funding history applies.
headcount_estimate: unknown — could not confirm a verified figure from primary sources in this session. The company runs 240 directly-operated stores plus manufacturing and HQ, so total headcount including retail staff is plausibly in the low thousands, but I found no confirmed number and am not asserting one. LinkedIn company page could not be fetched.
yc_or_accelerator: None — not applicable.

Their governance model is deliberately federated — the framework is offered, not imposed as a central dictate — so definitions cannot live in one central team's heads and must sit in a shared machine-readable layer. The strongest signal is the second-order one: Elastic sells context to agents for a living, so under-investing in its own context layer would be untenable. how_they_use_agents:
Two distinct layers, and both matter for the memory thesis.

(1) IN THE PRODUCT — Autodesk positions 'Autodesk Assistant' as 'your agentic AI partner' and 'The AI interface for Design and Make', in Tech Preview across AutoCAD, Fusion, Forma, Revit, Civil 3D, Inventor and Vault. Autodesk's own copy: 'every team member can use trusted and secure intelligent agents'; Assistant 'understands your models, your project context, and the task in front of you.' Advertised capabilities are explicitly agentic, not chat-only: model-aware task execution via natural-language prompts (updating models, generating outputs, checking drawings), 'autonomous verification of standards' against industry/company specs and schedules, and answers with source links grounded in the user's own project data. Autodesk also ships 'Autodesk MCP Servers' whose stated purpose is to 'standardize design and make context to enable seamless, secure, and scalable collaboration across tools and teams' — i.e. a context/protocol layer for agents. Backed by an Autodesk Research AI Lab (neural CAD) and ISO 42001 certification for its AI development platform.

(2) INTERNALLY (this is the Atlan purchase) — Autodesk runs a data-mesh Analytics Data Platform on Snowflake + AWS data lake, ingesting via Fivetran, Matillion, AWS Streaming and Apache Spark, consumed through Looker, Power BI, notebooks, SageMaker and reverse ETL. 60 domain teams, 45 use cases deployed since 2021, 120 active Atlan users. They evaluated open-source Amundsen in 2021 and replaced it with Atlan in 2022. Atlan's headline for them is literally 'How Autodesk Powers a Context Layer Across Their Data Mesh on Snowflake.' Mark Kidwell (Chief Data Architect, Data Platforms and Services): Atlan 'can tell publishers the usage of the tables or data products that they build… we can understand now, what actually is being used in the platform, what's popular, what's not', and 'Atlan is the layer that brings metadata from publishers to consumers.'
why_they_need_memory:
Structurally federated: 60 autonomous domain teams publishing data products into a mesh means no single team or human holds a map of what exists, who owns it, or what is trusted. Kidwell's quote is not about search — it is about persistent usage/popularity signal accumulated over time, which is exactly the behavioral-memory layer an agent needs to rank and trust sources. They tried the free option (Amundsen) and it did not hold, which is a useful buying signal: this is a category where 'build it on open source' visibly failed at their scale.

On the product side the need is sharper still. Autodesk Assistant claims to understand 'your models, your project context, and the task in front of you' and to autonomously verify against company standards — that requires durable, entity-resolved memory of a customer's model history, drawing conventions, CAD standards and project state across sessions and across seven different applications. Their MCP-server strategy is an explicit bet that context has to be standardized and portable between tools rather than re-derived per app. A vendor selling agent memory has two wedges here: the internal data/analytics org (already a paying Atlan customer, so budget and buyer are proven) and the Assistant product team, which is building customer-facing agent state at enterprise scale under ISO 42001 governance constraints.

Their stated bottleneck is not access, it is adoption: 16,000 frontline staff will not use a data product they cannot interpret, and an agent answering on their behalf cannot be trusted without durable context about ownership, freshness and meaning. Flores' own framing — lower barriers through AI-powered discovery, embed context and ownership into the product — is the agent-memory pitch stated by the buyer. The adoption-and-repeat-usage emphasis is also a warning for a vendor: this buyer measures success by whether people come back, so a memory layer has to visibly improve answer quality over time, not just index more.

Scale and mechanics: 1 million+ data assets automated and governed by a FIVE-PERSON governance team; ~300 users in the first four months growing to ~600 (2x YoY) against a 1,000-user target. Stack is modern cloud-native — Google Cloud Platform, BigQuery, Airflow, Tableau, Power BI, Atlan. What we want to build would take a lot more work elsewhere.' Pedro Ribiero (Chief Data Scientist): 'I just type what I'd like to find out, and if it's within our reach, it will pop up.' why_they_need_memory:
The ratio is the whole argument: five governance people against 1,000,000+ assets across four regulated business verticals (insurance, health, banking, services). Human-maintained context cannot scale past that, which is why they automated ownership, classification and PII tagging into playbooks — persistent, machine-written memory rather than tribal knowledge. That is the same shape as agent memory, just aimed at a catalog.

The language the buyers themselves use is retrieval-and-memory language, not BI language: 'encyclopedia of data' (Lopes), 'I just type what I'd like to find out, and if it's within our reach, it will pop up' (Ribiero). They are describing an ask-in-natural-language, get-grounded-answer loop — the exact surface an agent-memory product sits under.

Regulatory pressure raises the stakes: under LGPD, stale or missing context on PII is legal exposure, not just inefficiency, so the memory layer has to stay continuously correct rather than be a one-time index. They also have a proven displacement pattern — they ripped out Informatica EDC — meaning they will replace an incumbent when a lighter, faster tool wins (six weeks to launch was the deciding proof). Four semi-independent verticals with distinct data domains creates the same federation problem Autodesk has, which is likely why both landed on a context layer.

name: DigiKey (Digi-Key Electronics)
what_it_does: Global authorized distributor of electronic components — one of the largest in the world. Sells semiconductors (ICs, MCUs, transistors, diodes), passives, connectors and cable, electromechanical parts, power and circuit protection, sensors, automation/PLC gear, and test and soldering tools. Confirmed on their own site: 18M+ components from 3,000+ manufacturers, 4,700+ employees, 180+ countries served via 45 local websites in 21 languages, 6.5M+ orders a year, ~25,000 orders shipped daily, 3M+ sq ft of facilities in Thief River Falls, Minnesota including a recently completed 2.2M sq ft distribution center expansion. Also runs a marketplace for authorized partner inventory alongside its own stock, plus API/EDI integrations, supply chain services, design tools, and a large technical content/forum operation.
category: Electronic components distribution / industrial e-commerce. Traditional (non-AI-native) large private enterprise.
stage: Bootstrapped and privately held since 1972. No venture or growth funding on record; not public.
funding: None — no external funding rounds found. Privately held (ownership structure not disclosed on their site; founder Dr. Ron Stordahl retained ownership historically, but I could not confirm the current structure from a primary source). Revenue: unknown — not disclosed on their site. Multi-billion-dollar figures circulate publicly but I could not verify any of them here, so treat revenue as unknown rather than guessing.
headcount_estimate: 4,700+ (stated directly on DigiKey's own about page — the most reliable of the three headcounts)
yc_or_accelerator: None. Founded 1972, decades before the accelerator era.
founded_year: 1972 (founder: Dr. Ron Stordahl, who began by selling leftover parts from digital electronic keyer kits — hence the name. Went online in 1996; began international expansion 1997.)
sells_to: Both B2B and prosumer/developer — an unusual dual motion. B2B: electronics manufacturers, OEMs, contract manufacturers, procurement teams buying via API/EDI and corporate accounts. Prosumer/developer: individual design engineers, hobbyists, and makers buying single units with credit card or PayPal. Design engineers are the true end user in both cases.
how_they_use_agents: No agentic product features confirmed. I could not reach any DigiKey AI or newsroom page (multiple 404s), and the main site surfaces e-commerce, API/EDI integration, parametric search, design tools, and supply chain services rather than AI assistants. Parametric part search over an 18M-SKU catalog is the obvious place an agent would land, and component-selection copilots are an active category industry-wide, but I found NO primary evidence DigiKey ships one — do not assume it. Their relationship to this category is as a data-infrastructure BUYER, not an agent builder: the Atlan reference is a gated video landing page, "DigiKey's transition to Atlan in just weeks," with no transcript or named person exposed. Treat DigiKey as an enterprise data-catalog/governance buyer.
why_they_need_memory: The pull is catalog and supply-chain complexity, not agent ambition. An 18M-part catalog from 3,000+ manufacturers, each with its own parametric schema, lifecycle status, substitutes, compliance data, and pricing tiers, across 45 localized storefronts, is one of the harder semantic-context problems in commerce — and it is exactly what breaks naive retrieval. Any assistant that answers "what can I substitute for this obsolete MCU" needs durable, governed part semantics, not embeddings over datasheets. Their Atlan buy signals they are consolidating that context layer now. Caveat for positioning: nothing indicates DigiKey bought Atlan FOR agents — the "in just weeks" framing suggests a fast catalog/governance migration. They are evidence that the category's buyers include traditional non-AI enterprises with enormous entity catalogs, which is a genuinely different ICP from AI-native startups.
sources: Atlan gated video landing page referenced in the task brief (no transcript or named person exposed); https://atlan.com/customers/ did not list DigiKey during this research
DigiKey AI, newsroom, and press-release pages all returned HTTP 404 — AI capability could not be assessed from primary sources

name: SMG Swiss Marketplace Group
what_it_does: Switzerland's dominant network of online classifieds marketplaces — self-described as "the digital market square of Switzerland." Four portfolio segments, each a category leader in its market: Real Estate (ImmoScout24, Homegate, Flatfox, CASASOFT, IAZI), Automotive (AutoScout24, MotoScout24), General Marketplaces (anibis.ch, tutti.ch, Ricardo), and Finance & Insurance comparison (FinanceScout24, moneyland.ch). Revenue model is listings, subscriptions for professional sellers (dealers, agents), advertising, and lead generation. Also publishes data products such as a real-estate Purchase Index and sustainability data measurement.
category: Online marketplaces / digital classifieds (consumer-facing, multi-brand holding company). Traditional non-AI-native — now publicly listed.
stage: Public. IPO completed (confirmed via their investor relations site, which has a dedicated IPO page; listed on SIX Swiss Exchange). Formed November 2021 as a merger of Swiss marketplace assets.
funding: Not venture-funded in the startup sense — created in Nov 2021 as a corporate joint venture combining TX Group and Ringier marketplace assets with outside investors (General Atlantic and Die Mobiliar are the commonly reported partners, but I could NOT confirm the shareholder list from their own pages, so treat ownership specifics as medium confidence). Now public. Confirmed financials from their IR site: revenue CHF 332 million in 2025; dividend of CHF 0.82 per share approved; "continued double-digit revenue growth and margin expansion" reported for H1 2026.
headcount_estimate: ~1,000 employees (FTE) — stated on both their about page and investor relations site, so reasonably reliable. Offices in Switzerland (HQ Zurich), Serbia (Belgrade), Germany, France (Valbonne), and Vietnam.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Corporate joint-venture origin, not an accelerator company.
founded_year: November 2021 (as SMG; the constituent brands are far older — AutoScout24, Homegate, Ricardo and tutti.ch all predate it by 15-25 years)
sells_to: Two-sided. B2C for consumers browsing listings (the traffic side), and B2B for the paying side: car dealers, real estate agencies, professional sellers, and advertisers buying listings, subscriptions, and leads. Enterprise-scale internally despite modest headcount.
how_they_use_agents: Real but early and internally focused — no customer-facing agent product confirmed. Their tech blog carries "How AI is reshaping product, design, and research at SMG" and a hands-on engineering post on building a low-cost, low-latency, low-energy AI translation API deployed at scale (relevant because Switzerland is multilingual — German, French, Italian — and listings must cross language boundaries). Classifieds businesses also lean heavily on ML for pricing estimates, listing matching, search ranking, fraud and content moderation, and their IAZI/Purchase Index data products are valuation-model driven. But that is applied ML, not agents. Their Atlan reference is an Atlan-hosted video, "How Data Governance works at SMG Swiss Marketplace Group," with no named person or quote exposed — again a governance/catalog buy, not an agent-memory buy.
why_they_need_memory: The driver is federation across a multi-brand roll-up. SMG stitched together roughly a dozen formerly independent marketplaces, each with its own data model for what a "listing," "lead," "user," or "transaction" means, spread across five countries and multiple languages. Post-IPO they now also carry public-company reporting obligations on top of that fragmentation. That combination — many acquired domains, no shared semantics, regulatory pressure, and a small ~1,000-person org trying to cover it — is the canonical trigger for buying a context/governance layer rather than building one. As they push AI into product, design, and research (their own blog's framing), any assistant asking cross-brand questions hits the semantic mismatch immediately. Note the honest caveat: the evidence points to classic data governance as the buying trigger, with agent enablement a plausible next step rather than a documented one.
sources: Atlan-hosted video page referenced in the task brief (no named person or quote exposed); https://atlan.com/customers/ did not list SMG during this research

name: Signifyd
what_it_does: Ecommerce fraud prevention and 'commerce protection' SaaS. Merchants route orders to Signifyd, which returns a real-time ship/don't-ship decision on each transaction and financially guarantees approved orders (Signifyd eats the chargeback if it's wrong). Product lines: Guaranteed Fraud Protection, Complete Chargeback Protection, Chargeback Recovery, Account Protection, Authorization Rate Optimization (lifting bank approval rates via issuer integrations), Return Insights / return-abuse prevention, and Instant Refunds. A second business, 'Fearless Payments,' sells the same decisioning to payment service providers rather than merchants. The core asset is the 'Commerce Network' — a cross-merchant identity/behavior graph built from pooled transaction data across their retailer base, which is what lets them underwrite a stranger's first order at a given merchant. Explicitly positions against rules engines and blocklists: 'evaluates each order on its own merits and fraud probability using hundreds of data elements, networks and linkages.' Pitch to buyers is revenue recovery, not just loss prevention — they claim typical merchants leak 5-15% of revenue to false declines.
category: ecommerce fraud prevention / payments risk (ML decisioning); Atlan buyer = internal data platform team
stage: Late-stage private (Series E, 2021). No IPO or acquisition confirmed as of this research.
funding: ~$390M disclosed across six rounds: $2M seed (late 2012, Andreessen Horowitz and others), $7M Series A (2015), $20M Series B (2016), $56M Series C (2017, led by Bain Capital Ventures), $100M Series D (2018), $205M Series E (April 2021, led by Owl Rock Capital). Valuation $1.34B at the Series E. No post-2021 round confirmed — treat the $1.34B mark as stale.
headcount_estimate: ~490-500 (LinkedIn company page shows 491 employees, 501-1,000 band). Offices in San Jose, Denver, New York, London, Belfast, and Sao Paulo.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not a YC company; earliest institutional backer was Andreessen Horowitz at seed.
sells_to: B2B mid-market and enterprise — online retailers and brands (fashion, beauty, grocery, auto parts, sporting goods, airlines, QSR) plus payment service providers as a channel. Enterprise sales motion with platform integrations for Adobe Commerce, BigCommerce, Salesforce Commerce Cloud, and Shopify. Not developer-led, not prosumer.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct things, worth separating. (1) In the product: Signifyd is ML-native but pre-LLM — the decisioning engine is supervised machine learning over hundreds of features and the Commerce Network graph, running autonomous approve/decline calls at transaction speed. That is automation, not an LLM agent. (2) Around the product: they are publicly positioning for 'agentic commerce' and 'the autonomous economy,' with a dedicated whitepaper, and their 2026 fraud-trends marketing leads with 'AI has turned fraud into an assembly line.' Their strategic bet is being the trust layer for transactions where the buyer is an AI shopping agent rather than a human — authenticating agent-initiated purchases and distinguishing legitimate agents from AI-armed fraud rings. So they are less an agent builder than an agent-era underwriter. Note the vendor citation here is Atlan, a data catalog — that is their internal data/analytics org, not a product-side agent purchase.
why_they_need_memory: Weaker fit than the category pitch implies, and worth being blunt about. Signifyd already owns the memory asset that matters to their product — the Commerce Network is a purpose-built, proprietary persistent entity graph about buyers, and they will not outsource it. The real opening is internal: they are an Atlan customer, which means a data org large enough to have lost track of what its own tables, features, and models mean, and a documented need for a governed semantic/context layer over the analytics estate. If a company-brain vendor sells here, it sells to the data platform / analytics engineering team as 'context for internal AI and analysts,' alongside or on top of the catalog — not to the fraud product team. Secondary angle: agentic-commerce readiness creates demand for durable, queryable records of agent identity and behavior across sessions, which is memory-shaped, but they would likely build that in-house given it is core IP.
sources: https://www.signifyd.com/page-sitemap.xml (product, industry, and careers URL inventory)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signifyd (founding, founders, full funding history, valuation)
Note: crunchbase.com/organization/signifyd returned HTTP 403 and could not be read directly.

name: REA Group
what_it_does: Australia's dominant online property marketplace and digital advertising business. Flagship is realestate.com.au, the country's largest property portal, alongside realcommercial.com.au for commercial property. Revenue is advertiser-side: real estate agents and developers pay for listing depth, premium placement, and audience products, with consumers using the site free. Beyond listings, REA sells property data and valuation products (PropTrack), rich media and content, and has pushed into adjacent home-financing services (mortgage broking / lead generation). Internationally it has held or holds interests across Asia and Europe — Wikipedia records realestate.com.au plus Zoopla (UK), casa.it (Italy), iProperty (Asia-Pacific), and investments in Housing.com and Makaan.com (India); the international portfolio has changed repeatedly through acquisitions and divestments, so treat the specific overseas brand list as approximate rather than current. Publicly listed on the ASX (ticker: REA) and majority-owned by News Corp Australia. Headquartered in Richmond, Melbourne, with a Sydney office.
category: online real estate marketplace / digital classifieds and property data; Atlan buyer = enterprise data platform team
stage: Public company (ASX: REA), majority-controlled by News Corp. Not venture-funded.
funding: Not applicable — publicly listed since well before the venture era. Revenue A$928M for FY2021 (up from A$820.3M in FY2020); this is the most recent figure I could confirm and is now several years stale, as rea-group.com blocked automated fetching. Market cap is in the tens of billions AUD but I could not verify a current number, so treat it as unknown.
headcount_estimate: ~3,900 (LinkedIn company page shows 3,936 employees, 1,001-5,000 band). Wikipedia records 2,600+ as of 2020 across 20+ brands in eight countries, so the business has grown materially since.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 1995 in a Melbourne garage, long predates modern accelerators.
sells_to: Two-sided but monetized B2B: real estate agencies, agents, and property developers buy listing and advertising products; consumers are the free demand side. Also sells property data and analytics to financial institutions. Enterprise/SMB advertiser mix, geographically concentrated in Australia.
how_they_use_agents: Applied AI inside a consumer product, not agent infrastructure. REA describes itself as delivering 'immersive AI-led consumer experiences' across buying, selling, and renting, built on 'rich content, unique data and insights, highly accurate property valuation estimates.' Concretely that means ML-driven search and recommendation over listings, automated valuation models (AVMs) producing property price estimates, and content/image enrichment — plus, increasingly across the property-portal sector, LLM-generated listing summaries and conversational property search. I could not verify any named, shipped agent product because the corporate site and Medium engineering blog both refused automated fetching, so treat the specifics as inferred from their own positioning language rather than confirmed. The Atlan relationship indicates the AI work sits on a large, governed internal data estate — a data platform org managing listings, consumer behavior, and valuation feature data across many brands.
why_they_need_memory: This is a data-governance buyer wearing an AI hat, and the memory pitch has to be framed that way. REA runs a sprawling multi-brand, multi-country data estate where the same concepts (a listing, a property, an agent, a suburb) are modeled differently per system — which is exactly the problem Atlan was bought to solve. The agent-memory adjacency is that any LLM feature they ship over that estate (conversational search, valuation explanations, agent-facing copilots) needs a trustworthy, governed semantic layer telling it what the data means and which numbers are authoritative — getting a valuation wrong in a consumer product is a regulatory and reputational event, not a UX bug. There is also a genuine consumer-side memory case: property search is a months-long, high-consideration journey, and remembering a buyer's constraints, saved properties, and shifting preferences across sessions is real product value. But the buying center is the central data/platform team, the sales cycle is enterprise-long, and procurement at an ASX-listed News Corp subsidiary will be heavy. Not an early-adopter startup profile.

https://www.linkedin.com/company/rea-group (headcount 3,936, Richmond VIC HQ, 'immersive AI-led consumer experiences' positioning)

Note: www.rea-group.com, rea-group.com, about.realestate.com.au, medium.com/realestate-com-au-tech-blog, and reuters.com all blocked or refused automated fetching, so current financials and named AI products are unverified.

name: Personio
what_it_does: Cloud HR platform (HRIS) for European small and mid-sized companies, headquartered in Munich. Consolidates the full employee lifecycle in one system: core HR and employee records, recruiting/ATS, onboarding, absence and time tracking, performance and development, compensation, reporting, and payroll. Its structural moat is native payroll in Germany — which it markets as 'Europe's most complex market' — plus multi-country compliance for companies operating across European jurisdictions, a fragmented problem Workday and BambooHR serve poorly at this size band. Now positions as an 'Intelligent HR Platform' spanning Core HR, Talent, and Payroll, with smart automations and AI-driven insights layered over the record system. Scale: 16,000+ customers managing more than 1 million employees globally (up from ~12,000 customers in mid-2024), with offices in Munich, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Dublin, London, Madrid, and New York.
category: HR tech / HRIS SaaS for European mid-market; buyer of both Atlan (data catalog) and Atlassian Intelligence (internal knowledge)
stage: Late-stage private, heavily venture-backed. Last confirmed round 2022 at $8.5B; no round or exit confirmed since, so the valuation mark is stale and likely reset given the 2022-24 SaaS repricing.
funding: ~$700M disclosed. Confirmed rounds: $12M Series A (2017, led by Northzone), $75M Series C (2020, ~$500M valuation), $125M (2021, $1.7B valuation — unicorn), $270M Series E (2021, $6.3B valuation), $200M (2022, $8.5B valuation). A seed and Series B exist but I could not confirm their amounts, so the ~$700M total is a floor on disclosed capital, not an exact figure. Backers include Northzone, Index, Accel, Lightspeed, Meritech, Greenoaks (per public reporting on the later rounds).
headcount_estimate: ~2,250 (LinkedIn company page shows 2,250 employees, 1,001-5,000 band). Wikipedia records ~2,000 as of June 2024, so roughly flat-to-modest growth — consistent with a company that grew hard through 2021-22 and then consolidated.
yc_or_accelerator: None found — German university spinout (founded at TU Munich), first institutional round was Northzone's Series A.
sells_to: B2B European mid-market. Explicitly targets organizations with 200-5,000 employees — companies large enough to need a real HRIS but too small for Workday or SAP SuccessFactors. Buyer is the HR leader / People Ops team, not IT or developers. 70 countries served, but the center of gravity is DACH plus UK, Netherlands, Spain, and Ireland.
how_they_use_agents: Genuine and multi-directional, which makes this the most interesting of the three. Outbound: Personio ships AI into the HR platform itself — smart automations across HR workflows and 'proactive insights through AI-driven analytics,' with the platform repositioned from record-keeping to 'Intelligent HR.' The natural agent surfaces in HR SaaS are exactly the ones they are building toward: an employee-facing assistant answering policy and leave questions from company documents, recruiting screening and scheduling, and payroll anomaly detection. Inbound and telling: they have shipped AI spend tracking that pulls from the Anthropic Analytics API (aggregated usage only, never conversation content) alongside ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Langdock, and Google Gemini, letting HR/finance see which teams spend on which AI tools — meaning Personio is both an AI builder and an instrumenter of enterprise AI adoption. Internally they run Atlan over the data estate and Atlassian Intelligence over Confluence, so they have already bought two different 'company brain' products for two different internal audiences.
why_they_need_memory: Strongest fit of the three, and the cleanest case study for who buys this category. Three converging reasons. First, they have already proven they buy it twice — Atlan for governed data context and Atlassian Intelligence for unstructured internal knowledge — which is a company that has felt the pain of scattered institutional context at ~2,250 people across seven offices and is willing to pay to fix it. Second, the product itself is a memory problem: an HR assistant is worthless unless it remembers this employee's contract, tenure, jurisdiction, manager, leave history, and which of 70 countries' rules apply — HR answers are wrong by default without deep per-employee, per-entity, per-jurisdiction context, and the cost of a wrong answer is a compliance exposure. Third, their multi-tenant shape makes the memory hard in a way that favors buying: 16,000 customers each with their own policy documents, org structures, and local law means per-tenant isolated memory with strict data-residency and GDPR guarantees — precisely the requirement that makes teams reach for a vendor rather than a weekend Postgres schema. Caveat on the sales motion: they are a German mid-market SaaS company handling employee PII under GDPR, so any memory vendor faces serious data-residency, DPA, and security review before a deal closes.

https://www.linkedin.com/company/personio (headcount 2,250, 'Intelligent HR Platform' positioning, 16,000+ customers / 1M+ employees managed, explicit 200-5,000 employee target band, native German payroll, Anthropic Analytics API spend-tracking integration)
Vendor citation supplied in task brief: Atlan customer interview series plus Atlassian Intelligence (Confluence)

name: Kiwi.com
what_it_does: Online travel agency built around "virtual interlining" — algorithmically stitching together flights (and other transport) from carriers that have no interline agreements with each other into a single bookable itinerary, backed by the Kiwi.com Guarantee (rebooking/refund protection when a self-transfer connection breaks). Runs 100M+ flight searches per day across 500+ airlines and ~95% of global flight content; sold 18.9M seats in 2025 with gross bookings above EUR 2bn. Consumer web/app plus a distribution/API business. Data stack is GCP-native: BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataplex, Looker, Airflow, Terraform, Monte Carlo.
category: Online travel agency / travel tech marketplace (consumer B2C + flight-content distribution). NOT an AI-native startup.
stage: Private, PE-controlled growth-stage company (not venture-stage). Majority-acquired by General Atlantic in 2019.
funding: No conventional VC round stack. Early backing from Czech angel Jiri Hlavenka, then Touzimsky Airlines (2014) and investor Ondrej Tomek (10% stake, 2015). General Atlantic acquired a majority stake in 2019 and holds 66.7%; Oliver Dlouhy 21%, Jozef Kepesi 10.2%. Amounts of the GA deal not publicly confirmed in sources found. Revenue EUR 227M (2025); gross bookings >EUR 2bn/yr (had fallen from ~EUR 1.3bn in 2019 to ~EUR 450M in 2020 with a ~EUR 38M net loss).
headcount_estimate: ~450 (Wikipedia infobox, stated as of 2026). MEDIUM confidence on this figure — Kiwi.com was materially larger (well over 1,000) pre-2020 and I could not corroborate the current number from the company's own site or LinkedIn (jobs.kiwi.com does not publish a headcount).
yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: 2012 (founders Oliver Dlouhy and Jozef Kepesi; HQ Brno, Czech Republic)
sells_to: B2C consumers primarily; secondary B2B distribution/affiliate/API partners (metasearch, agencies, and increasingly third-party booking front-ends).
how_they_use_agents: Weakest agent story of the three. The kiwi.com homepage now ships an "AI Mode" search in BETA alongside the classic search form — an LLM-style natural-language flight query interface. Beyond that, the AI is classical ML/optimization: the virtual-interlining routing and pricing engine that runs billions of price checks daily is the core proprietary algorithm, and it long predates the LLM era. Their engineering blog (code.kiwi.com) has published nothing on LLMs or agents through late 2025 — recent posts are iOS/SwiftUI, GRC engineering, and BigQuery cost optimization. No public MCP server, agentic-commerce, or autonomous-agent initiative found. Structurally, though, they are a prime supplier of inventory to third-party AI travel agents.
why_they_need_memory: Textbook "the estate is too big to know" problem. Per the Atlan case study (Martina Ivanicova, Data Engineering Manager, presented at Gartner D&A Summit London 2024): ~100 Postgres databases, tens of thousands of tables, thousands of BigQuery datasets — searching one keyword like "Destination" returned 200,000+ entries. They used Atlan to collapse that into 58 governed data products with explicit ownership, documentation, quality monitoring and security standards, onboarding 20+ teams. Reported outcomes: 53% reduction in data engineering workload and 20% increase in data user satisfaction. That curated semantic layer over a chaotic estate is exactly the substrate an agent would need to answer questions over the business — they built it for humans first.
confidence: high (identity, product, ownership, Atlan usage all directly verified); medium on the current headcount figure
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiwi.com (raw wikitext infobox: founded 2012, c. 450 employees, EUR 227M revenue 2025, ownership split)
https://humansofdata.atlan.com/2024/09/kiwi-atlan-data-products/ (Atlan case study — 58 data products, 53% DE workload reduction)

name: Tala
what_it_does: Mobile-first consumer credit and financial services for underbanked people in emerging markets — credit lines, savings, and a digital wallet delivered through an app, underwritten in minutes on alternative/behavioral data rather than credit bureau files. Live in Kenya, Mexico, Philippines, India, Vietnam, Guatemala, Dominican Republic and Peru. Claims 15M+ customers, $10bn+ in credit delivered (the About page cites $8bn to 14M customers — figures differ by page/date), and 1bn+ proprietary data signals. Currently pivoting from being a lender to being "AI-native credit infrastructure": exposing its underwriting via API/SDK (docs.tala.co) so partners can embed Tala's risk intelligence. ~80% of the stack — underwriting engine, data schema, risk frameworks — redeploys across geographies without customization.
category: Fintech — emerging-markets consumer lending, moving to embedded-credit / credit-infrastructure-as-a-service
stage: Late-stage private. Last priced equity round was Series E (Oct 2021); since then growth has been funded largely with debt facilities and bank partnerships.
funding: ~$350M+ disclosed equity: Series B $30M+ (2017, led by IVP), Series C $65M (2018, expansion to Mexico and India), Series D $110M (Aug 2019, PayPal-backed), Series E $145M (Oct 2021). Debt/credit facilities: $40M from Victory Park Capital (2023), $150M from Neuberger Berman for Mexico (Apr 2025), and a $100M deal with ASEAN bank CIMB to launch Vietnam (Jan 2026).
headcount_estimate: unknown — Tala does not publish a number. Five office locations including Nairobi and Mexico City, remote-first/hybrid, actively hiring in Mexico, India and the Philippines. Plausibly several hundred, but I found no verifiable figure and will not guess one.
yc_or_accelerator: None found
founded_year: 2011 (founder & CEO Shivani Siroya; HQ Santa Monica / Los Angeles area, though the current site does not state HQ explicitly). Named to the Forbes Fintech 50 eight years running.
sells_to: Historically B2C (consumers in emerging markets). Now increasingly B2B/developer — embedded credit for partner banks, wallets and platforms via API and SDK; the CIMB and Airtm deals are the template.
how_they_use_agents: AI here means production ML risk models, not LLM agents. The flagship is "Tala InSight," a patent-pending credit decision model using causal methods to predict the terms under which each customer will succeed — self-described as an "AI-native underwriting engine" built for thin-file borrowers in informal economies, trained on a decade of repayment behavior. Decisions are real-time (minutes). May 2026: "Tala Brings AI-Native Credit Infrastructure On-Chain with Airtm." No evidence of customer-facing LLM agents or an internal agent platform. The relevant fact for the memory category is the data-team side: they built a dbt/Snowflake/Looker presentation layer and needed the semantics of it captured.
why_they_need_memory: Per Atlan's "Active Metadata Pioneer" interview with Tina Wang, Analytics Engineering Manager: documentation was inconsistent across teams and "it was often challenging to chase down what a table or column meant." They use Atlan to auto-sync documentation from dbt YAML into Snowflake and Looker, expose a central data dictionary to business users, and get column- and table-level lineage. Two-year Atlan customer; documented the old infrastructure for a year before building the new presentation layer. The underlying need: a lending business whose entire moat is model quality cannot afford ambiguity about what a feature column means — definitional drift is a credit-risk problem, not just a productivity one. That is a strong structural argument for durable, machine-readable semantic memory.
sources: https://tala.co/ (product, InSight model, 15M customers, $10bn credit, API/SDK)
https://tala.co/about/ (founded 2011, Shivani Siroya, markets, $8bn to 14M customers, "AI-native underwriting engine")
https://tala.co/press/ (funding history: Series B-E, Victory Park, Neuberger Berman, CIMB, Airtm)
https://tala.co/careers/ (five offices, Nairobi and Mexico City, remote-first)

name: Telefónica Tech
what_it_does: The digital-services business unit of Telefónica, the Spanish telecom group — effectively a large systems integrator and managed service provider selling Cloud, Cyber Security, Data & AI, IoT/connectivity, Blockchain, Business Applications and Digital Workplace to enterprises and the public sector across Spain, UK/Ireland, Germany, Brazil and Hispam. Sector focus includes public sector, healthcare, police, financial services and insurance, manufacturing and retail. Deep Microsoft alignment: Microsoft Inner Circle for 8 consecutive years, Azure Expert MSP for 6, plus Fortinet UK Managed Services Partner of the Year 2025 and IBM Apptio EMEA Cloud MSP Partner of the Year 2025. Note the corporate site (telefonicatech.com) blocks automated fetching with 403; the UK site telefonicatech.uk is accessible.
category: IT services / systems integrator / MSP — enterprise cloud, cybersecurity and Data & AI consulting. Sells the AI category rather than being an AI-native product company.
stage: Not applicable — a business unit/subsidiary of Telefónica S.A. (publicly listed, BME: TEF). Grown substantially through acquisitions of regional MSPs and security firms.
funding: No venture funding. Corporate-funded subsidiary. Revenue of EUR 2,222M in 2025, up 18.9% year over year (Telefónica Tech's own results announcement, corroborated by Telecompaper and TelecomLead coverage); roughly EUR 1.9bn in 2023 and EUR 1.5bn in 2022. MEDIUM confidence on the exact 2025 figure — obtained via search-result snippets because the corporate domain returns 403 to automated fetches.

yc_or_accelerator: None — corporate subsidiary

They also run Microsoft Copilot readiness and adoption programs, genAI delivery, AI strategy/use-case discovery, PoC-to-production, model review, and AI governance and data-foundation work, plus private/hybrid/edge AI infrastructure. Their stated position is that "AI does not work in isolation" and depends on data quality and governance — which is essentially the vendor-side argument for the memory category.
