This is the classic enterprise driver for the category: leverage (few experts, many consumers) plus blast-radius/impact analysis, not AI ambition per se. It also makes them a credible reseller/channel signal — a company that buys a metadata brain internally is likely to recommend one to its own enterprise clients.

name: Optimizely
what_it_does: Digital experience platform (DXP) for enterprise marketing teams. Originally an A/B testing / experimentation tool (Optimizely Inc., 2010), now a consolidated suite spanning web content management (CMS), content marketing/orchestration (ex-Welcome), experimentation & feature flagging, personalization, commerce, and product analytics (ex-Netspring, ex-Zaius CDP). As of 2026 the whole platform is repositioned as 'the AI platform for marketing,' sold as three pillars: Agentic CMS, Agentic Experimentation, and the Optimizely Agent Platform. Claims 10,000+ brands including Nike, Zoom, Salesforce, Visa.
category: Martech / digital experience platform — now positioning as a marketing AI agent platform
stage: Private, PE-owned. Post-VC; majority-owned by Insight Partners (confirmed via an Insight Partners portfolio page for Optimizely). Not a startup — this is a mature ~$300-400M-revenue-class enterprise software vendor.
funding: Optimizely Inc. raised roughly $146M+ in disclosed VC before being acquired: $1.2M angel (2010), $28M Series A (2013), $57M Series B (2014), $58M Series C (2015). Acquired by Episerver in October 2020 (terms not officially disclosed) and rebranded to Optimizely in January 2021. Episerver itself was acquired by Insight Partners in 2018 (reported ~$1.16B, not verified in this research). Current funding/valuation: not disclosed. Do not treat the acquisition price as a known number.
headcount_estimate: ~1,600+ (self-reported on optimizely.com/about, 2026). Wikipedia listed 1,400+ as of May 2024, so headcount appears to have grown modestly. LinkedIn was not accessible (auth wall) during this research.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Traditional VC-backed (Benchmark, Bain Capital Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, Accel among reported early investors); never in an accelerator.
founded_year: 2010 (Optimizely Inc., by Dan Siroker and Pete Koomen, both ex-Google). The surviving legal/operating entity traces to Episerver, founded 1994 in Sweden. HQ widely reported as New York, NY — I could not confirm a corporate address on optimizely.com.
sells_to: B2B enterprise — CMOs, digital/marketing leaders, content and growth teams at large brands. Also mid-market. Developer-adjacent (feature flagging, headless CMS) but the buying center is marketing, not engineering.
how_they_use_agents: Deeply and explicitly. Optimizely ships an Agent Platform with 50+ out-of-the-box marketing agents plus a no-code agent builder, and in August 2026 launched 'Virtual Teammates' — persistent AI coworkers with defined roles, responsibilities and org permissions: Chief of Staff, SEO & AI Search Analyst, Marketing Analyst, Personalization Strategist, CRO Manager. Agents are dragged into multi-step workflows with scheduled triggers so they run autonomously; every output is scored against the customer's standards before human review. In September 2026 they announced marketing-specific post-trained models claiming 10x cost efficiency vs frontier LLMs, plus 'Mark-Bench,' an open-source benchmark of 285 marketing tasks (they report 67% vs 60% for Claude at half the cost). Their own boilerplate now says they give 'AI agents the content they come looking for.'
why_they_need_memory: This is close to a textbook buyer. Two separate memory problems. (1) Product-side: their own marketing announcement says Virtual Teammates 'retain relevant context from previous conversations, projects, and decisions so marketers do not have to continually re-explain how their organization works' — persistent cross-session agent memory is the headline feature they are selling. They built an internal data layer called Mark-IQ that holds each customer's experimentation and analytics history as brand context for the models. (2) Internal-side, which is why Atlan sold them: per Atlan's Oct 2024 'Active Metadata Pioneer' interview with Senior Data Architect Nevenka Perisic, Optimizely came out of multiple mergers with badly siloed data, stood up a new central Data Services function on Snowflake, and bought Atlan to build a single catalog of glossaries, dictionaries, lineage and data flows so anyone can pull 'all these data artifacts together with attributes linked to the right terms.' Her stated concern — exposing meaningful data 'without creating an unusable swamp' — is exactly the curation problem an agent-memory layer claims to solve. A company selling agentic marketing needs its own context layer to be trustworthy.

name: Global Excel Management Inc.

Group companies: Global Excel Europe, Global Excel Latam, Global Excel Indonesia, Hines & Associates, ACM (Active Care Management), CanAm, Vitori Health, First Assistance.
category: Healthcare / insurance services — medical cost containment, claims administration, TPA (not a software company)
stage: Private, independently owned. Explicitly describes itself as 'a privately owned company.' No disclosed VC or PE round found. Grown by a long string of acquisitions rather than by fundraising.
funding: unknown — no disclosed funding rounds. Privately held with no public financials. The only quantified figures are operational: $2.1B in claims processed annually, 1,900+ corporate clients. Acquisition history (self-reported): MedSave, Olympus, HCS, ChargeCare International, ACM & CanAm (2014-2018), Prima Sarana Jasa/Global Excel Indonesia (2017), investment in telemedicine provider Maple (2018), Hines & Associates (2021), WeeCompany/WeeMedic (2023), Vitori Health and First Assistance (2025). Deal values not disclosed.
headcount_estimate: 1,280+ employees across 9 countries (self-reported on globalexcel.com/aboutus). LinkedIn was not accessible (auth wall) during this research, so this is the company's own figure.
yc_or_accelerator: None — not applicable. This is a 1990s-founded services business, not a startup.
founded_year: 1996 — created as a claims-administration/case-management subsidiary of etfs, which was founded 1984 in Sherbrooke, Quebec. etfs was sold to Royal & Sun Alliance (now Intact) in 2011, at which point Global Excel became independent. HQ: 73 Queen Street, Sherbrooke, Quebec, Canada; US office at 777 Brickell Ave, Miami; plus Mexico City, Jakarta and European offices.
sells_to: B2B enterprise — insurers, reinsurers, assistance companies, third-party administrators, and self-funded health plans. Long sales cycles, regulated, PII/PHI-heavy. The end beneficiaries are policyholders and providers, but the buyer is an insurance carrier.
how_they_use_agents: Essentially none in the product, based on available evidence. Nothing on globalexcel.com or in their newsroom describes AI agents, copilots or automation products; their published content is about claims workflows, provider networks and cost containment. The only AI touchpoint found is as a *consumer*: in Atlan's Sept 2024 interview, Senior Data Analyst Kevin Nutbrown says 'Atlan AI' was a differentiator in their evaluation — natural-language, 'Google-style results' search so non-technical business users can ask what a data term means. This is AI-assisted data discovery for internal staff, not agents in the product. Treat any claim that Global Excel is an agent company as unsupported.
why_they_need_memory: Their driver is semantic consistency across acquired systems, which is the unglamorous core of the 'company brain' pitch. Nutbrown's stated problem: after ~30 years of acquisitive growth they had a table called 'Claim' in one system and a different table called 'Claim' in another, so different teams pulled the same metric and got different numbers, and long-tenured employees like him had become the human memory of what the data meant. They bought Atlan to make that institutional knowledge explicit — business glossary, lineage across Snowflake and MSSQL, data ownership, and PII access clarity — so business users can self-serve instead of routing every question to the tech team. Regulated PHI/PII adds a governance reason to have a curated, permissioned context layer rather than pointing an LLM at raw claims data. But note: the pain is data-governance and tribal-knowledge decay, not agent memory.

Business model is asset-light: ChargePoint mostly sells hardware plus a recurring cloud subscription to site hosts (businesses, fleets, multifamily, retail, municipalities) who own the stations, rather than owning charging assets itself. Self-reported: ~5,000 customers including 82% of the Fortune 50, 453M charges delivered, ~342,000 charging spots on the network as of Jan 2025.
category: EV charging infrastructure — hardware plus network SaaS (cleantech / industrial IoT)
stage: Public. NYSE: CHPT since a February 2021 SPAC merger with Switchback Energy. Currently a distressed/turnaround-stage public company, not a growth story: revenue has declined three straight years and it completed a reverse stock split after a Feb 2025 NYSE non-compliance notice for a sub-$1 average closing price.
funding: Public company — verified from SEC filings. FY2026 (year ended Jan 31, 2026): total revenue $411.2M (Networked Charging Systems $216.5M, Subscriptions $162.4M, Other $32.3M), gross profit $125.6M, net loss $220.2M. Prior years: FY2025 revenue $417.1M, FY2024 revenue $506.6M. Note the shape: hardware is shrinking ($360.8M to $216.5M over two years) while subscriptions grow ($120.4M to $162.4M) — the business is mixing toward software. Has 2028 Convertible Notes outstanding with a going-concern-adjacent reclassification risk flagged in the 10-K. Pre-SPAC private funding (strategic investors including Daimler, Siemens, BMW i Ventures) is widely reported at >$600M but I did not independently verify that figure.
headcount_estimate: ~1,440 worldwide employees as of January 31, 2026 (stated verbatim in the FY2026 10-K — this is a hard, filed number). Down from 1,650 in 2024, consistent with the revenue decline and restructuring. LinkedIn was not accessible during this research.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Founded 2007 as a venture-backed hardware startup, went public via SPAC.
founded_year: 2007, as Coulomb Technologies, by Richard Lowenthal, Dave Baxter and Harjinder Bhade. HQ: 254 East Hacienda Avenue, Campbell, California (per SEC filings). CEO Rick Wilmer; chairman Bruce Chizen.
sells_to: Mixed, but primarily B2B enterprise and commercial — site hosts (workplaces, retail, hospitality, multifamily, stadiums), commercial and municipal fleet operators, and auto dealers. Secondary prosumer channel for home chargers, plus a free consumer driver app that is the demand-side network effect rather than a revenue line.
how_they_use_agents: Real but narrow and operational, not agentic-native. Shipping today: an 'AI Data Assistant' inside their software that answers natural-language questions over charging telemetry and generates visualizations; AI-driven pricing optimization based on energy patterns, dwell time and utilization; and an 'AI-powered Installer Toolkit' that automates up to 95% of station activation tasks. The flagship case (announced 2024, described in the Atlan interview) is AI-assisted field diagnostics: a driver photographs a malfunctioning station, and the AI cross-references cloud telemetry to diagnose the fault, identify the parts needed, and route the repair — cutting support contacts and station downtime. Their FY2026 10-K also carries an explicit risk factor that the business could suffer if it fails to 'identify, develop, integrate and deploy artificial intelligence and other advanced automation technologies' — so AI is now a board-level competitive concern, not a side project.
why_they_need_memory: The buying trigger was cross-system data discovery, and the forward-looking reason is AI dataset assembly. Per Atlan's Sept 2024 interview with Senior Data Engineer Hans Howard, ChargePoint's analytics team was burning days manually reconciling phone, sales, manufacturing and quality-control systems that each tracked different things — figuring out which system held a field, who owned it, and filing access tickets before any work could start. Atlan became the 'one-stop shop' search layer across all of it. Critically, Howard frames the next step in exactly agent-memory terms: the questions he wants answered are 'I want to combine session, alarm, and ticket data to feed a machine learning algorithm' and 'we have a large language model and need to analyze certain things — how do I bring that data together?' He says Atlan will play a key role in their AI initiatives 'starting with discovering available data, assessing its size and quality, and helping build datasets.' That is the clearest articulation across these three of why an industrial company buys a context layer: not to give an agent a diary, but to let humans and models find and trust the operational data that already exists across a fragmented estate.

name: Scripps Health

category: Healthcare provider (nonprofit integrated health system) — data-governance/catalog buyer, not an AI vendor
stage: Not applicable — 100-year-old nonprofit 501(c)(3), no venture stage
funding: None (nonprofit, no venture funding). Financial scale instead: total revenue $4,140,209,334 FY2023; $4,062,352,256 FY2022; $3,760,946,800 FY2021 (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, EIN 95-1684089)
headcount_estimate: ~13,000+ employees (Wikipedia, undated) plus 2,500+ physicians (scripps.org). Could not confirm a current figure on Scripps' own site — treat as approximate.
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: B2C / patients — healthcare services to consumers and payers in San Diego County. Internally the data-tooling buyer is enterprise analytics + data engineering.

I decoded the actual case-study PDF (hosted at f.hubspotusercontent30.net/hubfs/6880682/Scripps Health Case Study (2).pdf, still linked from atlan.com/customers/): its real title is 'Why a $3 billion healthcare provider chose Atlan as its MODERN DATA CATALOG' — not 'context layer'. Holly Hallman's framing is the memory pitch verbatim: solving problems 'without having to ask three of your teammates.' If they ever put LLM copilots on Snowflake/Power BI, this catalog is the grounding layer — but that is an inference, not something Scripps claims.

name: Contentful
what_it_does: API-first headless CMS, now marketed as a 'composable content platform' / DXP: content is modelled as structured entries once and delivered over REST, GraphQL and CDN APIs to web, mobile, and any other channel, decoupled from presentation. Serves 4,800+ brands (IKEA, Spotify, Red Bull, KFC, British Museum, Urban Outfitters, Twilio, Kraft Heinz). Current product surface (from the Aug-2026 archived site): Content Platform, Studio (visual experience assembly), Personalization (from the Aug 2024 Ninetailed acquisition), Analytics (beta — pitched as 'agentic analytics directly in your workflow'), plus capabilities AI Actions, AI Suggestions, Automations, Experimentation, Media/Asset Management, and a newly launched product called Palmata for 'AI discovery' (managing how a brand shows up in AI answers). Founded Berlin 2013 by Sascha Konietzke and Paolo Negri; current CEO Karthik Rau; offices Berlin, Denver, San Francisco, NYC, London. CAVEAT ON SOURCING BELOW — I could not verify Contentful as an Atlan customer.
category: Content infrastructure — headless CMS / composable DXP. Sold to developers + digital/marketing teams. (Now a Salesforce product.)
stage: ACQUIRED. Salesforce signed a definitive agreement June 1, 2026 and completed the acquisition September 1, 2026. Previously Series F (2021). This materially changes its status as an independent buyer of anything.
funding: $290.5M total venture: Series D $35.5M (2018, OMERS, Benchmark, Balderton, General Catalyst, Sapphire Ventures, Salesforce Ventures); Series E $80M (June 2020, Sapphire, General Catalyst, Salesforce Ventures); Series F $175M (July 2021, led by Tiger Global's PE arm at a $3B valuation). Acquired by Salesforce, closed Sept 1 2026 — purchase price NOT disclosed in the press release.
headcount_estimate: 700+ ('700+ Contentfulers, 100+ countries, 70+ nationalities' — their own about-us page, archived Aug 2026). Wikipedia's 592 figure is stale (2021).
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: B2B enterprise and mid-market (their own site segments 'Enterprise' and 'Mid-market'), with developers as the primary technical buyer and growth/web/content marketing teams as the economic buyer.
how_they_use_agents: Genuinely deep and current agent surface, verified from their GitHub org (all pushed Sept 2026): (1) contentful-mcp-server — MCP server over the Contentful Management API, so an assistant can create entries, update content types, upload assets, and author AI Actions in natural language; (2) a HOSTED remote MCP endpoint at mcp.contentful.com plus a local 'contentful-personalization' MCP server; (3) a 'skills' repo — 'Your AI agent knows how to code. These skills teach it Contentful' — 7 agent skills shipped as a Claude Code plugin (/plugin marketplace add contentful/skills), covering their five APIs and SDK patterns; (4) 'skill-kit', a TypeScript SDK for building agent skills as typed state machines with ArkType schemas and progressive-disclosure reference loading — i.e. they are building agent-context tooling, not just consuming it. In-product: AI Actions, AI Suggestions, Automations ('eliminate busywork with AI'), agentic analytics beta, and Palmata for AI discovery. Salesforce's stated rationale is exactly this: Contentful becomes 'the content layer it needs' for Agentforce, so agents can 'query, assemble, and deliver content dynamically without manual publishing steps.'
why_they_need_memory: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: I could not confirm Contentful is an Atlan customer. Contentful appears NOWHERE on atlan.com — not on /customers/, not on /wall-of-play, not on /wall-of-love/, not in Atlan's sitemap, and no archived Atlan URL contains 'contentful' (Wayback CDX). No 'Robert Clifford-Jones' appears on any Atlan page I fetched, and atlan.com/blog/contentful-chooses-atlan/, /success-stories/contentful/ and /customers/contentful/ all 404. Two likely explanations: (a) confusion with CONTENTSQUARE, which IS a documented Atlan customer with a live success story (atlan.com/success-stories/contentsquare/, quoted by Otávio Leite Bastos, Global Governance Lead) and is on the wall of love; or (b) Atlan's own marketing site is BUILT on Contentful (their JS bundles are literally named contentful-image-optimizer.*.js and contentful.*.js), so a scrape could have picked up the vendor relationship in the wrong direction. Treat the testimonial as unverified. On the substantive question of whether they'd need this category: yes, plausibly — a 700-person, 4,800-customer platform company with its own agents writing into customer content models needs schema/lineage context, and the quoted pains (lineage to find a pipeline failure fast; analysts spending time fielding repeat data questions) are the standard profile. But that is inference, not evidence.

name: DataCamp
what_it_does: Online learning platform for data, analytics and AI skills. Browser-based interactive courses (video + in-browser coding exercises), career/skill tracks, certifications, and hands-on projects covering Python, R, SQL, BI tools, LLM applications, prompt engineering and 'AI agent fundamentals'. Three go-to-market motions: individual subscriptions (B2C), DataCamp for Business (team/enterprise licences with custom learning paths and admin reporting), and DataCamp Classrooms (free for educators). Self-reported reach: 19M+ learners, 5,000+ companies, ~80% of the Fortune 1000, 3,000 academic organisations, 180+ countries. HQ at 1 Pennsylvania Plaza, New York, with offices in Leuven (Belgium) and London — the Leuven office reflects its Belgian origin. It also ships its own software product, DataLab, an AI-enabled data notebook. NOTE: this is DataCamp the edtech company, not the unrelated 'Datacamp' CDN/bare-metal hosting provider (datacamp.co.uk / CDN77 group) — the Atlan case study is unambiguously the education platform (interviewee is DataCamp's Director of Analytics, and the story references their Workspace/DataLab notebook and Donates & Classrooms programs).
category: EdTech / data & AI skills learning platform (SaaS, B2C + B2B). As a buyer, they are an active-metadata / data-catalog customer — i.e. a data-team buyer, not an AI-agent-startup buyer.
stage: Private, VC-backed but late-stage/mature (founded ~2013, no new round confirmed in this research). Not a startup in the seed/Series A sense.
funding: unknown — could not confirm. No funding figure appears on datacamp.com, its press page, or any source I was able to fetch; Crunchbase/Growjo returned 403 and my web-search budget was exhausted before I could verify. Widely-circulated but UNVERIFIED figures put total raised in the ~$30M range (a Series A around 2017 and a Series B around 2020 led by Spectrum Equity) — treat as a lead to check, not as fact.
headcount_estimate: unknown — not stated on the about or careers pages and I could not access LinkedIn. Scale indicators only: three offices (New York, Leuven, London), 19M learners, 5,000+ business customers. Commonly cited estimates of a few hundred employees are unverified.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. No YC or accelerator affiliation surfaced on their site or in any source fetched. Company originated out of Leuven, Belgium (KU Leuven ecosystem) rather than a US accelerator.
founded_year: unknown — not stated on their about/careers pages. Commonly reported as 2013 (Leuven, Belgium), but I could not confirm this from a primary source in this session.
sells_to: Mixed: prosumer/B2C (individual learners paying for subscriptions) + B2B SMB and enterprise (DataCamp for Business, incl. ~80% of Fortune 1000) + education institutions. The enterprise L&D buyer is the highest-value segment.
how_they_use_agents: AI appears in two places in the product, both assistive rather than autonomous. (1) AI Tutor inside courses — gives instant feedback and code explanation when a learner is stuck on an exercise. (2) DataLab, their AI-enabled data notebook (called 'Workspace' at the time of the Atlan interview) — an AI Assistant that lets users 'chat with your data', generating and running Python and SQL in the background to answer questions about metrics, trends, root cause and comparisons. The most relevant detail for a memory vendor: DataLab explicitly states it does not just forward the question to an LLM — it 'smartly enhances your question with your unique work context', including previous queries, connected data sources and organisational context. That is a context/memory-injection layer they built themselves. DataCamp deliberately frames DataLab as an 'AI Assistant' rather than an autonomous agent, and stresses that it writes reviewable code so users can audit it against hallucination. They also teach agents as curriculum ('AI agent fundamentals', 'Associate AI Engineer' track) — that is content, not internal agent deployment. No evidence of autonomous agents running in their own operations.
why_they_need_memory: Directly documented in the Atlan interview (Jorge Vasquez, Director of Analytics, Oct 2023). Their metadata and documentation were scattered across multiple tools, so non-technical users could not discover data; and they had no lineage visibility, which made a data-warehouse and clickstream migration risky and made it hard to know what was safe to deprecate. They bought Atlan for column-level lineage plus discoverability (Chrome plug-in, better UI/UX) — i.e. a single durable place where the meaning of every data asset lives. The second, stronger pull: their own DataLab AI Assistant is only useful if it knows the customer's work context (past queries, connected sources, org vocabulary), so DataCamp is simultaneously a buyer of a context layer and a builder of one. That makes them a buyer whose motivation is 'my AI answers are only as good as the context behind them', not 'my agent forgets between sessions'.
confidence: high on the company being real and on what it does and why it bought a context/metadata layer (primary sources: their own site plus a named, dated Atlan customer interview). low on funding, headcount and founded_year — none of these were confirmable with the tools available.

name: Foundry (Foundry Digital LLC)
what_it_does: IDENTITY CORRECTION — READ FIRST: the URL supplied with this task (https://foundryco.com) is the WRONG company. foundryco.com is Foundry, the B2B tech-media and marketing business formerly known as IDG Communications (publisher of CIO, CSO, Computerworld, InfoWorld, Network World, Macworld, PCWorld; founded 1964; sells intent data and demand-gen to tech marketers). The Atlan customer story titled 'Foundry: An Active Metadata Pioneer' is about a completely different Foundry: Foundry Digital LLC, the blockchain-infrastructure subsidiary of Digital Currency Group. The Atlan article describes Foundry as 'an organization dedicated to empowering decentralized infrastructure for institutions seeking tools for mining and staking digital assets' and 'best-known for the Foundry USA Pool, which is currently the world's largest Bitcoin mining pool' — language that matches foundrydigital.com's own careers page ('empowering institutions with the tools they need to mine digital assets') and does not match foundryco.com at all. WHAT FOUNDRY DIGITAL ACTUALLY DOES: operates the Foundry USA Pool (at points in 2024 Foundry plus Antpool controlled roughly 60% of the Bitcoin mining pool market), sets up and manages bitcoin mining operations across the US and Canada, and supplies financing, ASIC mining hardware procurement/logistics, deployment and fleet-management software, and staking services to institutional miners and blockchain companies. Founded 2019 as a DCG subsidiary; in 2021 it relocated over $300M of mining equipment out of China to North America; it charged no pool fees until April 2023; in January 2025 DCG spun Fortitude Mining out as a separate self-mining subsidiary. Headquarters is Rochester, New York (widely reported; I could not confirm this from a primary source because foundrydigital.com is behind Cloudflare bot protection).
category: Crypto / blockchain infrastructure — bitcoin mining pool operator and institutional mining & staking services provider. (If the parent agent actually meant foundryco.com, the category would instead be B2B tech media and intent-data marketing — a completely different buyer profile.)
stage: Not venture-stage. Wholly-owned operating subsidiary of Digital Currency Group (DCG), a private crypto holding company. No independent funding rounds.
funding: unknown / not applicable in the usual sense — Foundry Digital is capitalised by its parent Digital Currency Group rather than by outside venture rounds. No standalone round confirmed. DCG's own funding is a separate question and was not researched here.
headcount_estimate: unknown — foundrydigital.com is Cloudflare-blocked to automated fetches, their Greenhouse board currently shows zero open roles, and I could not access LinkedIn. No credible figure obtained. Do not guess: the company went through crypto-winter contraction and a 2025 subsidiary spin-out, so any older headcount number would be stale.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Corporate subsidiary, incubated internally by Digital Currency Group in 2019 — not an accelerator alumnus.
sells_to: B2B enterprise / institutional. Customers are institutional bitcoin miners, staking customers, and blockchain companies — not consumers and not developers. High-value, low-count, relationship-driven accounts.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agent usage found — and I looked. The Atlan interview (with Richard Goerwitz, Data Engineering Architect; Brian Kim, Data Analyst II; Amit Kini, Data Engineer III) contains exactly one AI reference: Richard said Atlan 'has made some strategic moves into AI' and that this was one factor in vendor selection. That is forward-looking vendor-selection reasoning, not a deployed agent. Their stated work is conventional data engineering — an enterprise data warehouse and data lake built during a period of fast organisational maturation, and a planned move to a domain-oriented data mesh. Treat this account as an early-signal buyer (a data team that wants their catalog vendor to be going somewhere with AI), not as an agent-deploying company.
why_they_need_memory: Documented in the Atlan interview (Sept 2023). Two concrete drivers. (1) Discovery: as Brian Kim put it, 'people outside of the data team are uncertain of where and what data we can provide' — the data team was the bottleneck for every question, so they needed self-service. (2) Shared language: the article is literally titled 'Driving a Shared Language for Data with Atlan' — they needed aligned terminology and a business glossary across departments, especially as they decentralised into a domain data mesh where each domain would otherwise invent its own definitions. This is the classic pre-AI reason to buy a company-brain product: institutional knowledge lives in a few engineers' heads and does not survive fast growth or decentralisation. Crypto-specific pressure adds a governance/audit dimension (institutional counterparties, regulatory scrutiny) that raises the value of provable lineage.
confidence: medium. HIGH confidence that Foundry Digital is a real company, that it is the entity Atlan actually profiled, and on why it bought a metadata/context layer — three named employees with titles in a dated first-party interview, corroborated by Wikipedia's DCG entry and by matching language on Foundry's own Greenhouse board. MEDIUM overall only because the URL supplied with this task points at a different company entirely, so the parent agent may have intended foundryco.com; the parent should confirm which Foundry it wants. LOW on headcount and on HQ city (Cloudflare-blocked primary source).

name: Sands Capital
what_it_does: Independent, staff-owned investment management firm — 'an active, long-term investor in leading innovative growth businesses, globally'. Founded 1992, headquartered in Arlington, Virginia (1000 Wilson Blvd, Suite 3000) with offices in London, New York, San Francisco and Singapore. $50 billion in client assets under management as of 30 June 2026 (it was $45B when the Atlan story was published in September 2023, so it has grown materially since). Operates an integrated platform across three strategies: public equity (concentrated growth portfolios), growth equity, and venture. Clients are institutions and fund sponsors — pensions, endowments, sovereign wealth, professional investors — in more than 30 countries. Note the double relevance for an agent-memory vendor: Sands Capital is both a buyer of data infrastructure AND, through its growth-equity and venture arms, an investor in high-growth technology companies, so its analysts consume enormous volumes of research on exactly the kind of companies a memory vendor sells to.
category: Financial services — institutional asset management / growth-equity and venture investing. As a buyer of this category: a regulated, research-intensive financial firm buying a data catalog and governance layer on top of Snowflake.
stage: Not applicable — private, independent, staff-owned firm, 34 years old, never venture-funded. It is on the other side of the table (it deploys capital rather than raising it).
funding: Not applicable / unknown. Sands Capital is a staff-owned partnership with no disclosed outside funding. The relevant scale number is AUM: $50B as of 30 June 2026 (up from $45B in September 2023).
headcount_estimate: unknown — the firm does not publish an employee count on its site and I could not access LinkedIn. Structural indicators only: five offices (Arlington HQ, London, New York, San Francisco, Singapore); the careers page describes investment research analysts, portfolio specialists, operations/planning/analytics, finance, legal, HR and events functions, and calls the firm 'tight-knit' and 'staff-owned'. That language plus $50B AUM is consistent with a few hundred people, but I will not put a number on it without a source.
yc_or_accelerator: None — not applicable. A 1992-founded asset manager, no accelerator history.
sells_to: B2B enterprise / institutional — sells investment management services to institutions, fund sponsors and professional investors across 30+ countries. Not developers, not prosumers.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents found, and no AI mentioned at all in the Atlan case study or on the pages I read. Their stack as described is conventional modern analytics: Snowflake as the cloud data warehouse, SQL, with Atlan integrated into Salesforce, Jira and Slack so that context surfaces where people already work. The Slack integration is the closest thing to an 'assistant' pattern — pushing data-quality alerts and answers into the chat surface rather than making people go find them. This is a knowledge-distribution problem being solved with integrations, not agents. If a memory vendor pitches here, the wedge is analyst research context and Slack-surface answers, not autonomous agents; and expect heavy compliance/audit constraints typical of a registered investment adviser.
why_they_need_memory: Documented in the Atlan customer story 'Advancing Literacy, Access, and Quality with Atlan and Snowflake' (Sept 2023), interviewing Akriti Shrestha (Business and Data Associate) and Adam Rosenbaum (Data Governance Analyst). The pain: business users could not understand what transformations had been applied to data or locate the right asset, so every question routed back to a small number of data engineers — 'We realized there was a need for a Metadata Management tool.' They bought to enable self-service discovery, cut repetitive questions to engineers, and push proactive data-quality alerts into Slack. The deeper driver, and the one that generalises: an investment firm's edge IS its accumulated analytical context — why a metric is defined a certain way, what a transformation assumes, which dataset a thesis was built on. When that lives only in analysts' heads it does not survive staff turnover, and in a regulated firm it also has to be auditable. Note the title of the piece Atlan chose — 'Building a Data Community' — this buyer's framing is cultural (data literacy and community) as much as technical, which is a useful signal for how to pitch the category to financial-services buyers.
confidence: high on the company existing, on what it does, on AUM, founding year and offices (all confirmed from the firm's own homepage and careers page), and on the buying rationale (named, titled interviewees in a dated first-party Atlan story). low specifically on headcount, which is not published anywhere I could reach. Confident there is no agent deployment to report — absence confirmed across three sources, not merely unsearched.

name: carVertical (legal entity: cV Group / CV Group, UAB)
what_it_does: VIN-based vehicle history reports. A buyer enters a VIN and carVertical aggregates records from 1,000+ international databases (national vehicle registries, insurers, law enforcement, official garages, auction and service records) into a single report covering damage history, odometer/mileage fraud, title and theft status, ownership changes, specs, safety ratings and market price estimates. Sold two ways: (1) direct-to-consumer single reports and multi-report packages to used-car buyers, (2) B2B/API to dealerships, insurers and leasing companies, including an 'Advanced vehicle history report API' and a VIN Decoder API. Operates in ~37 markets across Europe, North America and Australia; a US DOJ-approved NMVTIS data provider. Site claims 6,000,000+ users to date, ~2M unique users/year, 12.4M+ vehicles checked, 1B+ verified records. Per Atlan's 2023 interview: 27 markets, 1.5M monthly users, 22.3M VINs processed, 900+ connected data sources.
category: Automotive / vehicle data aggregation and reporting (consumer data marketplace + B2B data API). Not dev tools, not an AI product company.
stage: Private, post-ICO. No publicly confirmed VC equity rounds; appears founder-owned and revenue-financed. Effectively 'bootstrapped after a 2018 token sale.'
funding: ~EUR 16M raised via an initial coin offering (the cV token) in 2018 — the only confirmed external raise. No Crunchbase/PitchBook-confirmed VC rounds found. Revenue is public-ish via press: ~EUR 75-75.8M (2024/2025 reporting). Ranked #26 on the 2023 FT1000 fastest-growing European companies list and again a 2024 FT winner.
headcount_estimate: ~150-156. Company 'About us' page states '150+ Employees'; Wikipedia cites 156 as of 2025. At the time of the Atlan interview (Sept 2023) it was ~120 total, with ~20 in the data department.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not a YC company; no accelerator affiliation identified.
founded_year: 2017 (Wikipedia; Lithuanian company). The company's own About page markets 2019 as the launch of 'the first global car history register.'
sells_to: Mixed: prosumer/consumer (individual used-car buyers, the bulk of revenue) plus B2B SMB (dealerships, leasing, insurers) and developers via API.
how_they_use_agents: No evidence of LLM or agentic AI anywhere in the product. What exists is classical ML: carVertical runs a dedicated Machine Learning Engineering team as one of four teams inside its ~20-person data department (alongside Data Acquisition, Data Engineering, Data Analytics), and the site markets 'We use artificial intelligence to generate insights and identify inconsistencies across databases' plus a 'machine learning-powered VIN Decoder API' for cross-market variant identification. So: ML for record reconciliation, damage detection and VIN decoding across ~1,000 messy heterogeneous sources — not agents, and no agent memory.
why_they_need_memory: The Atlan purchase was driven by knowledge sprawl, not AI. Per CDO Arunas Vaitkus and Data Engineer Vidmante Ciziene, as the company scaled, institutional knowledge about data scattered across platforms and ad-hoc conversations, and management needed it consolidated to keep growing. Structural drivers: ~900-1,000 external data sources of wildly varying quality, 22.3M VINs, a four-discipline data org where ML engineers and analysts must trust upstream acquisition pipelines, and ISO 27001 compliance requiring documented data lineage. Stack: BigQuery, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, S3, Airflow, dbt, Tableau, AWS Lambda, JSON schema validation. Stated buying criteria were easy integration and a modern UI that would actually get adopted.

Add heavy regulation — federal student loan servicing contracts, payments, K-12/FERPA student data — and you get demand for a governed, documented, searchable context layer. Explicit buying criterion was adoption by non-technical as well as technical users: 'Atlan's intuitive UI was the biggest component for me.'

name: SouthState Bank (holding company: SouthState Bank Corporation, formerly SouthState Corporation)
what_it_does: A large US regional commercial bank headquartered in Winter Haven, Florida. Full-service consumer and commercial banking: checking/savings/money market/time deposits, commercial real estate, C&I, residential mortgage and consumer lending, debit/credit cards, treasury management (ACH, lockbox, remote deposit capture, merchant), trust, wealth and asset management, brokerage and annuities, and online/mobile banking. Notably also runs a nationwide correspondent banking and capital markets business (bond accounting for correspondent banks, asset/liability consulting, international wires, clearing) that reaches well beyond its branch footprint. Branch footprint ~371 locations across FL, SC, NC, GA, AL, VA, TX and CO. Renamed from SouthState Corporation to SouthState Bank Corporation in September 2025.
category: Regional commercial bank / retail and commercial financial services. Heavily regulated incumbent, not a fintech.
stage: Public. Listed as SSB (NYSE per current S&P Global data; historically quoted on Nasdaq — the listing appears to have moved). IPO 28 January 1997. S&P MidCap 400 component.
funding: Not applicable — public company since 1997, no venture funding. Scale metrics instead: $68.9B total assets (Q2 2026), $46.4B (2024). Share price ~$108 (Sept 2026). Last major capital event was the ~$2B stock acquisition of Independent Bank Group (announced May 2024, closed Jan 2025).
headcount_estimate: ~6,190 per S&P Global Market Intelligence (2026), up from ~5,100 in 2024 pre-merger.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Traces to First National Bank, Orangeburg, South Carolina, 1933.
sells_to: Both. B2B — commercial and small-business banking, treasury management, and a coast-to-coast correspondent banking/capital markets franchise selling to other banks. B2C — over one million retail consumer and mortgage/wealth customers across eight states.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agent usage found in any source reviewed, and the bank's own site was not fetchable (HTTP 403 to automated requests). The Atlan deployment is explicitly a governance program, not an AI program: a 'Data Intelligence Program' run by a hybrid team on a modern cloud stack. The features Gabrielle Tyll called decisive — 'native connectors,' 'bi-directional tagging,' and the 'impact analysis feature' for data engineers — are catalog/lineage features, not agent infrastructure. Treat this one as a data-governance buyer with no disclosed agent story.
why_they_need_memory: Bought by Gabrielle Tyll, SVP and Director of Business Initiatives (16+ years at the bank, background in consumer banking, operations, risk and program management) — a business leader, not a data engineer, which is itself telling. Stated need: 'a platform that not only provided centralized insights into our data environment, but also a user-friendly tool that supports the activities of our data owners and data stewards,' in order to operationalize governance and enable self-service; a specific pain was analysts burning time on data joins and merges. Structural drivers are strong: bank-grade regulatory and model-risk requirements demanding provable lineage; a serial-acquirer history (CenterState, then Independent Bank Group) that repeatedly bolts together incompatible core banking data estates; and a deliberately 'front-end agnostic,' consumption-priced cloud stack, which makes a stack-independent context layer valuable.

name: CouponFollow (NextGen Shopping LLC, a System1 company)
what_it_does: Consumer coupon-code search engine and deals directory, plus the Cently browser extension that auto-tests and applies discount codes at checkout, and Smilematic. Monetizes almost entirely through affiliate commissions on clicks/purchases driven to 5,000+ brand partners; the core acquisition channel is organic SEO ('Macy's coupon' type queries). Since ~2023 it has been diversifying into white-labeled/branded shopping experiences built for partner publishers and content sites. Site is geo/bot-blocked (Varnish 405) from this environment; content read via Wayback snapshot and its own SEC-filed acquisition release.
category: Consumer e-commerce / affiliate marketing (coupon and deals site). NOT an AI company; not agent-native.
stage: Acquired — operating brand/subsidiary of System1, Inc. (NYSE: SST). Bootstrapped and founder-owned before that.
funding: No disclosed venture funding — founder-bootstrapped from 2010. Acquired by System1 on 2022-03-04 for 'up to $115 million' in cash and stock inclusive of three-year earnouts (per System1's 8-K Ex-99.1). Still a System1 company as of 2026 (site footer: 'Copyright 2026 NextGen Shopping LLC, A System1 Company').
headcount_estimate: ~69 employees listed on LinkedIn (LinkedIn size band 51-200). Small team; the data function was a single BI/data-engineering team of a handful of people in 2023.
yc_or_accelerator: None found — no YC or accelerator affiliation; bootstrapped by founder Marc Mezzacca.
founded_year: 2010 (per CouponFollow's own About page: 'CouponFollow was born in 2010'; legal entity NextGen Shopping, Inc./LLC). Earliest Wayback capture of couponfollow.com/home/about is 2009.
sells_to: Primarily B2C (millions of consumer shoppers, email newsletter subscribers, extension users), with a B2B affiliate/partnership side selling placement and exclusive-coupon deals to 5,000+ retail brands, and an emerging white-label B2B offering to publishers/content sites.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agent product found — this is the honest answer. Their own About page describes ranking 'algorithms' that reorder coupons multiple times a day plus a human 'Coupon Operations' team that verifies codes; no LLM or agent framework is claimed. In the Atlan interview (Nov 2023) the BI director said the team was only in 'the early stages of pushing into Machine Learning and Data Science projects.' Their purchase of Atlan was a data-catalog/metadata purchase (documentation, lineage, glossary), not an agent-infrastructure purchase. Note the strategic irony: agentic commerce is arguably a threat to their SEO-plus-affiliate model rather than something they build.
why_they_need_memory: Textbook shared-context pain, articulated directly by Ted Andersson, Director of BI: documentation written in Confluence was 'already out-of-date' by the time it was written and 'nobody looked at it'; metric definitions drifted (one team's CTR meant something different from another's, each with their own dashboards); and 'CouponFollow ingests a tremendous amount of data from all kinds of different places, and it's very challenging to keep track of all of it.' He explicitly wanted Atlan to be 'the glue that pulls all of this together, and provide a single, shared place where everybody can go to understand the data, how it flows, and where it comes from' — i.e. a durable, queryable company memory to replace tribal knowledge and stale wiki pages, for humans first. name: North (formerly North American Bancard / NAB Holdings)
what_it_does: Merchant acquirer and payments technology company — the sixth-largest independent (non-bank) acquirer in the US. Sells card processing, POS hardware and software, e-commerce and mobile payments, billing/invoicing, gift and loyalty, fraud prevention, ATM services and developer APIs to merchants directly and through a ~3,000-strong network of sales partners, ISOs, ISVs, banks and credit unions. Serves restaurants, retail, convenience, franchise/enterprise and high-risk verticals. Brand family includes Payanywhere, Payments Hub, PayTrace, EPX and Capital for Merchants. Rebranded from North American Bancard to 'North' in 2024; operates as a registered DBA of NorthAB, LLC.
category: Payments / fintech infrastructure (merchant acquiring and POS). Traditional, non-AI-native mid-to-large private company.
stage: Private, founder-owned and founder-led (Marc Gardner, founder/CEO/President). Not venture-backed; no disclosed institutional rounds.
funding: unknown — no venture or growth round disclosed in any source I could confirm. Privately held by its founder since 1992; the company is self-funded/acquisitive (it has bought PayTrace, EPX and others) rather than VC-backed. Scale proxy: processes more than $100 billion per year in electronic transaction volume (the Atlan interview from 2023 cited ~$45B annually, so the figure has grown or is measured differently).
headcount_estimate: ~1,600 employees per LinkedIn (northpayments); Wikipedia cites ~1,300 as of 2024. Call it 1,300-1,600. Serves 350,000+ merchants.
yc_or_accelerator: None — not applicable; a 1992-founded, bootstrapped, founder-owned company.
founded_year: 1992 (founded by Marc Gardner; HQ Troy, Michigan)
sells_to: B2B — mostly SMB merchants (restaurants, retail, convenience, services) plus enterprise/franchise accounts, sold both direct and through a large indirect channel of ISOs, ISVs, banks and credit unions.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agent product of their own that I could confirm. Their public AI footprint is (a) marketing/thought-leadership content — a blog post on 'agentic commerce optimization' that positions North as the payments and data infrastructure underneath other people's shopping agents, not as an agent builder; and (b) a vendor partnership with Hawk AI for AML/compliance monitoring. Internally they run a Data Science and Reporting team and 'advanced analytics' but nothing described as agentic. Their Atlan purchase was governance-driven: PII discovery and masking/tagging in Snowflake, glossary, lineage, Snowflake cost optimization, and an Atlan Chrome extension overlay on Sigma dashboards. Note: north.com returns 403 to automated clients, so this read is from their sitemap, the Atlan interview, LinkedIn and Wikipedia rather than a full site crawl.
why_they_need_memory: Daniel Dowdy (Director, Big Data Analytics) describes a self-service analytics blast radius problem: after consolidating a sprawl of source systems into Snowflake, queries that took 30 hours now take 30 seconds, which 'increased the volume of the requests coming in' — hundreds of Sigma users answering their own questions, with no shared definitions behind them. The stated needs are a robust data glossary and dictionary for 'consistent metrics and reporting solutions', in-context definitions/comments/tickets surfaced right inside the Sigma dashboard so analysts stop round-tripping to engineers, lineage so they can safely widen Sigma access, and automated detection/tagging of newly added sensitive fields (this is a payments company — masking and exposure reduction are existential). The buying trigger was hard-requirement tooling integration (the Sigma Chrome plug-in) plus governance, not agents.

name: Mindbody (a Playlist company)
what_it_does: Vertical SaaS business-management platform for fitness, wellness and beauty businesses — class and appointment scheduling, integrated payments (Mindbody Payments, on Stripe), staff scheduling and payroll integration, CRM and lead pipeline, automated email/SMS marketing, reporting, and branded websites — paired with a consumer-side marketplace app that connects 3M+ consumers to those businesses. 40,000+ businesses run on Mindbody. It is now one brand inside Playlist, alongside ClassPass, Booker, Kite (franchise/enterprise) and EGYM (smart fitness hardware and corporate wellness).
category: Vertical SaaS (fitness/wellness/beauty business management) + consumer marketplace. Not AI-native, but as of 2026 actively shipping agent products.
stage: Late-stage private, PE-backed, at very large scale — effectively pre-IPO. Was public (NASDAQ: MB) 2015-2019.
funding: ~$107M in venture pre-IPO (Tech Coast Angels/Pasadena Angels $1M 2005; Bessemer/Catalyst $11M 2010; $35M 2012; $50M 2014); $100M IPO June 2015; taken private by Vista Equity Partners in Feb 2019 for $1.9B; acquired ClassPass Oct 2021 and Booker ($150M, 2018). In Jan 2026 Playlist and EGYM announced a merger with $785M in new equity, closed Mar 31 2026, valuing the combined company at $7.5B enterprise value — led by Affinity Partners with Vista Equity Partners, Temasek and L Catterton participating.
headcount_estimate: Mindbody brand ~1,418 on LinkedIn (band 1,001-5,000); Playlist group states 'over 3,000 employees globally' post-EGYM merger. HQ San Luis Obispo, CA, with UK, Australia and India offices and a remote-work policy since 2023.
yc_or_accelerator: None — bootstrapped as HardBody SoftWare in 1998, then angel- and VC-funded; no accelerator.
founded_year: 1998 (as HardBody SoftWare, Blake Beltram); incorporated as an LLC Feb 13 2001 with Rick Stollmeyer; Bob Murphy joined as co-founder 2003. CEO Fritz Lanman since Sept 2022 (now CEO/co-founder of Playlist).
sells_to: B2B SMB and mid-market primarily — boutique studios, gyms, spas and salons — extending up to large chains and franchises (via Kite) and enterprise employers (via EGYM Wellpass). Also a direct consumer marketplace (Mindbody app, ClassPass).
how_they_use_agents: This is the one of the three with a real shipped agent. Playlist launched AI Concierge on 2026-07-08, first for Mindbody customers: a 24/7 virtual front-desk assistant that answers missed calls, replies across web chat and SMS, books classes and appointments automatically, captures and qualifies leads, routes conversations to staff when needed, and lets operators set tone and guardrails, all monitored from one inbox. The release states it is 'powered by Playlist's vast data scale and the latest AI models and agentic frameworks' and — the key line for this category — that unlike generic chatbots it 'integrates directly into a business's system-of-record, understanding its services, pricing, availability, and client history,' ready from day one with real-time schedules and client activity. Reported results: 90%+ of messages handled without staff involvement; ~25 hours/month saved per active user as of April 2026. It is explicitly 'the first in a growing suite of shared AI products from the Playlist platform.' EGYM separately contributes AI-personalized training plans, and Playlist ships an AI-powered website builder (Customized Websites, Aug 2026).
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct layers, and they are the clearest illustration of why this category gets bought. (1) Human/organizational memory: Thomas Evans, Director of Data Platform, described 'a 20 plus year old company that made it this far without having a data catalog of really any order', a stack that is 'the product of multiple mergers and acquisitions' (Mindbody + ClassPass + Booker, now + EGYM), duplicate and conflicting glossaries — 'Are you talking about the BI glossary or the RevOps glossary?' — and a dependence on 'tribal knowledge pools' that he called 'a dangerous game', with knowledge otherwise 'lost in Slack'. They needed one enterprise glossary, discoverability, lineage to migrate acquired systems safely, and usage telemetry to protect hot assets and deprecate dead ones. (2) Agent memory: AI Concierge only works because it is grounded in each business's live system-of-record — services, pricing, availability, client history — which is exactly the per-tenant context store an agent-memory vendor sells. A company that spent 2023 consolidating five acquisitions' semantics into one catalog is the same company that in 2026 needs those semantics machine-readable for an agent talking to customers. Stack: Snowflake, Fivetran plus in-house Python/SQL pipelines orchestrated on Databricks, dbt and Airflow, Looker (Mindbody) and Tableau (ClassPass).

name: Yape
what_it_does: Peru's dominant payments super-app, owned by Banco de Crédito del Perú (BCP), part of Credicorp (NYSE: BAP). Started as free P2P transfers by phone number or QR code and expanded into a full consumer financial ecosystem: microloans and standard credit up to S/10,000, bill pay and mobile top-ups, FX, inbound remittances, SOAT insurance, a marketplace (Yape Tienda), and event ticketing (Joinnus, acquired 2023). Credicorp's FY2025 20-F reports 15.9M monthly active users, 19.1M registered users, 10.04 billion transactions, and total payment volume of S/437.7 billion, with an average of 66+ transactions per active user per month. Also operates in Bolivia (replacing BCP Bolivia's Soli app) and has announced cross-border links with EBANX and Colombia's Nequi. Roughly 1M+ Peruvian micro-merchants accept Yape QR payments.
category: Consumer fintech / digital payments super-app (buyer of data catalog + metadata tooling, not a vendor of it)
stage: Corporate subsidiary — not venture funded. Built in-house by BCP's Centro de InnovaCXIón (CXI); commercial entity Yape Market S.A.C. established July 2022, 99.99% owned by Grupo Crédito S.A. (Credicorp).
funding: unknown / not applicable — no external venture round found. Funded internally by Credicorp, a NYSE-listed financial group. Do not attribute a startup funding figure to Yape.
headcount_estimate: unknown — Credicorp does not break out Yape headcount separately in its 20-F, and I could not access LinkedIn to verify. The Atlan interview implies a data organization with at least four distinct specializations (data engineering, data science, ML engineering, analytics translators), so the overall org is well into the hundreds, but I will not put a number on it.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Internal corporate venture out of BCP's Centro de InnovaCXIón (CXI), created 2016, launched to the public 2017.
founded_year: 2016 (created inside BCP; public launch 2017). Yape Market S.A.C. incorporated July 2022.
sells_to: B2C — Peruvian consumers (financial inclusion focus: 6.6M Peruvians financially included via Yape/BCP savings accounts 2020-2025), plus ~1M+ micro-merchants and SMBs accepting QR payments and a business profile tier for merchants above S/25,000/month.
how_they_use_agents: No LLM or autonomous agents evidenced anywhere I could verify — this is important. Yape's AI is classical ML, not agentic. Per the Atlan interview, Yape runs a dedicated Machine Learning Engineering team handling model creation, deployment and MLOps, plus a Data Science team, on Azure + Databricks lakehouse + Event Hub/Confluent Kafka + Power BI. The highest-value ML application is credit underwriting for thin-file users: 1.3 million individuals accessed their first formal loan via Yape since 2022, and about 3M of 15M users were in the lending product as of 2025. Also fraud controls — Yape added three-digit transaction verification codes in 2025 to counter 'yape falso' screenshot-fraud. Yape's stated reason for picking Atlan included 'Atlan AI' as part of staying current with emerging technology, but that is vendor capability, not an agent Yape built. Neither yape.com.pe nor Credicorp's 20-F markets an AI assistant or agent in the product.
why_they_need_memory: Governance-driven, not agent-driven. Yape bought a metadata/context layer because a fast-scaling four-discipline data org (engineering, science, MLE, analytics translators) plus non-technical business users needed shared definitions over an Azure/Databricks estate growing at 10B transactions/year. They explicitly wanted native support for Data Mesh and Data Contracts, and a UI usable by non-technical staff to democratize access. Selection was rigorous — a scored evaluation (Atlan 4.8/5) and a three-week POC covering 5 use cases and 21 activities. The pain is 'nobody agrees what this field means across a federated org,' which is the same fragmentation an agent-memory product addresses, but the buyer here is a data platform lead (Jorge Plasencia, Data Catalog & Data Observability Platform Lead), not an AI team.

name: Commonwealth Financial Network (NOT the nonprofit at buildcommonwealth.org — the supplied URL is wrong)
what_it_does: IDENTITY CORRECTION FIRST: the input listed Commonwealth as https://buildcommonwealth.org. That is a different organization. Atlan's 'Commonwealth: An Active Metadata Pioneer' interview is explicitly with Kelsey Coffin, Senior Data Governance Manager at Commonwealth Financial Network, a broker/dealer serving independent financial advisors. Commonwealth Financial Network is the largest independently owned wealth management firm in the US: an independent broker-dealer and registered investment adviser providing back-office, compliance, research, marketing, technology and practice-management services to ~2,900 independent financial advisors managing ~$285 billion in brokerage and advisory assets. Founded 1979, headquartered in Waltham, MA, with offices in San Diego, CA and Blue Ash (Cincinnati), OH. Ranked #1 in Independent Advisor Satisfaction by J.D. Power 13 times. LPL Financial Holdings (NASDAQ: LPLA) agreed on 28 March 2025 to acquire it for $2.7 billion in cash; the deal has closed and commonwealth.com now states 'Commonwealth is now part of LPL Financial.' FOR THE RECORD, the org at the supplied URL: 'Commonwealth' (legal name Build Commonwealth Inc., EIN 04-3540147, Boston MA) is a real 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded 2001 as Doorways to Dreams (D2D), rebranded 2016, CEO Timothy Flacke, President Peter Tufano; FY Sept-2025 revenue $1.78M against $6.40M expenses, net assets $8.32M, salaries ~$3.44M implying roughly 25-35 staff. It does substantial financial-AI research (Emerging Tech for All, 'Financial AI for Good' guide and chatbot) — but it is not Atlan's customer.
category: Wealth management / independent broker-dealer and RIA (financial services). Buyer of data catalog and governance tooling.
stage: Was privately held and founder-owned (founder Joseph Deitch) for 46 years; since 2025 a wholly owned subsidiary of LPL Financial Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: LPLA). Sellers in the transaction were Gratitude Holdings, Inc. and Odd Couple, Inc.; the acquired entity was CFN Holding Company, LLC.
funding: No venture funding — bootstrapped and founder-owned from 1979 until acquisition. Exit value: $2.7 billion in cash paid by LPL Holdings, Inc., announced 31 March 2025 (agreement signed 28 March 2025), financed with corporate cash, revolver borrowings, and a $2.6 billion Morgan Stanley bridge facility plus debt/equity issuance.
headcount_estimate: ~1,400-1,500 home-office staff, inferred — not directly disclosed. Commonwealth publicly states a 2-to-1 advisor-to-staff ratio against ~2,900 advisors, which implies roughly 1,450 employees. Treat this as a derived estimate, not a reported figure. (The ~2,900 advisors themselves are affiliated independents, not employees.)
yc_or_accelerator: None.
sells_to: B2B, mid-market to enterprise — independent financial advisors and advisory practices (dually registered firms, 100% advisory practices, RIAs, hybrids). Average affiliated advisor gross revenue was reported at $814,075, the highest among independent broker/dealers.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents evidenced — the Atlan interview contains no mention of AI or agents at all, and this is the least AI-oriented of the three. The stack described is conventional enterprise BI: Azure, Snowflake, Power BI, Salesforce CRM, plus third-party market/custodial data feeds. Atlan is used for four things: (1) moving business terms and metrics out of Excel into a central glossary, (2) a documentation hub that links out to material scattered across SharePoint and Confluence, (3) technical lineage across pipelines and applications, and (4) data ownership assignment and data-quality scoring. Governance is run by a working group that meets twice weekly with representatives from across business units.
why_they_need_memory: The purchase is a pure knowledge-fragmentation play in a compliance-heavy industry. Definitions lived in spreadsheets; documentation was scattered across SharePoint and Confluence; nobody could tell where a number came from or who owned it. Kelsey Coffin's stated design constraint — 'within two clicks, people need to be exactly where they want to' — shows the real risk they were buying against was adoption, not model quality. This is the archetypal 'company brain' buyer: a regulated, non-technical-heavy enterprise with a small central governance function trying to make institutional knowledge findable across thousands of distributed users. Note the acquisition: post-LPL, the buying center for this category may have moved or been consolidated into LPL's stack.

Atlan's 'Purple: An Active Metadata Pioneer' interview describes Purple as 'a digitally native company, and the designer, manufacturer, and retailer behind a suite of market-leading mattresses, pillows, and bedding products,' classified as Manufacturing/Retail with brick-and-mortar, wholesale and eCommerce channels — that is Purple Innovation, Inc. FOR THE RECORD, the company at the supplied URL: purple.ai is Purple WiFi Limited (UK Companies House no. 06444980, incorporated 4 Dec 2007 as Promotions 24 Ltd, renamed Purple Wifi Oct 2012), a cloud guest-WiFi, staff-WiFi and multi-tenant-WiFi analytics platform in Oldham, England, CEO Gavin Wheeldon, claiming 86k+ venues and 350M unique users, with customers including McDonald's, Harrods and NHS trusts. It is not Atlan's customer.
category: DTC consumer products — vertically integrated mattress/bedding manufacturer and omni-channel retailer. Buyer of data catalog and governance tooling.
stage: Public. Listed on Nasdaq as PRPL since 2 February 2018 via reverse recapitalization with SPAC Global Partner Acquisition Corp (incorporated in Delaware 19 May 2015); Coliseum Capital Partners participated in the transaction subscription. Purple Innovation, Inc. is sole managing member of operating entity Purple Innovation, LLC (~99.9% of common units).
funding: Publicly traded, so 'funding' is market financing rather than venture rounds. Went public via SPAC in Feb 2018. FY2025 net revenue $468.7M, net loss $51.5M — currently loss-making and shrinking. I did not find and will not invent a private round history or current market cap.
headcount_estimate: ~1,100 employees as of 30 March 2026, per the FY2025 Form 10-K, spanning manufacturing, R&D, corporate functions, wholesale, e-commerce and Purple showrooms. (For contrast, the misattributed purple.ai / Purple WiFi Ltd averaged 76 employees in FY Jan-2025.)
yc_or_accelerator: None.
founded_year: Brand and operating company mid-2010s; Purple Innovation, Inc. (the listed shell) incorporated in Delaware 19 May 2015 as Global Partner Acquisition Corp, with the Business Combination completing 2 February 2018. The 10-K describes 'more than 30 years of expertise in comfort innovation' inherited from the founders' prior licensing business, so a single clean founding year is genuinely ambiguous — I did not confirm a specific one.
sells_to: B2C primarily (DTC e-commerce and own showrooms), plus B2B wholesale to large retail partners (Mattress Firm, Costco, third-party online retailers).
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents, and notably no AI product at all. Purple Innovation's FY2025 10-K mentions artificial intelligence exactly twice, both in risk factors — once as a technological-obsolescence risk, once as a cybersecurity risk from its own and partners' increasing AI use. There is no AI feature, assistant, or agent in the product or the go-to-market. The Atlan engagement is entirely conventional data governance on a modern-data-stack setup: NetSuite ERP, Snowflake warehouse, Fivetran and Matillion for ingestion, dbt for transformation, Looker for reporting.
why_they_need_memory: The clearest 'company brain' pain of the three, and it is organizational rather than technical. Purple runs a hub-and-spoke data org — a central Data Enablement team (Analytics, Data Engineering, Omni-channel Analytics, Operations Analytics, Data Governance) plus federated analysts embedded in eCommerce, FP&A, Innovations, Accounting, Marketing and the Contact Center. Tony Baker, Data Governance Manager, framed the problem as 'the Great Data Debate': the same metric defined differently by each function, plus uncatalogued Shadow IT. The governance program was only ~7 months old at interview, and the phased plan was business glossary first, then data stewardship, then root-cause analysis. So the buyer is an early-stage governance function inside a mid-cap retailer trying to make one set of definitions stick across ~1,100 people in six-plus business units.

name: Generate Capital, PBC
what_it_does: North American sustainable-infrastructure investment and operating platform, structured as a public benefit corporation. Generate builds, owns, operates and finances real assets rather than just writing checks: distributed energy and power infrastructure, data centers and digital infrastructure, energy efficiency and electrification, and 'sustainable and specialty' infrastructure (waste-to-energy, anaerobic digestion, vertical farming/greenhouses, green hydrogen, EAF steel). category: Sustainable / energy infrastructure investment and asset operator (climate finance + project development). As an Atlan buyer, they sit in the 'mid-size data team inside a capital-intensive non-tech enterprise' segment.
stage: Mature private investment platform — not a venture-stage startup. No priced VC rounds in the usual sense; capitalized by institutional equity commitments and corporate credit facilities.
funding: More than $14 billion raised since inception per their Feb 2025 CEO-appointment release (an earlier Nov 2024 release said '$10B+ raised since inception'). Specific events: $1.5B equity raise in 2024; $1.2B corporate revolving credit facility and term loan announced 20 Nov 2024; over $1B raised in the 12 months to 6 Nov 2025 from insurance companies, pension plans and existing shareholders. Homepage cites ~$1.5B+ in recent equity commitments and $1B+ in annual credit facility closings. Holds 'more than $9 billion in assets across credit and equity strategies' (Nov 2025) and 2,000+ assets globally with 50+ technology and development partnerships. Early backer named at launch: Ceniarth (family office).
headcount_estimate: unknown — not disclosed on the website, careers page, or in any press release reviewed. No verifiable LinkedIn figure obtained (LinkedIn company page not fetchable). Do not assume a number.

founded_year: 2014 (launch announced 4 December 2014)
sells_to: B2B enterprise — corporate energy buyers, data-center/large-load operators, project developers, technology companies, and cities/campuses/municipalities. Also raises from institutional LPs (insurers, pension plans).
how_they_use_agents: No evidence of AI agents anywhere in their product or operations. The Atlan relationship is human-in-the-loop data governance, not agent infrastructure. Per the Sept 2023 Atlan interview with Abraham Tom, Director of Data: stack is Snowflake (warehouse), StreamSets (ingestion), dbt (transformation), Tableau (BI). Atlan use cases are (1) a data dictionary and lineage documentation that goes beyond what dbt exposes, (2) impact analysis wired into GitHub pull requests so developers see downstream breakage before shipping to production, and (3) business-glossary definitions tied to the system dictionary for governance. Stated payoff: product managers write more detailed specs by researching lineage themselves, cutting back-and-forth with developers. why_they_need_memory: A small central data function supports a business whose economics live in thousands of heterogeneous project-level assets across six sectors, each with its own counterparty, performance and financing data. The buying trigger is shared institutional context: engineers, PMs and analysts all need one trusted answer to 'what does this field mean, where did it come from, and what breaks if I change it' without routing every question through the data team.
