sells_to: B2B across the full range — fast-scaling SMB/startups through global enterprise, plus a genuine developer motion via its MCP server and APIs. Increasingly targets AI-native companies as a named vertical.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct directions. (1) Chargebee as agent infrastructure: it ships Chargebee MCP, marketed as 'headless billing for any AI client,' so an external AI agent can read and act on billing through the Model Context Protocol without a UI. (2) Chargebee for agent economics: an 'Agentic Billing' product that prices agent actions and tracks usage in real time, 'Billing for Gen AI' supporting token-, credit- and agent-based pricing models, and 'Payments for AI' that powers payment decisions using billing context. The inai acquisition added AI-driven payments intelligence. So Chargebee both exposes itself to agents and sells the meter that other companies use to charge for their agents.
why_they_need_memory: Any agent transacting through Chargebee MCP needs persistent context — which customer, which plan, what entitlements, what has already been invoiced, what the pricing rules are — because billing actions are irreversible and a stateless agent will double-charge or mis-provision. Internally, the cited Atlan engagement is about escaping the 'data as a service' trap: a central data team fielding endless ad hoc requests, replaced with reusable, governed data products. That is the same shape as an agent-memory purchase — the buyer is trying to make institutional knowledge self-serve and machine-readable instead of routed through people.

name: Docker, Inc.
what_it_does: Docker is the container platform company. Core products: Docker Desktop (local dev environment), Docker Hub (image registry, 20M+ developers claimed), Docker Scout (supply-chain/vuln analysis), Docker Hardened Images (minimal, continuously patched, SLSA L3 base images), and Docker Offload. Since 2025 the roadmap has pivoted hard toward agent infrastructure: Docker Sandboxes (microVM isolation per agent session, `sbx` CLI, supports Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, Codex, OpenCode, Kiro), MCP Enterprise Gateway, Docker AI Governance (org-wide sandbox + MCP policy console with identity-bound audit logs), Docker Model Runner (local LLM inference), and Gordon (Docker's own AI assistant). Tagline on the homepage: 'Full autonomy for any agent. Full confidence for your security team.' Enterprise business (Docker Enterprise) was sold to Mirantis in Nov 2019; the remaining company is the developer-tools business.
category: Developer tools / container + AI-agent runtime infrastructure
stage: Late-stage private (growth). Most recent disclosed round is a Series C.
funding: $105M Series C announced March 2022, led by Bain Capital Ventures (widely reported at ~$2.1B valuation — treat the valuation figure as medium confidence). Pre-restructuring Docker raised much more, including a $95M Series D in April 2015 that first made it a unicorn; cumulative historical funding is several hundred million dollars. Board seats held by Benchmark (Peter Fenton), Insight Partners (Jeff Horing), and Bain Capital Ventures (Enrique Salem). In-Q-Tel was disclosed as an investor in 2016. No IPO.
headcount_estimate: 501-1,000 (LinkedIn company page band). Likely toward the lower half of that band post-2019 restructuring.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Docker began as dotCloud, which went through Y Combinator's Winter 2010 batch — but that is the predecessor entity, not Docker Inc. as it is marketed today. Treat as effectively non-YC.
founded_year: 2013 (renamed from dotCloud on 2013-10-29; dotCloud itself founded 2008 in Paris by Solomon Hykes, Kamel Founadi, Sebastien Pahl)
sells_to: Developers (bottom-up PLG via Docker Desktop/Hub) plus B2B enterprise (Hardened Images, Scout, AI Governance, MCP Enterprise Gateway are seat/contract sales to platform and security teams)
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct things, and it matters for the category question. (1) As a VENDOR, Docker now sells the substrate agents run on: per-session microVM sandboxes so coding agents can run with --dangerously-skip-permissions safely, an MCP gateway/catalog for tool access, a governance console for MCP and sandbox policy, and Gordon as an in-product assistant. (2) The Atlan relationship has NOTHING to do with agents — the Atlan customer interview ('Docker: An Active Metadata Pioneer,' Jun 2023, interviewee Heidi Jones, data analysis and program management lead) is about Docker's internal analytics team on Snowflake + dbt + Looker adopting a metadata catalog for self-service documentation. So Docker appears on this logo wall as an internal data-governance buyer, not as an agent-memory buyer.
why_they_need_memory: The stated pain in the Atlan interview is textbook 'company brain': Docker's data team had been dependent on a single person who held all the documentation and institutional understanding, and wanted to move off the 'ask my favorite data person' pattern. Their core team of data engineers/analysts plus embedded data people in Marketing, Sales, Product and Finance had grown fast (several senior hires in 9 months), so tribal knowledge did not scale. They bought a shared context layer so non-technical staff could find trusted, certified assets themselves and data professionals could spend time on modeling instead of answering questions. Buying trigger = team growth + distributed/embedded analysts + key-person documentation risk, not agents.

name: Octane (Octane Lending, Inc.)
what_it_does: Tech-enabled specialty consumer lender and dealer marketplace for recreational purchases — powersports (motorcycles, ATVs, UTVs, personal watercraft), outdoor power equipment, RVs, and increasingly cars. Consumer side: soft-pull prequalification with real rates ('Octane Prequalified'), instant credit decisions, prime / credit-builder / first-time-buyer programs. Dealer side: the Octane Dealer Platform, SafeCheck (fraud/identity), Octane Preferred, and lead-gen from 80+ OEM brand partners and 4,000+ dealer partners. It underwrites and holds paper through its wholly owned in-house lender Roadrunner Financial, Inc. (launched 2016) and funds itself in the capital markets via ABS — a separate SEC filer, Octane Receivables LLC, files ABS-15G for the securitization shelf. HQ 535 8th Ave, New York; offices in Manhattan, Irving TX, plus remote.
category: Fintech — specialty/POS consumer lending (powersports, RV, outdoor equipment)
stage: Late-stage private / growth. 12 Form D exempt-offering notices with the SEC from July 2014 through November 2025; no S-1 or registration statement on file, so still private as of this research.
funding: Most recent round is verifiable from SEC Form D (CIK 0001613576, accession 0000950103-25-014596, filed 2025-11-12): equity, total offering amount $57,178,499, total amount sold $57,178,499, date of first sale 2025-11-03. Cumulative lifetime equity raised is NOT disclosed — do not quote a total. Directors named on that filing (useful as investor signal, affiliations are medium confidence): James Fitzgerald (Contour Venture Partners), Jesse Beyroutey (IA Ventures), Reuben Kobulnik (Valar Ventures), Jennifer Hill (likely independent). Executive officers/directors: Jason Guss (co-founder, CEO), Steven Fernald (co-founder, President & CFO), Mark Davidson, Mark Molnar, Sean Fernandez-Ledon, Mike Dushane, Maria Aveledo, Murali Vajjiravel. Separately, the business is substantially debt-funded through warehouse lines and Octane Receivables ABS deals.
headcount_estimate: 501-1,000 (LinkedIn company page band)
yc_or_accelerator: None found
founded_year: 2014 (marketplace launched 2014; Roadrunner Financial in-house lending added 2016)
sells_to: B2B2C — sells a financing platform to dealers and OEMs, and originates loans to consumers. Not an enterprise SaaS seller.
how_they_use_agents: No LLM agents in the product that I could verify. The AI/ML that exists is classical: a data science team building predictive machine learning models for credit risk and underwriting, which is what powers the 'instant decision' and soft-pull prequalification experience, plus SafeCheck for fraud/identity. The public consumer site never mentions AI or ML at all. Their Atlan case study (Jun 2023) is about analytics documentation, not agents. Internal stack at the time of the case study: AWS, Amazon Athena, Redshift, Apache Airflow, Tableau — notably a hand-rolled AWS stack, not the Snowflake/dbt norm.
why_they_need_memory: Strongest documented ROI story of the three. Two separate data organizations (one for financial reporting, one for BI — the BI team had data engineers, a data analyst, a product manager, and an engineering manager) had drifted into silos with fragmented documentation, and post-pandemic remote work broke the 'walk over and ask' fallback. Alex Bendix (Data Product Manager) framed it as teams using data in different ways with no common understanding of assets. Reported results: ~200 engineering hours saved per month from reduced support requests, 40% fewer messages in data-help Slack channels within three months, monthly active catalog users from under 5 to 70, at least ten previously non-technical people now querying independently, and engineers recovering 10-20% of their time. The buying trigger is interrupt load on a small data engineering team from a much larger non-technical org, in a regulated, heavily-audited lending business.

name: Austin Capital Bank SSB
what_it_does: A chartered Texas state savings bank (FDIC cert 58082, established 2006-01-09, Austin TX, 8100 Shoal Creek Blvd) that operates like a fintech holding company with a bank charter — it calls itself 'community banking on a national scale' and defines its community by shared problems rather than geography. Consumer fintech brands: Credit Strong (fully digital credit-builder loans and lines of credit for people with no or damaged credit — the flagship and by far the best-known product), FreeKick (first-to-market product letting parents build credit for minors and young adults aged 14-25 via an FDIC-insured savings account), Fort Knox Bank (high-yield 'secure savings' with biometric/passwordless verification, delayed withdrawals and closed-loop transfers as anti-fraud), MAGNUM, Rainy Day emergency savings, Jackpot Savings, money market and CDs. Founder and CEO Erik Beguin, who is regularly quoted in the press as a bank-fraud expert. Site claims 1M+ users and 50+ engineers, and Inc. 5000 listing for seven consecutive years. Note the size mismatch to keep in mind: as of the 6/30/2026 FDIC call report it holds only $395.5M in total assets and $308.4M in deposits across 15 offices — a very small bank running a large-volume consumer fintech book.
category: Community bank / consumer fintech (credit building, secure savings)
stage: Not venture-stage. Privately held bank, founded and led by its founder; funded by deposits, retained earnings and bank capital rather than priced equity rounds.
funding: unknown — no venture or growth equity round could be confirmed. There is no SEC Form D, no Crunchbase-style round I could verify, and nothing on the site. Treat as bootstrapped/self-funded; do NOT attribute a funding number to this company.
headcount_estimate: 51-200 (LinkedIn band); ~76 employees have LinkedIn profiles tagged to the company. The site's claim of '50+ engineers' is plausible only if that counts contractors or the Credit Strong entity, so treat it as marketing.
yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: 2006 (FDIC established date 2006-01-09)
sells_to: Consumer / prosumer (B2C direct-to-consumer credit-building and savings products), with the bank charter itself as the moat
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents found anywhere in the product or on the site. The only AI-adjacent items are forward-looking: the Atlan case study says future plans include fraud-detection models and marketing-spend optimization algorithms. Fort Knox's security story is biometric/passwordless auth and closed-loop transfers, which is rules-and-identity engineering, not ML. This company is an AI non-adopter that bought a metadata/context tool for humans.
why_they_need_memory: Classic 'tiny data team, whole company depends on it' case. Ian Bass (Head of Data & Analytics) ran a lean 2-3 person team and built the entire stack from scratch in 16 months — Snowflake, dbt, Fivetran, ThoughtSpot, Atlan, Tableau, Power BI, reverse ETL — replacing disconnected AWS and PostgreSQL databases. Two forces drove the purchase: (a) regulated, sensitive consumer-credit data means governance and access control are non-optional, and (b) a 2-3 person team cannot be the query interface for the whole bank, so they needed non-SQL staff to self-serve. Reported outcome: launching FreeKick required only ~2 hours of implementation effort using Atlan Insights, plus same-day/next-day marketing and product impact measurement and real-time executive metric visibility. Buying trigger = regulatory data governance + extreme data-team leverage constraints, not AI.

name: Advocates for Human Potential, Inc. (AHP)
what_it_does: For-profit behavioral-health consulting firm and government contractor. AHP provides technical assistance, training, research/evaluation, grant and funds management, and program implementation to federal (HHS/SAMHSA) and state agencies. Its work covers opioid and substance-use treatment and prevention, mental health systems, homelessness/housing, criminal justice, and treatment-facility buildout and licensing oversight. Named clients include the State of California (behavioral health infrastructure, housing, workforce investments), Massachusetts (Access to Recovery), the Philadelphia Department of Prisons (MAT programs), Tribal Nations, and SAMHSA. Its data team does 'gap analysis' (where grant money will have the most impact), pipeline/throughput analytics, and outcome measurement. It also builds an internal customer-facing app, the 'AHP Portal.'
category: GovTech / behavioral-health consulting and grant-program services (data catalog buyer, not AI)
stage: Private, independent, for-profit; no venture or PE backing found
funding: unknown — no VC/PE funding found. Revenue comes from federal and state contracts; USAspending shows HHS awards including $7.06M (CCBHC expansion evaluation), $6.23M (BH-HIV TA Center), $3.73M (Recovery to Practice)
headcount_estimate: 201-500 (LinkedIn band; ~492 employees listed)
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2B enterprise / B2G — federal and state government agencies
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents found anywhere in AHP's product or operations. They are a pure data-catalog/governance buyer, not an agent company. In the Atlan interview, Nick Murray (Senior Product Manager, product owner of the AHP Portal and their data governance platform) describes Atlan as a discovery layer for non-technical staff and an educational tool for junior analysts learning SQL. Stack is AWS-heavy: S3 data lake, Amazon Redshift in GovCloud, dbt for transformation, Power BI. Future interest listed is automation, not agents: dbt-driven quality tests surfaced in the catalog, auto-tagging of sensitive/PII data for government clients, and auto-tagging data from less-verified sources.
why_they_need_memory: Classic 'multiple sources of truth' pain. Large numbers of non-data-team users (project teams, coaches) pull raw data from scattered sources into Excel and BI tools and 'go off on their own,' producing conflicting numbers and, in Murray's words, misinformed decisions on how grant money is allocated. A lot of effort goes into mapping where the truth lives across the organization. They need one place that says what a dataset means, whether it is trustworthy, where it came from, and whether it contains sensitive government data. Their warehouse being in AWS GovCloud adds a compliance dimension that makes provenance and tagging load-bearing rather than nice-to-have.
sources: https://web.archive.org/web/20231003072311/https://humansofdata.atlan.com/2023/08/ahp-an-active-metadata-innovator/ (the source testimonial; page deprecated from Atlan's live site, recovered via Wayback — identifies AHP as Advocates for Human Potential and Nick Murray as the interviewee)
https://www.linkedin.com/company/advocates-for-human-potential (founded 1986, Sudbury MA, 201-500 employees, offices in Chicago IL and Pasadena CA)

name: Mistertemp' Group (legal entity: Alphyr SAS)
what_it_does: French temporary-staffing and recruitment group built on a franchise model. It operates ~230 agencies across four brands: Aquila RH (generalist temp staffing), Lynx RH (white-collar/executive recruitment), Vitalis Medical (healthcare temp staffing), and Mistertemp' (digital-first temp work). Two-sided business: it places temp workers with client companies, and it sells agency franchises to entrepreneurs (personal investment from ~EUR 25,000). Claims EUR 500M network revenue, 62,000 people placed, 400,000 contracts completed; the Atlan case study cites 12,000+ clients and 55,000 workers as of 2022. Positioning tagline is 'digitaliser sans deshumaniser' — digitize without dehumanizing. Runs an in-house R&D team in Paris's JobTech scene building the agency-management interface and dashboards.
category: HR tech / staffing marketplace (JobTech) — data catalog buyer, not AI
stage: Private, founder-led; no disclosed venture rounds
funding: unknown — no funding rounds found. Holding company Alphyr SAS filed EUR 7.86M revenue and EUR 12.2M net profit for 2025 with EUR 307,500 share capital (French registry via Pappers); the EUR 500M figure is network-wide franchise revenue, not the holding company's
headcount_estimate: ~198 direct group employees (LinkedIn); holding entity Alphyr SAS reports 38 employees in its French filings; LinkedIn lists a 1,001-5,000 band that includes the franchise network. Direct corporate headcount is the low hundreds.
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2B SMB — client companies hiring temp workers, plus franchisee entrepreneurs
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents in the product or in the Atlan case study. Their site lists machine learning alongside AWS, Kubernetes, Node.js, Elasticsearch and 'Big Data' as part of the R&D stack, but nothing agentic is described. The Atlan engagement is entirely classical data governance: a four-person data team using Fivetran -> Snowflake -> Looker with Airflow and dbt, using Atlan's column-level lineage and popularity metrics.
why_they_need_memory: A four-person data team had accumulated heavy technical debt by ingesting data indiscriminately. Atlan's lineage and usage metrics revealed that over half of their 1,500 Snowflake tables and 60% of their Looker dashboards had no downstream consumers; they deprecated roughly two-thirds of their assets. The stated payoff is confidence — 'we are confident as a team when we're talking about a data asset.' The need is a durable, queryable map of which asset is authoritative and who actually uses it, so a tiny team can maintain a sprawling estate. This is the pre-agent version of the memory problem: context about the data, not context for an agent.

name: Buildertrend
what_it_does: Vertical SaaS for construction management, aimed at residential home builders, remodelers, specialty/trade contractors, and increasingly commercial general contractors. One platform covering preconstruction (estimating, bidding, proposals), project management (scheduling, daily logs, change orders, submittals, plans), financials (budgeting, job costing, invoicing, payments, bill capture), and a client-facing portal for homeowner communication. Claims 1M+ all-time construction professionals, 2M+ projects, 1.5M+ app downloads, 100+ countries, and markets to '20,000+ builders.' Also runs adjacent businesses: Buildertrend University, onsite consulting, and CBUSA, a group purchasing organization for home builders.
category: Construction tech / vertical B2B SaaS — actively becoming an agentic AI platform
stage: Private, growth-equity backed (Bain Capital Tech Opportunities portfolio company)
funding: Bain Capital Tech Opportunities investment, portfolio entry listed as 2020; amount undisclosed. Acquisitions: CBUSA (2023), BizJet AI, Inc. (July 2026). Total raised: unknown — no dollar figures disclosed publicly on the sources I could reach.
headcount_estimate: unknown current figure; company's own about page states '500+ employees' as of 2019. LinkedIn was not reachable this session.
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2B SMB — home builders, remodelers, and trade contractors, mostly small and mid-size firms
how_they_use_agents: This is the one of the three with a real, explicit agent strategy, and it is recent. Shipping AI features today: AI Client Updates (auto-generated project updates sent to homeowners without manual writing), AI Bill Capture (extracting and coding vendor bills), and AI-powered Submittals and Plans. In July 2026 Buildertrend acquired BizJet AI, Inc., described as an 'agent-native' company combining a multimodal data platform with multi-agent AI systems to automate builder workflows — cost estimating, scheduling, and a project assistant. BizJet co-founder Ruhaab Markas (ex-Amazon Alexa, AWS Bedrock, Google) joined as VP of Product, AI, and John Baker (ex-Google, Amazon) as Distinguished Engineer. Markas's stated goal: 'Buildertrend is uniquely positioned to become the agentic AI platform for homebuilders, remodelers and specialty contractors because it already serves as the system contractors rely on.' CEO Dan Houghton frames it as software that 'doesn't just track the work, it helps move it forward.'
why_they_need_memory: Two overlapping reasons. (1) The original Atlan driver, from Preston Badeer, Director of Data Engineering: a tiny data engineering team (started at two engineers) supporting 20+ data scientists and 10+ customer researchers across BigQuery, dbt, Fivetran, Hightouch, GitHub Actions, Tableau and Dataiku, with no documentation — 'it was just, kind of, the wild west.' Explicit anti-tribal-knowledge philosophy: 'Everyone on the team should be able to pick up any project that anyone has worked on without any kind of Joe knows about that thing and he's on vacation.' Badeer's stated goal is that every employee has trusted, documented, role-relevant data on day one, alongside their email. (2) The 2026 agent pivot compounds it: multi-agent systems doing estimating and scheduling need exactly the trusted, documented, lineage-aware context layer the catalog was built to provide, plus persistent per-project and per-builder context across long-running construction jobs. A stated preference of 'throw tools at problems before people' means they buy this layer rather than build it.

name: New York Life Insurance Company
what_it_does: The largest mutual life insurer in the U.S., in operation since 1845 (chartered 1841 as Nautilus Mutual Life). Sells term, whole, universal and variable universal life insurance, long-term care and individual disability insurance, income and deferred annuities, mutual funds/ETFs, 529 plans, wealth management, estate planning and small-business coverage. Distribution is overwhelmingly human: 12,000+ agents and advisors across 120+ offices. New York Life Investments is the global asset-management arm (Candriam, MacKay Shields and other affiliated boutiques); the general account investment portfolio is ~$371B. FY2024 revenue ~$27.2B, total assets ~$244.9B; paid $2.5B in dividends to policyholders in 2025, its 171st consecutive year. Policyholder-owned, so no outside shareholders and no equity ticker.
category: Life insurance / financial services incumbent (Fortune 100, mutual). NOT an AI-native startup — this is an enterprise buyer of a data/context governance platform.
stage: Public-interest mutual company, 180 years old. Not venture-backed; no stage in the startup sense.
funding: none — mutual company owned by its policyholders, no outside shareholders and no VC/PE funding. (It is an investor itself: New York Life Ventures, its corporate VC arm, founded 2012.)
headcount_estimate: ~15,000 corporate employees (15,384 as of 2023); company states '23,000+ employees and agents,' of which 12,000+ are agents and advisors (2025).
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2C consumers (individual life, annuities, retirement) plus B2B for group benefits and small-business coverage; sold through a captive agent/advisor force rather than self-serve.
how_they_use_agents: AI is internal-productivity and advisor-augmentation, not agentic product. CIO Deepa Soni frames AI as 'a human amplifier' that cuts admin work so advisors spend time with clients, and explicitly calls it 'a cultural and a people transformation' resting on 'strong data, governance and cybersecurity foundations.' Their newsroom runs an 'Everyday AI' series profiling employee-built tools — an AI tool for compliance reviews (Noah Robbins) and a predictive-outcomes model built by a data scientist (Ceci Chen). Soni's line 'Long history gives us that long data,' converted into 'enterprise intelligence' for personalized service, is the clearest statement of intent. No public evidence of autonomous multi-step agents in production; no attributed Atlan quote or case study — logo only on Atlan's homepage 'trusted by' wall.
why_they_need_memory: Textbook enterprise-context buyer: 180 years of accumulated policy, actuarial and claims data across a heavily regulated business where an AI answer that cannot be traced to a certified definition is a compliance problem. Atlan's pitch — data graph + business logic + governance so 'every AI output is traceable' back to who certified it — maps directly onto an insurer's need to let advisor copilots and internal LLM tools reach trusted data without leaking or hallucinating regulated facts. The buying motion here is almost certainly a central data-governance/CDO org, not a product team.

name: W.W. Grainger, Inc. (Grainger)
what_it_does: Broad-line industrial distributor of maintenance, repair and operating (MRO) supplies — motors, lighting, material handling, fasteners, plumbing, tools, safety equipment — plus inventory management and technical support services. Serves more than 4.6 million customers, primarily in North America and Japan. FY2025 revenue $17.9B ($17.2B in 2024). Two reportable segments: High-Touch Solutions North America (~2 million products, sold with sales/technical coverage to complex accounts) and Endless Assortment (the web-only businesses Zoro, ~13 million SKUs, and Japan's MonotaRO, ~29 million SKUs). Sold its U.K. Cromwell business in December 2025. NYSE: GWW, S&P 500 component, headquartered in Lake Forest, Illinois. Digital is the dominant channel — >70% of U.S. orders originated digitally as of 2019.
category: B2B industrial distribution / MRO e-commerce (Fortune 500). NOT an AI-native company — an enterprise buyer.
stage: Public company (NYSE: GWW), founded 1927, S&P 500 constituent.
funding: n/a — publicly traded since long before the venture era; no startup funding history. FY2025 revenue $17.9B.
headcount_estimate: ~25,000 team members worldwide as of Dec 31, 2025 per the FY2025 10-K (approx. 22,100 full-time, 2,900 part-time/temporary; ~90% North America, ~10% Asia). Wikipedia lists 26,000 for 2024.
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2B across the full size range — SMB and mid-market (largely via Zoro/MonotaRO self-serve) through large enterprise, healthcare, manufacturing and government accounts (High-Touch Solutions).
how_they_use_agents: Confirmed from the FY2025 10-K rather than marketing: Grainger is 'increasing investments in developing, managing and implementing AI, such as large language model technologies' and treats embedding 'AI capabilities into its digital platforms' as competitively critical. Its eCommerce operation already uses 'machine learning and other capabilities to provide simplified customer interactions' — i.e. product search, SKU matching and recommendation across a 13-29 million-SKU catalog, the classic MRO discovery problem. The 10-K also carries explicit AI risk-factor language (flawed algorithms, insufficient or biased datasets, failure to recoup AI investment). No public evidence yet of autonomous agents; the plausible near-term shape is a customer-facing product-finding assistant plus internal merchandising/pricing copilots. Logo only on Atlan's homepage wall, no quote or case study.
why_they_need_memory: The hard problem is product data at scale: tens of millions of SKUs with inconsistent manufacturer attributes, cross-references, substitutes and compliance data, spread across three semi-independent businesses (Grainger, Zoro, MonotaRO) and 80+ upstream systems. Any AI search or purchasing assistant is only as good as the certified attribute and taxonomy layer underneath it, and a wrong substitute recommendation on a safety or electrical part is a liability event. That is precisely the 'unify, enrich, certify, activate' pipeline Atlan sells. Their own 10-K risk language about insufficient/biased datasets is effectively the business case for buying a governed context layer.

name: HelloFresh SE (HelloFresh Group)
what_it_does: The world's largest meal-kit company: a subscription DTC platform that ships pre-portioned fresh ingredients plus recipe cards, and increasingly ready-to-eat meals. Founded in Berlin in 2011 by Dominik Richter, Thomas Griesel and Jessica Nilsson; IPO'd on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange 2 Nov 2017 (FWB: HFG). FY2025 net revenue €6.76B, ~850 million meals delivered, 29,000+ recipes, operating in 18+ countries. Brand portfolio spans HelloFresh (core meal kits), Green Chef (lifestyle/diet-specific), EveryPlate (value), Chefs Plate (Canada), Factor (ready-to-eat, the growth engine), Youfoodz (Australia), Pets Table (pet food) and Good Chop (meat/seafood). Currently running an efficiency/profitability program and shifting toward a higher-value customer base and a broader 'daily food companion' app positioning.
category: Consumer subscription e-commerce / DTC food (meal kits and ready-to-eat). NOT AI-native — a scaled consumer internet incumbent.
stage: Public company (Frankfurt Stock Exchange, FWB: HFG), listed 2017; formerly Rocket Internet-backed before IPO.
funding: n/a as a startup today — publicly listed since November 2017. FY2025 net revenue €6.76B. Pre-IPO it raised venture rounds (Rocket Internet, Insight Partners, Baillie Gifford among historical backers); no current private round to report.
headcount_estimate: ~19,065 employees (2025); company site states '18,000+'.
yc_or_accelerator: none (Rocket Internet company builder, not an accelerator in the YC sense)
sells_to: B2C consumer subscription across 18+ markets; no meaningful enterprise sales motion.

HelloFresh shipped a conversational-commerce app inside ChatGPT (US beta, late 2025) built on OpenAI's Apps SDK and the Model Context Protocol — a Python/FastAPI MCP server exposing HelloFresh menu APIs, plus a React/TypeScript widget rendering interactive recipe cards (images, cook time, difficulty, nutrition) with one-click handoff to hellofresh.com. Users filter by excluded ingredients, calories or cook time in natural language. The company states this is the first step toward native presence across ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, on the thesis that a significant share of e-commerce traffic will arrive through AI platforms. Add 29,000+ recipes across 8 brands and 18 markets with per-country menus and localized nutrition rules, and you get a taxonomy/lineage problem that has to be certified before it is 'activated' to an agent. That is exactly Atlan's MCP-and-API activation story. So the need is real on two fronts: (1) product-side, their agents are stateless across sessions and need durable repo/org context; (2) buyer-side, a ~2,500-person all-remote public company with a fragmented internal data stack needs a governed semantic layer before analytics agents can be trusted — the exact pitch Atlan makes as "The Context Layer for AI."

The agent pulls from Google Drive, Google Sheets, Guru collections, and Zoom's public help center, and is embedded directly in Slack where the questions were already being asked, with a lightweight feedback control. A videographer in a live, high-stakes deposition cannot wait on a human in Slack — latency is the whole problem, and roughly 50% of inbound was answerable from existing documentation. What they needed was a persistent, curated store of operational know-how (Zoom quirks, deposition room setup, escalation paths) sitting where the work happens, so tribal knowledge in a small support team's heads survives turnover and scales past the two people who hold it. stage: Late-stage private, PE-backed. CAUTION: the widely reported 2019 majority-stake acquisition by The Carlyle Group could NOT be re-verified in this session (the press release URL 404'd and my web-search budget was exhausted) — treat ownership as probable but unconfirmed here.

how_they_use_agents: Both in-product and internally, which makes them the most interesting of the three. IN PRODUCT: an "AI Hiring Agent" / Talent Engagement Agent that autonomously matches candidates to roles, runs candidate-led conversational screening ("feels like chatting with a recruiter, not a scripted bot") at scale, identifies skills and surfaces roles candidates hadn't considered, and automates scheduling. The March 2026 Hireguide acquisition was explicitly to ship a voice-based AI Interviewer and, per the CEO, "a series of conversational agents that will power smarter hiring workflows." INTERNALLY (the Guru deployment): the 30-person support team runs a custom Support Knowledge Agent in a dedicated Slack channel that draws on verified Guru collections AND ingests relevant Slack conversations from expert channels, returns linked Guru cards alongside AI answers, and uses prompts fine-tuned to HireVue's platform names and terminology; the team monitored 900+ early questions to tune accuracy. Also embedded via a Zendesk browser extension for in-ticket answers and Lessonly module integration for onboarding. Outcomes claimed: onboarding 5 weeks → 2 weeks (60% cut), Slack questions down 40% even as case volume rose 500+.
why_they_need_memory: The sharpest driver is M&A-induced product sprawl: acquisitions took the support surface "from supporting one platform to four," so institutional knowledge lived in tenured agents' heads and new hires were "completely reliant" on them. That is the canonical company-brain buying trigger — knowledge fragmented faster than documentation could keep up. Two secondary drivers: (1) a 30-person tiered support org with constant onboarding, where ramp time is a directly measurable cost; (2) HireVue operates in a heavily scrutinized regulatory domain (2019 EPIC/FTC complaint, a CVS AI-scoring suit settled 2024, a 2025 ACLU disability-discrimination complaint, plus NYC LL144 / EU AI Act exposure), which means internal answers must be verified and attributable rather than plausibly hallucinated — they bought a system with a verification primitive, not a raw LLM search box. Worth noting for positioning: as an agent vendor themselves, they are a sophisticated buyer who evaluated retrieval quality (900+ monitored questions) rather than taking demo claims at face value.

category: Nonprofit — K-12 food education and child nutrition, plus policy advocacy. No AI or software product whatsoever.
stage: Nonprofit — venture stage terminology does not apply.

Salaries and wages were $15.7M. The 2024 audit flagged a material weakness in internal controls. It is an AmeriCorps grantee (same structural model as Teach for America or Habitat for Humanity). how_they_use_agents: No agents in any product — there is no product. Purely internal knowledge management. FoodCorps adopted Guru as a federated search and verification layer sitting ON TOP of Google Drive, Box and Slack rather than migrating content into a new system, using enterprise search, the browser extension, the Slack integration, and Guru's card-verification workflow. Rollout was deliberately low-lift: a 30-day trial plus bulk migration tooling. Guru's AI Knowledge Agents and Pages (department-specific hubs) were described as PLANNED future expansion, not yet deployed at the time of the case study — so of the three companies here, this is the least mature agent deployment.
why_they_need_memory: Two explicit and highly transferable buying criteria. First, AGNOSTIC/FEDERATED INGESTION: "We didn't have to move everything into Guru. Instead, it connected us to where files already lived." A ~100+ person distributed remote nonprofit with years of tool sprawl across Drive, Box and Slack has neither the budget nor the ops capacity for a content-migration project — the memory layer has to index in place. Second, VERIFICATION AND TRUST: "The fact that Guru lets us verify information is huge. It means we can trust what we're seeing, which wasn't always the case before." A staleness/provenance signal was a named purchase driver, not a nice-to-have. Structurally they also have designed-in churn — service-member cohorts rotate annually — so institutional knowledge walks out the door every year by construction. The Director of Operations & IT framed the whole problem as retrieval rather than storage: "It's less about where the information lives and more about how you get to it."

what_it_does: Business travel and spend management platform. Books flights/rail/hotels/cars via 25+ NDC connections, then handles the money side: expense capture, receipt matching, invoice intake through ERP entry, VAT recovery, policy enforcement and approvals. Also runs a group/events booking line. Named features include FlexiTravel (80% refund on cancelled trips), Traveler Tracker, Lodge Card and Perk Card. Self-reported scale: 10,000+ business customers, $2.5B+ annualized booking volume, a booking every 5 seconds. Grew by acquisition — Click Travel (2021, UK), NexTravel (2021, YC-backed), and Yokoy (2025, Swiss AI expense management, 'nine figure' price) — and rebranded from TravelPerk to Perk as the scope widened from travel to travel+spend+events. travelperk.com now 301-redirects to perk.com.
category: Business travel & spend management SaaS (T&E) — not AI-native; a 10-year-old vertical SaaS company with a large customer-care org
stage: Late-stage private (Series E)
funding: ~$860M total equity + debt. $200M Series E in Jan 2025 led by Atomico at a $2.7B valuation (nearly double the prior $1.4B), with EQT Growth, Noteus Partners, Kinnevik and General Catalyst. Prior rounds: $104M (Jan 2024), $115M Series D equity+debt (Jan 2022, unicorn), $160M (Apr 2021), $60M Series C extension (2019), $44M (2018), $21M (2018), $7M Series A (2016). Investor base also includes SoftBank Vision Fund, Felix Capital, Blackstone and Sequoia Capital (per Perk's own media center).
headcount_estimate: ~1,800+ (self-reported on perk.com and in the Guru case study); LinkedIn band 1,001-5,000. Customer care alone is >1,000 people, up from ~150 total employees in 2019, with 300+ new care agents onboarded in 2025.
yc_or_accelerator: None. (Notably, Perk *acquired* YC-backed NexTravel in 2021 — the YC connection is on the acquired side, not Perk itself.)
sells_to: B2B — SMB through enterprise. Multiple personas inside each account: finance teams (spend control, reporting), travel managers (program admin), and individual employee travelers. Named customers include Wise, On Running, Breitling.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places. (1) In the product: Perk markets 'one AI across travel, spend and events' that auto-categorizes expenses, matches receipts to card transactions, extracts invoice line items, validates suppliers, populates cost objects from historical patterns, flags policy breaches and routes approvals — claimed ~100,000 tasks/day. They also ship an MCP server so customers can run reports and approvals from Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini. (2) Internally, which is the Guru relationship: custom Guru Knowledge Agents scoped by care-agent tier and by booking platform, so the agent recognizes which platform a rep is working in and surfaces only relevant content. Reported usage: 908 monthly active AI users, 1M+ Card views, 173 announcements sent, 200 agent comments/month. Guru also hosts an Incidents Page that replaced Slack/email alert sprawl.
why_they_need_memory: Classic scale-of-support pain, not agent-infra pain. A customer care org that went from ~150 to 1,000+ people, onboarding 300+ new agents in a single year, with critical operational updates buried across Slack, email and internal databases. Layer on three acquisitions (Click Travel, NexTravel, Yokoy) with different products and booking platforms, nine country locales, and travel-supplier rules that change constantly — the answer a rep needs is both role-specific and platform-specific. Their stated mantra is 'Everything is in Guru.' The buying trigger was headcount growth plus M&A-driven knowledge fragmentation, and the AI layer was adopted on top of an already-governed knowledge base.

name: Lemonade
what_it_does: Full-stack, AI-first insurance carrier (not a broker — it underwrites its own risk). Sells renters, homeowners, car, pet and term life insurance direct to consumers in the US, plus contents/liability in the UK, France, Netherlands and Germany. Onboarding and claims run through chatbots rather than agents or forms; the company claims ~98% of policies are bound via AI and 60%+ of claims handled by AI, with nearly half of claims paid in seconds. Certified B-Corp with a 'Giveback' program donating leftover premium to charities chosen by customers ($10M+ to date). Acquired Metromile (2022); announced a Tesla partnership for autonomous-vehicle insurance in Jan 2026.
category: Insurtech — AI-native consumer insurance carrier, publicly traded
stage: Public company (NYSE: LMND)
funding: Publicly traded. IPO 1 July 2020 on NYSE, 11M shares at $29 (~$319M gross). Pre-IPO venture backing from SoftBank Vision Fund, Sequoia Capital, GV, Allianz X, General Catalyst and others — I could not confirm a precise pre-IPO total in this research, so treat that figure as unknown. FY2024 reported revenue $527M, net loss $202M, total assets $1.85B.
headcount_estimate: ~1,235 employees per the FY2024 annual report; LinkedIn currently lists ~1,475 (band 1,001-5,000). The Guru case study cites 500+ globally distributed 'Makers' (content contributors) across Customer Experience, Claims and Underwriting.
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: Consumer / D2C (prosumer). ~2-2.9M customers across US, UK and Europe. Not a B2B seller — which makes it an unusual profile for this vendor category; the buyer here is an internal ops/enablement function, not a product team.
how_they_use_agents: Two layers again. Customer-facing: Maya and Jim, the AI bots that quote policies and adjudicate claims, are the company's core product mechanic. Internally — the Guru relationship — CX, Claims and Underwriting run on Guru as an 'AI source of truth' integrated with Slack, Zendesk and their LMS (360Learning), with Guru AI Answers surfacing verified policy inside Zendesk via browser extension and permission-scoped collections for sensitive content. They built a Slack-first intake workflow (Zapier automations + Google Sheets tracking) where stakeholders submit the first draft and the L&D team edits for clarity and linkage. Reported: 5,000+ Guru Cards, 2,000+ verified Pet Claims Cards, 200-300 knowledge requests processed monthly, 90% weekly adoption, 100% trust score, 93% accuracy in annual audits, and one full week cut from new-hire training.
why_they_need_memory: Regulated, high-churn knowledge. Insurance content varies by US state, by country, and by product line (renters vs. home vs. car vs. pet vs. life), and it changes with filings and underwriting rules. When your customer-facing AI answers claims questions, the governance layer underneath is a compliance requirement, not a convenience — a stale card becomes a wrong regulatory answer. Add 500+ distributed contributors and 200-300 change requests a month and you need provenance, verification cycles and expiry, not just a search box. Their explicit framing is visibility and capacity: proving to stakeholders what the knowledge team is doing and what it's worth.

name: Empathy
what_it_does: B2B2C platform for 'life's hardest moments' — bereavement, estate administration, legacy planning, caregiving and leave. Sold to life insurers, banks/wealth managers, employers and benefits consultants, then delivered free to their policyholders or employees. Product lines: Loss Support (probate, funeral logistics, benefits claims, closing accounts, grief support), LifeVault (AI-guided estate/legacy planning and document vault), Caregiving Support, Leave Support, and Connect (a client-relationship layer for the institution). The model is explicitly 'AI + human care': software handles the paperwork and logistics, human Care Managers handle the rest. Claims families save an average of 189 hours and $3,007. Coverage footprint: 50M+ policyholders and 9M+ employees, North America and UK. Distribution partners named on-site include MetLife, New York Life, Prudential, Guardian, Allianz, Aflac, Munich Re, Citi, Securian, TIAA, MassMutual, Aviva and AT&T. Grief author David Kessler is 'Chief Empathy Officer.'
category: Benefits tech / insurtech services — AI-assisted bereavement, estate and caregiving support sold through insurers and employers
stage: Series B (last confirmed); likely one later undisclosed round — see funding note
funding: $162M+ total raised per Empathy's own site. Confirmed rounds: $13M seed (Apr 2021), $30M Series A (Sept 2021), $47M Series B (Mar 2024) — that's $90M, so roughly $70M+ of the stated total comes from a round I could NOT confirm in this research. Do not treat a Series C as verified. Investors listed by the company: Index Ventures, Gradient Capital, Adams Street Partners, Entrée Capital, Aleph, LionTree, Latitude, Semper and Primetime. No valuation disclosed anywhere I could reach.
headcount_estimate: ~231 employees listed on LinkedIn (company self-selects the 51-200 band). Smallest of the three by an order of magnitude.
yc_or_accelerator: None found
sells_to: B2B enterprise — life insurers, banks and wealth managers, large employers, and benefits consultants. Delivered B2B2C to end families. Enterprise sales cycle, insurance-grade procurement.
how_they_use_agents: In the product: AI-guided estate planning flows in LifeVault, AI drafting (they shipped an AI obituary generator in 2023), and AI triage of the logistics of loss, backed by human Care Managers. In operations — the Guru relationship — they hit a jurisdiction-grounding failure: a single knowledge agent was answering Manitoba estate-fee questions with Ontario law. Their fix was to split into two separate Knowledge Agents, US and Canada, each scoped to its own knowledge base, wired to country-specific Guru Pages, flagged with 🇺🇸/🇨🇦 emoji in the UI, embedded in the Chrome extension where Care Managers actually work, and prompted to refuse to generalize across provinces/states. They also rewrote content from tables into headers because the retrieval layer parsed headers more reliably.
why_they_need_memory: The sharpest need of the three, and the most instructive for this category. Their answers are jurisdiction-bound legal-adjacent guidance — probate and estate rules differ by US state and by Canadian province — delivered to grieving families by non-lawyer Care Managers under insurer-brand liability. A retrieval error isn't a bad search result, it's wrong legal information at the worst possible moment. That forces hard partitioning of the knowledge base by region, provenance on every answer, and content authored for machine retrieval rather than human skimming. Every new market (Canada, UK) multiplies the partitions, so the agent architecture has to scale by jurisdiction. This is a genuine agent-grounding problem, not a wiki-search problem.

name: Paraco Gas (Paraco Gas Corporation)
what_it_does: Family-owned propane distributor and energy services company serving the Northeast US. Sells residential and commercial propane delivery, tank installation and leasing (56–1000+ gallon), oil-to-propane conversions, budget billing and service contracts, HVAC services (Paraco HVAC), plus commercial/industrial lines: forklift fuel (cylinder exchange), restaurant and construction fuel, AutoGas, agricultural propane, and BBQ tank exchange. Per its own executive-team page it serves ~120,000 residential and commercial customers from 27 distribution locations and is the 13th largest propane marketer in the US; HQ in Rye Brook, NY. Founded 1968 by Pat Armentano as Patsems, Inc., a welding supply distributor in Mount Vernon, NY; Joseph Armentano became CEO in 1987 and is still CEO/Chairman. Grew mainly by acquisition (Paraco Fuel 1979, Suburban Propane's Long Island ops 1985, Furman Gas 1994, AmeriGas locations 2004–05, Colonial Gas 2006, Blackstone Propane and Blue Flame 2007, and many more through 2021), with direct operations or JVs touching NY, PA, NJ, CT, MA, RI, VA, NC, CO, FL, TN, IL and GA.
category: Propane / fuel distribution and home energy services (non-tech incumbent; the buyer is the contact-center / workforce-management function)
stage: Private, family-owned; no venture funding (Tracxn lists it as an unfunded company)
funding: None disclosed — privately held and self/debt-financed since 1968. Third-party data aggregators estimate revenue in the $100M–$500M range (IncFact) with point estimates around $181M (RocketReach) to $220M (Zippia); these are unverified vendor estimates, not company-reported figures.
headcount_estimate: 425+ company-wide (stated on Paraco's own executive-team page); CEO Joe Armentano's LinkedIn profile says 'more than 400 employees.' Contact-data vendors list ~200, but the company's own figure is the more reliable one.
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: B2C homeowners plus B2B SMB and mid-market commercial/industrial accounts (restaurants, construction, agriculture, forklift fleets). As a software buyer it is a traditional mid-market enterprise buyer.
how_they_use_agents: 'Agents' here are human contact-center agents, not AI agents — this is the important distinction for this category. Paraco's customer experience team uses Guru as the knowledge layer behind live phone support: Knowledge Cards for processes, policies and pricing; a Microsoft OneDrive integration to pull in existing documents; and Announcements to push real-time price and policy changes to the floor. Guru's AI search surfaces answers across those sources mid-call ('it's pulling information from multiple sources pertaining to the topic'). The case study notes future plans for Guru Pages and custom GPT integrations, so agentic use is aspirational rather than deployed. There is no evidence of AI agents in Paraco's own product or customer-facing channels; their tech story is delivery/usage-tracking telemetry and automatic delivery scheduling.
why_they_need_memory: Classic 'tribal knowledge trapped in email' problem at a roll-up. Decades of acquisitions (dozens of propane companies since 1979) left inconsistent policies, pricing and procedures across 27 locations, and price changes in a commodity business move constantly. Daniel Guglielmo: 'Hold times were high because agents couldn't find what they needed quickly, and that left customers on double holds. It was just a mess.' and 'We needed a tool that allowed us to centralize everything so our agents could stop digging through emails or relying on outdated systems.' Reported outcome: call handle time down 8% (from over 6 minutes to under 5:30), time-to-first-response improved 10 seconds within two weeks, faster onboarding with better training assessment scores, and call volume maintained with reduced workforce need. The buying trigger is contact-center cost and CSAT, not AI ambition — but a governed, current knowledge base is exactly the substrate an AI voice/chat agent would later need.

name: Faire (Faire Wholesale, Inc.)
what_it_does: Online B2B wholesale marketplace connecting independent retailers (boutiques, grocers, florists, bakeries, plant nurseries, gift shops) with 100,000+ mostly small and emerging brands. Faire de-risks wholesale buying for small retailers: low order minimums, 60-day interest-free payment terms, and free returns on a retailer's first order with any new brand — Faire takes the credit and returns risk and monetizes via commission plus a fast-growing ads business (>5% of revenue). Founded 2017 by Max Rhodes (CEO), Marcelo Cortes (co-founder/Chief Architect), Daniele Perito and Jeff Kolovson — several ex-Square. Y Combinator alum (W17). Offices in San Francisco (HQ), New York, Toronto, Waterloo, London and São Paulo. Company-stated scale as of Nov 2025: ~$3B GMV expected for 2025, $500M+ annualized revenue, 40%+ YoY growth in Q3, GMV growth accelerating 8 consecutive quarters, net dollar retention above 110%, retailers in 70,000 cities.
category: B2B e-commerce marketplace / wholesale commerce platform (late-stage growth tech, not an AI-native startup)
stage: Late-stage private (Series G+); post-correction. Peak $12.4–12.6B valuation Nov 2021; repriced to a $5.2B employee tender in Nov 2025.
funding: Roughly $1.4B–$1.7B raised total across ~7–9 rounds — sources disagree, so treat the exact number as uncertain. Anchors that are well-sourced: a $400M Series G (Nov 2021) co-led by Durable Capital and Dragoneer at a $12.4B valuation, which the company said took total funding past $1B; a $416M extension (May 2022) from Y Combinator, Sequoia and others; and a Nov 2025 secondary/employee tender at $5.2B led by WCM Investment Management with Baillie Gifford and True North Fund. Investors across rounds include Sequoia Capital, Y Combinator, Lightspeed Venture Partners (Series B), Khosla Ventures, Forerunner Ventures, Founders Fund, Dragoneer and Durable Capital. Tracxn puts total funding at $1.7B over 9 rounds from 28 investors.
headcount_estimate: Roughly 900–1,300. Revelio Labs estimates 1,270 as of March 2026; Unify estimates 931; another aggregator cites 1,500 as of 2024. Faire laid off 20% of staff in Nov 2023. No company-confirmed figure is public, so treat this as an estimate range.
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator (W17); YC also participated in the 2022 $416M extension round
sells_to: B2B SMB primarily — independent/local retail store owners — plus the small brands supplying them. Internally it is a large tech org, so it also buys enterprise-grade internal tooling.
how_they_use_agents: Agents appear in three distinct places. (1) Customer-facing product: natural-language search ('find me dresses made in Paris, under $100') parsed into structured filters, image-based search via vision models, and 'Project Burrito' — Python agents paired with Kotlin services that compose multi-step buying flows by reading a retailer's profile and assembling a product assortment. Faire has publicly committed to an 'AI buying assistant' that helps retailers visualize and build cohesive assortments, plus AI-driven product-listing optimization (auto-improved descriptions, images and product types, with an opt-out) and AI+logistics for consolidated multi-brand shipping. (2) Internal engineering: 'Project Cyberpunk,' an in-house agentic development platform with pre-warmed dev workspaces and an orchestrator that decomposes tasks into smaller sub-agent prompts (settings cleanup, test authoring, code quality), plus GitHub Copilot invoked programmatically through MCP servers to do things like find expired feature flags and open cleanup issues. (3) Internal ops/CX: Guru Knowledge Agents — a 'CX Policy Assistant' agent answering CX policy questions, and a second Knowledge Agent supporting marketplace operations. Notion is the connective tissue across 20+ work apps, with Notion AI used for meeting notes, synthesizing customer feedback, drafting docs and cross-tool search; Faire ran a 30+ person AI hackathon and embeds 'AI Captains' on every team.
why_they_need_memory: Two different memory problems, which is why Faire shows up on two vendors' customer lists. On the Guru side it is knowledge decay: Carly Byrge inherited a Guru instance with trust scores of 40–50% and hundreds of unverified cards, and was manually QA-ing content ~6 hours/week — 'I spent probably an average of six hours a week trying to stay on top of and catch up with all of our unverified cards. It was a lot.' Quality automations (auto-verify/auto-unverify on engagement signals) cut that to under an hour a week and raised the trust score from 76% to 96% (Guru also claims ~20% higher AI accuracy). The unlock was explicitly that the knowledge base had to be trustworthy before the team would let a Knowledge Agent answer from it — bad knowledge produces confidently wrong AI. On the Notion side it is context for agents: 7+ years of business knowledge, roadmaps, PRDs and sprints linked across Jira/GitHub/Figma so that, in Notion's framing, AI 'acts with full context rather than starting from scratch' and future agents inherit business context from day one. Reported Notion outcomes: workflows 30% faster, ~9 hours/week saved per person, 81% report smoother meetings, 71% call Notion AI their most valuable AI tool, 94% call Notion mission-critical, 8x claimed ROI. This is the archetypal buyer: an AI-forward but not AI-native company whose agent quality is bottlenecked by the freshness and governance of its internal knowledge.

name: PetDesk (PetDesk, LLC; formerly parent-branded Petvisor)
what_it_does: Vertical SaaS for veterinary practices — client engagement and front-office software that integrates directly with 25+ practice information management systems (PIMS) such as ezyVet, Cornerstone and AVImark. Modules: Client Communications (two-way texting, mass messaging, unified Comms Inbox), PetDesk Phones (veterinary-specific VoIP with PIMS-aware caller ID showing pet history, vaccine status and upcoming appointments, call queues, routing decision trees, 2-year call history), Online Booking, PetDesk Scribe (AI ambient documentation / SOAP notes), a pet-parent mobile app, payments, veterinary websites and marketing. Company-stated scale: 12,000+ veterinary practices, 18.5M+ pets annually, 44M+ appointments/year; marketing claims 25–30 hours/week saved per clinic, 50% lower phone volume, 90% lower no-show rate. Founded 2013, HQ at 2044 First Ave, San Diego, CA. The parent holding company was Petvisor, which rolled up PetDesk, Vetstoria (online booking), Kontak, WhiskerCloud (vet websites) and Groomer.io (pet grooming software); petvisor.com now redirects to petdesk.com, indicating the portfolio has been consolidated under the PetDesk brand.
category: Vertical SaaS — veterinary practice / pet-care client engagement software (PE-backed roll-up, AI-augmented not AI-native)
stage: Private equity-backed growth stage (majority/strategic growth investment, post-venture)
funding: Approximately $130M+ disclosed. Series B of $12M in Feb 2019. Frontier Growth made an initial investment in 2021. In Nov 2023 the Apax Digital Funds led a strategic growth investment of more than $100M into Petvisor, with participation from existing investors Frontier Growth, PeakSpan Capital and management. Frontier stated that since its 2021 investment Petvisor had scaled revenue and clients more than 3x, organically and via the PetDesk/Vetstoria/Kontak/WhiskerCloud/Groomer.io acquisitions. Exact total raised is not publicly consolidated — treat $130M+ as a floor, not a precise figure.
headcount_estimate: Roughly 200–350. Revelio Labs estimates 311 as of March 2026; ContactOut lists 164; a local business directory lists '200+'. No company-confirmed number is public. Note that headcount is split across the acquired brands (Vetstoria has UK/Sri Lanka presence), so US-only counts will read lower.
yc_or_accelerator: None found
sells_to: B2B SMB — independent veterinary clinics and small-to-mid multi-site vet groups (plus grooming businesses via Groomer.io). Some corporate/consolidator vet groups, but the core motion is high-volume SMB.
how_they_use_agents: In the product: PetDesk Scribe is an AI ambient scribe generating SOAP notes (as of Sep 2026 it is schedule-aware — 'Scribe now knows your schedule. Just tap and talk!'); PetDesk Phones includes AI call summaries of voicemails that write back into the PIMS, voicemail transcription, and Missed Call Text Back automation; the company has also written about chatbots for clinic front-desk work. Notably PetDesk is positioned in the market as a phone/front-office platform with AI call summaries rather than a full autonomous AI receptionist — third-party comparison sites consistently place it against dedicated voice-AI receptionists rather than as one. Internally: PetDesk's CX Ops team runs Guru Knowledge Agents over its support knowledge base with quality automations governing what those agents can answer from, and Shona Fenner participates in Guru's Innovation Partner Program and has spoken publicly on 'Bad Knowledge Breaks AI.'
why_they_need_memory: The purest roll-up memory problem of the three. Years of growth plus five acquisitions (PetDesk, Vetstoria, Kontak, WhiskerCloud, Groomer.io) left the knowledge base cluttered with duplicate and conflicting content from teams that had never shared one — Shona Fenner: 'We had eight different Guru cards from different teams about risk management, post-sale. Looking at these in isolation, you wouldn't know which way to turn.' Verification score was stuck at 60–70%, which meant nobody trusted the base and therefore nobody would trust an agent answering from it. Guru quality automations (flagging cards with repeated negative reactions, excluding admin views from activity signals) raised the verification score from 76% to 85% and, more importantly, changed what 'unverified' means — 'what's unverified now, it's not just noise anymore — it's the stuff that actually needs love.' Eight duplicate risk-management cards collapsed into one process, and previously disengaged stakeholders started participating. Automation was then extended to additional Knowledge Agents. The driver is M&A-induced knowledge fragmentation blocking AI deployment across a 12,000-clinic support operation.

name: Bonafide Health
what_it_does: Direct-to-consumer women's health supplement brand focused on perimenopause and menopause symptom relief. Sells hormone-free, clinically studied OTC products: Revaree / Revaree Plus (vaginal dryness), Thermella (hot flashes, marketed as a hormone-free NK3R antagonist), Ristela (sexual satisfaction), Serenol (mood), Clairvee (vaginal odor), Silvessa (skin/hair), Noctera (sleep), plus probiotics and multivitamins, sold individually, in bundles, and via subscription. Claims 1,565,000+ customers and 13,000+ recommending healthcare providers. Channels are DTC e-commerce (Shopify), retail (Target, per a Sept 2025 Drug Store News item), and an HCP/professional channel. HQ: 500 Mamaroneck Avenue, Suite 510, Harrison, NY. The storefront runs on the Shopify domain jds-therapeutics.myshopify.com, confirming Bonafide is the consumer brand of JDS Therapeutics.
category: consumer healthcare / DTC supplements (women's health, menopause) — NOT healthcare AI
stage: Acquired — operates as a brand within Pharmavite, itself a subsidiary of Otsuka Pharmaceutical
funding: No venture rounds confirmed. Acquired by Pharmavite in November 2023 for $425 million (per Wikipedia's Pharmavite entry). Prior to that it was the consumer brand of JDS Therapeutics. No pre-acquisition funding figures found — do not assume any.
headcount_estimate: unknown — no verified public figure found. Not independently listed; absorbed into Pharmavite. The Guru testimonial references a CX/support org with training and quality management, implying a contact-center team of at least a few dozen, but this is inference, not a sourced number.
yc_or_accelerator: none found
founded_year: unknown — no founding year stated anywhere on hellobonafide.com. Parent entity JDS Therapeutics predates the Bonafide brand. Do not cite a year without a source.
sells_to: prosumer / B2C consumer (women 40+ in perimenopause and menopause), with a secondary HCP-recommendation channel and retail distribution
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct and unrelated things. (1) Internal, which is the Guru relationship: their customer-experience org replaced Google Drive with Guru as the verified knowledge source, and moved to Guru's AI-generated Answers so human support agents can self-serve. Alexandria Hauer, Sr. Manager of CX Training and Quality, is quoted that AI Answers 'consolidates important information so agents don't have to rely as much on people for quick answers' and cites prior pain points of 'lack of verification, no formatting structure, and it was difficult to find anything.' Note that 'agents' in this testimonial means human support reps, not autonomous software. (2) External and inbound: their Shopify storefront exposes an agentic-commerce surface — a sitemap_agentic_discovery.xml pointing at /agents.md, a Universal Commerce Protocol profile at /.well-known/ucp, and an MCP endpoint at /api/ucp/mcp with search_catalog / create_cart / create_checkout tools for third-party shopping agents. This is Shopify platform default, not bespoke engineering by Bonafide, and it makes them a target of agents rather than a builder of them. Bonafide ships no AI agent in its own product; the product is physical supplements.
why_they_need_memory: Classic scaling-CX knowledge problem rather than an agent-infrastructure problem. Their support org fields repetitive, high-stakes questions about clinical claims, ingredients, contraindications, subscription and billing mechanics, and returns, where a wrong answer is a regulatory and trust liability because these are health products. Their own stated pain was unverified, unstructured, unfindable content in Google Drive. They bought a verified knowledge layer with AI retrieval so reps stop interrupting SMEs. Secondarily, the agentic-commerce endpoints mean external shopping agents now need accurate, machine-readable product and policy facts — another argument for a single canonical source of truth. But they are a knowledge-base buyer, not an agent-memory buyer in the developer-infrastructure sense.
confidence: high on existence, product, and Pharmavite ownership; medium on the $425M figure (single source, Wikipedia); low on founding year and headcount, which I could not confirm at all

name: Branch (Branch Insurance)
what_it_does: Insurtech carrier selling bundled home and auto insurance direct to consumers, plus renters, umbrella, condo, and term life. The differentiator is speed and embedded distribution: Branch pulls claims, driving, and credit data from third-party sources to prefill a quote from minimal user input, and per co-founder/CEO Steve Lekas is 'the only insurance company that can bind insurance through an API, and the only one that can bundle auto and home insurance in a single transaction.' It operates its own reciprocal exchange in Ohio (launched Aug 2020) rather than acting purely as an MGA. Distribution runs through direct-to-consumer, embedded point-of-sale partnerships with mortgage lenders and home-security companies (ADT, SimpliSafe, Homepoint), and since ~2021 an independent-agent channel. Community-flavored programs: My Community Discount, Community Pledge, SafetyNest, Community Drive with Cambridge Mobile Telematics. Certified B Corp as of January 2023. HQ in downtown Columbus, Ohio, with a distributed team.
category: insurtech / personal-lines P&C insurance (home + auto) — NOT an AI company
stage: Series C (reached unicorn status June 2022). No later round found; their press page's newest item is February 2023, so current stage is unverified.
funding: $229.5 million total raised since 2017 inception, per TechCrunch (June 2022). Rounds: $24M Series A announced July 2020; $50M Series B announced June 2021; $147M Series C announced June 8, 2022 at a $1.05 billion post-money valuation, led by Weatherford Capital. No funding events found after mid-2022.
headcount_estimate: 400+ as of June 2022 per TechCrunch (up from roughly 75 a year earlier). Current headcount unknown — the careers page discloses no numbers and I found no post-2023 source. A December 2020 Columbus Region release cited plans for 150 new jobs at the expanded HQ.
yc_or_accelerator: none found
founded_year: 2017 (per TechCrunch, June 2022); first state launch was Ohio in September 2019
sells_to: B2C consumer (homeowners and drivers), plus B2B2C embedded partnerships with lenders, realtors, and security providers, and a B2B independent-agent channel
how_they_use_agents: Important disambiguation: 'Agents' in Branch's own site navigation and product language means human independent insurance agents, not AI. Branch ships no AI agent in its consumer product; the automation in the product is data prefill and API-based binding, not LLM agents. The vendor relationships are internal enablement. Guru is the knowledge layer for their member-support and sales organization — Eli Logan, Director of Sales & Member Support Effectiveness, says 'People are finding answers themselves now rather than asking for help,' and describes the Slack workflow: 'when an agent asks a question in Slack, we answer their question and then direct them to where they can self-serve that answer, and Guru is the place we point them every time.' Kendall, Sales & Support Effectiveness Lead, frames the stakes as 'There's a massive ripple effect when an agent can't find an answer.' They are also cited as a Notion AI customer. Both are internal knowledge/AI-search tools for human reps.
why_they_need_memory: The strongest structural fit of the three. Personal-lines insurance knowledge is a combinatorial explosion: coverage rules, forms, rate structures, discounts, and regulatory language multiply across ~28+ states, four-plus product lines, a reciprocal exchange, and multiple embedded partners — and all of it changes on a regulatory clock. Support reps must give answers that are correct and compliant per-state, and a stale answer creates E&O and regulatory exposure. They explicitly built a Slack-to-Guru deflection loop because tribal knowledge in Slack did not scale. They also scaled headcount roughly 5x in twelve months, so onboarding velocity was the acute pain. The value is retrieval and verification of a large, stale-prone corpus, not agent autonomy. Worth noting for segmentation: this is a non-technical, non-AI-native SMB services buyer — the opposite end of the market from Trusted Health.

name: Cartwheel (legal entity: Cartwheel Care Inc.; care delivered by Cartwheel Health Services P.C. and affiliated PCs)

Guru actually delivers on the promise of automation' — alongside the stat '60% → 100% of knowledge assessed & verified, with Guru quality automations.' A stale card here is a clinical and regulatory risk, not an inconvenience — which is exactly why their quoted win is 'we no longer have to manually review knowledge accuracy' and why the metric they publicize is percent of knowledge *verified* rather than time saved. AI in the shipped product is narrow and assistive: an 'AI Campaigns Assistant' for drafting patient marketing campaigns, smart/automated form processing (smart form automation preview and GA release in the changelog), insurance-card scanning that auto-captures details into the verification form, and missed-call analysis with automatic text-back scheduling in NexHealth Phones. Their feature pages for scheduling, verification and phones consistently say 'automated' rather than 'AI-powered.' Knowledge was spread across Guru, Slack, Jira and Asana. The case study is unusually explicit about the two problems an agent-memory vendor sells against: verification ('Staying on top of verification is crucial. It's a job, but it's 100% worth it') and source trust when expanding what the AI can see ('We want to broaden Guru's view to include more resources, but want to ensure they are accurate, so it has been a work in progress'). The buyer and administrator is Carol Merriman, who manages the IT team; she says explicitly that she chose partly on whether she personally liked administering it and on the quality of vendor support ('I needed something I liked since I'm going to manage it. Value was delivered by thousands of human sales/CS reps executing playbooks, which is exactly why knowledge tooling mattered. Post-acquisition the AI layer lives at the Concentrix level: Concentrix now ships an "iX Product Suite" including iX Hello and iX Hero, markets "1000+ clients running AI in production," says iX Suite deals were up 400% YoY in Q2 2026, and handles "billions of human + AI interactions" annually. So the agent story here is a BPO retrofitting agents onto a labor-arbitrage business, not an agent-native product.
why_they_need_memory: The canonical non-AI-native buyer of a company brain. A distributed workforce of ~2,900 reps sells on behalf of many different client brands simultaneously — each rep needs client-specific pricing, SKU, renewal-policy and objection-handling knowledge at the moment of the call, and the correct answer differs per client, per geo, per language. Constant onboarding (BPO attrition) plus 45 languages and 175 countries makes tribal knowledge unworkable. The Guru quote — unifying "onboarding and sales processes information" — is precisely this: ramp time and answer consistency across a large, churning, multi-tenant rep pool. For an agent-memory vendor, the modern version of this account is grounding the AI agents that now answer alongside those reps: the knowledge base has to be the shared substrate for both humans and iX agents, with per-client isolation.

name: Better.com (Better Home & Finance Holding Company)
what_it_does: Digital-first US mortgage lender. Consumers apply online for purchase mortgages (including VA and a crypto-backed product), refinances, cash-out refis and HELOCs, with attached "Better+" services — title, closing, homeowners insurance (Better Cover), attorney matching. The engine underneath is Tinman, an in-house loan origination system that aggregates borrower data via APIs, applies automated decisioning logic and orchestrates underwriting through closing. FY2025: $164.9M revenue (+52% YoY), $4.7B funded loan volume (+32%), net loss $165.9M, total assets $1.505B. Headcount 1,329 (869 US, 426 India, 34 UK). Founded Feb 2014 by Vishal Garg; HQ 1 World Trade Center, NYC. Daniel Lewis replaced Garg as CEO in Aug 2026. Divested UK ops (Trussle/Better.co.uk) to OneDome May 2025; announced divestiture of Birmingham Bank April 2026.
category: Consumer fintech / mortgage origination, with an AI-augmented lending-tech platform sold B2B to other lenders
stage: Public — Nasdaq: BETR, via SPAC merger with Aurora Acquisition Corp, August 2023
funding: ~$860M+ disclosed private capital pre-SPAC: Series C $160M at ~$600M valuation (Aug 2019), Series D $200M at $4B (Nov 2020), Series E $500M from SoftBank at $6B (Apr 2021). SPAC merger (Aug 2023) brought ~$565M including a $528M convertible bond from SoftBank affiliates; those bonds were restructured April 2025. Now trades publicly; 2025 was still deeply loss-making (-$165.9M).
headcount_estimate: 1,329 as of end-2025 per the FY2025 10-K (869 US / 426 India / 34 UK). Historically volatile: ~11,000 in 2020, 900 laid off by videoconference Dec 2021, 3,000+ more cut Mar 2022, ~950 by 2023.
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: Primarily prosumer/consumer (US homebuyers, refinancers, homeowners tapping equity, VA-eligible veterans). Secondarily B2B enterprise — banks and financial institutions licensing Tinman.
how_they_use_agents: Two named systems plus a recent LLM layer. (1) Tinman — the AI/workflow-automation loan origination system doing automated decisioning and orchestration from application through close; the 10-K is explicit that parts of production still "require human involvement," so it is automation-with-oversight, not autonomous. (2) Betsy — a voice-based AI loan assistant that speaks to borrowers, answers mortgage-application questions and collects required information. (3) In March 2026 Better launched an OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise integration giving loan officers a conversational UI wired into Tinman's underwriting engine through a Model Context Protocol connector — i.e. an internal agent that reads the system of record. That MCP-connector move is the strongest signal in this cohort of a company actively building agent infrastructure over its own knowledge.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls, and the Guru testimonial captures the first. (1) Human knowledge bottleneck: the quoted SME says losing Guru would mean "30+ Slack notifications overnight, every night," each a basic question 1-3 other people would also ask — a small number of SMEs being drained by repeat lookups. Compounding that, headcount swung from ~11,000 to ~1,300 in four years, so institutional knowledge was repeatedly destroyed, and a second quote is a COVID-era remote hire relying on Guru to learn what new employees should know. (2) The agent pull: mortgage is state-by-state, product-by-product, and regulator-audited. Betsy talks to borrowers and the ChatGPT/MCP layer advises loan officers on underwriting — both need grounded, current, provenance-tracked policy knowledge, because a hallucinated mortgage rule is a compliance event, not a bad UX moment. This is the profile of a buyer who bought a knowledge base for humans and now needs the same substrate to ground agents.
