Product family extends to FusionGO (mobile app), Fusion Wave (digital signage), Fusion Play (intramural/league scheduling) and Fusion Club. Claimed scale: 320+ schools, colleges and municipalities, 5M active users, 500,000 daily check-ins, $200M in annual transactions processed. Named customers include University of Minnesota, Purdue, University of Utah, Wake Forest, University of Michigan and Wingate. Addresses: LinkedIn lists London, Ontario; the website contact address is 8133 Warden Avenue, Markham, Ontario.
category: Vertical B2B SaaS — campus and municipal recreation/facility management software
stage: Private, small — no funding rounds found; appears bootstrapped or founder-owned, but I could not confirm this, so treat as unknown
funding: unknown — no venture rounds, Crunchbase entry (403/blocked) or press coverage of financing found. Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence, though a 20-year-old 80-person vertical SaaS company with no funding footprint is most consistent with bootstrapped.
headcount_estimate: 51-200 band on LinkedIn, with ~80 employees actually listed on the company page. Call it roughly 80-100.
yc_or_accelerator: None found
founded_year: 2006 (per LinkedIn company profile)
sells_to: B2B institutional mid-market/SMB — university and college campus recreation departments, municipal parks-and-rec departments, and independent recreation/club facilities across Canada, the US and Europe. Buyer is a director of campus recreation or a municipal rec manager, not a technology buyer.
how_they_use_agents: None found. A full read of the product pages turned up no AI, LLM, copilot or agent functionality — the only automation mentioned is rules-based "automated messaging" for overdue equipment follow-up, plus scheduled reporting. Recent product news (Fusion Play, FusionGO shown at NIRSA 2026) is also non-AI. This company is a pure knowledge-management buyer with no agent story at all.
why_they_need_memory: The purest "institutional memory in a small company" case of the three, and the quote is explicit about it: nine years of failed attempts to make knowledge transfer work. An ~80-person company supports 320+ live institutional deployments, each configured differently (different membership rules, access-control policies, fee structures, campus integrations), against a customer base — campus rec departments — with heavy student-staff turnover on their side too. Implementation and support knowledge concentrates in a handful of long-tenured people; when one leaves, a customer's configuration history leaves with them. Note the buying signal for a memory vendor: this is a CEO-level purchase at a small company, driven by continuity/bus-factor risk rather than by scale or by agent grounding. It is the low-ACV, high-conviction end of the category, and it shows the buyer set is not only AI-native startups.

name: Greenhouse (Greenhouse Software, Inc.)
what_it_does: Applicant tracking system / hiring operating system. Greenhouse Recruiting covers talent sourcing, structured interviewing with scorecards, candidate experience (MyGreenhouse candidate portal), configurable approval workflows and permissions, onboarding, reporting, and 500+ integrations. Two newer AI-forward SKUs sit on top: 'Real Talent' (application fraud-signal detection using phone/email/IP/location, CLEAR-powered identity verification, and AI resume-to-criteria talent matching that recommends but never auto-advances or auto-rejects) and 'Voice AI', a two-way voice AI interviewing agent used at the top of funnel to replace resume screening. greenhouse.io now 301-redirects to greenhouse.com.
category: HR tech / recruiting software (ATS), B2B SaaS
stage: PE-owned (TPG majority since January 2021); previously venture-backed through Series D
funding: ~$108.8M venture before the buyout: $2.7M seed (2013), $7.5M Series A (2014), $13.6M Series B (2015), $35M Series C (2015), $50M Series D (2018). In January 2021 TPG invested $500M for a majority stake at an $820M valuation. No newer round confirmed in this session.
headcount_estimate: unknown — 125 employees as of the 2015 Series C (Wikipedia); current headcount is not published on greenhouse.com and LinkedIn was not reachable in this session. Company self-describes as 'midsize' (2024 Best Midsize Places to Work in Colorado award).
yc_or_accelerator: none found
sells_to: B2B — mid-market through enterprise talent acquisition / HR organizations (named customers include Okta, Zapier, Samsara, Adyen, Planet, Kaizen Gaming, SpotHero, hipages)
how_they_use_agents: Product side: Voice AI is a genuine conversational agent — recruiters define questions, scoring rubrics and role context; the agent runs a two-way voice interview with dynamic follow-ups at ~2s latency, answers candidate questions from a pre-approved information set, then returns transcripts, rubric scores and flagged inconsistencies for a human decision, with full audit trails. It is offered for Greenhouse and Ashby (Lever 'coming soon'). Real Talent adds AI resume/criteria matching and fraud-signal scoring. Internal ops side (the Guru testimonial): Director of Sales Operations Tori Moss re-implemented Guru at Greenhouse after using it at a prior company, and splits the knowledge base into internal-facing and external customer-facing content for a 50+ rep sales team.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. (1) Their own Voice AI agent is only as good as the role context, rubric and 'pre-approved answers' corpus it is grounded in — that is an agent-memory/context problem in their core product, and it is compliance-sensitive (auditable transcripts, no autonomous reject). (2) The buying motion actually observed is internal: a sales-ops leader arming 50+ reps with verified answers and a hard internal-vs-customer-facing content boundary — the classic 'company brain' pain of trusted, permissioned, current answers in the rep's workflow. Note the buyer here was Sales Ops, not engineering, and she was a repeat buyer who brought the tool with her across employers.

name: Boomi (formerly Dell Boomi)
what_it_does: Enterprise integration platform as a service (iPaaS), now self-branded 'The Data Activation Company'. The Boomi Enterprise Platform spans data integration and management (Data Hub, Meta Hub, Knowledge Hub), integration and automation (Flow, Event Streams, B2B/EDI management), and API management. On top of that sits a full agent stack: Agentstudio (build, govern, orchestrate AI agents), Agent Control Plane (agent registry, observability, guardrails), AI Gateway (controls AI and MCP interactions), Boomi Connect (governed access to 1,000+ enterprise apps for agents) and MCP connectors that expose enterprise assets as governed MCP tools. Claims 30,000+ customers, 250,000+ community members, 300,000+ application connections; Leader in the 2026 Gartner MQ for iPaaS and 2025 Forrester Wave. The Guru citation lists it under its old 'Dell Boomi' name — same company, not an ambiguous logo-wall entry.
category: Enterprise integration / iPaaS + AI agent infrastructure and governance
stage: Private, private-equity owned (Francisco Partners and TPG Capital, both with board representation)
funding: No venture rounds. Acquired by Dell in 2010; carved out from Dell to Francisco Partners and TPG in 2021 (purchase price widely reported around $4B — not verified from a primary source in this session). Current ownership by Francisco Partners and TPG is confirmed on Boomi's own leadership page.
headcount_estimate: unknown — not published on boomi.com; company describes itself as remote-first with multiple offices worldwide. LinkedIn not reachable in this session.
yc_or_accelerator: none — corporate/PE lineage, not accelerator-backed
founded_year: 2000 (commonly cited; not verified from a Boomi primary source in this session — what is confirmed is the 2010 Dell acquisition and 2021 PE carve-out)
sells_to: B2B enterprise — IT, integration, data and platform teams across manufacturing, healthcare, retail, financial services, higher education, public sector, energy/utilities; 30,000+ organizations from SMB to large enterprise
how_they_use_agents: Boomi does not merely use agents, it sells the agent substrate. Agentstudio designs custom agents (structured or conversational), grounds them with persistent memory, knowledge bases, glossaries and database connections, connects them to integrations/APIs/MCP servers, allows per-task model choice, and deploys cloud/hybrid/on-prem or behind the firewall. Agent Control Plane centrally registers and monitors agents with full audit logs, token-level analytics, anomaly detection and kill-switch. Marketing claims 'hallucination rates under half a percent'. Knowledge Hub is explicitly positioned as turning scattered documents and data into 'one governed, AI-ready knowledge layer for agents and search', with hybrid semantic+keyword retrieval, metadata filtering and access governance.
why_they_need_memory: Important nuance for category analysis: Boomi is arguably a *competitor* to the company-brain / agent-memory category rather than a natural buyer of it — Knowledge Hub plus Meta Hub is their own governed retrieval and semantic layer for agents. Their Guru relationship is an internal sales-enablement purchase (cited alongside Greenhouse in a Guru sales-enablement post), i.e. a big distributed GTM org needing consistent, current product answers across a fast-moving product line and 30,000+ accounts. So this logo tells you the category sells into large enterprise revenue orgs even at companies that build the underlying tech themselves.

name: Outdoorsy (Outdoorsy Group)
what_it_does: Peer-to-peer RV and campervan rental marketplace, now a four-part 'outdoor mobility' group: (1) Outdoorsy.com, the consumer marketplace connecting RV owners with renters, including delivered-and-set-up rentals, one-way rentals and national-park trip planning; (2) Roamly, an in-house insurtech providing RV/campervan insurance and, since 2026, real-time insurance for autonomous fleets; (3) Wheelbase, enterprise SaaS fleet/inventory management for professional RV rental operators (claimed used by 95% of U.S. professional hosts); (4) Outdoorsy Destination Network of campgrounds and glamping properties. Self-reported scale: 25,000+ unique rentals across 4,800+ cities and 11-14 countries, 10M+ booked nights, 100,000+ reviews averaging 4.87, 250M miles driven, $3B+ cumulative transactions as of Sept 2024, profitable since 2023, projecting $8B transactions by 2029. HQ Austin, Texas (15,000 sq ft on South Lamar).
category: Consumer travel marketplace + vertical SaaS (Wheelbase) + insurtech (Roamly)
stage: Private, venture-backed late stage; reports profitability since 2023 and hired a new CFO in Feb 2026
funding: unknown — total raised, round history and investors are not disclosed on any company-controlled source reachable in this session, and the web-search budget was exhausted before external funding databases could be checked. Do not treat as unfunded; it is simply unverified here.
headcount_estimate: unknown — not published on outdoorsy.com; careers page returned 403 and LinkedIn was not reachable in this session
yc_or_accelerator: none found
founded_year: 2015 (founder/CEO Jeff Cavins; co-founder/CMO Jennifer Young)
sells_to: Hybrid: prosumer/consumer two-sided marketplace (renters plus RV owners monetizing idle assets) with a B2B vertical-SaaS arm selling Wheelbase to professional RV rental fleet operators, plus a B2B2C insurance product
how_they_use_agents: No customer-facing AI agent was confirmed on their site. The 2026 corporate boilerplate describes Roamly as 'an AI-driven insurtech platform providing the risk-management infrastructure for the future of transport, from RVs to autonomous vehicles' — i.e. AI in underwriting/risk rather than a conversational agent. The Guru relationship is internal support enablement: the case study covers equipping support teams through extreme volatility (COVID furloughs, then a 200% booking increase in one week).
why_they_need_memory: Marketplace support and trust-and-safety is the archetypal knowledge-decay problem: policies span insurance coverage, cancellations, damage claims, delivery, one-way and cross-border rentals across 11-14 countries, and they change constantly. Headcount is seasonal and volatile (furloughs to a 200% booking surge inside a week), so ramp time for support reps is the binding constraint — exactly the pain a company brain, and later an AI support agent, is sold against. Note the buying center is customer support ops, not engineering, and the trigger was a demand shock rather than an AI initiative.

name: FullStack Labs (now branded "FullStack")
what_it_does: Nearshore software engineering consultancy and talent marketplace. Two divisions under one brand since April 2024: FullStack Labs (project-based custom software development, product design, DevOps, data/AI engineering) and FullStack Talent (a vetted network of pre-screened engineers placed as staff augmentation / "Forward Deployed Engineers"). US-led delivery with engineers largely in Latin America; HQ listed on LinkedIn as Brentwood, Tennessee. Marketing claims 600+ US client companies (Uber, Siemens, Ericsson, Deloitte cited), a network of 1,100+ engineers, and "deploy AI teams in 48 hours." Site has been aggressively repositioned around AI: "AI-native engineers," "Production AI Deployment," partnerships with AWS, Google Cloud, NVIDIA, Databricks, Snowflake. Leadership churned recently: Anton Tomchenko (ex-Hexaware, 18 years at EPAM) became CEO Oct 27 2025, replacing Dr. Benjamin Carle; three more C-level hires (CFO, CDTO, CMO) announced May 2026.
category: IT services / nearshore software development + engineering staffing (services business, not a software product); recently repositioned as an AI/agentic-AI implementation partner
stage: Private, ownership undisclosed. No venture or PE round found in any public source. Likely founder-owned/bootstrapped or quietly PE-recapped — the 2025-2026 wholesale executive replacement (new CEO plus three C-levels) is a pattern often associated with a control investor, but nothing confirms this.
funding: unknown — no disclosed funding rounds found. Their own press release lists an investors@fullstacklabs.co contact but discloses no investors, revenue, or ownership.
headcount_estimate: ~800. LinkedIn company page shows 797 employee profiles and a self-reported band of 501-1,000. Separately claims a broader network of 1,100+ engineers (network size, not payroll).
yc_or_accelerator: none found
founded_year: Not disclosed anywhere on their site. Approximately 2014-2015: the site says "more than a decade" of experience, and the earliest Wayback capture of fullstacklabs.co is April 2016.
sells_to: B2B — US mid-market and enterprise engineering orgs buying outsourced dev teams and individual contract engineers. Also sells to smaller companies. Buyer is a VP Eng / CTO / head of product, not a developer self-serving.
how_they_use_agents: They BUILD agents for clients rather than selling an agent product. Their custom-AI service page explicitly advertises "LLM-powered agents, agent loops, and multi-agent systems," plus computer vision, NLP/chatbots, and automated document workflows. Case studies cited on the homepage include an agentic assistant supporting 3M+ users and processing 20M+ data points, an AI call auditor for compliance review, AI document systems, and an AI research assistant. Their engineering blog covers Claude Code, LlamaIndex, and model comparisons. Internally, agents show up as an AI-assisted delivery pitch ("AI-native engineers," 48-hour pod deployment), not as a shipped product.
why_they_need_memory: Their entire margin structure depends on how fast a distributed, rotating engineering pod can absorb a client's codebase, conventions, and domain context — they literally sell "teams in 48 hours." The Guru testimonial is exactly this: CEO David Jackson describes a "Development Best Practices" board of checklists for version control, builds and deployment, cutting developer onboarding from weeks of ad-hoc questions to a couple of hours of reading, and replacing a 200-page HR manual with searchable cards. That is onboarding-context-as-a-product-input. Second, harder need: the agents they ship to clients (document systems, call auditors, research assistants) each require durable client-specific context, so agent memory is both an internal enablement need and a component they would resell inside client builds. Caveat: as a services firm they tend to build rather than buy infrastructure, and would evaluate a memory vendor as a component for client projects as much as for themselves.

name: Chili Piper
what_it_does: Inbound "demand conversion" platform for go-to-market teams — the layer between a web form fill and a booked sales meeting. Consolidates form routing, lead qualification, data enrichment, lead distribution/routing (territory rules, account ownership, weighted round-robin), website chat, and calendar scheduling. Products include Concierge/Instant Booker, Distro (lead distribution), Chat and Chat AI, Handoff, Chilical, and an admin Command Center. Named customers include Intuit, Spotify, Airbnb, Gong, Intercom, LinkedIn, SurveyMonkey. Founded 2016 by Alina and Nicolas Vandenberghe; 100% remote from day one, team spread across 33 countries, no offices.
category: GTM / sales tech — inbound lead routing, qualification and meeting scheduling; now pushing into the AI SDR category
stage: Series B (last disclosed round April 2021). No subsequent round found.
funding: $54M total disclosed. $18M Series A announced Aug 18 2020, led by Base10 Partners with Gradient Ventures (Google's AI fund) and Flashpoint VC; TJ Nahigian joined the board. $33M round announced Apr 15 2021 (they branded it "Series Spicy"), led by Tiger Global with Base10 and Gradient participating. Nothing newer is published on their site or findable.
headcount_estimate: ~270. LinkedIn shows 273 employee profiles; the company's self-reported LinkedIn band is a stale 51-200. For reference they stated 101 employees at the April 2021 round. Fully distributed across 33 countries.
yc_or_accelerator: none found (Gradient Ventures is Google's AI venture fund, an investor rather than an accelerator)
sells_to: B2B mid-market and enterprise. Buyer is the GTM/revenue-operations function — marketing ops, sales ops, demand gen leaders at growth-stage and enterprise SaaS companies with high inbound volume.
how_they_use_agents: Three distinct agent surfaces, all retrofitted onto the existing routing/scheduling engine. (1) AI Chat Agent — an always-on website assistant that qualifies visitors and books meetings 24/7. (2) AI Inbound SDR — responds to form fills and demo requests in the same session, runs "a real conversation informed by CRM data and enrichment" against the customer's ICP rather than a scripted decision tree, then routes by territory/ownership/round-robin and books onto the right rep's calendar; it writes meetings, transcripts and qualification context back into the CRM so context survives the human handoff. (3) Chili Assist — a natural-language configuration agent inside the Command Center that turns plain English into routing rules (condition types, cross-object references, ownership rules, nested logic), adds/removes team members via fuzzy name matching, and reads live distribution state; changes stay as unpublished drafts until a human approves.
why_they_need_memory: Two independent pulls. Product side: their AI SDR only works if it holds durable context it did not just receive — ICP definitions, territory and ownership rules, product/pricing knowledge, and prior interaction history with an account. They already hand-roll a partial solution by writing qualification context and transcripts back to the CRM for handoff continuity; that is a memory substrate built out of Salesforce fields, which is precisely the pain an agent-memory vendor sells against. Chili Assist's stated limitation is telling — it reads "the live state at the moment you ask" with no documented cross-session retention. Internal side: the Guru testimonial is about a fully remote, 33-country GTM org drowning in "dreaded repeat questions in Slack"; Jared Wexler (Solutions Consultant) describes hitting a Chrome extension to surface collateral in seconds mid-call, contrasted against an LMS. Fast-scaling remote sales org + agent product that needs account context = the archetypal buyer for this category.

name: Crisp (Crisp Thinking Group Limited) — no longer an independent company
what_it_does: UK-based real-time risk intelligence. Combined proprietary ML classifiers (their "Risk Intelligence Graph," classifying actors, content, groups and entities) with 24/7 human analyst teams to monitor "digital chatter" across social, fringe and bad-actor platforms and alert enterprises to emerging reputational, security and online-harm risks before they became crises. Three product lines: Corporate Risk Intelligence (C-suite/comms/security), Platform Risk Intelligence (Trust & Safety teams at social networks, apps and games), and Pharmaceutical Social Compliance (adverse-event detection for pharma marketing, sold with a zero-misses guarantee). Claimed to protect 1,000+ brands representing $6.5T of combined market cap. Company timeline: founded 2005 by Adam Hildreth with a mission to stop online child exploitation; 2010 social moderation platform; 2015 managed digital risk monitoring with a 24/7 global expert team; 2019 expanded to terrorism, conspiracy and election-interference actors; 2020 founding member of the Online Safety Tech Industry Association. NOTE: the "Crisp" in the Guru case study is this company — NOT crisp.chat (the French customer-messaging tool) and NOT Crisp/crispnow.com (the US retail supply-chain data firm). Confirmed via the Guru interview naming crispthinking.com and "250+ and growing" UK employees.
category: Risk intelligence / trust & safety / online-harms monitoring — an ML-plus-human-analyst managed service sold to enterprise risk and Trust & Safety functions
stage: Acquired. Bought by Kroll in 2022; crispthinking.com now redirects to Resolver, a Kroll business. Not an independent buyer today — any renewal decision now sits inside Kroll/Resolver procurement.
funding: $25M growth investment from Baird Capital in 2018 (announced alongside claimed 100% YoY growth and a plan to double headcount). Earlier rounds not disclosed; total raised unknown. Kroll acquisition terms undisclosed.
headcount_estimate: 250+ at the time of the Guru interview (~2021-2022), per Crisp's own statement in that piece. Standalone headcount today is not meaningful — absorbed into Resolver, whose LinkedIn shows ~698 employee profiles.
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2B enterprise. Buyers were corporate comms, security, HR, legal/compliance and Trust & Safety leaders at large global brands, social platforms, games companies and pharma manufacturers. Long enterprise sales cycles, managed-service delivery.
how_they_use_agents: No LLM agent product found — this predates the current agent wave. What they call AI is 16+ years of trained classification models ("AI/HI," artificial plus human intelligence) feeding a Risk Intelligence Graph that discovers, classifies and tracks risk actors and content, with human analysts adjudicating and escalating 24/7. The agent-shaped work here is done by people: analyst teams applying policy judgment at speed.
why_they_need_memory: This is the purest "human company brain" case of the three, and the weakest agent-memory case. Crisp hired a dedicated Knowledge Manager (Martin Theobald) specifically because 2020-2021 hypergrowth broke their knowledge flow; his job was converting implicit expertise held in analysts' heads into documented, discoverable, verified knowledge — knowledge maps, verification processes, and what he called a "knowledge champion community" that finally cemented Guru's adoption. The forcing function is that judgment quality IS the product: 24/7 analyst rotations must apply the same policy and threat-actor context consistently, so shared verified context is directly revenue-critical, not just nice-to-have. Two important caveats for targeting: (a) they bought a human-facing knowledge system years before agent memory was a category, and (b) they no longer exist as an independent purchaser.

name: Spotify
what_it_does: Audio streaming platform for music, podcasts and audiobooks, on a freemium model (ad-supported free tier plus Premium subscriptions), founded in Stockholm. Scale as of June 2026: 777M monthly active users and 300M paid subscribers; revenue was EUR 15.67B in 2024. Also runs a large advertising business and creator-facing tooling (Spotify for Artists, Megaphone/podcast ad tech). Note: this is the well-known streaming company, not a vendor in the agent-memory category — it appears purely as a logo on Guru's customer wall.
category: Consumer audio streaming / media platform (buyer of internal knowledge + AI-search tooling, not a seller in this category)
stage: Public - direct listing on NYSE in April 2018, ticker SPOT
funding: Public company; no current venture funding. Pre-IPO private raise total not verified in this pass - treat as unknown. Went public via direct listing (no capital raised at listing). 2024 revenue EUR 15.67B.
headcount_estimate: ~7,302 employees (June 2026)
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2C consumers (freemium/subscription) plus advertisers and creators; not a B2B seller
how_they_use_agents: Product-side: AI DJ (personalized, now takes real-time voice requests in 60+ markets and via Android Auto), AI Playlist (natural-language prompt-to-playlist, with iterative refinement like 'more upbeat', now in 40+ additional markets), audiobook Recaps, and AI-provenance tooling (AI persona badges, AI credits, SongDNA, Verified by Spotify). Spotify has also exposed itself as a connected tool for third-party assistants - users can link their account to Claude and to ChatGPT for taste- and history-based recommendations, which makes Spotify a target surface for external agents rather than only an agent builder. Internal/ops side: Spotify appears on Guru's customer logo wall (asset '2025_Solutions_Customer_Spotify.svg' and the /customers marquee), i.e. as a buyer of an AI knowledge layer for internal teams - logo only, no quote, so the internal deployment scope is unverified.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. (1) Consumer-product memory: every marquee AI feature (DJ, AI Playlist, external assistant integrations) is worthless without long-horizon listening history and taste state - personalization IS memory for them, though they build that in-house rather than buying it. (2) Org memory: ~7,300 employees across Stockholm/NYC/global offices in a famously autonomous 'squad' structure means internal knowledge is heavily fragmented across teams and tools; that is the classic Guru buying motive - support, sales enablement, and internal ops needing one verified answer instead of tribal knowledge. As a buyer they are the 'large, non-AI-native enterprise with knowledge sprawl' archetype, not the 'AI startup wiring memory into its agent' archetype.

name: Stripe
what_it_does: Financial infrastructure for the internet: payments acceptance (Checkout, Payment Links, Elements, Link, Terminal), billing and subscriptions/usage-based billing, plus adjacent financial services (Connect for marketplaces, Issuing, Treasury, Capital, Payouts), risk and compliance (Radar, Identity, Tax) and data products (Sigma, Data Pipeline). Processed $1.9T in payment volume in 2025; $5.1B revenue in 2024. Sold primarily to developers and finance teams at companies from startups to enterprises.
category: Payments / fintech infrastructure - and, since 2025, agentic-commerce infrastructure (developer platform)
stage: Private, late-stage / pre-IPO. Last published mark: February 2026 employee tender at $159B valuation (up ~70% from $91.5B in Feb 2025).
funding: Total raised not verified as a single figure - treat cumulative total as unknown. Verified milestones: $2M seed (May 2011; Thiel, Musk, Sequoia, SV Angel, a16z); $600M in March 2021 at a $95B valuation; $6.5B in March 2023 at $50B (largely for employee liquidity/RSU tax withholding); July 2024 secondary with a $70B 409A; Feb 2025 tender at $91.5B; Feb 2026 tender at $159B. Also an active acquirer: Bridge ($1.1B, Feb 2025), Privy (June 2025), OpenRouter ($7.5B, Aug 2026 - its largest acquisition).
headcount_estimate: ~8,500 employees (2025)
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator - Summer 2009 batch (as /dev/payments)
sells_to: Developers first, then B2B across the full range - SMB self-serve through large enterprise
how_they_use_agents: Stripe is positioning itself as the payment rail FOR agents rather than as an agent operator. Verified: the Agentic Commerce Protocol (announced Sept 2025, co-developed with OpenAI) lets any business accept purchases initiated from AI platforms without major re-plumbing; it powers Instant Checkout in ChatGPT (Sept 2025). It shipped an AI foundation model for payments (May 2025) trained on its transaction graph for fraud/authorization. Its homepage markets 'Building the economic infrastructure for AI', claims 88% of the Forbes AI 50 as customers, and references 'Stripe-integrated agents'. The $7.5B OpenRouter acquisition (Aug 2026) pulls an LLM-routing marketplace in-house. Internal/ops use of agents is not disclosed; Stripe appears only as a logo ('2025_Solutions_Customer_Stripe.svg') on Guru's /solutions pages, with no quote and no case study - and notably Stripe is NOT on Guru's main /customers page, so the relationship is weakly evidenced.
why_they_need_memory: As a buyer: ~8,500 people, a notoriously deep product surface (dozens of products, each with its own API semantics, regional rules and compliance edge cases), plus large support and solutions-architect orgs answering technical questions at volume - the exact conditions where a verified internal knowledge layer pays for itself. As a category-adjacent player: agentic commerce only works if the agent carries durable buyer context (payment credentials, prior orders, merchant relationships, spend limits) across sessions, so Stripe is arguably building its own memory/identity substrate for agents rather than buying one. Treat Stripe as an infrastructure peer to the agent-memory category, not just a customer of it.

name: Ro (Roman Health Ventures Inc.)
what_it_does: Vertically integrated direct-to-patient telehealth company: connects patients to US-licensed clinicians online and owns the downstream stack - nationwide telehealth, its own pharmacy/fulfillment, and lab/at-home diagnostics. Core lines are Ro Body (GLP-1 weight management, partnered with Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly - roughly 40% of revenue by end of 2024), Ro Man / Roman (ED and sexual health, ~33%), and a ~25% tail of dermatology, hair loss, fertility (Modern Fertility, acquired 2021) and diagnostics. Revenue $598M in 2024, up 66% from $360M in 2023. Founded by Zachariah Reitano (CEO), Saman Rahmanian and Rob Schutz. Its internal platform is branded 'ro.OS' and spans intake, prescribing, fulfillment, monitoring and renewal.
category: Direct-to-consumer telehealth / digital health (GLP-1 and men's health)
stage: Private, late-stage (Series D). Last priced round Feb 2022; carried at a $7B valuation. Some low-quality aggregator sites claim an S-1 filing or a $2.3B secondary mark - I could not confirm either and would not rely on them.
funding: ~$1B in primary capital raised. Verified rounds: $3.1M seed (2017, General Catalyst); $88M Series A (2018, FirstMark Capital); $200M Series C (2020); $500M Series D (2021) at a $5B valuation; $150M extension (Feb 2022, led by ShawSpring Partners) at a $7B valuation. No confirmed round since Feb 2022.
headcount_estimate: Uncertain. LinkedIn's company page reports the 201-500 band; third-party aggregators estimate ~900. Best guess ~400-900 - do not treat as precise.
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2C - consumers/patients paying cash for subscription care (membership + medication); not a B2B seller
how_they_use_agents: Concrete and clinical, not cosmetic. Ro published 'Powered by ro.OS: Using AI to triage patient messages' describing an AI system that triages inbound patient messages for adverse events - reported 94% accuracy and a drop in response time from 115 minutes to 33 minutes; the results were published and presented as a peer-reviewed abstract at Obesity Week 2025. That is an AI agent sitting in the middle of a regulated clinical workflow, routing to human clinicians. Separately, Ro appears in Guru's 'Trusted by thousands of teams' marquee on /customers (asset 'Ro Logo (Black).png') - logo only, no quote - consistent with Guru serving its care/support teams. Its design agent lives directly on the canvas and pulls context from four channels: uploaded files (user interviews, UX copy, data reports), pasted Figma file links (so it can read components, tokens, layouts and styles and reproduce existing design patterns), live web search, and MCP tool connectors to GitHub, Atlassian, Slack, Linear and Hex. It ships 'Skills' — saved prompts converted into slash commands that encode a team's creative direction and are shared across the team — plus generative plugins and shader tooling. Agent conversations are visible to file collaborators by default, deliberately, as 'a window into how someone thinks.' Code Connect feeds design-system knowledge to coding agents and cut token costs ~22.5% on average (Coinbase case study, Sept 2026). Figma also runs an official Figma MCP server. Separately cited as a customer by Guru, Notion AI and Granola — i.e. it buys internal-knowledge tooling for its own ~1,900-person org while building the design-context layer itself.
why_they_need_memory: Figma has effectively concluded that context IS the product: their own framing is that the difference between an agent that speeds you up and one that understands how you work is context. Skills are a hand-rolled memory layer — reusable, shareable, team-scoped encoded judgment — and the MCP connectors plus Code Connect are a hand-rolled retrieval layer over design systems and adjacent tools. That makes them a validating reference for the category and simultaneously a hard sell: they built their own. Their internal need (a 1,900-person public company with ten-plus product lines shipped in about eighteen months) is the more straightforward buying motion, and is presumably what the Guru/Notion/Granola citations reflect.

name: Assent Inc. (formerly Assent Compliance)
what_it_does: Enterprise SaaS for supply chain product compliance and sustainability, sold to complex manufacturers. Assent runs a 'Product Intelligence Network': it collects part-level material declarations and supplier data from a manufacturer's deep supply chain, validates it with in-house regulatory experts, and maps it to regulations so the customer can prove compliance and design compliant products. Three solution lines: (1) Product Material Compliance — REACH, RoHS, TSCA, PFAS, Prop 65, SCIP, PPWR; (2) Product Sustainability — CSRD/ESG reporting, product carbon footprint, EU Batteries Regulation, EUDR deforestation, conflict minerals; (3) Responsible Sourcing / trade compliance — forced-labour and sanctions screening, supplier diversity. Delivery is software plus a services/advisory layer that runs supplier-engagement campaigns on the customer's behalf. Scale claims: 780+ customers (GE, Boeing, Johnson & Johnson, Honeywell, Toshiba, ABB, Hologic, Corsair), 39M part data points, 1.3M supplier engagements, 80,000+ compliance campaigns run annually. Ottawa HQ, Certified B Corp, hubs in Ottawa, Pune, Amsterdam, Eldoret (Kenya) and Penang. Made its first acquisition ever in July 2026, buying IPOINT (LCA and product stewardship software, strong in automotive).
category: supply chain compliance & sustainability SaaS (regtech / ESG data network) — enterprise vertical SaaS, not AI-native
stage: late-stage private, PE-backed unicorn (post-Series D)
funding: $500M+ total across four rounds in five years. Largest: $350M in January 2022 led by Vista Equity Partners at a $1B+ valuation (described by the company as one of the largest raises in Canadian software history). Use '1,000+' as the defensible figure.

sells_to: B2B enterprise — large and complex manufacturers in medical devices, aerospace and defense, electronics, automotive and industrial equipment. Buyers are heads of product compliance, supply chain, sustainability/ESG and legal at multinationals.
how_they_use_agents: The most genuinely AI-adjacent of the three. In December 2025 Assent launched Request Manager, marketed explicitly as an 'AI-native solution', built on the Assent Sustainability Platform and priced from $250/month, GA to new customers January 2026. It targets the supplier side of the problem: a supplier receiving hundreds to thousands of inbound customer compliance questionnaires per year (a manufacturer averages ~350 requests/year, each taking ~3 hours; 80% still handled via email and spreadsheets). Request Manager uses AI-powered parsing to read and extract incoming requests, classifies them, matches them against already-verified declarations in the network, auto-fills responses from reusable data, and enables proactive declaration sharing. Marketing says 'the more you use it, the smarter it gets.' They call this 'Network Intelligence' rather than agents, and I found no explicit claim of autonomous agents or LLM tool-use. The July 2026 IPOINT acquisition was framed around applying 'AI across that combined data' to answer product and supplier questions on one platform. So: AI-powered document understanding and response generation over a proprietary regulatory data network, moving toward agentic workflow automation.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct needs. Internally, a 1,000+ person, remote-first, six-country organisation whose product IS regulatory expertise — rules change constantly (PFAS thresholds, EUDR, CSRD, PPWR, evolving sanctions), and account managers, regulatory experts and supplier-engagement teams must all answer from the same current interpretation. Stale internal answers become customer-facing compliance errors, which is why an enterprise knowledge tool like Guru is bought here. In the product, Request Manager is precisely a memory problem dressed as an AI feature: answer a supplier questionnaire once, remember the verified answer, and reuse it against the next 350 differently-worded requests. Their moat is accumulated, validated supply chain data reused across time and customers — persistent memory over a proprietary corpus is literally the value proposition, and an agent-memory vendor could plausibly sell into both the internal enablement side and the product side.
confidence: high — funding amounts, dates, lead investors, founding year, employee milestone, customer count, AI product launch and Guru logo all verified from first-party press releases and pages. Medium confidence only on current (2026) headcount.

name: Oura (Oura Health Oy)
what_it_does: Finnish health-technology company making the Oura Ring, a smart ring that continuously tracks sleep, activity, stress, readiness, heart rate/HRV, blood oxygen, body temperature, and menstrual cycle. Freemium hardware-plus-subscription model: buy the ring, then pay for Oura Membership to unlock 50+ metrics and advanced features in the iOS/Android app. Five ring generations shipped through June 2026; Ring 5 adds GLP-1 medication tracking, and 'Health Radar' continuously monitors biometrics for patterns worth flagging. 5.5M rings sold as of Sept 2025; company guided to close to $2B in 2026 sales. Acquired Veri (metabolic health) and Sparta Science (analytics) in 2024. Sold D2C and via retail partners.
category: consumer health wearable (hardware + subscription), digital health
stage: Late-stage private, pre-IPO — filed confidentially for a US IPO in May 2026
funding: $2.3M seed (2015); $100M Series C (May 2021); $200M Series D (Dec 2024) at a $5.2B valuation; $900M Series E (Oct 2025) at an $11B valuation.
headcount_estimate: 900+ employees
yc_or_accelerator: None found
founded_year: 2013 (Oulu, Finland; US operations in San Francisco)
sells_to: B2C / prosumer — direct-to-consumer hardware and subscription, plus retail partners; also enterprise, employer, and research programs
how_they_use_agents: The clearest agent story of the three, and it runs in both directions. In-product: Oura Advisor is an LLM-powered in-app health assistant that reads the user's Sleep, Activity, Readiness, and Resilience data, explains long-term trends, and builds plans. It explicitly supports 'Memories' — stored personal health context such as recovering from surgery — and draws on short- and long-term data plus previous interactions to tailor responses. In April 2026 Oura shipped its first proprietary LLM for women's health, reviewed by board-certified clinicians. Internally: Oura is on Guru's healthcare logo wall, so it also buys a governed knowledge layer with Knowledge Agents for its own teams.
why_they_need_memory: Oura is arguably the archetype buyer for this category. Its consumer agent is worthless without persistent per-user memory — health guidance that forgets a surgery, a pregnancy, or a GLP-1 prescription is not just unhelpful but unsafe, and Oura has already productized this as an explicit 'Memories' feature. On the internal side, a 900+ person hardware-plus-clinical-content company with a pending IPO needs governed, verifiable answers about medical claims, regulatory positioning, and support policy so that neither staff nor AI assistants improvise.

name: Covered Bridge Cabinetry
what_it_does: Truly-custom kitchen cabinetry brand. Manufactures made-to-order cabinets in North American hardwoods and premium enamel finishes, with customizable door styles, stile/rail widths and edge profiles, sold almost entirely through an independent dealer network (local kitchen & bath dealerships) to interior designers, builders, renovators and homeowners. IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL FINDING: this is NOT an independent company. It is a brand/subsidiary of FGI Industries Ltd. (Nasdaq: FGI, CIK 0001864943), a global kitchen-and-bath supplier headquartered at 906 Murray Road, East Hanover, NJ — the same address the Covered Bridge contact page lists. FGI's SEC subsidiary list (EX-21.1) shows the legal entity as 'Covered Bridge Cabinetry Manufacturing Co., Ltd' incorporated in Cambodia, i.e. the manufacturing arm; product is sourced from Southeast Asia. FGI's 10-K places 'Covered Bridge Cabinetry' alongside 'Craft + Main Cabinetry' in its 'Other' category and states custom kitchen cabinetry is 'less than 8% of our total sales' but is 'some of the highest margin, highest quality products that we sell' and a targeted growth/consolidation area. Site claims 'over 30 years of experience in cabinetry manufacturing.'
category: building products / custom kitchen cabinetry manufacturing (brand of a public kitchen-and-bath supplier)
stage: not venture-stage — brand/subsidiary of a Nasdaq-listed small-cap (FGI Industries Ltd., IPO Jan 2022)
funding: unknown / not applicable — no standalone funding. Parent FGI Industries is public (Nasdaq: FGI and warrants FGIWW); FY2025 total FGI revenue $130,528,652 (down 1.0% vs $131.8M FY2024) per its 10-K filed 2026-04-10. No revenue is broken out for Covered Bridge specifically beyond 'custom kitchen cabinetry <8% of total sales' (implies roughly <$10M).
headcount_estimate: unknown for the brand itself. Parent FGI Industries employed approximately 426 full-time employees company-wide as of December 31, 2025 (10-K Human Capital section). Covered Bridge is a fraction of that; realistically a small brand/dealer-support team in NJ plus a Cambodian manufacturing entity. LinkedIn headcount could not be retrieved (auth-walled).
yc_or_accelerator: none
founded_year: unknown as a legal entity; brand markets 'over 30 years of experience in cabinetry manufacturing.' First appears in FGI Industries' SEC subsidiary list in the FY2022 10-K (filed 2023-04-17), so it was under FGI ownership by end of 2022.
sells_to: B2B — sells through independent kitchen & bath dealers, and markets to builders, remodelers and interior designers; ultimate product is consumer/residential. Classic B2B2C dealer-channel model, SMB-scale operation inside a public parent.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents appear anywhere in their product or on their website — the product is physical cabinets. Their appearance on Guru's logo wall is as a BUYER of an internal knowledge/AI-agent tool, not a builder of one. Guru's construction & engineering page pitches 'Knowledge Agents' that 'tailor answers by role and context' and that 'verify and unverify info for you.' The plausible internal use case is dealer-facing and order-desk knowledge: door styles, wood species and grades, finish/color libraries, pricing and spec sheets, lead times, and warranty/claims answers that a small support team must give consistently to a distributed dealer network. Note this is inferred from the product model — Guru publishes no case study for them, only the logo.
why_they_need_memory: A truly-custom product with a combinatorial spec space (species, grade, door style, stile & rail widths, edge profiles, enamel colors) sold through third-party dealers means the same questions get re-asked constantly by people outside the company, and getting an answer wrong produces a scrapped custom order. Their knowledge is also spread across a US brand/marketing team, a NJ parent company, and an overseas manufacturing entity, so institutional memory does not live in one head or one system. This is the low-tech end of the agent-memory buyer spectrum: they want a verified answer layer over static product/process knowledge, not agent state for an autonomous system.

name: Cumming Group
what_it_does: International project management and cost consulting firm for the built environment — program and project management, cost and commercial management, planning and scheduling, project controls, dispute avoidance/resolution, energy and sustainability, building consultancy and technical due diligence. Sectors include data centers and advanced technologies, semiconductor/advanced manufacturing, healthcare, higher ed and K-12, government, hospitality, sports and themed entertainment, transportation and infrastructure, aviation, energy and utilities, rail, and residential. Claims '#1 Pure Play PM Firm in U.S.' and #12 on the ENR 100 PM/CM list, 3,000+ team members across 70+ offices, and $300B+ of projects delivered. Heavily acquisitive: mergers with OutForm Consulting and TLM Group (Aug 2026), RGD Project Management (May 2026), Vidaurri Management Group (Mar 2026), plus earlier absorption of Lehrer Cumming, PCM, Nova Partners and RGMK into one brand. Launched a global Advanced Technologies Division in March 2026 and marked its 30-year anniversary July 2026.
category: construction/AEC professional services — program, project and cost management consulting (ENR-ranked PM/CM firm)
stage: private equity–backed, mature (30 years old); not a startup
funding: PE-backed, amounts undisclosed. New Mountain Capital announced a growth partnership / investment on 2021-11-16 (terms not disclosed); prior sponsor Tailwind Capital remained a shareholder. At the time of that release New Mountain cited $35B+ AUM and Cumming had 1,850+ employees across 41 offices. No venture funding, no Crunchbase-style round history; revenue is not publicly disclosed (private).
headcount_estimate: 3,000+ (company-stated, 2026, across 70+ offices worldwide). Note their own contact page still carries a stale '2,500+ team members and 60+ offices' figure, and the 2021 New Mountain release said 1,850+ across 41 offices — so roughly 60% headcount growth in five years, largely by acquisition. LinkedIn not retrievable (auth-walled).
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: B2B enterprise — owners, developers, government agencies, hyperscalers/data center operators, health systems, universities and public-sector clients buying program and cost management on large capital projects. Long consultative sales cycles, enterprise procurement.
how_they_use_agents: AI shows up on the delivery/ops side, not as a product they sell. Their 'Digital Solutions' practice markets an integrated ecosystem branded 'Actual Useful Things (AUT)' and describes itself as 'data-driven, digitally enabled, AI-enhanced,' combining 'data, automation, and AI with real-world construction knowledge.' Named AI-bearing components: Procore with 'Procore Helix: AI Assist, Agent Builder' as the primary project delivery platform; AI-enabled cost estimating via Togal and Ediphi (alongside CostX and a proprietary cost database); AI-assisted progress assessment against schedule from reality-capture tools (DroneDeploy, Cupix, Multivista, OnsiteIQ); plus PowerBI/Tableau/Looker dashboards, Primavera P6/Synchro/Crystal Ball for scheduling and risk, and Join.build and Clearstory integrations. They explicitly frame integrated knowledge management as supporting 'responsible AI deployment.' They are an agent ORCHESTRATOR/consumer — assembling third-party agents (Procore Agent Builder) over their own project data — rather than an agent builder, which is exactly the profile that buys a company-brain layer.
why_they_need_memory: The sharpest fit of the three. Three compounding pressures: (1) serial M&A — at least four mergers in 2026 alone plus four legacy brands folded into one — means the firm is continuously absorbing other companies' processes, cost data, templates and client history, and needs a shared memory layer so acquired teams stop operating as islands; (2) 3,000+ people across 70+ offices and a dozen-plus sectors, where the same cost-estimating or schedule-risk judgment gets re-derived from scratch by each region; (3) they already run agents inside Procore Helix/Agent Builder over project data, and those agents are only as good as the verified, current knowledge behind them — Guru's pitch of agents that 'verify and unverify info for you' maps directly onto a consultancy where a stale unit cost or an out-of-date compliance rule flows straight into a client deliverable. Their proprietary construction cost database is the institutional memory that differentiates them commercially; the agent-memory purchase is about making that memory reachable by everyone and by their agents.

I verified the logo on Guru's page against both candidates: Guru's asset '2025_Solutions_Customer_intrax.svg' contains an isometric-cube icon to the LEFT of the wordmark whose path data ('M16.4628 5.1112L21.66 2.15464L27.5523 5.58958V12.4555L22.3669 15.4239V8.50301L16.4628 5.1112Z') is the same geometry, uniformly scaled ~2.83x, as the icon in intrax.com.au's own logo file ('M46.53,15.7 L59.91,8.16 L75.08,16.92 L75.08,34.43 L61.73,42 L61.73,24.35 L46.53,15.7 Z'). WHAT THEY DO: a national Australian multi-discipline professional services firm providing engineering, surveying and geotechnical services across the built environment, organized in four divisions — Housing (volume, custom, medium-density, modular/relocatable), Projects (living accommodation, education, retail, industrial, healthcare), Land (residential, commercial, industrial, infrastructure, marine, transport, utilities), and Remedial & Forensic. how_they_use_agents: No AI product and no customer-facing agents. Their site markets 'AI automation' as one of several 'cutting-edge technology' capabilities alongside 3D scanning, BIM and high-resolution drone surveying — i.e. AI applied inside a surveying/engineering workflow (likely automated processing of scan/drone capture and report generation), not an agent product. As with the other two, their presence on Guru's wall is as a buyer of an internal knowledge/agent layer, not a vendor. Guru pitches Knowledge Agents giving role- and context-specific verified answers to field supervisors, project managers and engineers, integrated with Procore, Autodesk, Raken and SafetyCulture.
why_they_need_memory: A 500-person engineering firm assembled partly by acquisition (ESG, Terramap, Advent, Insync, an NSW surveying firm) across 6 offices and 4 divisions has the classic knowledge-fragmentation problem: each acquired practice arrived with its own standards, templates and precedent. Their work is also compliance- and standards-bound — Australian building codes, soil classification and geotechnical standards, state-by-state surveying regulation — where the authoritative answer changes and a stale one creates liability, which is precisely the 'verify/unverify info for you' pitch. The Housing division's volume-builder work means thousands of near-identical jobs where a consistent, retrievable answer beats re-deriving it, and the Remedial & Forensic division depends on being able to recall what was specified and why on a project years earlier. name: Chime (Chime Financial, Inc.)
what_it_does: US consumer fintech / neobank — explicitly "a financial technology company, not a bank," with banking services provided by partner banks The Bancorp Bank, N.A. and Stride Bank, N.A. Products: fee-free checking with no minimum balance, high-yield savings (up to 3.75% APY for Prime members), SpotMe fee-free overdraft up to $200, early direct deposit (up to 2 days early), Credit Builder secured Visa card with no credit check, MyPay earned-wage advance up to $500/pay period, cash-back rewards (5% Prime / 2% Plus), 47,000+ fee-free ATMs, and Chime Invest (commission-free investing, launched July 2026). Premium tier Chime Prime launched 2026. Also distributes through employers (e.g. an Allied Universal partnership covering hundreds of thousands of employees). Sponsors MLS All-Star and the WNBA Portland Fire.
category: Consumer fintech / neobank (mass-market US banking)
stage: Public — IPO'd on Nasdaq (ticker CHYM) in June 2025; reported Q2 2026 results on Aug 5, 2026
funding: Public. Chime's own newsroom links Forbes coverage of the June 2025 Nasdaq debut: stock jumped 37% on day one, valuing it at $14.5B. Pre-IPO venture funding is widely reported at roughly $2.6B total with a $25B private valuation in a 2021 Series G, but I could not verify those private-round figures in this pass (web search budget was exhausted; investors.chime.com timed out repeatedly) — treat them as unconfirmed.
headcount_estimate: ~2,500 (LinkedIn company page lists 2,505 employees, band 1,001–5,000). HQ San Francisco, with offices in Chicago and New York.

sells_to: B2C — mass-market US consumers/hourly-and-salaried workers; some B2B2C distribution via employer partnerships
how_they_use_agents: Not an agent vendor; a heavy AI adopter internally. Chime's careers site states "84% of the code we shipped in March was developed with AI, up from 29% just four months ago," positions the company as "built for building in the AI era," and says AI "supercharges our products, so we can personalize at scale." It lists an open "Full-Stack Engineer, Human Agent Tooling" role — i.e. tooling for human support agents, which is exactly the surface a knowledge/memory layer plugs into. Newsroom also mentions an internal "AI Voyager" employee innovation program and AI cutting ad production time ~60% (per the CMO). No public claim of customer-facing autonomous agents; the consumer product pages mention no AI at all. why_they_need_memory: Regulated consumer finance at scale with 24/7 member support: front-line reps and AI answer systems need verified, permission-aware answers about fee policies, disputes/Reg E procedures, and differences between the two partner banks (Bancorp vs Stride) — all of which must be sourced and provably current for compliance. Product surface is churning fast (MyPay 2024, Prime and Invest in 2026), so knowledge goes stale quickly; Guru's pitch of Knowledge Agents that "verify and unverify info for you" targets exactly that decay. Being newly public adds disclosure discipline to what support may say.

category: Consumer fintech / personal-finance marketplace and media (NOT an AI vendor)
stage: Public (Nasdaq: NRDS, IPO November 2021)

yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: B2C consumers and B2B SMB (via Fundera); revenue actually comes from financial-institution partners who pay for referrals
how_they_use_agents: Consumer-facing: NerdAI, a conversational assistant embedded directly on the nerdwallet.com homepage (input labeled 'Ask NerdAI a question', placeholder 'Ask me about credit cards…') plus a persistent floating chat button — a NerdAIChat client component on the live homepage. FY2025 10-K states they use 'machine learning and rules-based systems to improve marketplace matching, predict user intent, and optimize performance,' says 'We currently incorporate AI technology in certain of our products and in our business operations,' and the risk factors explicitly name 'generative and agentic AI technologies.' They have initiated an internal AI governance framework. Note: 'NerdAI' returns zero hits in EDGAR full-text search, so the assistant is not yet a named, material line item in filings. why_they_need_memory: Their entire asset is 15,000+ pieces of expert-reviewed, compliance-sensitive financial content plus partner terms that change weekly (the homepage timestamps APYs to specific days). Any consumer-facing financial assistant must ground answers in verified, current, legally-reviewed facts rather than model priors — that is a retrieval-plus-verification problem, exactly what agent-memory/knowledge-layer vendors sell. Internally, 650+ remote employees across editorial, compliance, partnerships and support need one verified source of truth as product terms churn. Strategically urgent: credit-card revenue fell 24% in 2025 on 'continued pressures in organic search traffic,' and the 10-K flags AI-assisted search as a further threat — so structuring their knowledge to be consumable by agents is now a distribution survival question, not a nice-to-have.

category: Dev tools / web infrastructure (WebOps, managed hosting) — B2B SaaS
stage: Late-stage private (Series E, July 2021). Sameer Kazi appointed CEO November 2024; on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list.
funding: $200M+ total raised. Seed $1.3M (2010); Series A $5M Foundry Group (2012); Series B $21.5M led by Scale Venture Partners (2014); Series C $29M incl. $8.5M Industry Ventures (2016); Series D $40M Sageview Capital (2019); Series E $100M solely from SoftBank Vision Fund 2 (announced 2021-07-13) at a valuation over $1B. No publicly announced round since 2021. SEC Form D filings under CIK 0001509079 (Dec 2011, May 2014, Jul 2016, Mar 2019).

yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: B2B — developers and digital agencies, enterprise marketers, and IT leaders running large multi-site web portfolios. Verticals: higher education, government, media, nonprofit, consumer brands, technology, credit unions.
how_they_use_agents: This is the most genuinely agent-relevant of the three. Their Q3 2026 product update leads with 'Introducing Agentic Fleet Management. Make your entire web fleet visible and actionable to agents.' Concretely: (1) a Pantheon MCP Server (marked coming soon) that exposes sites, environments, workflows, backups and Secrets Manager to AI coding agents with scoped access, read-only mode and confirmed write actions; (2) fleet-level traffic insights that surface top IPs, user agents and paths across every site in a workspace and detect unusual/bot sources; (3) a new Site Administrator governance role for delegated, non-destructive control; (4) bulk upstream updates across all connected sites. A next-generation global CDN adds bot protection that challenges malicious scrapers before origin. They also run an MCP-server webinar (Content Publisher deep dive, real-time blog post deployment) and marketing around 'AI-ready infrastructure' and 'the war on agentic citations.' Autopilot (2021) is pre-LLM automation — automated updates plus visual regression testing. Internally they appear on Guru's business-services logo wall.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. Product side: they are building an agent control plane over 700,000 production websites. An agent that can update, deploy or roll back a customer site needs durable, scoped, per-site state — what this site is, its policy and environment, what was already attempted, what a human already approved — which is precisely persistent agent memory plus permissioning rather than a stateless tool call. Their own MCP design language ('scoped access, read-only mode, confirmed write actions') is that problem stated out loud. Ops side: ~440 employees plus 2,500 agency partners supporting three separate CMS ecosystems produce a large, fast-churning support and enablement surface; keeping verified answers consistent across support, sales, docs and partner enablement is the textbook Guru knowledge-layer use case.

how_they_use_agents: None observable. I found zero mentions of AI, artificial intelligence, machine learning, algorithms or agents on the homepage, the hire-electricians product page, or their most recent (Feb 2026) product blog post. The only automation on the site is rules-based: automatic TDLR license-expiry detection and alerts, automatic notifications for project transfers/terminations/time approvals, automatic Spanish translation of communications, and geofenced clock-ins. Founders are Moody (Denman) Heard, Michael Orcutt and Vu Brown. The Guru relationship is therefore internal knowledge management, not an agent in their product — they appear only on Guru's construction-and-engineering logo wall, with no case study.
why_they_need_memory: Classic 'non-technical, fast-scaling services org' buyer rather than an AI company. Their SLA is speed of human judgment — 75%+ of qualified candidates matched within 30 minutes — so recruiters and account managers need instant, correct answers. The knowledge is genuinely hard and state-specific: electrical licensing (Texas TDLR and equivalents), prevailing-wage and certified-payroll rules, I-9 and background-check policy, and per-contractor job requirements, all varying across 14+ metros in multiple states. They also grew by acquisition (Ladder, Dec 2024), which means merging two operating playbooks and onboarding a second recruiting team. That is a verified-knowledge-base problem, and it is why a company with no AI in its product still shows up on an AI-knowledge vendor's logo wall.

stage: Public (Nasdaq: WW), post-restructuring. Filed Chapter 11 in Delaware on 2025-05-06 to eliminate most of ~$1.5B of debt, was delisted from Nasdaq 2025-05-16, traded OTC, and re-listed in early July 2025 after emerging. Reporting quarterly results through Q2 2026.

how_they_use_agents: AI shows up in two places. (1) In the product, as ML features rather than autonomous agents: camera-based meal recognition that assigns Points values, automatic macro tracking, and the 2021 'PersonalPoints' system that used AI to customize point values and zero-point food lists per member. The consumer site does not market 'AI agents' by name. (2) Internally, as the Guru buyer: Guru's healthcare page pitches permission-aware Knowledge Agents that deliver verified answers into EHRs (Epic, Oracle Health, Athena), Slack/Teams and email with PHI masking — which matches WeightWatchers' clinic-side support and coaching operations rather than anything member-facing. Treat the agent usage as internal knowledge-assist, not agentic product.
why_they_need_memory: Large, distributed, high-churn frontline: coaches, member-support reps and now clinicians answering questions about a program whose rules change (Points system revisions), plus a regulated telehealth arm where GLP-1 eligibility, insurance coverage, prior-auth steps and clinical protocols must be answered identically every time. Content is scattered across clinical protocol docs, payer coverage rules, marketing offers and app release notes. That is the classic 'company brain' pain: verified, permission-scoped, PHI-safe answers pushed into the tools staff already use, so support does not improvise on regulated content.

Wrapped with Gravie Care (member support) and Gravie Pay (interest-free financing for out-of-pocket costs). Claims 3,300+ employer groups across all 50 states, 97% employer satisfaction, 92% CHOICE group retention. Confirmed as a Guru logo on getguru.com/solutions/healthcare and /solutions/insurance.
category: employer health benefits / ICHRA and level-funded insurtech (not an AI company)
stage: Late-stage private / growth-stage. Latest round announced 2026-07-30, led by General Atlantic; the round size was not disclosed in the press release, only the cumulative total.
funding: $463 million total raised as of 2026-07-30 (company-stated, in the PR Newswire release announcing the General Atlantic-led round and Eric Murphy's board appointment). Investors visible via board seats: General Atlantic (Jon Michael Reese), FirstMark Capital (Amish Jani), AXA Venture Partners (Alex Scherbakovsky). Individual round sizes and valuation are not disclosed publicly on their site.

Scale signal only: 3,300+ employer groups nationwide and an in-house member-support org (Gravie Care), which implies a meaningful services headcount — but I will not put a number on it.

how_they_use_agents: No AI or AI agents appear anywhere in Gravie's public product marketing — the homepage, about page and press releases are silent on it. Their agent exposure is entirely as a buyer: Guru's Knowledge Agents sitting behind Gravie Care support reps and broker-facing teams, retrieving plan-specific verified answers with PHI masking and permission-aware access. This is a back-office knowledge-assist deployment, not agents in the product.
why_they_need_memory: Benefits support is a knowledge-retrieval problem at its core. A Gravie Care rep must answer questions that vary by employer group (3,300+ of them), by plan type (level-funded vs ICHRA vs the new Edge hybrid), by state (50 different individual-market and insurance-regulation regimes), and by plan year — while touching PHI. Getting it wrong creates compliance and claims exposure. The knowledge lives in plan documents, carrier rules, broker collateral and internal SOPs that change every renewal cycle. That is exactly the 'verified, permission-scoped, always-current answer in the rep's workflow' use case a company-brain vendor sells, and it is why an insurtech with no AI product still buys agent-memory infrastructure.

name: 1Password (AgileBits Inc.)
what_it_does: Started as a cross-platform consumer password manager (encrypted vaults for passwords, licenses and secrets behind a master password, on iOS/Android/Windows/Linux/macOS/browser) and has repositioned as an enterprise 'unified access management' platform — its own framing is visibility and control for humans, machines and AI agents, built on a vault for identities, credentials and secrets. Enterprise surface includes Extended Access Management (device trust, SSO gap coverage), secrets management for infrastructure, passkeys (via the 2022 Passage acquisition), and an agentic-AI security line. Stated scale: 200,000+ business customers, 30%+ of the Fortune 100, two-thirds of the Forbes AI 50, 1.3B credentials secured. Confirmed as a Guru logo on getguru.com/solutions/it-services (asset '2025_Solutions_Customer_1password.svg'); also cited by Notion AI.
category: security / identity and access management, secrets management, and now AI-agent access control (dev tools adjacent)
stage: Late-stage private, Series C. CEO has publicly floated a possible 2026-2027 IPO. Not a startup by any reasonable definition.
funding: ~$920M total disclosed across three rounds: $200M Series A in 2019 led by Accel (the company's first outside capital after 13 bootstrapped years), $100M in 2021 at a $2B valuation, and a $620M Series C in January 2022 at a $6.8B valuation — at the time the largest Canadian venture round. Investors include Accel, ICONIQ, plus celebrity/operator angels (Ryan Reynolds, Robert Downey Jr., Justin Timberlake, Shopify and Slack executives). Revenue: surpassed $250M ARR in September 2023 and exceeded $400M ARR as of November 2025. Acquisitions: SecretHub (2021), Passage (2022).
headcount_estimate: 1,400+ global employees (stated on 1password.com/about). Remote-first with Toronto HQ at 4711 Yonge St.
yc_or_accelerator: none — bootstrapped from 2005 until the 2019 Accel Series A
founded_year: 2005 (company/product origin; the 1Password product release is often dated to June 2006)
sells_to: B2B enterprise (primary — Fortune 100, MSP edition), B2B SMB, developers (secrets management, CLI, CI/CD), and prosumer/consumer (the individual and family password manager that remains the brand's front door)
how_they_use_agents: 1Password is unusual in this list because agents appear on both sides. In the product, it sells agent infrastructure: a Credential Broker that verifies AI agents and machine workloads at runtime and issues only the credentials each is authorized to receive; discovery of shadow AI and local agents running on developer machines and in browsers; TOTP support so agents can satisfy MFA without a human; replacement of .env files with policy-driven vault access; time-of-use authorization, scoped credentials, real-time revocation, and unified audit across humans, agents and machines — marketed as 'zero standing privileges for humans and AI.' Notably the agentic-AI page does not name MCP. As a buyer, it runs Guru for IT/support knowledge and Notion AI as a workspace brain.
why_they_need_memory: A 1,400-person remote-first company supporting 200,000+ business customers across a product line that now spans consumer password manager, enterprise device trust, developer secrets and agent access control. Support and solutions engineers must answer version-, platform- and plan-specific questions with security-critical accuracy, and the internal knowledge is spread across docs, Notion, Slack and ticket history. That is the canonical company-brain buyer profile: high-headcount distributed org, fast-moving product surface, and answers where being stale is a security problem. There is also a strategic-affinity angle — a vendor whose own thesis is that agents need governed access to enterprise systems is a natural early adopter of agent-memory tooling, and a natural design partner/reference logo for it.

name: OnePay (formerly One / One Finance; Guru logo asset 'one financial')
what_it_does: Consumer fintech 'super app' majority-owned by Walmart. one.app now 301-redirects to onepay.com. Product set: mobile banking (checking + high-yield savings through partner banks Coastal Community Bank and Lead Bank), early pay (up to 2 days before payday), OnePay Debit and CashRewards Mastercard, the Builder secured credit card (launched Apr 2026, no late fees/interest), OnePay Later BNPL at Walmart (powered by Klarna), OnePay Wallet with Walmart rewards, stock investing from $1, crypto, IRAs, free credit-score monitoring, personal loans via Upgrade (Jul 2026), Apple Pay support (Aug 2026), and wireless plans. Separately runs OnePay Enterprise: embedded financial wellness and earned wage access ('@Work') sold to employers, payroll/HR tech platforms, and gig/staffing platforms. Also runs 'OnePay Next', an internal incubator described as 'AI-native, end to end'. HQ New York, NY.
category: Consumer fintech / neobank 'super app' (retail banking, BNPL, investing); secondary embedded-finance B2B line
stage: Late-stage private, corporate-backed (Walmart holds a majority stake; Ribbit Capital co-investor)
funding: Launched Jan 2021 as 'Hazel' by Walmart + Ribbit Capital; capitalized with over $250M when it merged ONE Finance and Even Responsible Finance under the ONE brand (Apr 2022); a $300M round co-led by Walmart and Ribbit Capital (2024). A January 2026 employee share buyback valued the company at more than $4B (Bloomberg). Total raised not publicly consolidated - treat ~$550M+ disclosed as a floor, exact total unknown.
headcount_estimate: ~500-1,300. LinkedIn company page lists the 501-1,000 employee band, with roughly 1,296 profiles listing OnePay as employer (Sept 2026).
yc_or_accelerator: None. Corporate-venture origin - incubated as 'Hazel' by Walmart and Ribbit Capital rather than through an accelerator.
founded_year: 2021 (as Hazel; the acquired ONE Finance dates to 2019). Rebranded from One to OnePay in 2025.
sells_to: Primarily B2C - mass-market and underbanked US consumers, heavily indexed to Walmart shoppers. Secondary B2B enterprise motion (employers, HR tech/payroll platforms, gig platforms) for embedded financial wellness.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places, both documented on their own newsroom. (1) IN THE PRODUCT: 'OnePay For Agents' (30 Jun 2026) exposes a OnePay MCP server so third-party AI assistants can securely pull a user's financial context - 'plan your trip, knowing how much to budget for it'. Their stated thesis: 'We believe the future of money will be increasingly agentic. As AI agents become how people shop, plan travel, compare options, and make decisions, money needs to be present there.' (2) INTERNALLY: 'Arnab' (27 May 2026), their internal AI agent / 'AI Co-Worker', shipped as a web app and natively in Slack to all employees. Arnab fronts 'a growing fleet of specialized agents across the business - engineering, operations, compliance, fraud, customer support'. Its developer agent is called 'Tokki'. Architecture is built on two open protocols: MCP for agent-to-tool access and ACP (Agent Communication Protocol) for agent-to-agent. Arnab supports 'hundreds of tools across dozens of integrations' (Slack, Gmail, Drive, GitLab, Datadog, ArgoCD, ERP, expense, legal, analytics), is model-agnostic with six selectable models, and hosts a marketplace of user-built 'Skills' and 'Apps'.
why_they_need_memory: They articulated the category's buying thesis themselves, in public. The Arnab post names 'the cold-start problem': a frontier model 'is brilliant in the abstract and a stranger in your environment. It doesn't know your business... your mission, your values, how your org is structured. It doesn't know what "Tokki" is, who runs the Risk team, or which Slack channel is the right one to ping when payments latency spikes.' They call that 'the single biggest reason AI adoption stalls inside organizations. The technology is ready. The context isn't.' Two of Arnab's five stated 'superpowers' are exactly this category: (a) Knowledge - it ships knowing mission, values, org structure, HR policy, product features, value props and customer FAQs, so it can answer 'who owns the Pay Later roadmap?' the way a teammate would; and (b) Memory - 'It Learns You', per-user memory of projects, collaborators, recurring questions and preferred answer formats, deliberately made inspectable and user-manageable ('Memory shouldn't be a black box'). Being a regulated financial institution adds auditability and single-source-of-truth pressure on top. NOTE the buying implication: OnePay is a Guru customer for human knowledge search AND built its own agent-memory layer in-house rather than buying one - a warning sign that well-resourced fintechs at this scale may build rather than buy.

name: Ramp
what_it_does: All-in-one financial operations / spend management platform for businesses. Corporate charge cards (Visa, unlimited physical and virtual, with per-vendor/category/amount controls and up to 5% cashback); expense management with receipt capture via SMS/Slack/mobile and automatic policy review; accounts payable (OCR invoice extraction, two- and three-way matching, zero domestic ACH fees); procurement and intake-to-pay (contract parsing, dynamic approval routing, auto-generated POs); corporate travel with policy enforcement at booking and automatic hotel rate re-shopping; and a treasury / FDIC-insured business account. Self-reported scale: 'Trusted by 70,000+ businesses', 27M+ hours saved, books closed 75% faster. HQ New York.
category: B2B fintech / spend management and finance automation SaaS, now heavily agentic
stage: Late-stage private (Series E and beyond)
funding: ~$1.96B+ in disclosed equity, plus undisclosed rounds and large debt facilities. Rounds: ~$15M Series A (Feb 2020), $30M (Dec 2020), $115M Series B (Apr 2021), $300M Series C (Aug 2021), $300M Series D (Aug 2023), $150M Series D-2 (Jun 2024), undisclosed Series E (Jun 2025), undisclosed (Jul 2025), $300M led by Lightspeed (Nov 2025), $750M led by ICONIQ Growth (Jun 2026). Latest valuation $44B (Jun 2026).
headcount_estimate: ~1,200-2,500. LinkedIn company page shows the 1,001-5,000 band and Wikipedia cites 1,200 for 2025; ~6,537 LinkedIn profiles associate with the name 'Ramp', which likely overcounts (name collisions / alumni). Treat 1,001-5,000 as the reliable range.
yc_or_accelerator: Ramp itself did not go through an accelerator. Founders Eric Glyman and Karim Atiyeh previously built Paribus, a Y Combinator-backed startup acquired by Capital One in 2016 - reported, not verified in this session.
founded_year: 2019 (March 2019; LinkedIn also lists Founded 2019). Founders: Eric Glyman (CEO), Karim Atiyeh (CTO), Gene Lee.
sells_to: B2B across the full size range - startups and SMBs through mid-market and enterprise. Named customers on-site include Notion, Shopify, Webflow, Eventbrite, Poshmark and Quora.
how_they_use_agents: 'Ramp Intelligence' is an AI layer embedded across the platform rather than a bolt-on. In accounts payable alone, 'four AI agents handle auto-coding, fraud prevention, approval routing, and automatic payment'. A named AI Policy Agent (shipped summer 2025) reviews 100% of expenses against company policy and escalates only exceptions. Other agentic surfaces: invoice transcription and line-item processing, three-way PO/receipt/invoice matching, contract parsing in procurement, real-time fraud and anomaly detection, duplicate-subscription flagging, vendor payment automation and cashback optimization, and automatic travel rate monitoring/rebooking. They claim 90% accurate auto-coding, learned from transaction patterns across 70,000+ customers. Explicit guardrail: 'no money ever moves without human confirmation' and 'all decisions transparent and auditable'.
why_they_need_memory: Two independent pulls. (1) PRODUCT SIDE - their agents are useless without durable per-tenant context, and their own marketing says so: agents are 'trained on your policy and controls', 'learn from past invoices', and 'learn from your company's spend patterns'. Coding an invoice or approving an expense correctly requires remembering this customer's chart of accounts, vendor history, approval chains, prior exceptions and reversals - that is agent memory, whether built or bought. (2) INTERNAL SIDE - a 1,000-5,000-person company compounding at this rate has a severe onboarding and single-source-of-truth problem across sales, support, finance and compliance, which is the classic Guru buy. Notably Ramp appears as a cited customer of Guru, Onyx (formerly Danswer), Notion AI and Granola simultaneously, which suggests they buy context/knowledge tooling broadly across the stack rather than standardizing on one - a positive signal for category demand but a crowded competitive field, and a hint they are also a favourite logo for vendors to cite.
