IMPORTANT DISAMBIGUATION: there is a second, unrelated company named Zello (linkedin.com/company/zello) — a UAE-based occupational health/workforce health services provider founded 2021 — that also shows 51-200. The Guru customer is the Austin, TX push-to-talk software company, confirmed by the zello.com site and the zello-inc LinkedIn page.
yc_or_accelerator: none found
founded_year: 2007 (original Loudtalks product by Alexey Gavrilov, announced Sept 17, 2007); company incorporated/established in Texas circa 2011-2012 — Wikipedia says 2011, LinkedIn lists 2012
sells_to: B2B, spanning SMB to large enterprise, sold into frontline operations — retail chains, airlines, logistics/transportation fleets, construction, hospitality, public safety. Buyer is ops/frontline leadership rather than IT. There is also a large free consumer/prosumer user base that acts as bottom-up distribution into the paid Zello Work product.
how_they_use_agents: Zello is unusual here: it both BUYS and BUILDS in this category. (1) BUILDS: 'Zello AI' with an assistant named Ella, marketed as 'the only frontline AI powered by real conversations' — an AI assistant that answers a frontline worker's question instantly from the company knowledge base, pitched on faster training/onboarding, better customer service and less downtime. Zello also turns its own PTT conversation stream into operational intelligence, and shipped AI Message Search plus an anonymized Message Vault (engineering blog, May 5, 2026). Live voice translation and transcription are further ML features. They have a dedicated executive for this: Raphael Varieras, SVP of AI & Data. Ella is essentially a company-brain product for deskless workers, sitting on top of a proprietary voice corpus that competitors do not have. (2) BUYS: Zello's logo appears on Guru's /solutions/it-services page, i.e. Guru is being used internally for knowledge/service-desk answers. Caveat: no Zello case study or quote exists on Guru's site, so the internal team and depth of usage are inferred from logo placement.
why_they_need_memory: The sharpest ICP of the three. Zello's own product thesis IS agent memory: Ella is only useful if it can retrieve accurate, current company knowledge (SOPs, product info, store policy) and answer a worker mid-shift, hands-free. That means they have a live, in-house need for knowledge ingestion, freshness/verification, permissioning and retrieval quality — the exact problems an agent-memory vendor sells into — and a strategic reason to evaluate the category rather than only consume it. Separately, as a 51-200 person company scaling from viral consumer app to enterprise sales (new CRO hired June 2025), their internal support and IT knowledge is growing faster than headcount, which is the standard Guru trigger. Watch for the buy-vs-build tension: a company shipping its own knowledge assistant may prefer to build memory infrastructure rather than buy it, or may buy it as embedded infrastructure — that distinction is worth qualifying in a sales conversation.

Their AI layer is 'Signals', marketed as 'hospitality's first foundation AI model' — a causal-AI engine that analyzes ~4B data points hourly across market demand signals plus a property's own PMS data to forecast revenue (claimed up to 95% forecast accuracy, 18% RevPAR lift). On top of Signals sit: (1) 'Ask Signals', a conversational AI interface launched May 2026 that lets hotel staff query operational, guest, and revenue data in natural language and assembles composite guest profiles (booking source, channel history, payments, ancillary spend, review history, recent comms) — currently in early pilot; (2) a guest-facing AI chatbot handling inquiries over web, WhatsApp, and SMS; (3) automated review responses, campaign generation in the guest CRM, and AI-assisted site building/SEO. Their explicit positioning is that AI only works on unified data — 'see the whole hotel, not a slice of it' — which is a data/context argument rather than an autonomous-agent argument. I found no evidence of multi-step autonomous agents, MCP support, or an agent memory layer in their product.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls, and the Guru purchase is almost certainly the first one. (1) Internal: a ~650-person, 40+-country distributed org supporting 20K+ properties across a very broad product surface (PMS, payments, channel manager, revenue, marketing, websites) — support, IT, and CS agents need one trusted answer layer, which is exactly the internal-knowledge/company-brain use case Guru's IT-services page sells. Note Cloudbeds appears only on Guru's logo wall, not as a published case study, so the depth of that deployment is unverified. (2) Product-side: 'Ask Signals' is a natural-language interface over fragmented hotel data, and their whole marketing argument is that context completeness is the differentiator — that is a retrieval/unified-data thesis rather than a persistent-memory thesis. Fit for an agent-memory vendor is medium: strong internal-knowledge buyer, weaker as an agent-memory infrastructure buyer.

Named customers include Virgin Voyages, Coach, Revolve, Forbes, L.L. Bean, and Tapestry (announced Apr 2026). Founded by Jeremy Swift (CEO), who previously founded and sold BlueHornet, and Adam Gillespie (CTO).
category: martech — cross-channel customer engagement / CDP + messaging platform, with an aggressive AI-agent product line
stage: Series C (announced July 26, 2022). No later round announced in their press archive through Sept 2026, so they are ~4 years past their last disclosed raise.
funding: $85M total raised. Most recent: $50M Series C, July 26, 2022, led by NewSpring, with ABS Capital (new), High Alpha and Upfront Ventures (existing) participating. Their about page also lists PeakSpan, Blossom Street Ventures, and Ankona Capital as investment partners. Valuation never disclosed.
headcount_estimate: ~200-260. LinkedIn shows the 51-200 bracket with 257 associated employee profiles. Fully remote team, San Diego HQ (402 W. Broadway, Suite 700).
yc_or_accelerator: none — but High Alpha, an early investor, is a venture studio/accelerator
sells_to: B2B enterprise — enterprise retail, travel, and media brands. Buyer is the marketing team, with technology/data teams as co-buyers. Not SMB, not developer-led.
how_they_use_agents: This is the strongest agent story of the three, and it is unusually explicit. Cordial has shipped a run of agent-infrastructure releases: (1) 'Cordial Edge AI' (Jan 2025), multimodal AI with brand-specific custom models, claimed 35%+ lift in marketing-driven purchases; (2) an MCP interface (launched Aug 28, 2025) that lets external AI assistants — Claude is named explicitly — query live customer and campaign data, pull performance insights and templates, and build/analyze audiences in real time; their pitch is explicitly that competitors expose 'limited endpoints' while Cordial gives agents 'structured access to data, assets and campaign context' and 'the full context needed to finish jobs'; (3) 'Cordial Foundry' (Sept 2025), agent-first tooling to move agents 'from draft mode to delivery' — agents search and retrieve brand assets, apply visual rules pulled from Figma design files, and execute campaigns end-to-end with preview and QA; (4) 'SAM' (Smart Asset Manager), an ML-tagged brand asset library that enforces brand guardrails so agents stay on-brand, with derivative asset generation; (5) a partnership with Wunderkind for 'autonomous marketing' (Aug 2026). CEO framing: 'Real agents don't stop at suggesting subject lines — they build and ship, to finish the job.'
why_they_need_memory: Best-fit buyer of the three, and fits on both axes. Product-side: they are explicitly building agents that execute multi-step campaign workflows and have publicly staked their differentiation on context completeness — 'the full context needed to finish jobs' is nearly a verbatim agent-memory pitch. Agents that retrieve brand assets, enforce per-brand visual and voice guardrails, and ship campaigns across many enterprise clients need durable, per-brand, per-account memory that survives across sessions; today they appear to solve this with MCP retrieval plus SAM's metadata rather than a memory layer, which is exactly the gap an agent-memory vendor sells into. Internal-side (the likely Guru purchase): ~200 remote employees supporting complex enterprise accounts like Tapestry, Coach, and Virgin Voyages, where solutions and support engineers need one governed answer layer. Note Cordial appears only on Guru's logo wall, not as a published case study, so deployment depth is unverified. Caveat on timing: last raise was 2022, so budget may be tighter than the AI-release cadence suggests.

Note the About page's 'five years ago' phrasing implies ~2018-2019, which likely refers to a relaunch or a specific initiative rather than founding — the 2016 anniversary post is the more reliable anchor.
sells_to: Two channels: consumers (DTC bottle sales, UK-centric shipping) and corporate/B2B buyers purchasing co-branded bottles as merchandise or gifting.
how_they_use_agents: Nothing agentic in their product — it is a physical bottle and a refill directory. Their presence is purely as a Guru customer on the getguru.com/solutions/nonprofit logo wall ('Give Me Tap'). Plausible internal use is a small shared knowledge base for customer-support and order/returns queries plus corporate-partner and co-branding request handling, answered through Guru's AI search and Knowledge Agents. I could not verify any case study, testimonial quote, or depth of usage — the only evidence is the logo.
why_they_need_memory: Weakest fit of the three and worth discounting in any ICP analysis. A sub-10-person consumer brand does not have the knowledge-fragmentation problem this category is sold against; the likeliest explanation is a free or heavily discounted Guru nonprofit/social-impact tier, which makes the logo a marketing placement rather than evidence of demand. If there is a real need it is thin: keeping impact claims, water-pump attribution and co-branding terms consistent across a tiny team fielding partner and press queries.

name: The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research
what_it_does: The world's largest nonprofit funder of Parkinson's disease research, founded in 2000 by actor Michael J. Fox with co-founder Deborah W. Brooks (now CEO). Deploys research grants against a self-set strategic research agenda; cites ~$3B invested since inception and 180+ therapies in or entering human testing, and has been described as funding more Parkinson's research than the US government. Flagship asset is PPMI (Parkinson's Progression Markers / Precision Medicine Initiative, launched 2010): a longitudinal observational study with 5,000+ in-clinic participants across 50 medical centers in 12 countries, 50,000+ online volunteers, mail-in screening (including scratch-and-sniff smell tests), and de-identified data and biosamples released to outside researchers under confidentiality pledge. Also runs patient education ('Parkinson's 101', newly-diagnosed guides, medication guidance), the Buddy Network peer-connection program, policy advocacy, and Team Fox peer-to-peer community fundraising. States 89 cents of every dollar goes to mission programs.
category: Nonprofit medical research funder and patient advocacy organization (neurology / Parkinson's). Not an AI company, though PPMI's open dataset is a heavily used substrate for third-party ML biomarker research.
stage: Not applicable — nonprofit, 501(c)(3), tax exemption issued December 2000.
funding: Philanthropic. IRS Form 990 via ProPublica, FY2024: total revenue $505,288,760; total expenses $452,470,597; net income $52,818,163; net assets $195,881,852; 97.0% of revenue ($490.2M) from contributions, 2.6% investment income. Five-year revenue trend: 2023 $316.1M, 2022 $362.4M, 2021 $353.4M, 2020 $202.3M. Executive compensation totals $4.7M (1.0% of expenses); CEO Deborah W. Brooks $1,467,004 in 2024. By revenue this is by far the largest of the three organizations.
headcount_estimate: Unknown — not stated on the site and not confirmed in any source I could reach (LinkedIn unreachable, web search budget exhausted). For calibration only: a ~$450M/year grant-making and clinical-research operation of this type typically runs several hundred staff, but I am not putting a number on it.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Celebrity-founded nonprofit, no accelerator affiliation.
sells_to: Not a seller. Fundraises from individual donors, the Team Fox community-fundraising network, corporate and pharmaceutical partners, and major philanthropy; serves two distinct audiences — Parkinson's patients and caregivers (education, helpline-style support, trial recruitment) and academic/industry researchers (PPMI data and biosamples).
how_they_use_agents: Nothing agentic in what they publish externally — the michaeljfox.org and PPMI pages I fetched contain no mention of AI or machine learning in their own operations. Their appearance is as a Guru customer on the getguru.com/solutions/nonprofit logo wall, i.e. internal staff-facing AI knowledge search and 'Knowledge Agents' with automated content verification, integrated with nonprofit CRMs (Salesforce, Bloomerang, Kindful, DonorPerfect). Adjacent but distinct: PPMI's de-identified longitudinal dataset is widely used by external researchers for ML-driven biomarker and progression modeling — that is third parties doing AI on MJFF data, not MJFF running agents.
why_they_need_memory: Strongest structural fit of the three. Large staff plus a very wide volunteer and community-fundraising surface (Team Fox) plus a patient- and caregiver-facing information function where answers touch medication, symptoms and trial eligibility. Anything patient-facing must be medically accurate, consistently worded, and provably current — which maps directly onto Guru's verification-and-expiry workflow rather than onto generic retrieval. Add trial-site coordination across 50 centers in 12 countries and a research-grants operation with its own process knowledge, and you get exactly the fragmented-internal-knowledge profile this category is sold against.

name: ACLU (American Civil Liberties Union)
what_it_does: 106-year-old US civil-liberties advocacy nonprofit. Litigates constitutional-rights cases in courts nationwide, lobbies legislatures, runs grassroots organizing campaigns, and publishes public education material ("Know Your Rights") across ~17 issue areas including free speech, reproductive freedom, immigrant rights, LGBTQ rights, voting access, and privacy/surveillance. Structurally two national entities — American Civil Liberties Union Inc, a 501(c)(4) that can lobby without limit (EIN 13-3871360), and the ACLU Foundation, a 501(c)(3) that takes tax-deductible gifts and does the litigation (EIN 13-6213516) — plus at least one autonomous affiliate in every state, DC, and Puerto Rico, each with its own ED, board, staff and budget. Not a product company; it does not sell software and has no commercial offering.
category: Nonprofit / civil-rights legal advocacy. NOT an AI company, not SaaS, not a startup. Buyer-side only: it appears on Guru's nonprofit logo wall as a knowledge-management customer.
stage: n/a — nonprofit membership organization, no equity, no venture stage
funding: Not venture-funded. Member/donor funded. IRS Form 990 via ProPublica: ACLU Foundation (13-6213516) FY2024 revenue $185.1M, expenses $201.7M, total assets $828.6M; FY2023 revenue $201.2M. ACLU Inc, the c4 (13-3871360), FY2023 revenue $146.7M, expenses $174.5M, assets $181.4M. Wikipedia cites a combined national budget of ~$383M for 2024, excluding the state affiliates' separate budgets. 1.7M members (2024).
headcount_estimate: unknown exact. Wikipedia cites ~500 staff attorneys at the national organization plus several thousand volunteer/cooperating attorneys; total employment across national plus 50+ autonomous state affiliates is plausibly in the low thousands but no verified figure was found (the 990s do not report employee counts and the careers page gives no number).
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: n/a — does not sell a product. Serves members, donors, plaintiffs and the public; a mission organization rather than a commercial vendor. As a software buyer it behaves like a mid-to-large distributed enterprise (300-1000+ seats at national, plus federated affiliates).
how_they_use_agents: No AI agent appears anywhere in ACLU's own work product — the ACLU is on the other side of the AI question publicly, campaigning against facial recognition, automated license plate readers (specifically Flock Safety), and algorithmic surveillance through its Speech, Privacy & Technology work. Agents enter only as a purchased internal tool: the ACLU logo sits on Guru's /solutions/nonprofit page under "Join the thousands of companies that use and love Guru," where Guru markets AI search over Slack/Gmail/Drive and "Knowledge Agents" that read who is asking and why and answer from verified sources. The ACLU does maintain an in-house "Digital, Tech & Analytics" department that builds tech platforms, so there is real technical staff, but no public evidence of ACLU building or deploying agents of its own. There is no ACLU case study on getguru.com/customers — the logo wall is the only evidence of the relationship, and its depth (which teams, how many seats, whether it is current) is unverified.
why_they_need_memory: A federated organization where knowledge is the actual asset and it is scattered by design: 50+ autonomous affiliates each running their own litigation and comms, national departments spanning legal, communications, development, advocacy and operations, and rapid-response campaign work where staff must find precedent, prior filings, messaging guidance and donor context fast. High campaign-cycle turnover means institutional memory walks out the door. Classic "company brain" buyer: not because they build agents, but because their answers live in Slack threads, Google Drive and the heads of long-tenured staff, and the same questions get re-asked across affiliates.
confidence: high on the organization existing and on its financials (IRS filings). Medium-low on the Guru relationship — confirmed only as a logo on Guru's nonprofit solutions page, with no case study, quote, deployment size, or date.

name: DonorsChoose
what_it_does: Nonprofit crowdfunding marketplace for US public-school classrooms. Public school teachers post itemized project requests (books, art supplies, lab equipment, class trips) with line-item budgets; individual donors, corporations and foundations fund them; DonorsChoose vets every request, buys each item itself and ships the materials directly to the school rather than sending cash to teachers. Donors get project photos and teacher letters, and $50+ donors get handwritten student thank-you notes. Also runs matching campaigns, gift cards, account credits, donor-advised-fund and stock giving, and corporate partner programs (iHeartRadio, Panda Cares and similar campaigns appear on their blog). Reports $551 average project cost, 79% of projects fully funded, and projects posted from 86% of US public schools. Publishes open classroom data for developers.
category: Nonprofit edtech / charitable giving marketplace. Two-sided platform (teachers ↔ donors) with a real fulfillment and vetting operation behind it. Not an AI company.
stage: n/a — 501(c)(3) public charity, philanthropically funded, no equity or venture stage
funding: Not venture-funded. Grant- and donation-funded. Wikipedia lists major supporters including the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Google.org, PNC Bank, Staples and Target. IRS Form 990 via ProPublica (EIN 13-4129457): FY2022 revenue $187.3M, expenses $175.6M, total assets $131.3M; FY2021 revenue $158.1M. Wikipedia cites 2023 revenue of $155.7M. Note most of this flow-through revenue is donor money passing to classrooms, not operating budget. Cumulative platform totals on their own site: $314M+ raised from ~1.9M donors across 2M+ funded requests.
headcount_estimate: ~115 employees (Wikipedia). NYC headquarters at 134 W 37th St with remote staff nationwide; team described as including many former teachers.
yc_or_accelerator: none — founded by a teacher in his classroom, not through an accelerator
sells_to: n/a as a vendor. Two-sided nonprofit: serves K-12 public school teachers (supply side, free) and individual donors plus corporate/foundation partners (demand side). Corporate partnership sales motion resembles B2B enterprise; the teacher-facing side resembles prosumer self-serve at very large volume.
how_they_use_agents: No AI agent is visible in the product. Nothing on the homepage, About, Impact or blog mentions AI, ML or automation; the vetting process is described in human terms ("we vet all requests, purchase each item, and ship materials directly") with no technical detail. They do publish open classroom data and cite "DonorsChoose Data" in research posts, so there is analytics capability, but no evidence of agent-building. Agents appear only as a bought internal tool: the DonorsChoose logo is on Guru's /solutions/nonprofit page alongside ACLU and Forum for the Future. No DonorsChoose case study exists on getguru.com/customers, so the deployment is unverified beyond the logo.
why_they_need_memory: The operational profile is a knowledge-heavy support machine: ~115 staff serving millions of teachers and donors, every one of 2M+ project requests screened against eligibility and vetting rules, plus a thick layer of corporate-partner campaign rules (match terms, geographic restrictions, eligible item categories) that change per campaign and per funder. Support and screening staff need one consistent, verified answer to "is this eligible?" and "what does this partner's match cover?" — exactly the repeated-question, policy-drift problem Guru sells against (their FoodCorps case study describes the same pattern at a similarly sized, remote-heavy nonprofit: knowledge scattered across Drive, Box and Slack, same questions re-asked, no way to confirm what is current).
confidence: high on the organization, its scale and its financials (own site, Wikipedia, IRS filings). Medium-low on the Guru relationship — logo wall only. High confidence that they are NOT an AI-native company.

name: Forum for the Future
what_it_does: International sustainability nonprofit and systems-change consultancy. Works in paid and funded partnership with corporations, governments and civil-society organizations to redesign systems rather than run single projects, concentrating on energy, food and agriculture, and business/economic transformation. Runs multi-stakeholder coalitions and futures/scenario work, and reports partnerships with 100+ organizations across business and the public sector. Effectively sells strategic advisory, convening and applied research — a consultancy with a charitable wrapper, not a software product.
category: Nonprofit sustainability consultancy / systems-change advisory. Not AI, not SaaS, not a startup.
stage: n/a — UK registered charity plus a US 501(c)(3) affiliate; no equity, no venture stage
funding: Not venture-funded. Revenue comes from partnership fees, project funding, grants and philanthropy. Wikipedia cites annual turnover of around £5.2M for the UK organization. The US arm, Forum For The Future US Inc (EIN 47-4667055, 521 5th Ave, New York), reports on IRS Form 990: FY2023 revenue $3.78M, expenses $3.16M, assets $1.53M; FY2022 revenue $1.94M; FY2021 revenue $2.10M — roughly doubling revenue between 2022 and 2023.
headcount_estimate: ~66 staff per Wikipedia (UK-centric figure). Adding the US, India and Singapore offices, total is plausibly in the 70-120 range, but no verified consolidated number was found — treat 66 as the only sourced figure and note it may be dated.
yc_or_accelerator: none
founded_year: 1996 (founded by Jonathon Porritt, Sara Parkin and Paul Ekins; Hannah Pathak is CEO, Sally Uren OBE is Executive Director / Chief Acceleration Officer)
sells_to: B2B enterprise plus government and civil society — large corporate sustainability teams, public-sector bodies and foundations buying multi-year partnership and advisory engagements. Small number of high-value relationships rather than volume self-serve.
how_they_use_agents: None in what they deliver. The output is human consulting: workshops, scenarios, coalitions, reports. Their own site could not be fetched during this research (the host returned 403 / an SSL handshake failure to the fetch tool), so I could not check for any AI practice area or published AI-and-sustainability work — that gap is unresolved. Agents appear only as a purchased internal tool: the Forum for the Future logo is on Guru's /solutions/nonprofit page, where Guru pitches AI search across Slack/Gmail and "Knowledge Agents" that answer from verified sources and auto-verify/unverify content. No Forum for the Future case study on getguru.com/customers.
why_they_need_memory: The sharpest fit of the three for a company brain, and for the most ordinary consultancy reason: a small headcount (~66) spread across the UK, US, India and Singapore, working project-by-project with 100+ partner organizations across incompatible time zones. Their sellable asset is reusable IP — frameworks, futures methodology, sector research, prior client context, funder reporting language — and it decays into personal Drive folders and Slack DMs between engagements. Consultants need to find what the firm already knows about a sector or a client before a pitch, and a distributed staff cannot rely on tapping a colleague's shoulder.
confidence: medium. The organization is unambiguously real and the Guru logo is confirmed, but I could not reach their own website (403/SSL failure on both www and apex), so the description of what they do rests on Wikipedia plus IRS filings for the US entity. The 66-staff and £5.2M turnover figures are Wikipedia-sourced, unverified against filings, and possibly stale. Guru relationship confidence is low-medium: logo wall only.

name: SOCAN (Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada)
what_it_does: Canada's largest member-based music rights management organization and performing rights organization (PRO). Licenses the public performance, communication and reproduction of music to businesses, venues, broadcasters and digital services; collects and distributes royalties to songwriters, composers and publishers in Canada and, via reciprocal agreements with foreign PROs, worldwide. Confirmed scale: 'more than 185,000' Canadian member creators/publishers (homepage), representation of ~4 million creators and publishers globally, a record $512M in royalties distributed in 2024, and self-described administration of ~170 billion individual performances per year. Runs subsidiaries/divisions: SOCAN Foundation, Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame, and Entandem (a joint licensing venture with Re:Sound). Has consolidated the Canadian rights market by acquisition: MediaNet Digital (2016), Audiam (2016), SODRAC (2018), and CMRRA (announced complete on the current site). CEO Jennifer Brown; President/board chair Marc Ouellette. HQ Toronto, with offices in Vancouver, Montreal, Nashville and Los Angeles. Also runs a developer portal at developer.socan.ca.
category: Music rights management / performing rights organization — non-profit. For Guru's segmentation, it sits in the 'nonprofit' vertical, not tech.
stage: Not applicable — non-profit member organization, no venture stage. Established 1990 by merger of CAPAC and PROCAN.
funding: None (no venture funding). Self-funded via licence fees and administrative deductions from royalty flows. The relevant financial figure is throughput, not capital: $512M distributed in royalties in 2024.
headcount_estimate: ~250-500. LinkedIn shows the 201-500 band with roughly 436 associated profiles; SOCAN's own LinkedIn copy references 'over 250' people. Spread across five offices (Toronto HQ, Vancouver, Montreal, Nashville, LA). Not independently audited.
yc_or_accelerator: None. SOCAN itself runs a program called the Canadian Creative Accelerator Music Program for member creators — it is an accelerator operator, not an alumnus.
sells_to: Two-sided and neither is classic B2B SaaS: it licenses B2B (businesses, venues, broadcasters, streaming services, from SMB bars to enterprise DSPs) and it serves 185,000+ individual creator/publisher members who are effectively its constituency rather than its customers.
how_they_use_agents: No evidence SOCAN builds or ships AI agents — there is nothing agentic in its product and no AI feature marketing. It appears only as a logo on Guru's /solutions/nonprofit wall (confirmed present, alongside ACLU, GiveDirectly, DonorsChoose, Michael J. Fox Foundation, Forum for the Future, Give Me Tap). So the 'agent' in play is Guru's own Knowledge Agent deployed internally: staff in member services, licensing and distribution asking natural-language questions and getting sourced answers from verified internal cards, surfaced in Slack/Teams/Gmail. Notably, SOCAN's public posture toward generative AI is adversarial: on 2026-09-02 it filed suit against Suno Inc., alleging training without consent on virtually all readily-accessible online music and citing 150 Suno outputs matching its repertoire (Tom Cochrane, Avril Lavigne, Alexisonfire, K. Maro, Daniel Balavoine). It advocates 'ART principles' (Authorization, Remuneration, Transparency) and opposes new text-and-data-mining exceptions. This is a buyer that will be sensitive to how a memory vendor trains on and retains its data.
why_they_need_memory: Textbook institutional-knowledge problem. Its operating rules are dense and externally mandated — tariff schedules, Copyright Board rulings, distribution rules, reciprocal agreements with dozens of foreign PROs — and must be answered consistently in English and French across five offices for 185,000+ members. Four acquisitions (MediaNet, Audiam, SODRAC, CMRRA) merged four sets of process knowledge, systems and legacy answers into one org, which is exactly the state that produces contradictory internal documentation. Long-tenure staff at a 36-year-old non-profit means much of the operating knowledge is in people's heads and walks out at retirement. Guru's nonprofit pitch (find donor details, grant deadlines and compliance requirements instantly; retain institutional knowledge despite staff transitions) maps directly.

name: Glossier
what_it_does: Beauty and personal care brand, spun out of Emily Weiss's Into The Gloss blog in 2014 on a 'Skin First. Makeup Second.' positioning. Sells skincare, makeup, body care, fragrance (Glossier You), the Balm Dotcom line and branded merch. Originally a pure DTC e-commerce brand with experiential retail stores; has since shifted to a hybrid wholesale model, distributing through Sephora, Space NK and Mecca alongside glossier.com. Retail footprint is contracting: per Wikipedia, of twelve stores it is closing nine over roughly two and a half years, retaining New York, Los Angeles and London. Colin Walsh is CEO (sources disagree on start date — LinkedIn says October 2023, Wikipedia says October 2025 — treat the date as unconfirmed); Emily Weiss is executive chairwoman. HQ 233 Spring Street, New York. Discontinued experiments include Glossier Play (2019-2020) and GlossiWEAR apparel. Partnerships with the WNBA (2020) and USA Basketball (2024).
category: DTC / omnichannel beauty and consumer retail. Guru's 'retail' vertical.
stage: Late-stage private, venture-backed, post-peak. Raised through at least Series D/E, then contracted: layoffs in 2020, 2022 and again in February 2026, plus a large store-closure program. Not a growth-stage buyer — a cost-conscious one.
funding: Confirmed from Wikipedia: $2M seed from Forerunner Ventures; $24M Series B (December 2016); an additional ~$150M raised across 2018-2019, valuing the company at $1.2B. That gives a confirmed floor of roughly $176M. Widely reported but NOT independently confirmed in this research pass: a $100M Series D in 2019 (Sequoia) inside that $150M, and an $80M Series E in July 2021 led by Lone Pine Capital at a $1.8B valuation, bringing the commonly cited total to ~$266M. Treat anything above ~$176M as unverified here. Revenue is not publicly disclosed.
headcount_estimate: ~300-460. LinkedIn shows the 201-500 band with about 459 associated profiles. Wikipedia records a February 2026 layoff of approximately 54 employees described as roughly one-third of the (corporate) workforce, which conflicts with the LinkedIn count — the LinkedIn figure likely includes retail staff and stale profiles. Corporate HQ headcount is probably closer to 150-250; total including stores nearer 400.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Traditional VC path (Forerunner Ventures seed; later rounds reported to include Index, IVP and Sequoia).
sells_to: Consumers (B2C). DTC via glossier.com plus its own stores, plus wholesale through Sephora, Space NK and Mecca. It has no B2B product, so any agent/memory purchase is purely an internal-operations spend, not something embedded in what it sells.
how_they_use_agents: No AI anywhere in the product — the homepage contains zero mention of AI, chatbots or automation. Glossier appears strictly as a logo on Guru's /solutions/retail wall (confirmed present, alongside Brooklinen, Hatch, Etsy, The Farmers Dog, Minted and Vuori); there is no Glossier case study on Guru's /customers page. The agent is therefore Guru's Knowledge Agent used internally: Guru pitches this vertical as 'in-the-moment retail insights powered by enterprise AI search' for e-commerce merchandisers, store operations managers, customer support and inventory teams, with agents that 'understand who's asking and why,' auto-verify content, and fire knowledge triggers — surfaced in Slack/Teams/Gmail and wired to Shopify/Square. Glossier is a consumer of someone else's agent, not a builder of one.
why_they_need_memory: Frontline retail is the use case. Store associates (historically high-churn, seasonally staffed) and CX agents need one authoritative answer on shade matching, ingredients and allergens, promo mechanics (the site was running a 30%-off Labor Day sale with a gift-with-purchase during this research), returns, and international shipping across many currencies. The launch cadence of a beauty brand means product facts change constantly and go stale fast — precisely what Guru's verification/expiry model targets. The channel shift compounds it: the same product and policy facts must now stay consistent across glossier.com, three remaining owned stores, and Sephora/Space NK/Mecca wholesale partners. And after repeated layoffs (2020, 2022, February 2026), a shrinking team is holding the same operational surface area — the classic 'we lost the people who knew this' trigger for buying a company brain.

name: Hatch (Hatch Baby, Inc.)
what_it_does: Smart sleep company selling connected hardware plus a paid content subscription. Confirmed product lines: Hatch Baby (Rest, Rest+, Rest Go — sound machine, night light and 'time to rise' clock for infants and children), Restore 3 (a phone-free adult smart sleep clock with sunrise alarm and wind-down routines), Hatch Sleep Clock (a contactless nightstand sleep tracker that requires no wearable), plus Hatch Go, accessories and a refurbished line. Software side: the Hatch Sleep App (iOS/Android) and a Hatch+ subscription (free trial offered) carrying original audio — sound baths, meditations, sleep music, audiobooks and 'The Nightly,' a call-in podcast hosted by Matt Bragg, Josh Gondelman and Greta Johnsen. Positioning is 'the power of a good bedtime routine' rather than sleep-score optimization. Claims to have helped over half a million families sleep better; the Google Play listing cites 4 million+ people. Founded by Ann Crady Weiss (CEO) and Dave Weiss, who met at BabyCenter where she was SVP of consumer experience; the company got its visibility break on Shark Tank in 2016. Legal entity is Hatch Baby, Inc. HQ Menlo Park, CA, with a heavily distributed workforce (hires across 30+ US states and BC/ON/SK in Canada). Great Place to Work certified 2024. NOTE ON AMBIGUITY: hatch.co is distinct from Hatch Ltd (hatch.com, the global engineering and consulting firm) and from several unrelated startups named Hatch. The identification is solid — Guru's retail logo wall places 'Hatch' among DTC consumer brands (Glossier, Brooklinen, Etsy, The Farmers Dog, Minted, Vuori), and the brief supplied hatch.co directly.
category: Consumer sleep hardware (IoT) plus subscription content. DTC/retail — Guru's 'retail' vertical.
stage: Private and venture-backed; exact stage unconfirmed. Confirmed only that Hatch is a current True Ventures portfolio company ('Smart sleep devices helping people build healthy sleep habits,' categorized as consumer hardware). Maturity signals point to growth stage or later: 12 years old, ~260 employees, multiple product generations, retail distribution, equity offered to all full-time staff.
funding: Unknown. No round amounts, dates or totals could be confirmed. Crunchbase returned HTTP 403; an SEC EDGAR company search for 'Hatch Baby' Form D filings returned no matching companies; news searches surfaced nothing on funding. The only confirmed investor is True Ventures (current portfolio listing). Do not attribute a raise figure to this company without a primary source.
headcount_estimate: ~200-300. LinkedIn shows about 259 associated profiles; LinkedIn's self-reported band says 51-200, which appears to understate the current size. Distributed across 30+ US states and 3 Canadian provinces with a Menlo Park HQ.
yc_or_accelerator: None found. Appeared on Shark Tank in 2016, which is media exposure, not an accelerator.
founded_year: 2014 (per LinkedIn). The company's own about-us page frames 2016 — the Shark Tank appearance — as the launch moment, so both years appear in sources.
sells_to: Consumers (B2C), DTC through hatch.co and through retail channels, with a subscription attach (Hatch+). Two distinct buyer personas — parents of infants/toddlers, and adults buying for their own sleep — which effectively doubles the support knowledge base.
how_they_use_agents: No AI in the product and no AI language on the site. The Sleep Clock does contactless sleep sensing and the company references learning sleep patterns and 'personalized recommendations,' but Hatch never attributes any of it to AI or ML — a deliberate-looking positioning choice for a bedroom device where sensing and privacy are sensitive. Current open roles (Staff Backend Engineer, Senior Embedded Systems Engineer, Staff Mobile Engineer, Director of Growth Strategy) include no AI/ML positions. Hatch appears only as a logo on Guru's /solutions/retail wall, with no case study on Guru's /customers page. The agent is Guru's Knowledge Agent used internally — near-certainly for customer support and store/retail-partner enablement given the hardware troubleshooting load.
why_they_need_memory: Connected hardware generates the densest support knowledge base of the three. Support agents must hold: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth pairing across at least six device SKUs and multiple hardware generations (Rest, Rest+, Rest Go, Restore, Restore 3, Sleep Clock), firmware versions and their known issues, app-to-device compatibility matrices, warranty and returns including a refurbished line, Truemed/HSA-FSA eligibility, and separate Hatch+ subscription billing and cancellation flows. Two customer segments each need different tone and troubleshooting. The workforce is fully distributed across 30+ states, so there is no hallway to overhear the answer in — documented, retrievable knowledge is the only channel. And demand is seasonal: baby gifting drives Q4 and new-parent spikes that require ramping temporary support staff fast. That combination — high SKU complexity, remote team, seasonal surge hiring — is the exact shape of company that buys a knowledge/agent-memory layer.

name: Avis (Avis Budget Group)
what_it_does: Avis is the flagship car-rental brand of Avis Budget Group (Nasdaq: CAR), a Parsippany, NJ vehicle rental and mobility holding company. It rents cars, SUVs, vans, EVs/hybrids and luxury vehicles to leisure travelers, corporate travel accounts, government and group/meeting customers, with one-way, long-term and business-account programs, plus protections/insurance add-ons, roadside assistance and the Avis Preferred loyalty program (skip-the-counter, points, upgrades). The parent group runs ~10,250 rental locations across 180+ countries under Avis, Budget, Budget Truck, Payless, Zipcar, Flexcar, Apex and Maggiore. FY2025 revenue $11.65B (down ~1.2% YoY); TTM revenue ~$11.71B; net loss of $889M in 2025 (improved from a $1.82B loss in 2024); market cap ~$4.9B as of Sept 2026. This is emphatically not a startup — it is a capital-intensive, low-margin, currently unprofitable legacy transportation incumbent.

stage: Public company, Nasdaq: CAR
funding: n/a — publicly traded, not venture-funded. Market cap ~$4.9B (Sept 2026); FY2025 revenue $11.65B; FY2025 net loss -$889M
headcount_estimate: ~24,500-25,000 employees globally (company site says ~24,500; market data sources say ~25,000)
yc_or_accelerator: none
founded_year: 1946 (Avis brand); the Avis Budget Group holding company took its current form in 2006
sells_to: B2C (leisure renters) plus B2B enterprise and SMB corporate travel accounts, government, and group/meeting bookings

yc_or_accelerator: None found. No YC or accelerator affiliation surfaced in any source; funded through conventional venture rounds from 2017 onward.
founded_year: 2014 (PitchBook); launched to customers July 2016. Founded by Jonathan Regev and Brett Podolsky - the careers page describes them as 'two dog dads' frustrated by the gap between how pet food is marketed and how it is made.
sells_to: B2C consumer subscription (dog owners), with an important professional influence channel: veterinarians and vet techs who recommend the product, served through a dedicated Vet Team Portal. No enterprise or developer sales motion.
how_they_use_agents: Buyer, and notably more human-agent-heavy than AI-agent-heavy. It runs a large in-house Customer Experience organization - an SVP of Customer Experience (Pete Boudreaux), 24/7 support, and a dedicated CX Quality Assurance program - and appears on Guru's retail logo wall, using Guru's Knowledge Agents as the internal answer layer for that team. Its other named vendors are contact-center and outreach tooling rather than autonomous AI: UJET (a case study credits it with a 50% improvement in first-call resolution) and Regal, whose case study is explicit that HUMAN agents make the personalized outbound calls and texts (57% lift in conversion, 32% answer rate, 15% lift in month-one retention, quoted by Product Manager Manuj Goyal). I found no public evidence as of Sept 2026 of The Farmer's Dog deploying a customer-facing autonomous AI agent. So the 'agent' Guru serves here is primarily a human CX rep being fed verified knowledge.
why_they_need_memory: The whole product is per-dog state, which is the hardest thing for a stateless support system to handle. Every subscriber has a distinct plan keyed to their individual dog - breed, weight, weight-loss or gain goal, allergies, recipe mix, transition schedule from kibble, and a delivery cadence tied to freezer space and consumption rate. Common contacts ('my dog won't eat it', 'my box came early', 'can I change the recipe', 'my dog's vet wants a different calorie target') are unanswerable without the dog's history, not just the order record. Layer on: (1) a 24/7 CX org spread across NYC, Nashville and Boca Raton plus outsourced partners, all of whom must give the same answer; (2) nutrition and health claims where a wrong answer carries animal-health and AAFCO/regulatory exposure, so knowledge must be verified and current rather than merely retrieved; (3) an expanding SKU set (Fresh, the new shelf-stable Instant Fresh, treats) that resets what reps need to know; and (4) a vet channel with its own separate body of clinical knowledge. That combination - long-lived per-customer context plus a distributed frontline team needing one verified source - is precisely the company-brain/agent-memory pitch.

name: Vuori

Business model is omnichannel: DTC e-commerce, a large and growing fleet of owned retail stores (Wikipedia cites ~40 US stores plus international locations including London; other trackers cite more), and wholesale through Nordstrom, REI and Equinox. Customer-facing policy centerpiece is the 'Investment in Happiness' guarantee (free returns / love-it-or-send-it-back), which the brand also frames internally as its approach to employees and community. International expansion began 2022 into the UK, France, Germany, Ireland, Netherlands, Australia and Canada. HQ Carlsbad, CA.
category: DTC + brick-and-mortar retail apparel / athleisure (retail, not AI)
stage: Late-stage private and profitable (reached profitability in 2017); frequently discussed as an IPO candidate but still private. Founder Joe Kudla remains CEO and majority owner.
funding: ~$1.27B total per Tracxn, but note that the largest tranche was a secondary tender rather than primary capital. Documented: $45M (2019, Norwest Venture Partners); $400M (Oct 2021, SoftBank Vision Fund 2); $825M (Nov 2024, secondary tender led by General Atlantic and Stripes) at a ~$5.5B valuation, which remains the latest known mark. headcount_estimate: ~2,500-2,570. Revelio Labs reports 2,527 in 2026 (up from 2,365 in 2025 and 1,768 in 2023); PitchBook lists 2,570. TrueUp's 1,300 figure appears to lag. The majority of this headcount is retail store staff rather than corporate.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Bootstrapped-then-VC path: Kudla self-funded early, the company was profitable by 2017, and its first institutional round was Norwest in 2019. No accelerator affiliation.
founded_year: 2015, by Joe Kudla in Encinitas, California (the name means 'mountain' in Finnish)
sells_to: B2C consumers through e-commerce and its own stores, plus B2B wholesale accounts (Nordstrom, REI, Equinox).
how_they_use_agents: Buyer only, and the weakest agent story of the three. Vuori appears on Guru's retail solutions logo wall as a knowledge-management customer, which in Guru's retail framing means its 'Knowledge Agents' surface product, policy and promo information to store associates and CX teams (Guru advertises retail integrations with Shopify, Square, Toast and Erply). I could find no public evidence - no case study, no press, no product surface on vuoriclothing.com - that Vuori has built or deployed a customer-facing AI agent, and targeted searches for Vuori AI agent deployments returned only unrelated results. The relevant 'agent' at Vuori is the human retail associate on a store floor, with AI search behind them. Treat any claim that Vuori runs autonomous agents as unsupported.
why_they_need_memory: Vuori's need is the classic distributed-frontline knowledge problem rather than a stateful-customer-context problem. ~2,500 employees, most of them store associates spread across dozens of US and international locations, with the turnover and seasonal hiring typical of retail floors - every new hire needs to be productive fast. The assortment turns over every season and is built on proprietary fabric technologies (AllTheForm, FormRefined, the Sunday and Restore collections) that associates are expected to explain accurately to justify a premium price point. Operating across the US, UK, EU, Australia and Canada plus wholesale partners means region- and channel-specific policies on returns, pricing and promotions, and the 'Investment in Happiness' free-return guarantee makes policy accuracy a direct margin question. So the buying trigger is: one verified, always-current answer delivered to store floor, e-commerce CX and wholesale teams at once - which is why Guru's 'verify and unverify info for you' and 'knowledge triggers' framing targets exactly this profile. Per-customer long-term memory is a much weaker driver here than for Minted or The Farmer's Dog.

name: Community Phone
what_it_does: Landline-replacement phone service: a base station that plugs into a wall and connects over cellular networks (no internet, no VoIP), with a 26-hour backup battery, number porting from copper lines, spam/scam-call blocking, and a cloud dashboard + mobile app. Two customer bases: (1) residential, heavily skewed to seniors and the adult children buying for them — plans from ~$45/mo, plus an $89/mo 'monitoring and safety' tier that adds scheduled automated wellness check-in calls, a caregiver portal with real-time call logs, safelist management and missed-check-in alerts; (2) small businesses that need a real business line but do not run a call center — shared business number, call routing/rollover, greetings/IVR, two-way SMS, voicemail transcription, missed-call auto-reply, multi-location. Claims 99.9% reliability, all 50 states, and 25,000-30,000+ paying customers. Its careers page frames the mission as modernizing telecom for small businesses and 'communities across America'; its YC listing now frames it as 'the peace-of-mind layer for aging in America.'
category: Consumer + SMB telecom (wireless landline replacement / cloud phone system); aging-in-place adjacent. Not an AI company.
stage: Seed-stage on paper (YC W19) but effectively revenue-financed at scale — YC profile claims eight-figure ARR heading to nine figures; careers page claims healthy cash flow and financial stability. No priced Series A/B has been publicly reported.
funding: Unknown / largely undisclosed. Investors named by the company: Y Combinator, the YC Continuity Fund, and SNR.vc. Third-party trackers only capture a tiny disclosed amount and disagree: Tracxn reports $150K in 1 round from Y Combinator (Mar 2019); LeadIQ reports $250K total as of Jul 2026. No credible reported round size beyond the YC seed — do not treat $150K-$250K as their true total capitalization, it is simply all that has been disclosed.
headcount_estimate: ~100-200. Y Combinator's directory lists 101 (2026). Third-party aggregators disagree widely: RocketReach 140-193, LeadIQ 201-500, SignalHire 51, Seamless 11-50. 100% remote, globally distributed team spanning sales, engineering, support, marketing and ops.
yc_or_accelerator: Y Combinator, Winter 2019 batch (listed as 'Community Phone Company'); later backed by the YC Continuity Fund.
sells_to: Mixed B2C and B2B SMB. Consumer: seniors aging in place and their family caregivers. Business: very small businesses (single- and multi-location) that want a business line without a contact center. Not enterprise, not developers.
how_they_use_agents: Two layers. (1) Internal — they are on Guru's 'trusted by thousands' logo wall for utilities/telecom, i.e. Guru is the knowledge layer / knowledge agent for their distributed remote support and sales org (their pitch is 'reach real humans in less than 2 minutes,' so human agents answering fast is the core promise Guru underwrites). (2) Product — the YC listing states 'our AI-powered check-in calls surface how seniors are really doing,' and the company says it uses 'AI to protect customers and reimagine connectivity' and to prevent phone scams. On the public marketing site those same features are described as 'automated' rather than AI: scheduled automated check-in calls with button confirmation, automatic blocking of known fraudulent numbers, voicemail transcription, missed-call auto-reply. No AI receptionist / voice-agent answering product is marketed today, though PitchBook's description mentions 'automated answering tools.'
why_they_need_memory: Their differentiator is human support speed at consumer price points, delivered by a 100% remote, globally distributed CS team — that only works if answers are consistent and instantly retrievable. The knowledge surface is unusually messy: per-state and per-carrier porting rules from copper decommissioning, hardware/base-station troubleshooting, coverage checks, plan and device SKUs, senior-specific handling, and small-business routing configs. Add high-empathy elderly customers where a wrong answer causes churn, and rapid hiring into support. If they push the AI check-in calls further, they also need per-customer longitudinal context (what the senior said last week, what the caregiver already knows) — which is agent memory rather than static knowledge.
confidence: high on existence and product; medium on headcount; low-to-medium on funding (only YC seed is disclosed and aggregators conflict)

name: Essent
what_it_does: Essent N.V. is the largest energy retailer in the Netherlands — electricity, gas, heat and energy services to residential and business customers in NL and Belgium (also operates the energiedirect.nl brand). Headquartered in 's-Hertogenbosch, founded 1999 from the merger of PNEM/MEGA Groep and EDON Groep; owned by RWE (2009-2016), then innogy, and since 2019/2020 a subsidiary of German utility E.ON. Roughly 2.3-2.5 million electricity customers and ~2 million gas customers. This is a large incumbent utility, not a startup. Note: distinct from Essent Group Ltd (NYSE: ESNT), the US mortgage-insurance company — the Guru logo wall is on a utilities/telecom page and Essent's own engineering blog confirms Guru usage, so the Dutch utility is the right match.
category: Retail energy utility (B2C + B2B), enterprise-scale incumbent. Not AI-native, but an aggressive agentic-AI adopter in customer operations.
stage: Not venture-backed — wholly owned subsidiary of E.ON SE (public, ~79-80k employees group-wide).
funding: N/A — corporate subsidiary of E.ON, no venture funding. Revenue was ~EUR 6.3B (2013, last figure surfaced); current figures not confirmed.
headcount_estimate: ~3,100 employees at Essent N.V. (Revelio Labs, March 2026), ~94% in Western Europe. Other aggregators put it near 2,600 (EasyLeadz, Feb 2025). Customer-service org specifically: 700+ agents. (The 20,000 figure in older Wikipedia text refers to the pre-breakup 2007 Essent group and is not current.)
yc_or_accelerator: None
sells_to: B2C households and B2B/commercial customers in the Netherlands and Belgium. Buyer for this software category is internal: customer-operations / customer-service leadership and their IT team.
how_they_use_agents: The clearest, best-documented agent-memory use case of the three. Essent built 'Bolt,' an award-winning agent-assist bot living in Microsoft Teams, serving 700+ customer service agents. Architecture explicitly stated by Essent's own IT blog: Guru is the internal knowledge base / source of truth; an AWS pipeline (Lambda, Step Functions, API Gateway, S3) syncs Guru content daily into S3 and transforms it into Cognigy's Knowledge Store format; Cognigy AI provides the conversational RAG layer that answers agents' natural-language questions with answers, summaries and links. Reported impact: 85% of helpdesk tasks automated, >1 minute cut from average handling time, ~20,800 additional successful interactions per year, and ~EUR 1.8M annual cost savings, plus faster agent onboarding. Customer-facing side: chatbot 'Robin' serves Essent and energiedirect.nl 24/7 across four channels (CogX award winner), and a 2026 talk describes Essent automating over 55% of all customer chats with agentic AI at 2.5M-customer scale.
why_they_need_memory: They are the canonical buyer: 1,100+ knowledge articles that change constantly (tariffs, contract terms, regulatory changes, seasonal billing and outage procedures), 700+ agents who previously wasted handle time searching or escalating to a helpdesk, and now two consumers of the same knowledge — the internal agent-assist bot and the customer-facing bot. Without a governed, continuously synced knowledge layer, the RAG bots drift out of date and give customers wrong regulated information. Their own architecture treats the 'company brain' as a separate product tier (Guru) from the conversational layer (Cognigy), with a daily freshness pipeline in between — exactly the problem an agent-memory vendor sells into.

Named investors: Bonfire Ventures, Crosscut Ventures, Double M Partners, BAM Ventures (12 investors total per PitchBook). yc_or_accelerator: None
founded_year: 2014 (founded by Patrick Maloney)
sells_to: B2C — US residential electricity customers ('members') in deregulated retail energy markets. Software buyer is internal member-care/customer-support operations.
how_they_use_agents: No public evidence of AI agents in the customer-facing product — the offering is an energy plan, not software, and the site makes no AI claims. The only confirmed signal is internal: Inspire appears on Guru's utilities/telecom logo wall, i.e. Guru serves as the knowledge layer / AI answer surface for its member-support organization (support runs a toll-free care line plus an online Answer Center). This is a knowledge-management-for-support buyer rather than an agent-building company; treat any stronger claim about agentic deployment as unverified.
why_they_need_memory: Retail energy support is a knowledge nightmare that changes weekly: plan terms, variable vs fixed rates, and enrollment/cancellation rules differ per state and per host utility across nine jurisdictions plus DC, with regulator-mandated disclosure language and rate lookups that must be answered correctly. Add seasonal billing-spike surges that push volume into contract/BPO agents, high consumer-complaint sensitivity in retail energy, and now a post-acquisition merge of Inspire's and Rhythm Energy's knowledge bases and support teams. That combination — regulated, per-jurisdiction, fast-changing answers delivered by a churning support workforce — is what drives a company brain purchase.
confidence: medium — existence, product, founding, and both acquisitions are confirmed; funding totals conflict between sources, headcount is a single third-party estimate that predates integration, and their use of AI agents is inferred from the Guru logo wall rather than a case study

name: ArchiTxt (architxt)
what_it_does: NOT A COMPANY. architxt is a solo-maintained open-source GitHub repository (garethjcooper/architxt, Apache-2.0), self-described as 'a document processing pipeline and web UI that ingests documents — extracts structured content via an LLM-augmented pipeline (Docling, denoising, vision analysis, entity detection) — and produces clean, versioned, entity-tagged knowledge.' PDF is the preferred input; DOCX/XLSX/PPTX are supported but 'have received minimal testing.' It is a self-hosted Node.js 22 app requiring the user to supply their own LLM provider (Ollama local/cloud, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or Anthropic). Its organizing concept is the 'Temporal Mosaic': the best-known state of a system is a composite of the freshest knowledge per scope rather than any single document. Repo metrics as of research: 4 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor (garethjcooper) with 22 commits, created 2026-06-11, last push 2026-07-31, no homepage URL set, no license-holder entity, no company org. There is NO product website, no pricing, no legal entity, and no evidence of commercialization. Note: a DIFFERENT project, Neplex/ArchiTXT (an academic Python library by Nicolas Hiot, Research Engineer at Universite d'Orleans, GPL-3.0, 5 stars, created 2024), shares the name but is unrelated — the Hindsight post refers to the Gareth Cooper repo, which explicitly links to Hindsight in its README.
category: Open-source document-processing / knowledge-extraction tooling (individual developer side project, not a vendor)
stage: Not a company — personal open-source side project. Its author's GitHub profile self-reports employment at 'Spark NZ' (Spark New Zealand, the telecom), located Wellington, New Zealand, with only 1 public repo total.
funding: unknown — no company exists, no funding raised or sought
headcount_estimate: 1 (single GitHub contributor; effectively one person's side project)

sells_to: Nobody — it is not sold. Free, self-hosted open source aimed at developers/knowledge-management practitioners who run it locally with their own LLM keys.
how_they_use_agents: LLM calls are the core of the pipeline rather than a bolt-on: an LLM-augmented extraction chain (Docling parsing, denoising, vision analysis, entity detection) turns documents into entity-tagged structured knowledge. Its distinctive agent construct is 'mental models' — reusable LLM prompts that analyze an entity from a specific angle, which are re-run automatically against the Hindsight memory bank as new documents are ingested. Results can be human-reviewed and edited before being pushed to Hindsight.
why_they_need_memory: Hindsight is used as the persistence and reasoning substrate, not as chat memory: extracted facts are stored as timestamped, source-referenced observations so the system can do cross-document reasoning and enterprise-scale semantic search. The Temporal Mosaic idea specifically needs time-aware memory to know which fact is freshest per scope when documents contradict each other across time; incremental re-ingestion means facts are retained and mental models re-run without reprocessing the corpus.

Architecturally the founder runs a SELF-HOSTED Hindsight deployment (chosen explicitly for compliance reasons in a regulated industry) using a single memory bank with two tag layers — a 'shared' tag for company-wide/institutional knowledge and 'user:<id>' tags for per-user isolation — queried with tagsMatch: 'any_strict' so a single retrieval surfaces both the user's own history and shared knowledge. Separately, a git hook scans the codebase and retains architectural decisions, code patterns and function behaviors under the 'shared' tag, so the coding agents inherit institutional engineering context. why_they_need_memory: The founder's core claim is that memory was a day-one architectural requirement, not a later feature: 'Memory was not something I could add later; it had to be part of the design from the beginning.' The product's differentiation depends on accumulating months of context about each user's preferences and portfolio, so an assistant starting from scratch each session would be materially worse. Multi-tenancy is the hard part — per-user isolation with shared institutional knowledge on top — and self-hosting was required because a regulated financial product could not send portfolio data and conversation history to a third-party managed memory service.

name: AI Data Technician
what_it_does: NOT A COMPANY — an individual academic project by Yuan Sui, whose GitHub bio reads 'PhD @ Caltech'. AI Data Technician is an agentic system for scientists working with high-dimensional, high-sample-rate time series (multi-channel neural recordings at 1-2 kHz, wearable sensor streams, industrial vibration data). It converts raw signals into intermediate representations LLMs can reason over (spectrograms, PSD plots, statistical features), then uses interactive human-AI collaboration to formalize expert judgment into interpretable detection rules for artifact rejection, event marking and signal classification. Architecture: three agents — Orchestrator (Claude Sonnet with a 4,000-token extended-thinking budget, up to 25 tool-use iterations), Task agent (autonomous multi-step execution with bash/read/write/vision, 15 iterations), and Think agent (memory extraction, context compaction, session reflection). Tools include bash, read (PDF + MATLAB .mat v4-v7.3), write, vision (Gemini Flash), plot (Plotly + matplotlib), recall, remember, task, ask and todo, over a pre-installed scientific stack (NumPy, SciPy, MNE, antropy, ruptures, h5py, scikit-learn). Real-time WebSocket browser UI with streaming chat, live activity panel, interactive plots and a todo tracker. GitHub: 6 stars, 2 forks, repo created 2026-03-15, last push 2026-03-19, sole contributor. Demo at yue-crew-projects.org is gated behind Cloudflare Access (approval required). No company name, team page, pricing, website or legal entity exists.

how_they_use_agents: Agents are the entire product: a three-agent loop where the Orchestrator plans with extended thinking and delegates, the Task agent autonomously executes multi-step analysis (loading files, computing features, generating and testing code), and the Think agent manages knowledge. Agents call vision models on generated plots to describe and compare signal images, and pause to ask the scientist clarifying questions via a browser modal when genuinely blocked.
why_they_need_memory: Deep, well-specified dependency — arguably the most sophisticated memory design of the three. Three-layer architecture: Session (per-conversation turn/tool logs, plus raw chat turns pushed to EverMemOS via store_chat_turn() for passive fact extraction), Project (project_memory.md rewritten by the Think agent every 5 messages and injected into the system prompt each turn; in EverMemOS stored under a project-scoped group_id hashed from the project path, classified as episodic_memory vs profile and keyword-indexed for semantic retrieval), and Global (cross-project procedures and user preferences under group_id 'adt_global', populated by end-of-session reflection). The 'remember' tool writes to file and EverMemOS simultaneously in hybrid mode; 'recall' does keyword + semantic search across project and global layers then synthesizes via the Think agent. Deployment is either self-hosted Docker (ghcr.io/.../evermemos:latest) or the managed cloud service at api.evermind.ai. The stated rationale: no universal thresholds exist in signal analysis, so learned parameters, artifact signatures and labeling procedures must persist and compound across sessions.

Buying rather than building was the shortcut for a solo maker: he got per-user multi-tenant memory isolation without building a memory stack. Only verified datapoint: 82 employees as of March 2024, with a stated plan to double by end of that year. Given 7 offices and an $11B valuation the real figure is certainly far higher, but I could not confirm it — do not use a number.
yc_or_accelerator: Not YC and not an accelerator company, but seeded by the OpenAI Startup Fund (Nov 2022), which is the closest analogue.
sells_to: B2B enterprise — large law firms (AmLaw 100 / Magic Circle), in-house legal departments at global corporates, and Big Four / professional-services firms. High-ACV, security- and confidentiality-sensitive buyers.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the core product: purpose-built legal agents that run complex matter work end to end against a firm's own document corpus in Vault, plus contract review/negotiation agents and workflow agents. This is customer-facing product, not internal ops. Because the agents operate over a firm's private precedent and matter files, the quality ceiling is set by how well the agent knows that specific firm.
why_they_need_memory: Harvey's own framing is turning 'unstructured context into compounding agentic knowledge bases.' Cofounder/President Gabe Pereyra in Engram's launch PR: 'We're working with Engram to build learned enterprise memories that are secure, cost-efficient, and turn unstructured context into compounding agentic knowledge bases.' The joint benchmark is the concrete evidence: Engram's 17 Aug 2026 research post 'Understanding a Law Firm through Study,' bylined 'Engram, in partnership with Harvey,' builds an agent for a synthetic firm (Calderwood & Harkness — 100M tokens, 266 matters, 9,286 files) and reports $0.13/30% all-pass versus $1.32/25% for Opus 4.8 — a ~10x cost reduction with better accuracy. So the driver is: firm corpora are far too large to re-retrieve per query, and cost-per-matter is the binding constraint. STRONGEST EVIDENCE OF THE THREE — claimed by both sides: Harvey's own post-training blog says it 'partnered with Engram to train a Qwen3.8-27B model that encodes the firm's knowledge into parametric memory and structured text notes,' thanks Engram in acknowledgements, and links Engram's post; Harvey's LAB post credits five named Engram staff (Dan Biderman, Jessy Lin, Mayee Chen, Neel Guha, Shizhe He). I independently confirmed harvey.ai/blog/author/engram exists as a live author page on Harvey's own site with a post 'LAB: Law Firm Knowledge' (7 Aug 2026), describing Engram as 'an AI research company building models that learn from the people and organizations that use them.' CAVEAT: this is a research collaboration and open-source benchmark co-development, not a disclosed paid production deployment.
confidence: high — company, product, funding history and the Engram collaboration are all independently corroborated on both vendor and customer sites. Headcount is the only genuinely unknown field.

name: Kiteworks (formerly Accellion, Inc.)
what_it_does: Governance and security control plane for sensitive data exchange — marketed as the 'Private Data Network' / 'Zero Trust Data Exchange in One Platform,' with the tagline 'Control, Protect & Track Every Data Workflow.' It is a single-tenant-by-design virtual appliance that puts one compliance and audit layer across every channel sensitive content moves through: secure email, secure file sharing, managed file transfer (MFT), SFTP servers, web forms, APIs — and, notably, an MCP server for AI agent data access. Four stated foundational controls: authenticated identity (SAML, MFA, certificates, scoped delegation tokens), policy-enforced access (ABAC/RBAC), encrypted handling (TLS 1.3, AES-256, FIPS 140-3 validated), and immutable SIEM-integrated audit trails. FedRAMP Authorized and IRAP-assessed to PROTECTED. Claims 3,800+ enterprise customers and 100M+ end users across government, healthcare, financial services, legal, manufacturing, pharma/life sciences and tech. HQ San Mateo, California.
category: Secure content communications / data governance and compliance infrastructure — now positioning into AI data governance and agent access control
stage: Private, private-equity/growth-equity backed unicorn (not venture-stage). Long-established company, 27 years old.
funding: $456M from Insight Partners and Sixth Street Partners (Aug 2024) at a valuation above $1B. Earlier: $120M from Bregal Sagemount (Apr 2020); $12.2M from Riverwood Capital (Jan 2012); ~$35M total raised as of 2011.
headcount_estimate: 400+ employees (per Wikipedia). Not disclosed on the company's own site — treat 400+ as approximate.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 1999, long predates the accelerator era.
founded_year: 1999 (founded in Singapore as Accellion, Inc.; later relocated to Palo Alto/San Mateo, CA; rebranded to Kiteworks in October 2021)
sells_to: B2B enterprise and government — regulated industries and public sector where compliance failure is existential (FedRAMP, IRAP PROTECTED, CMMC-type buyers). Classic high-touch enterprise security sale, not PLG.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places, and the distinction matters for understanding this buyer. (1) IN PRODUCT: native AI agent governance is a stated differentiator — agents authenticate with scoped delegation tokens, get task-limited permissions, and every operation is logged and policy-governed exactly like a human workflow; Kiteworks ships an MCP server as one of its governed data-access channels. So Kiteworks sells agent governance. (2) INTERNALLY, which is what the Jedify testimonial is about: CIO Kumud Kokal describes building 'a fleet of AI agents — covering customer health, sales modeling, and engineering risk.' This is an internal ops/IT deployment, not embedded in the shipped product.
why_they_need_memory: Per the testimonial, the agents were the easy part; the hard part was 'giving every agent a shared, governed understanding of our business so they reason consistently and act safely' — and doing it 'without rebuilding our entire data layer.' The buying driver here is consistency and safety across a fleet of internal agents plus avoiding a data-platform rewrite, which is a materially different motivation from the Notion/Harvey cases (token economics on huge private corpora). Note also the ideological fit: a company whose whole pitch is governed data access is a natural buyer of a governed context layer. EVIDENCE CAVEATS: the testimonial and the homepage logo-wall placement are both on Jedify's site (jedify.com, which jedify.ai redirects to); Jedify's customer list also names Openweb, The Weather Company, Exodigo, Snappy, RubyPlay, DealHub and SoundCloud, with Snowflake as a partner. I could NOT independently verify Kumud Kokal — he does not appear on Kiteworks' own management page (which lists Jonathan Yaron as Chairman/CEO, Kurt Michael CRO, Yaron Galant CPO, Tim Freestone CSO, Jessica Pursell CFO, Frank Balonis CISO, Amit Toren CBO, and others, with no CIO role listed at all), and a site search of kiteworks.com for 'Kokal' returns zero results. Kiteworks itself has published nothing about Jedify. The company is unambiguously real; the specific person/title and the deployment are vendor-attested only.
confidence: high — that Kiteworks is a real, large, well-funded company and that its product genuinely centers on AI-agent data governance. medium/low — on the Jedify deployment specifics and on Kumud Kokal's CIO title, which are asserted only by the vendor and are absent from (and unsearchable on) Kiteworks' own site.

name: Rokid
what_it_does: Chinese AI + AR smart-glasses maker, founded July 2014 in Hangzhou. Started as an AI voice-assistant/smart-speaker company (Rokid Alien, Rokid Pebble) and pivoted into eyewear. Now on its 11th generation of mass-produced AI/AR glasses: Rokid Glasses (marketed as the lightest full-feature AI+AR glasses), Rokid AI Glasses Style / Neo (Jan 2026, first Rokid model shipping with ChatGPT and Gemini integrated; display-free, launched at CES 2026 and widely covered as a Ray-Ban Meta alternative), Rokid AR Spatial and Rokid Max 2 (tethered viewers for gaming/multitasking), plus the enterprise X-Craft industrial headset. Runs its own spatial OS, YodaOS, with an open developer platform (open.rokid.com). Self-reported: 300+ patents, 60% of resources in R&D, sold in 80-100+ countries, millions of users, and the most-funded XR project ever on Kickstarter (>$3.6M in 45 days).
category: AI/AR smart glasses and spatial-computing hardware (consumer + industrial); adjacent to the AI-wearable / always-on-assistant category
stage: Late-stage private. Reported to be planning a Hong Kong IPO (South China Morning Post, 7 April 2026, headline 'Chinese AI glasses maker Rokid planning Hong Kong IPO', cited as a footnote in Wikipedia's RayNeo article).
funding: ~$378M total raised as of March 2022 (TechCrunch). Known rounds: $50M at a $450M valuation (Nov 2016); $100M Series B extension (Jan 2018) to build US presence; Series C closed March 2022 — TechCrunch's article text says $160M raised across two tranches while the article slug says $110M, so treat the exact Series C figure as $110M-$160M. Series C investors were not disclosed beyond 'related ecosystem players' (clients and supply-chain partners). Any post-2022 rounds could not be confirmed — this session's web-search budget was exhausted and Crunchbase/LinkedIn/PitchBook returned 403/404 to direct fetch.
headcount_estimate: ~380 employees as of March 2022 (TechCrunch). Current headcount unknown — LinkedIn and Crunchbase were not fetchable. Given 11 product generations and global distribution it is very likely materially larger now, but I am not estimating a number.
yc_or_accelerator: none found
sells_to: Primarily consumer/prosumer hardware (D2C via store.rokid.com, Amazon US/India, Kickstarter, retail in 80-100+ countries), plus B2B enterprise/industrial for the X-Craft line (field service, inspection, 5G/GPS ruggedized headsets) and a developer platform at open.rokid.com.
how_they_use_agents: The assistant IS the product. Rokid Glasses ship a voice-first AI assistant on YodaOS doing real-time translation, audio transcription, hands-free photo/video capture and teleprompter; the Style/Neo models route to third-party LLMs (ChatGPT and Gemini) rather than a purely in-house model. Rokid's technology page also describes digital-human agents with ASR/TTS language understanding 'connected to AIGC' (30+ actions, one-click avatar adaptation, ~80% automated) aimed at NPC and office-automation uses, plus voice-interaction services, centimetre-accurate visual positioning/SLAM and gesture recognition as the interaction substrate. Note: EverMind's own GitHub README marks the 'Rokid AI Assistant with EverOS' entry 'Coming soon' with no code and no live link — so on the evidence available this is an announced/planned integration, not a shipped deployment, and Rokid should not be counted as a confirmed paying customer.
why_they_need_memory: An always-on wearable is the canonical agent-memory buyer: the glasses see and hear a continuous stream of the wearer's day, but each LLM call is stateless, so without a persistent layer the assistant re-meets its user every session. EverMind's own framing for the (unshipped) integration is 'long-term memory for all of your smart activities'. Concretely: remembering people, places, prior conversations and standing preferences across sessions and devices; making transcription/translation history retrievable later; and personalising a voice-only interface where there is no screen to re-enter context on. Rokid is also multi-LLM (ChatGPT + Gemini), which pushes memory out of any one model provider and into a portable layer — exactly the pitch of a 'company brain' vendor.
