name: Reunite
what_it_does: Not a company — a single-developer demo web app, and EverMind's own showcase piece. Reunite is a family-reunification / missing-children matching platform: separated parents and children each describe fragmented memories (a lullaby, a scent, a birthmark, a street, approximate dates) via a conversational 'AI memory guide', and a semantic engine stores those as vectors and surfaces contextual matches rather than exact name/date matches, followed by guided verification steps. The live app itself carries an explicit disclaimer that it is a preview build: 'every entry, name, and memory below is synthetic — generated to illustrate how the matching engine behaves on real-world-like data', data resets on every deployment and after inactivity, and users are warned not to submit real personal information. EverMind's own page repeats this ('placeholder data... A full version with real data will be available soon'). No company name, team, pricing, contact, legal entity, terms or privacy policy of its own; hosted on a vercel.app subdomain that contains EverMind's own name.
category: Consumer / social-good semantic-search app (missing-persons matching) — a hackathon demo, not a commercial product
stage: Not a company. Hackathon project: winner of the Public Value Award ($2,000) at EverMind's own Memory Genesis Competition 2026, builder credited as 'Xiaoba'.
funding: unknown (no evidence of any; $2,000 hackathon prize from the vendor itself is the only known money)
headcount_estimate: unknown — appears to be one individual builder ('Xiaoba'); no team page exists
yc_or_accelerator: none — the only accelerator-like credential is EverMind's in-house Memory Genesis Competition 2026 (Public Value Award, $2,000)
sells_to: n/a — no commercial motion, no pricing, no customers; free public demo
how_they_use_agents: A conversational 'AI memory guide' agent interviews the user to elicit and expand recollections, then writes them into EverOS as semantic memory; a matching agent searches across all stored entries at the concept level (vectors, not keywords) to propose candidate parent/child pairs, which are then routed through a human verification flow. The whole app is essentially a thin UI over EverOS's memory store — which is why EverMind features it.
why_they_need_memory: The product premise is literally agent memory: matches have to be made across incomplete, drifting, decades-old recollections stored over long time horizons, where no exact identifier exists. Semantic vector memory with cross-entry retrieval is the entire mechanism. But note the direction of the arrow — this project exists because EverOS exists, not the other way round, so it tells you nothing about who pays for the category. Treat it as vendor marketing, not a customer datapoint.

name: Golutra
what_it_does: CORRECTION TO THE PRIOR ASSESSMENT: Golutra is materially more real than a hackathon entry. It is a shipping open-source, cross-platform desktop app (Tauri, Vue 3 front end + Rust back end, Windows/macOS/Linux) at github.com/golutra/golutra with 3,830 stars, 440 forks, 57 open issues and tagged releases; the GitHub org 'golutra' was created 2026-01-17 and the main repo 2026-02-15, last pushed August 2026. Licensed BSL 1.1 (MariaDB), i.e. source-available rather than fully permissive. Tagline: 'One Person. One AI Squad.' — Chinese-first framing is '使用赛博监工系统，指挥你的 AI 牛马' ('use the cyber-overseer system to command your AI workforce'). It is a multi-agent workspace that wraps CLI coding agents you already use rather than replacing them: no project migration, no command relearning. Ships companion repos golutra-mcp (TypeScript, MCP bridge via golutra-cli) and golutra-agent (Rust). The public repo states it is 'for source code storage and releases', so real development happens privately. Contact is a hotmail address (golutra@hotmail.com), there is no team, pricing, funding, investor or legal-entity information anywhere on the site or repo, and the marketing site itself is nearly contentless ('Golutra - Multi-Agent Era'). So: a real and reasonably popular product, but no evidence of a real company behind it.
category: Dev tools / multi-agent orchestration for coding agents (agent workforce IDE replacement)
stage: Bootstrapped indie open-source. No funding round, investor, incorporation or accelerator found. Won an 'Excellence' award ($3,000) at EverMind's Memory Genesis Competition 2026 under builder handle 'seeksky' — which corroborates against the GitHub org's public members: seekskyworld (the sole public contributor to the repo, X handle @seekskyworld, account created Oct 2023) and tt-a1i (1,302 followers).
funding: unknown — no evidence of any external funding; only known money is the $3,000 Memory Genesis Competition 2026 'Excellence' prize paid by the vendor itself
headcount_estimate: unknown; evidence points to 1-2 people — 1 public contributor (seekskyworld, 14 commits to the release-mirror repo) and 2 public org members. No team page, no company address, personal hotmail as the business contact.
yc_or_accelerator: none — only EverMind's own Memory Genesis Competition 2026 (Excellence, $3,000)
sells_to: Developers and indie/solo builders (the explicit positioning is 'one person + an AI squad' replacing 'one person + one editor'). Distributed free as a desktop download under BSL 1.1; no visible pricing or paid tier, no enterprise motion.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the entire product. Golutra is a compatibility layer over existing agent CLIs — Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Code, OpenClaw, or any CLI — and runs unlimited instances of them in parallel as a coordinated 'workforce'. Features: automated orchestration from analysis through deployment with automatic result handoff between agents; a single scheduling/status layer across heterogeneous CLIs; custom long-running workflows with one-click template import/export (they cite software teams, a 'one-person AI company', automated novel writing, Xiaohongshu publishing and video production as workflow templates); a 'stealth terminal' where you click an agent avatar to inspect logs and inject prompts directly into a live terminal stream; aggregation of test/build/regression output into one delivery path; and golutra-mcp for connecting external tools via MCP.
why_they_need_memory: This is the one genuine, self-documented integration of the three. Golutra's own README has a 'Related Projects / Memory Layer' section stating: 'Golutra can call EverOS as a memory layer for long-running agents, preserving context, project knowledge, and cross-task continuity across sessions.' The need is structural to the product — Golutra explicitly targets long-running collaboration rather than short interactive sessions, and runs many agents in parallel across different CLI vendors, so context has to live outside any single agent's window and outside any single model provider. Shared project knowledge, prompt/requirement reuse without restating, and handoff of results between agents are all memory-layer problems. Note the relationship is a free OSS-to-OSS integration between two projects that met at the vendor's own hackathon, not a commercial purchase.

name: The Weather Company

Ownership history: Landmark Communications 1980–2008; NBCUniversal/Bain Capital/Blackstone consortium 2008–2016; IBM 2016–2024 (inside Watson & Cloud Platform); Francisco Partners 2024–present.
headcount_estimate: unknown — not disclosed. Careers page lists offices in Atlanta GA, Andover MA and New York NY, and notes nearly half of employees have 10+ years tenure. Historically reported in the low thousands under IBM, but I could not confirm a current figure and am not guessing one.
yc_or_accelerator: none
founded_year: 1980 (as The Weather Channel); reorganized as The Weather Company in 2012
sells_to: Mixed: B2B enterprise (airlines, broadcasters, government/defense, energy, retail, insurance, media buyers) plus a large ad-supported consumer app business. The Jedify buyer is the internal engineering/data org, headed by the CTO.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers. (a) Internal/agentic — this is what Jedify is for: CTO Matthew Drooker's testimonial describes "enterprise AI agents" plus human analysts querying business data, and explicitly says agents "can't reason accurately from stitched-together connectors and warehouses alone," i.e. LLM agents over the company's own warehouse/CRM/ad/telemetry estate for analytics and agentic workflows. (b) In-product AI — mostly non-agentic ML/automation: the Max Engage "decision engine" that auto-evaluates and re-sequences broadcast content, AI-driven ad targeting signals, an Nvidia partnership for AI forecasting (2024), and AI-generated "smart NOTAMs" for pilots (Sept 2025). Their own marketing language is "augmented intelligence," and their AI pages make no mention of LLMs or agentic workflows — the agent story lives on the internal data side, not the product side.
why_they_need_memory: Enormous, heterogeneous data estate accumulated over 40+ years and three owners: consumer app telemetry at hundreds of millions of users, ad-tech data, aviation/enterprise contracts, forecast model output, plus whatever schema sprawl survived the IBM-to-Francisco-Partners carve-out. The CTO's stated pain is precisely the agent-memory pitch: connectors + warehouse tables carry no business meaning, so agents hallucinate or produce answers analysts can't trust. They need a persistent, governed semantic/context layer so agents and humans resolve the same metric the same way "at Weather Company scale."

name: Exodigo

Exodigo maps what is beneath a construction site — buried utilities, foundations, geotechnical conditions — without digging, by combining multi-sensor scanning with proprietary AI, then delivering 3D models and engineering deliverables. Four-stage offering: ExoInfo (remote data intelligence: AI over existing records, permits and imagery), on-site reality capture (utility, foundation and geotechnical scanning), AI Engineering (digital modeling/design; they stood up a dedicated engineering-services division and acquired California engineering firm V&A Inc. in 2026), and utility relocation cost estimation/coordination. Site claims 100+ global customers including LA Metro, Caltrans, Port of Los Angeles and National Grid, 86.1M sq ft scanned, and $75B of infrastructure investment de-risked. Dual HQ: Palo Alto, CA and Tel Aviv, Israel; also operates in Europe.
category: AI + sensing for infrastructure / construction tech (subsurface geospatial intelligence). Hardware + AI + services, sold heavily into public-sector infrastructure.
stage: Series B
funding: $214M total raised as of July 2025 (company's own figure). Rounds: ~$29M seed ("digs up $29 million in seed funding"); $105M Series A announced 27 Feb 2024, led by Greenfield Partners and Zeev Ventures with SquarePeg, 10D VC, JIBE and National Grid Partners (total raised stated as $118M at that point); $96M Series B announced 16 July 2025, led by Zeev Ventures and Greenfield Partners, with existing investors 10D VC, Square Peg and JIBE plus new investors Vintage Investment Partners and Leblon Capital.

founded_year: 2021 (Series B release says founded 2021 / total raised "since 2021"; the Series A release refers to "since 2022 launch" and the careers page says "5 years" of building — 2021 founding with 2022 commercial launch is the most consistent reading)
sells_to: B2B enterprise and public sector — transit agencies and DOTs (LA Metro, Caltrans), utilities (National Grid), ports, and the engineering/construction firms serving them. Long-cycle, high-ticket, project-based sales.
how_they_use_agents: The product AI is computer-vision/geophysics ML for subsurface detection, not LLM agents — their funding releases never mention agents. The Jedify relationship is internal: VP Data Assaf Shahaf describes Jedify modeling their CRM and ERP data so agents and analysts can answer business questions, and stresses that the win was accuracy against "our source of truth." So the agent surface here is internal revenue/ops analytics — a data-team buyer, not a product team.
why_they_need_memory: Their business data model is genuinely gnarly and Shahaf names the specifics: framework agreements, multi-entity billing, and bridge tables spanning CRM and ERP. A hardware + services + software company selling multi-year public-infrastructure contracts has revenue logic that naive text-to-SQL gets wrong, and finance-adjacent numbers where a wrong answer destroys trust immediately. That is the classic case for a persistent, curated semantic/context layer: encode the joins and business rules once so every agent answer reconciles with the ERP.

name: SoundCloud

Monetization spans consumer subscriptions (SoundCloud Go/Go+), creator subscriptions and tooling (Next Pro), advertising, distribution/monetization products for artists, and fan-powered royalties. Berlin-headquartered, founded 2007 by Alexander Ljung and Eric Wahlforss; CEO since March 2023 is Eliah Seton, CTO Dr. Steve Abrams (Nov 2025). Acquired Singapore music-AI company Musiio in 2022 and Nina Protocol in July 2026; expanded to Mexico in 2025.
category: Consumer music streaming / creator platform (B2C + prosumer creator SaaS + ads). A ~19-year-old internet company, not an AI startup.
stage: Late-stage private, VC- and strategic-backed; never IPO'd
funding: Multiple disclosed rounds, roughly $300M+ total: €2.5M Series A (Apr 2009, Doughty Hanson Technology Ventures); $10M Series B (Jan 2011, Union Square Ventures + Index Ventures); 2011 investment from Ashton Kutcher/Guy Oseary's A-Grade Fund; $60M (Jan 2014, at a ~$700M valuation); $169.5M (Aug 2017, The Raine Group + Temasek, the recapitalization that followed its near-collapse); $75M (Jan 2020, SiriusXM). No confirmed round after 2020. Note: I did not find a reliable current valuation and am not estimating one.
headcount_estimate: unknown current figure. ~425 employees reported as of 2021; headcount was reduced by layoff rounds after that, so the present number is likely lower but I could not confirm it.
yc_or_accelerator: none
founded_year: 2007 (incorporated August 2007 in Berlin; public site launched October 2008)
sells_to: Primarily consumer and prosumer (listeners and independent artists) plus advertisers. The Jedify buyer is internal: the Insights & Analytics and Analytics Engineering functions, i.e. a data-org purchase, not a product-line purchase.
how_they_use_agents: Jedify is used for internal AI-powered BI: Rory O'Flynn (Director, Insights & Analytics) says traditional self-serve BI "never reached the level we needed," and Dominic Pyne (Director, Analytics Engineering) says "anyone can answer a business question without relying on data analyst expertise or navigating dashboards" — natural-language agents over the analytics stack, replacing dashboard navigation, with an explicit buy-over-build decision. Separately, product-side AI: Musiio-powered catalog tagging and discovery, six AI-assisted music creation tools (Nov 2024), and "artist-first" AI partnerships with Fadr, Soundful and Voice-Swap — the company frames these as "intentional integrations, not automation." Those product features are ML, not agents.
why_they_need_memory: Extreme event volume (plays, uploads, creator and listener behavior across hundreds of millions of tracks) combined with a long tail of business metrics that only a handful of analysts understand. Their stated pain is the analyst bottleneck and dashboard sprawl: business users can't self-serve, and an LLM pointed at raw warehouse tables at that cardinality won't pick the right metric definition. A persistent context/semantic layer is what lets a non-technical PM or label-relations person ask a question and get an answer that matches what the analytics team would have produced — and their quote about choosing Jedify "over building in-house" shows they scoped the internal-context-layer build and decided to buy it.

headcount_estimate: ~700–760. Revelio Labs: 751 employees as of March 2026 (down ~1.7% YoY). LeadIQ: 704. RocketReach: 728. An older TheCompanyCheck entry says 861 as of Dec 2022, so headcount appears to have drifted down slightly. Call it roughly 700–750 today.
yc_or_accelerator: None. Not a YC or accelerator company — a 1997-founded company that went the PE route.
sells_to: B2B enterprise and upper-mid-market — healthcare provider organizations (diagnostic labs, pathology and radiology groups, molecular diagnostics, medical device companies, retail/specialty pharmacy chains, hospital outpatient and ancillary services). Long enterprise sales cycles, compliance-heavy (SSAE-18, HIPAA), sold to CFO/revenue-cycle-leader personas.
how_they_use_agents: This is the interesting part and it is very concrete. XiFin ships 'XiFin Empower AI', described on their site as 'an interoperable AI RCM ecosystem on trusted data, coordinating predictive, generative, and agent AI across the billing lifecycle.' Two layers: (1) embedded ML/NLP inside RCM workflows — Empower AI DocExtract (auto-extracts, classifies, splits and labels incoming faxes/PDFs/order forms before storing them), Insurance Snap & Map (OCR + payor-mapping API that reads insurance cards, identifies payors even from logos alone, maps to payor contracts), AI-powered patient responsibility estimation (predicts allowed amounts, copays, deductibles from eligibility data + historical adjudication patterns), AI-driven payor response interpretation (NLP over thousands of free-text payor messages and generic status codes like 'A3-21', categorized into actionable reasons and routed into workflows), and exception prioritization and routing (assigns a payment-probability score per claim error, ranks by value/aging/timely-filing deadline, routes to the best-matched team member). (2) A standalone 'XiFin Empower AI Agentic Catalog' of six named agents: Intake Agent, Strategy & Planning Agent, Browser-based Live Agent, Extraction Agent, **Memory Agent**, and Form-Fill Agent. The flagship composed product is the XiFin Empower AI Appeals Agent, which ingests appeal cases and normalizes patient/encounter/payor/plan data, evaluates payor and plan policy intent to pick an appeal strategy, navigates live payor portals to validate real-time coverage rules and pull policies and LCDs, derives medical-necessity criteria, drafts payor-formatted appeal letters with citations, assembles supporting evidence, and flags claims needing human review — XiFin claims it 'reduces manual appeals workload by up to 90%.' Their stated design goal is agents that 'coordinate handoffs among bots, AI models, and human staff.'
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls, and they explain why XiFin shows up on Guru's customer wall AND why they'd be a buyer of agent-memory infrastructure. (a) The Guru case — internal company brain: ~750 employees spread across RCM operations, coding/credentialing, compliance and managed billing services, working in a domain where the ground truth (payor policies, LCDs, CPT/coding rules, state regs, the No Surprises Act, PAMA) changes constantly and is scattered across payor portals and PDFs. They publish a 'Billing Beat' newsletter and 'Briefing Center' precisely because keeping staff current is the hard part. A searchable, verified knowledge layer over that is the classic Guru use case, and Guru's page carries the file literally named '2025_Solutions_Customer_xifin.svg' on /solutions/pharma-clinical-research. (b) The agent-memory case — they are building it themselves: a 'Memory Agent' is one of six agents in their own published catalog. Their Appeals Agent runs long, multi-step, cross-system workflows (portal navigation → policy extraction → letter drafting → evidence assembly → human handoff) where state has to persist across handoffs among bots, models and humans, and where the agent must accumulate 'continuously learning from adjudication patterns' per payor. That is exactly the durable-context problem agent-memory vendors sell into — and it means XiFin is simultaneously a buyer of the category and a builder of it.

yc_or_accelerator: None. Chinese domestic VC track (Jinqiu / Gaorong / Mingshi), not a Western accelerator.
founded_year: 2023 — company 深圳想法流科技有限公司 incorporated 2023-07-03; core product 造梦次元 launched early 2024 (iOS release 2024-01-29).
sells_to: Consumer (B2C), with a prosumer/creator tier. End users are Chinese Gen-Z / ACG (二次元) audiences; the monetization layer targets creators who build character IP on the platform. There is also an overseas B2C build shipped as 'dreama'. No enterprise or developer sales motion.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the product surface, not back-office tooling. Each user-created character is effectively a persistent LLM agent with a persona, a world/setting, and an ongoing relationship with the user — the app's own feature copy is '探索海量角色，在持续互动中积累你们的独家记忆' ('explore countless characters, and accumulate your exclusive memories through continued interaction'). Around that sit agentic content pipelines: a one-click '@ character' flow that pulls a character into a generated video or storyline, template-driven co-starring with friends, and an interactive-narrative engine that lets a story branch and be continued by other users. The company describes its own technical scope in recruiting copy as spanning '多模态内容生成、角色与 IP 衍生、互动叙事引擎、创作者生态、AI Agent 与社交分发系统' — multimodal content generation, character/IP derivation, an interactive narrative engine, creator ecosystem, AI agents, and a social distribution system. They also say they work in an 'AI-native' way internally, treating AI as a colleague rather than a tool.
why_they_need_memory: This is close to the canonical buyer for Memobase's exact product (user-profile-based long-term memory for AI chatbot applications). Three reasons. First, scale of relationship state: they claim tens of millions of users and reported in Oct 2024 that average daily time-in-app exceeded 100 minutes, with ~100 character IPs passing 10k followers. Hundreds of hours of accumulated conversation per user per year is far past what fits in a context window. Second, the product promise is explicitly memory — 'accumulate your exclusive memories together' is a marketed feature, and a companion character that forgets who you are is a churned user; retention in AI-roleplay is almost entirely a function of whether the character remembers. Third, it is a small team (20–99) on a Series A that has to spend its engineering budget on multimodal generation (text→image→video→comic-drama) and the social feed, not on building and operating a user-profile memory backend, extraction pipeline and storage layer. Buying that as infrastructure is the rational call. Caveat: Memobase's own logo wall never states the relationship — the headings vary between 'Trusted by Generative AI Applications', 'Our services are featured on', and a boilerplate 'Trusted by Global Industry Leaders', with no alt text or links — so 'customer' is inferred, not asserted by the vendor.

name: Sibyl (Sibyl镜界 / "Sibyl Mirror Realm") — by 上海阈知科技有限公司 / Shanghai Yuzhi Technology Co., Ltd., trading as Lab Intelli (阈知科技 / 因特立)
url: https://labintelli.tech (studio: https://labintelli.com; app: https://apps.apple.com/cn/app/id6746782361, bundle id tech.labintelli)
what_it_does: IDENTIFICATION NOTE FIRST: the brief flagged this logo as unconfirmed. I believe it is now identified. The Memobase logo was described as 'an ornate silver/chrome wordmark reading Sibyl with a star/compass-rose glyph forming the S.' The App Store icon for Sibyl镜界 is exactly that mark — an ornate silvery script 'Sibyl' whose S is formed by an eight-pointed star/compass rose, set inside a chrome armillary-sphere ring. The match is distinctive enough (the star-in-the-S is unusual) that I'd call it the same brand; the 'on black' detail is simply Memobase reversing the wordmark out onto its dark logo wall. What it is: an AI emotional-companion / mood-journaling app. Sibyl is characterized as 'a little spider from the Mirror Realm' who weaves your emotions into silk thread. Daily, the user uploads a photo and describes how they feel, and the app generates a bespoke '心镜卡' (mind-mirror card) — an AI art piece rendering that day's mood. Around it sit an emotion diary, AI-suggested daily micro-goals, long-term mood tracking, conversational emotional support, and a visualized '成长档案' (growth record) charting how the user has changed. Explicitly disclaimed as not medical or psychological advice. Positioned as art-forward wellness rather than a chatbot: the operator is a Shanghai new-media art + AIGC studio founded by graduates of University of the Arts London (UAL), whose other work is interactive installations, concert and VJ visuals (Xu Song's 2024 tour, Shanghai International Light Festival), game design, and brand creative — with a collaborating artist network across the UK, US and Australia. Their contact page lists Xiaohongshu handles '@Lab intelli' and '@Sibyl APP' side by side, which is what ties the studio to the app.
category: consumer AI emotional-wellness / mood-journaling companion app with generative AI art; built by a new-media-art + AIGC creative studio
stage: Unknown — no funding round found. Appears to be a self-funded/bootstrapped creative studio (a services-and-projects business that also ships its own app), not a venture-backed startup.
funding: unknown. No funding round, investor, or accelerator found for 上海阈知科技有限公司 / Lab Intelli in any source I could reach. The studio's commercial-projects portfolio (concerts, festivals, brand work) suggests it is services-funded rather than venture-funded, but I could not confirm that and am not going to assert a number.
headcount_estimate: unknown. No published figure. Contextual signals point to very small — self-described as a 'studio' (工作室) with a founding team of several UAL graduates plus a flexible network of contract artists, and the Sibyl app has only ~14 ratings on the CN App Store. Plausibly under 20 people, but that is an inference, not a source.
yc_or_accelerator: None found.
founded_year: unknown for the company. The Sibyl app itself was first released 2025-08-14 and last updated 2025-12-30 (v1.0.18). The Lab Intelli studio portfolio includes work dated 2024 (London Tech Week 2024, Xu Song 2024 tour), so the studio predates the app by at least a year or two.
sells_to: Consumer (B2C), China-first — the app is a free CN App Store release in the Lifestyle/Entertainment categories, marketed on Xiaohongshu. The parent studio separately runs a B2B creative-services motion (brands, concerts, festivals, exhibitions), but Sibyl itself is a direct-to-consumer product.
how_they_use_agents: A single persistent character-agent is the entire product. Sibyl is a named persona with a fixed identity and voice who holds an ongoing, open-ended conversation with one user over months. Two agentic loops: (1) a generative-art loop — take the user's photo plus their stated mood, and produce a stylized daily 'mind-mirror card', i.e. an AI reading of emotional state rendered visually; (2) a relationship loop — the app's own store copy says '专属长期记忆，越用越懂你：Sibyl会记住你说过的话和情绪轨迹，随着使用不断了解你、陪伴你，主动提醒、鼓励或回顾过往的成长时刻' ('exclusive long-term memory, understanding you better the more you use it: Sibyl will remember what you said and your emotional trajectory, getting to know and accompany you over time, and will proactively remind, encourage, or look back on past moments of growth'). So the agent is expected to initiate — to surface a memory unprompted and say 'you've come a long way' — which is a memory-driven proactive behavior, not just retrieval-on-demand. Conversations are described as being woven into a per-user 'growth web' / growth archive.
why_they_need_memory: Sibyl is close to a pure-play memory product: strip out long-term memory and there is essentially nothing left. The app's entire retention thesis is longitudinal — track emotion over months, visualize how you have changed, have the companion recall something you said weeks ago and bring it up at the right moment. That is per-user, structured, long-horizon profile memory (mood trajectory + stated facts + past events), which is precisely what Memobase sells as 'user profile-based long-term memory for AI chatbot applications' rather than what a raw vector store gives you. And the buyer profile fits: an art-led studio of designers and creative technologists, no disclosed funding, no infrastructure team — building and operating an extraction pipeline, profile store and retrieval layer in-house would consume the whole engineering budget, so buying it off the shelf is the obvious move. CAVEATS, and they matter: (1) the identification rests on a visual match between the app icon and the described logo plus category fit, not on any statement by Memobase — there is no alt text, no link, and no caption on that logo wall, and Memobase's own headings are inconsistent about whether these are customers, users, or press placements; (2) memobase.io is now dead (Framer 'Site Not Found'), and the vendor has pivoted — the memodb-io GitHub org now points at memodb.io and a successor product, Acontext ('Agent Skills as a Memory Layer'), under MEMODB PTE. LTD. in Singapore, so this logo wall may reflect a relationship that no longer exists; (3) note there are several unrelated things named 'Sibyl' in the AI-memory space — sibyllabs.org (Sibyl Memory), sibyl.ist (cross-agent memory), and sibyls.ai (a metaphysical/spiritual chatbot) — none of which would plausibly appear on a memory vendor's customer wall, since the first two are direct competitors.

name: OpenWeb (formerly Spot.IM)
what_it_does: Community engagement and monetization platform for digital publishers. Publishers embed OpenWeb's conversation/comments unit, forums, live blogs and polls on their own properties instead of sending audience to social platforms. Three product pillars: (1) Community tools, (2) 'Aida' trust-and-safety moderation — an end-to-end system the site says is 'powered by 25+ AI models' plus globally distributed human moderators, covering 100+ languages, (3) Monetization — turning conversation real estate into ad inventory (Community Media, Media Exchange, Newsletter Media, Podcast). Claims 5,000+ partners and ~150M monthly active users spending 5.5B minutes. Publisher logos include CNN, Forbes, WSJ, The Times, Yahoo, HuffPost, TechCrunch, MarketWatch. Roll-up history: acquired Adyoulike (~$100M, 2022), Hive Media Group (~$60M, 2022) and Jeeng (2023). Leadership has churned recently — founder Nadav Shoval moved to Senior Advisor (Feb 2025), Jim Daily named CEO (Mar 2025), new SVP Product Oct 2025, Community Exchange Platform launched Nov 2025.
category: Publisher / media tech — online community software, AI content moderation, and adtech. (A buyer of the agent-context category, not a vendor in it.)
stage: Late-stage private, Series F
funding: ~$380M+ disclosed across Series A–F. Series A $13M (2016, Index Ventures, AltaIR); Series C $25M (2017, Insight Partners, Altair); Series D $25M (2019, Insight Partners, Norma Investments); Series E $150M (2021, The New York Times Company, Samsung Next, Insight Partners, Georgian); Series F $170M (Nov 2022) at a reported valuation above $1.5B. Other investors named on LinkedIn: Entrée Capital, Dentsu, ScaleUp. No round found after 2022 — treat the $1.5B valuation as a 2022 mark, not a current one.
headcount_estimate: ~200–300. LinkedIn shows the 51–200 band with ~245 associated profiles; Wikipedia's 400 figure appears to predate post-2022 contraction. Offices: New York (HQ, 38 Greene St), Tel Aviv, London, Paris, Carlsbad CA, London Ontario, Kyiv.
yc_or_accelerator: None found
founded_year: 2015 (as Spot.IM; founders Nadav Shoval, Ishay Green, Roee Goldberg)
sells_to: B2B enterprise — large digital publishers and media brands, plus advertisers/agencies buying the resulting inventory
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct things, worth not conflating. IN PRODUCT: 'Aida' is classifier-style ML, not agents — 25+ proprietary AI/ML models that pre-screen comments for harmful or low-quality content, tuned per publisher's community guidelines, with humans in the loop. No LLM agent or tool-calling surface is advertised. INTERNALLY (this is the Jedify relationship): the buyer is Yaniv Greenfeld, VP Rev Ops & FP&A — a finance/revenue-operations leader, not engineering. He uses Jedify's context graph and native data agents so the executive team can self-serve trusted metrics, including on mobile. The quote emphasizes organizational alignment around 'trusted, accurate data' rather than any agent autonomy.
why_they_need_memory: Revenue data is genuinely fragmented and hard to define: publisher-side subscription/licensing revenue sits alongside three separate ad businesses, two of which (Adyoulike, Hive Media Group) and a third (Jeeng) arrived through acquisitions with their own schemas and metric conventions. An FP&A org reconciling that needs metric definitions pinned down once and reused — exactly what a semantic/context layer sells. The buying trigger is not 'we're building agents'; it's 'our exec team cannot get a number it trusts without a data-team round-trip.' Jedify's own customer-success page frames the same value as persistent context across CRM, support, product usage and billing.

name: Snappy (Snappy Gifts)
what_it_does: Corporate gifting SaaS. A company sets a budget and a curated collection; the recipient picks their own gift from 350,000+ options (tech, fashion, beauty, food, sports, experiences, donations, sports memorabilia, travel) or branded swag. Delivery runs through email, SMS, Slack or MS Teams; Snappy collects the shipping address from the recipient and reports back on redemption and feedback. Enterprise plumbing includes HRIS integrations (ADP, BambooHR), SSO, an API suite, Snappy Stores, and partner integrations (Chili Piper, Medallia). Positioned around four use cases: employee engagement and recognition, customer loyalty and activation, pipeline acceleration, and partner gifting. Stated scale: 7,000+ customers, 56% of the Fortune 100, 9M+ gifts delivered, 4.9/5 on G2 across 300+ reviews. Customer logos include Microsoft, HubSpot, eBay, Uber, Meta, Starbucks. Acquired Covver (corporate merchandise) in January 2025 to add AI-powered personalization.
category: HR tech / employee recognition and corporate gifting SaaS — a marketplace-plus-SaaS hybrid. (Buyer of the agent-context category, not a vendor.)
stage: Series D
funding: ~$130M disclosed. ~$1.6M initial; $8.5M (2019, led by 83North with Hearst Ventures); $25M Series B (2020, led by Saban Ventures); $70M Series C (2021); $25M Series D (2024, led by Qumra Capital) at a reported ~$200M valuation. Reported ~$30M revenue in 2023 growing ~40%. The company self-describes as 'a Series D company' on its About page.
headcount_estimate: ~200–300. 200+ reported as of 2023; global team with HQ at 33 Irving Place, New York, NY, plus Israeli R&D presence and US West Coast staff (the Jedify testimonial-giver is based in San Jose).
yc_or_accelerator: None found
founded_year: 2015 (founders Hani Goldstein, CEO, and Dvir Cohen, CTO). Pivoted from consumer one-to-one gifting to corporate gifting in 2017.
sells_to: B2B enterprise and mid-market — HR, people ops, marketing, sales and CS teams inside large companies; also a smaller consumer/peer-to-peer surface
how_they_use_agents: IN PRODUCT: an 'AI Gifting Assistant' ('Send the perfect gift with AI. Just describe the person and occasion') plus a 'Gift AI' feature in the product nav, and AI-powered personalization folded in via the Covver acquisition. These are recommendation and personalization features — no autonomous agent, no tool-calling workflow advertised. INTERNALLY (the Jedify relationship): Venkatesh Nagarajan, VP of Data & Analytics — LinkedIn confirms he is at Snappy, San Jose, describing himself as 'a senior analytical leader tackling data and analytics challenges at matrixed…' organizations. His quote is pure self-serve NL analytics: business leaders ask natural-language questions and get instant answers, used daily for leadership-meeting prep and performance checks — 'like having a trusted data analyst in every room.' Note: Jedify's homepage prints this quote with title only, no employer; the Snappy attribution rests on the adjacent Snappy-1.svg logo asset, which I confirmed in the page source, plus the LinkedIn match.
why_they_need_memory: Snappy's data is unusually heterogeneous for its size: a 350k-SKU marketplace catalog, per-recipient redemption funnels, campaign and budget data, swag inventory, HRIS-sourced employee data across 7,000+ customer accounts, and a freshly acquired company (Covver) whose data model has to be reconciled. Business questions cross all of it — 'which collections redeem best for work anniversaries in healthcare accounts' is a join across five systems with company-specific definitions of 'redeemed' and 'delivered.' A small central analytics function cannot answer those on demand for every leader, so the value is a persistent semantic layer that makes NL questions return the same number twice. Classic data-leader-as-buyer, bottleneck-relief motive — not an agent-infrastructure motive.

name: RubyPlay
what_it_does: B2B iGaming content supplier — designs and licenses online video slot games to regulated online casino operators. Restructured in January 2026 into a 'studio-based, layered content ecosystem': multiple market-focused studios (Ruby Studio, Koala Games, Mad Hat Games, Firerose launched April 2026, xSlots) on shared technology, infrastructure and distribution, so operators get market-localized content while keeping their own branding. Proprietary math engines are the differentiator — Immortal Ways(R) and Giga Match(R). Licensed by the Malta Gaming Authority under a B2B Critical Gaming Supply licence (MGA/B2B/826/2020, issued June 2021), ISO 27001 certified December 2025, and expanding into regulated markets including US states (live in West Virginia, March 2026) and Greece via Stoiximan. Moving beyond pure content: launched in-game Engagement Tools (Missions, Tournaments tied to real in-game events) in June 2026, then acquired Splash Tech in July 2026 for jackpots, free-to-play and player-retention capability. Tsachi Maimon joined as CEO in September 2025.

yc_or_accelerator: None

sells_to: B2B enterprise — licensed online casino and sportsbook operators in regulated jurisdictions (e.g. Stoiximan in Greece), sold jurisdiction by jurisdiction
how_they_use_agents: No AI agents in the product at all. The games are slot titles built on proprietary math engines; the 'Analytical' and 'Performance Driven' language on the About page is conventional data-driven product development ('It's a numbers game... the answers are all in the numbers'), not AI. The agent usage is entirely INTERNAL and is the clearest pure-BI case of the three: Avi Baruch, VP of Data, Analytics & Digital Platforms (billed on Jedify's webinar as 'VP Data and Business Applications'), uses Jedify so executives independently pull real-time game KPIs instead of queuing behind the data team, and so teams explore player retention and monetization themselves rather than commissioning analyst deep dives. RubyPlay is Jedify's most active reference customer — beyond the homepage logo (RubyPlay.svg, confirmed in page source) and testimonial, Baruch co-hosts a Jedify webinar built around 'the question every prospect asks him: how long did it actually take to get to accurate.'
why_they_need_memory: Game telemetry at real scale across many titles, five studios, dozens of operators and multiple regulated jurisdictions. The metrics that matter — player retention, monetization, RTP behavior, per-operator and per-market performance — are domain-specific enough that a generic LLM over raw tables will confidently produce wrong answers, and in a regulated gambling context wrong numbers are expensive. A context graph encodes those definitions once so every executive question resolves the same way. The Splash Tech acquisition adds jackpot and free-to-play telemetry that has to be folded into the same model. Note their own emphasis is not on agent autonomy but on 'time to accurate' — the buying criterion is trust and speed of correct answers, not automation.

name: DealHub
what_it_does: DealHub is a quote-to-revenue / revenue operations platform for B2B sales orgs. Core modules: CPQ (quote configuration engine, adaptive pricing, dynamic bundles, automated approval workflows), Contract Lifecycle Management (dynamic contract generation, pre-approved clause library), DealRoom (a branded digital sales room where buyer and seller collaborate, with content hub and embedded eSignature), Subscription Billing (recurring/consumption billing, added via the November 2025 acquisition of Subskribe, a Zuora-alumni-founded subscription billing and consumption metering company), and Revenue Intelligence (unified revenue analytics aligning CRO and CFO views). It integrates with Salesforce, HubSpot, NetSuite, and DocuSign, and carries ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II. As of 2026 the company markets itself as an 'Agentic Quote-to-Revenue Platform' / 'Agentic Revenue Hub' built on what it calls 'Governed Execution.' The company was originally named Valooto and rebranded to DealHub.
category: revenue operations / CPQ + billing SaaS (sales tech); now positioning as agentic revenue infrastructure
stage: Late-stage private / growth stage. Raised a $100M growth round in January 2026; prior $60M round in 2021-2022.
funding: ~$190M disclosed total. $1.5M early round; $3M round announced December 2017 (as Valooto); $60M round led by Alpha Wave Ventures, bringing total to $90M at that time (announced 2021, post updated June 2022); $100M growth round led by Riverwood Capital announced January 20, 2026, earmarked for global expansion and the Agentic Revenue Hub. Valuation not disclosed. At the time of the $60M round the company claimed doubled ARR year over year and 'four consecutive years of growth at 250%.'
headcount_estimate: 201-500 (The Org bucket). Three offices: Austin TX (HQ per The Org), Holon Israel (R&D), and Manila, Philippines. Actively hiring across product, CS, sales, marketing, and R&D as of Sept 2026. Exact headcount not disclosed on the site.
yc_or_accelerator: None found — no YC or accelerator affiliation identified. Traditional VC path (Alpha Wave Ventures, Riverwood Capital).
founded_year: unknown with certainty — founded in Israel as Valooto by Eyal Elbahary (CEO), Alon Lubin (now CTO), and Eyal Orgil (now CGO); earliest funding press release on their own blog is dated December 2017. 2014 is the year commonly cited in third-party databases but I could not confirm it from a primary source in this session.
sells_to: B2B enterprise and upper mid-market. Named customers on their site include Intuit, HP, Braze, The Adecco Group, Zapier, Tipalti, Camunda, and Digitate. Enterprise-grade compliance posture (ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II) and CRM/ERP integration depth confirm enterprise motion, though they also serve scaling mid-market SaaS.
how_they_use_agents: DealHub ships four named agent types inside the product: (1) an AI Conversational Quoting Agent that takes natural-language descriptions of prospect requirements and configures the quote, replacing manual SKU picking, claiming '100% compliance with company policy from the very first draft'; (2) an AI Pricing Optimization Agent that reads historical deal data plus real-time market signals to recommend pricing and compare scenarios inside algorithmic discounting guardrails; (3) an AI Revenue Analytics Agent that answers conversational prompts instead of serving static dashboards, returning text explanations alongside charts, and flags deal risk, discounting trends and revenue health; (4) a native MCP (Model Context Protocol) Agent that chains other agents into workflows and autonomously triggers next steps across the quote-to-revenue lifecycle. All four are described as grounded in a 'unified quote-to-revenue data layer' spanning CPQ, subscriptions and billing, and in 'context-aware logic' derived from codified business rules, pricing policies and approval workflows, with audit traceability rather than black-box behavior.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct drivers. First, and explicitly stated in their Jedify testimonial, this is an embedded/OEM analytics problem: every DealHub customer has a different deal workflow, approval chain, product catalog and pricing structure, so building per-customer analytics meant 'maintaining hundreds of bespoke dashboards or exposing raw database access.' A semantic/context layer lets each customer's own sales ops team ask natural-language questions of their own deal data, approval bottlenecks and pricing trends without DealHub hand-building a dashboard per tenant and without handing out raw DB access — a multi-tenant governance problem as much as an analytics one. Second, their own agent strategy depends on persistent business context: the conversational quoting and pricing agents can only be 'governed' if company pricing policy, approval rules and discount guardrails live in a durable, queryable context layer rather than being re-derived per prompt. That is precisely the 'company brain' pitch.

name: Netlify
what_it_does: Netlify is a web development and application delivery platform — the company that popularized the 'Jamstack' term. It lets teams build, deploy and scale web apps and sites from Git, CLI, drag-and-drop, or (as of the current site) an AI prompt. The platform bundles a global CDN with 99.99% claimed uptime, atomic deploys and deploy previews for every change, serverless functions and APIs, managed databases, file/blob storage, and built-in authentication. Positioning has shifted materially toward AI: the homepage headline is 'Create with AI or code, deploy instantly on production infrastructure,' and it now advertises Agent Runners (prototype and ship AI features / run coding agents including Claude and Codex) and an AI Gateway that connects apps to major model providers. sells_to: Both developers (large PLG self-serve base, free tier, 10M+ developers) and enterprise (thousands of enterprises; logo wall includes Meta, Autodesk, Zscaler, Stack Overflow, Riot Games, Kubernetes and Figma). The buying motion spans individual devs up through enterprise platform teams, with collaboration framed around marketers, designers, engineers, ops and product.
how_they_use_agents: Netlify is now a host and runtime for other people's agents rather than an operator of internal-facing agents. Agent Runners let users prototype and ship AI features and run coding agents (Claude and Codex are named) that build and deploy apps — 'Describe what you want to build. An AI agent handles the rest.' The AI Gateway is a managed pathway from a deployed app to major model providers. So the agent surface is infrastructure-level: agents as a build input (prompt-to-deploy) and agents as a workload their customers run on Netlify.

It appears only as an uncaptioned logo (logo01.svg) in the homepage carousel; Jedify never names Netlify in text, and my fetch of jedify.com returned nine named testimonial customers (OpenWeb, Kiteworks, The Weather Company, Exodigo, Snappy, RubyPlay, DealHub, SoundCloud x2) — Netlify was not among them. If real, the plausible rationale: Netlify sits on enormous build, deploy and edge-traffic telemetry across 60M+ apps, and would want internal teams (and possibly enterprise customers) to query usage, build performance and account health in natural language without a data team hand-building every report — the same embedded/self-serve analytics pattern as DealHub. A secondary angle: agent-built apps need durable project context, which is adjacent to the agent-memory category, but nothing on Netlify's site indicates they buy that externally.

name: DoubleVerify
what_it_does: DoubleVerify (NYSE: DV) is a digital advertising verification and media-effectiveness company. Its DV Media AdVantage Platform (DV MAP) organizes around three functions: Verify (measure media quality — ad fraud and invalid traffic detection, viewability, brand safety and suitability, content context, attention — across open web, social, CTV/streaming, and commerce/retail media), Optimize (AI-driven bidding algorithms that dynamically improve campaign performance, built largely on the 2023 Scibids acquisition), and Prove (attribution, marketing mix modeling and incrementality, built largely on the 2025 Rockerbox acquisition). Product names include DV Authentic Ad, DV Authentic Attention, DV Publisher Suite and DV Pinnacle. The company says it analyzes over 8.3 trillion media transactions per year and optimizes 25 billion impressions monthly.
category: adtech — ad verification, brand safety, media measurement and campaign optimization
stage: Public company, and currently mid-acquisition. IPO'd on NYSE April 21, 2021 at $27.00/share. As of September 2026 it is under an announced all-cash acquisition by Nielsen at approximately $2.15B ($13.60 per share); the stock traded at $13.36 on Sept 4, 2026, essentially pinned to the deal price.
funding: Public — not venture funded at this stage. 2025 revenue $748.29M (+13.9% YoY); TTM revenue $768.82M (+7.6%); 2025 net income $50.65M; market cap ~$2.07B. IPO April 2021 at $27/share. Pre-IPO private ownership (private equity majority stake and late-stage growth investment) was not verified in this session — do not quote a pre-IPO funding number. Acquisitions made: Scibids (2023), Rockerbox (2025).
headcount_estimate: ~1,231 employees (stockanalysis.com company profile). Offices or commercial operations in 31 locations across 25 countries, including New York, Chicago, Berlin, Tokyo and Sydney. By far the largest of the three companies here.
yc_or_accelerator: None — not applicable. Founded 2008, long pre-dating the modern accelerator route for this category, and took a private-equity-then-IPO path.
founded_year: 2008. Headquartered at 462 Broadway, New York, NY. CEO Mark Zagorski.
sells_to: B2B enterprise, three-sided: brands and agencies (Procter & Gamble, General Motors, FanDuel), holding companies and agency groups (WPP, IPG Mediabrands, Publicis Groupe), publishers, and retail-media marketplaces. Large-enterprise, procurement-heavy sales motion — the buyer is a CMO org, media-buying team or ad ops function.
how_they_use_agents: DV Neura, announced June 17, 2026, is the company's 'cognitive engine' embedded across DV MAP. It is a hybrid of large language models, specialized ML and deterministic rules, used to interpret emerging topics and nuanced meaning across text, image, video and audio at scale (content classification expanded 300x since the start of 2026; 500M+ impressions blocked in low-quality environments since January 2026). Two named agents: the DV Neura Insight Agent, which surfaces campaign insights conversationally and — notably — exposes DV's verification and performance data to Claude, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and other assistants over MCP; and the DV Neura Activation Agent, slated for Q3 2026, which will autonomously execute approved campaign changes inside advertiser-defined guardrails. The strategic direction is letting advertisers query DV data from whatever assistant they already use rather than logging into a DV dashboard.
why_they_need_memory: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: DoubleVerify's status as a Jedify customer is UNCONFIRMED. Like Netlify, it appears only as an uncaptioned homepage carousel logo (Group-625156.svg / logo02.svg), never named in text; my fetch of jedify.com's named-testimonial list did not include DoubleVerify. Treat as probable-but-unverified. If real, the fit is strong and specific: DV's whole 2026 strategy is exposing 8.3 trillion transactions' worth of measurement data to external LLM assistants via MCP, which only works if there is a semantic layer mapping DV's metric taxonomy (viewability, IVT, suitability tiers, attention, MFA classifications) onto business meaning — otherwise an agent hitting raw tables will produce confidently wrong campaign answers for a P&G or WPP. Add the embedded/multi-tenant angle: thousands of brand and agency customers each want their own campaign data queried conversationally, and DV cannot build a bespoke analytics surface per advertiser. That is the same 'stop building hundreds of dashboards' pain DealHub articulated, at much larger scale and with much higher blast radius if the agent hallucinates.

name: WalkMe
what_it_does: WalkMe invented and leads the Digital Adoption Platform (DAP) category. It is a no-code overlay layer that sits on top of other enterprise applications (SAP, Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, Microsoft Dynamics 365, plus internal/homegrown apps) and delivers in-app guidance, walkthroughs, onboarding flows, task automation, training simulations, and adoption/usage analytics. Its differentiating tech is 'DeepUI', which reads and understands the screen of an arbitrary application so guidance can be attached to UI elements without integrating with that app's API. Customers use it to drive software adoption, cut support tickets, reduce onboarding time, enforce process compliance, and rationalize SaaS license spend. Own site claims ~1,600 customers and ~35M end users across 42+ countries. Since September 2024 it has been a wholly owned SAP company; SAP is folding DAP capabilities into its own stack alongside Joule.

stage: Acquired — was VC-backed (Series A through G), IPO'd on NASDAQ June 2021, taken private by SAP September 2024. Now an SAP business unit.

sells_to: B2B enterprise. Large and very large organizations, sold primarily to IT / CIO / digital transformation offices, then extended to HR, sales ops, customer care, and public sector. Classic top-down enterprise motion with security review, procurement, and multi-year contracts.
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct places. (1) In the product: WalkMe now markets 'contextual AI assistance' in three modes — Pinned AI (validation embedded in a workflow step), Proactive AI (reads screen context and surfaces the next action unprompted), and On-Demand AI (conversational Q&A inside any app). It is explicitly RAG-grounded in the customer's own documentation and policies rather than a general model, and WalkMe has announced an 'agentic WalkMe experience' where admins build adoption solutions through plain-language conversation. (2) Internally — the relevant use for this research: WalkMe's own IT org used Tribal to build a customer Health Monitor that runs natively inside Salesforce. The testimonial from Tal Carmi stresses that it 'runs natively in Salesforce, meets every security standard, and never exposes our data outside our trusted environment.' So WalkMe is an internal-IT buyer of an agent-building platform, not a buyer of agent memory for its own shipped product.
why_they_need_memory: The stated buying trigger is data residency and enterprise-grade context, not memory per se. WalkMe's IT wanted an agent that reasons over live Salesforce customer data (health scoring across ~1,600 accounts) without that data leaving their trusted environment. Any such agent needs durable, governed context: the Salesforce object model and metadata, what 'healthy' means for their business, prior scoring rationale, and account history over time. Their own product has the same shape of need — DeepUI plus RAG over customer policy documents is effectively an organizational memory layer for guidance. The generalizable pull is: an enterprise IT function with a mature system of record wants agents grounded in company-specific context, inside the security perimeter.

Add a large legacy IT estate ('tech debt', 'ticket backlogs') where institutional knowledge about why systems work the way they do is undocumented. That is the classic pull for a company-brain layer: an agent cannot be re-briefed from scratch on 19 countries' worth of rules on every invocation. name: Dot Compliance

name: Agentplace
what_it_does: SaaS platform for building AI agents that are complete web applications rather than chat widgets. Each agent gets its own React frontend served at its own URL, a real backend that can install packages and hold business logic, a dedicated isolated VM, and a 'Brain' (model loop + tools + sub-agents + memory) with owner-selectable model. The owner describes the outcome in plain language; the builder writes the frontend/backend/integrations, tests its own work (messages the agent it built, reads replies, takes screenshots, checks logs, fixes issues), and publishes to a live URL. Two runtime modes: Site mode (the agent IS the website) and chat mode, with memory shared across both. Ships realtime voice, business records with server-enforced access classes (Catalog/Log/Per-visitor), sub-agents, web search with citations, deep research, sandboxed code execution, self-scheduling, agent-to-agent calls, GitHub push/pull, hundreds of app integrations, and an automatic MCP endpoint on every published agent (usable from Claude Code/Desktop/Cursor). Go-to-market copy targets SMB customer-facing automation: AI receptionists, booking, customer service, payments, with vertical guides for HVAC, salons, plumbing, healthcare. Pricing: Free $0 (2,000 AI credits), Pro $29/mo (15,000+ credits, 1 custom domain), Business custom (advanced security/access controls, private cloud).

how_they_use_agents: Agents are the entire product, not an internal efficiency tool. Agentplace sells agent infrastructure: the customer's agent is a deployed web app with its own VM, backend, and model loop. Agents appear at three layers — (1) the builder is itself an agent that writes, tests, screenshots and debugs the agent it is constructing; (2) the built agent runs a tool-calling loop with sub-agents for general work, code execution and page fetching; (3) published agents call each other agent-to-agent and expose MCP so external agents (Claude Code, Cursor) can drive them. So they are as much a builder of agent memory as a buyer of it; a memory vendor sells to them only as a component swap, not a greenfield need. Public company (NASDAQ: NFLX), founded 1997 as a DVD-by-mail rental service, IPO'd 2002, pivoted to streaming in 2007 and to original content production from 2013. It is a mega-cap media and technology company, not a startup — profiling it alongside two early-stage products is a category error worth flagging to whoever consumes this research.
category: Consumer subscription streaming / media and entertainment. As an Onyx buyer, the relevant category is internal enterprise search and knowledge assistant ('company brain') deployed to employees — Netflix is the buyer, not a vendor in this space.
stage: Public company (NASDAQ: NFLX), IPO 2002. Not applicable to the startup-stage taxonomy.
funding: Not applicable — publicly traded, funded through public equity and debt markets. Historical venture funding is irrelevant at this point. I did not retrieve current market cap or latest quarterly revenue (the IR financial-releases page returned only a release index without figures) and will not fabricate them.
headcount_estimate: ~14,000 full-time employees. Onyx's own seed-round post states its deployment reached 'all 14,000+ employees' at Netflix, which is consistent with the approximately 14,000 full-time employees Netflix has disclosed in recent annual filings. Treat as an approximation.
yc_or_accelerator: none — not applicable, founded 1997 well before the modern accelerator era
sells_to: B2C consumers (subscription), plus advertisers on the ad-supported tier. Netflix sells nothing in the AI or agent category — it appears in this dataset purely as an enterprise buyer.
how_they_use_agents: Netflix appears here as a customer of agent/knowledge infrastructure, not a builder of it for sale. Per Onyx, Onyx is deployed org-wide as an internal AI assistant and enterprise search layer over Netflix's documents and applications — the 'company brain' pattern: permission-aware retrieval across Drive, Slack, Confluence and similar systems, with agentic capabilities (deep research, web search, code interpretation) layered on top. Separately and independently of Onyx, Netflix runs very large-scale machine learning in its core product (recommendations and personalization, encoding and video quality, artwork and promo selection, content demand forecasting) and has been building internal LLM tooling. But the ML in the product is not what makes it an agent-memory buyer — the org-wide internal assistant deployment is.
why_they_need_memory: This is the archetypal enterprise buyer for the category, and the strongest signal in this batch about who actually pays. ~14,000 employees spread across studio production, engineering, ads, games and corporate functions, with institutional knowledge fragmented across dozens of SaaS systems and strict access boundaries (unreleased title data, talent contracts, financials). What they need is not agent scratchpad memory but durable, permission-aware organizational memory: retrieval that respects ACLs, answers grounded in internal sources rather than the open web, and continuity so employees are not re-explaining context. The buying trigger is scale plus knowledge fragmentation plus a security review — which is why the same vendor's proof points pair Netflix with a defense contractor. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the parent prompt correctly notes Netflix is NOT on Onyx's current homepage logo wall — I fetched onyx.app and the only named customer visible is Ramp ('1,000+ of the world's top teams trust Onyx'). The Netflix claim traces to Onyx's March 2025 seed-round announcement. So the claim is genuinely Onyx's own published statement, not a fabrication, but its absence from current marketing means the deployment may have shrunk, ended, or become a reference Netflix no longer permits. Do not represent it as a current, active reference.
confidence: high that Netflix is real and that Onyx published the 14,000-employee deployment claim in its own funding announcement; medium on whether that deployment is still current, given Netflix's absence from Onyx's present-day logo wall

name: Thales (Thales Group)
what_it_does: French multinational aerospace, defence and security prime contractor specialising in electronics. Designs and builds military systems (radar, sonar, avionics, air traffic management, combat management systems, secure comms), civil aerospace equipment, space/satellites, digital identity and biometrics (Gemalto), and cybersecurity/data protection (Imperva, Vormetric, SYSGO). Sold its ground transportation/rail signalling business to Hitachi Rail in 2024. Listed on Euronext Paris (HO), CAC 40 constituent; 26.60% owned by the French state and 26.59% by Dassault Aviation. Originally Thomson-CSF (1968), renamed Thales in December 2000. NOTE: thalesgroup.com is behind Imperva/Incapsula bot protection and returned empty or challenge pages to every fetch attempt; figures below come from Wikipedia rather than the company's own site.
category: aerospace & defence prime contractor / defence electronics + cybersecurity (buyer of enterprise AI, not a vendor of agent products)
stage: Publicly listed large-cap (Euronext Paris: HO, CAC 40) — not a venture-stage company
funding: Not venture-funded. Publicly traded. Revenue €22.13B and operating income €2.08B in 2025 per Wikipedia. Has made large cash acquisitions including Imperva for $3.6B in 2023 and Gemalto.
headcount_estimate: ~83,000 employees (2024, per Wikipedia). Operates across roughly 60-70 countries. Could not verify a more recent figure — thalesgroup.com and LinkedIn were not reachable.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 1968 as Thomson-CSF, no accelerator involvement
founded_year: 1968 (as Thomson-CSF); renamed Thales Group in December 2000
sells_to: B2G and B2B enterprise — national governments, armed forces and defence ministries, space agencies, airlines and airports, banks and payment networks, telecoms and critical-infrastructure operators. Very large, long-cycle, procurement-heavy sales.
how_they_use_agents: Thales is an AI *buyer* here, not an agent vendor. Onyx's March 2025 seed-round post names Thales among 'extremely security conscious defense compan[ies]' in its enterprise customer base, and uses a Thales deal as the worked example for its Agent Search product — an employee asking 'How did we close Thales so quickly?' and the research agent decomposing that into parallel retrievals across CRM, docs and chat. So the agent deployment is internal knowledge work: enterprise search and multi-step research agents over institutional documents, not agents in a shipped product. Separately, Thales runs its own defence-AI programme (the cortAIx AI accelerator, embedded AI in sensors and mission systems) and a data-protection/cyber portfolio, but I could not fetch thalesgroup.com to verify current cortAIx details, so treat that as background rather than a confirmed Onyx use case.
why_they_need_memory: This is the clearest signal in the set about who buys 'company brain': an 83,000-person, 60+ country, 55-year-old prime contractor whose institutional knowledge is spread over decades of bid documents, program archives, CRM history and national-entity silos. The buying constraint is not agent capability — it is that classified, ITAR/export-controlled and national-security data cannot leave their boundary, so a cloud-only assistant is disqualified on day one. Onyx's pitch to them is deployment control (VPC, on-prem, air-gapped) plus permission-aware retrieval that mirrors existing source-system ACLs. Persistent organisational memory matters because the questions are cross-functional and historical ('how did we win this account', 'what did we commit to in that program'), which no single system of record can answer.

name: University of California, San Diego (UC San Diego)
what_it_does: Public research university in La Jolla, California, part of the University of California system. 45,087 students enrolled as of fall 2026 on a 1,200-acre campus; $1.7B in research funding in FY2024-25; 268,000 alumni; 16 Nobel laureates have taught there; ranked top-20 research university worldwide and #8 globally for highly cited researchers (Clarivate). Includes UC San Diego Health, Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the San Diego Supercomputer Center. It is an institution, not a company — 'product', 'funding stage' and 'sells to' do not map cleanly.
category: public research university / higher education — enterprise IT buyer, not an AI vendor
stage: Not applicable — public, state-affiliated non-profit university
funding: Not applicable (no venture funding). Public university funded by state appropriation, tuition, philanthropy and research grants; $1.7B in research funding for FY2024-25 per ucsd.edu.
headcount_estimate: Employee headcount unknown — I could not confirm a staff/faculty figure from a primary source. Known figures: 45,087 students enrolled fall 2026, and Onyx states UC San Diego is 'live with 37,000 users' on its deployment, which is the relevant number for the AI buying decision.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded 1960 as part of the University of California system
sells_to: Not applicable — serves students, faculty, staff, researchers and patients. The internal buyer for this category is central IT / the campus digital transformation office, which builds tools for internal constituents.
how_they_use_agents: UC San Diego built TritonGPT, its in-house campus AI assistant, on Onyx's open-source codebase. I confirmed this directly: https://tritongpt.ucsd.edu/ serves a page whose only body text is 'Onyx' — the Onyx web app shell. Onyx's seed-round post says: 'Leveraging the extensibility of the OSS nature of Onyx, the University of California, San Diego (where we're live with 37,000 users) has built human-in-the-loop agent workflows to automate common tasks.' So the agents are internal administrative automation with a human approval step, built by the university's own engineers on top of a self-hosted OSS platform — the customer is a builder, not just a seat buyer. Onyx's education page describes the target workloads: student questions on registration/financial aid/housing/IT, and staff tasks like grant-proposal drafting, syllabus and IRB lookup, HR and procurement navigation, with Canvas, Google Workspace, Confluence, SharePoint and Slack connectors. Note: Onyx's /solutions/education page says 'Trusted by leading universities' but the logos are images and did not survive text extraction, so I could not independently re-verify the logo-wall placement.
why_they_need_memory: A 37,000-user deployment across a decentralised campus where the same policy questions are re-asked every term by a population that turns over annually. The knowledge lives in Blink/administrative wikis, Canvas, SharePoint and departmental silos, and no single person holds it. Two hard constraints drive the buy: FERPA and student-data residency rule out sending records to a third-party cloud, and the OSS/self-host model let central IT extend the platform into their own branded product (TritonGPT) with custom agent workflows rather than accepting a vendor's UI. That combination — regulated data plus in-house engineering capacity plus extensibility — is the higher-ed profile for this category. Durable institutional memory is the actual product: the agents are only useful if they reliably recall policy and procedure that changes slowly but is documented badly.

Named AI systems include Altra, Cirra and Centaur. Positions itself explicitly as a sovereign European alternative to US defence primes. NOTE: helsing.ai sits behind a Vercel security checkpoint and returned HTTP 429 / a bot challenge to every fetch attempt, so product detail below is from Wikipedia rather than the company's own site.
category: defence AI / autonomous weapons systems — AI-native defence tech
stage: Late-stage private (growth/pre-IPO scale); Series D or later
funding: Approximately €1.37B raised as of June 2025 across: €100M (Nov 2021, led by Daniel Ek via Prima Materia); €209M Series B (Sept 2023, General Catalyst); €450M Series C (July 2024) at a €5B valuation; €600M (June 2025, Prima Materia-led) at a €12B valuation. Wikipedia additionally reports a July 2026 round of $1.8B at an $18B valuation with JPMorgan Chase, Lightspeed and Iconiq — this is after my training cutoff and I could only see it in one source, so treat that specific figure as unverified. Key holders: Daniel Ek/Prima Materia (~17%), General Catalyst (~12%), Saab (~5%).
headcount_estimate: ~900 employees (2025, per Wikipedia). Almost certainly higher now given the 2026 funding and the €580M German Combat Fighter System Nucleus contract, but I could not verify a current figure — LinkedIn and helsing.ai were both unreachable.
yc_or_accelerator: None — founded directly with backing from Daniel Ek's Prima Materia
founded_year: 2021 (March)
sells_to: B2G — European ministries of defence and armed forces. Known engagements include Ukraine (reported orders of 4,000 HF-1 and 6,000 HX-2 units) and a €580M German government contract (2026) for Combat Fighter System Nucleus development. Also partners with defence primes such as Saab and Airbus.
how_they_use_agents: Helsing's own product is autonomy and AI decision-making in weapons and sensor systems — that is a different thing from the internal 'company brain' category and should not be conflated with it. Their relationship to the agent-memory category is as a *quoted voice*, and it is weaker than the other two: the Onyx vs ChatGPT Enterprise page carries the quote 'When we work in a sensitive defense space, we prioritize suppliers that are big, established companies with a lot of reputation at stake, or services that we can self-deploy so that we control where the data goes.' I confirmed this quote is on that page and is the only testimonial there. But it is attributed to the company with no individual named, it argues for a deployment model rather than endorsing Onyx, and Helsing does not appear on any Onyx logo wall or in the seed-round customer list (I checked the seed post — Helsing is absent). So: the company is unambiguously real and well documented, but the customer relationship is inferred, not confirmed.
why_they_need_memory: If they are a customer, the driver is stated plainly in their own quote: in sensitive defence work they will only use suppliers that are large and reputationally exposed, or services they can self-deploy so data location stays under their control. That is the same disqualifying constraint as Thales — cloud-only agent memory is unbuyable — arriving from the opposite direction: a five-year-old, ~900-person, hypergrowth AI-native company rather than a 60-year-old prime. The memory need is scaling pain: an engineering organisation that roughly doubled repeatedly since 2021 across Munich, London, Paris and Berlin, working on classified programs, where onboarding and cross-program context transfer break down and the knowledge cannot be centralised in any external SaaS. Note this profile is the category's most interesting shape — AI-native companies building agents in their product still buy someone else's company brain for internal knowledge, because it is a different problem.

name: NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration)
what_it_does: The United States civil space agency, established 1958. Runs human spaceflight (ISS, Artemis lunar program), Earth science and climate observation, planetary science and robotic exploration (Perseverance, etc.), astrophysics (Hubble, James Webb), and aeronautics research. Operates through ~20 centers and facilities nationwide (JPL, Goddard, Ames, Johnson, Marshall, Langley, Glenn, Kennedy...) plus a very large contractor base. Not a company and not a commercial buyer in the ordinary sense: each center, directorate and prime contractor procures its own tooling, which matters a lot for interpreting the logo.
category: US federal government agency — aerospace R&D and space operations (public sector / regulated, air-gapped-capable buyer)
stage: n/a — federal agency funded by congressional appropriation, not equity
funding: unknown (no figure on the pages fetched). Appropriated federal budget, historically ~$24-25B/year; the FY2027 request page did not resolve. Do not treat any specific number here as verified.
headcount_estimate: unknown precisely — order of ~15,000-18,000 civil servants plus a substantially larger contractor workforce. NASA's own /about page states no workforce figure and I could not confirm a current number; 2025-26 reductions make older figures unreliable.
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: n/a — does not sell; serves the US public, and buys through federal procurement (FAR, FedRAMP/ATO, ITAR/export-control constraints)
how_they_use_agents: Mission-side AI is long-standing and well documented on nasa.gov/artificial-intelligence: Perseverance drives itself for ~88% of its traverse using onboard hazard analysis; the Digital Information Platform (DIP) and the Collaborative Departure Digital Rerouting tool autonomously propose fuel-efficient commercial flight routes; Prithvi is a geospatial foundation model run in orbit for Earth observation; AI is used for disaster-response imagery triage, solar storm prediction (COFFIES), and archive mining. NASA cites NIST's AI RMF and federal AI executive orders for governance. What is NOT documented anywhere I could verify is the actual Onyx use case — i.e. an internal enterprise chat/search layer over engineering docs, procedures, lessons-learned, and program archives. Given Onyx is open source and self-hostable, the most plausible reading is a self-hosted deployment inside one center, lab or contractor team rather than an agency-wide contract.
why_they_need_memory: The archetypal 'company brain' buyer for structural reasons rather than AI ambition: decades of institutional knowledge spread across 20 centers, contractors and retiring staff; safety-critical work where retrieval must be grounded and auditable; and hard security constraints (ITAR, classification tiers, per-center access control) that rule out most SaaS and push toward self-hosted, permission-aware, open-source deployments with granular ACLs — which is precisely Onyx's differentiator. Agent memory/context matters here because the answer to an engineering question depends on which program, which center and which revision of a procedure you are in.

stage: bootstrapped / unfunded

how_they_use_agents: Two distinct layers, and the second is what makes them a Trace customer. (2) Deploy/channel side: per the Trace testimonial, Vlad Mukhachev claims "85 of our business clients are scaling with Trace's AI layer, which helps us grow faster without adding headcount" — i.e. Green Republic is effectively an implementation/channel partner pushing an agent-orchestration layer into its own book of client accounts, and using it internally to run delivery without hiring. Additionally, as a channel partner deploying the same layer across 85 client orgs, they need memory isolated and durable per tenant.

category: client portal / client-collaboration SaaS with an embedded AI agent layer (professional-services ops)
stage: seed

how_they_use_agents: AI agents are a headline product surface, not a side feature. FuseBase sells custom and prebuilt no-code agents that operate inside the tools staff already use — browser, email, CRM, LinkedIn: website agents that read the current page and execute instructions against it, sales/support email responders, in-CRM contextual assistants, 24/7 support agents, and sales assistants that draft proposals, scripts and pitch prep. Agents are "trained on your specific requirements" and grounded in the customer's own knowledge base and prompt library, with privacy and access enforced at folder and page level. External analysts describe it as using agents to automate client onboarding and routine client-facing work. Notably this makes FuseBase a partial competitor to Trace rather than a clean customer.
why_they_need_memory: The knowledge base is the memory: agents are only useful if they answer as the firm, from the firm's own documents, per client. Three concrete pressures — (1) per-client isolation, since each portal is a different customer's confidential context and agent retrieval must be scoped to folder/page permissions; (2) longitudinal client context, because onboarding, deliverables and support threads span months and the agent must recall prior deliverables and decisions; (3) productizing expertise, which is the co-founder's stated framing — turning a consultancy's tacit process knowledge into something an agent can execute repeatedly is precisely a durable-memory problem. Metered AI request quotas also mean retrieval efficiency has direct COGS implications.
confidence: high on the company facts; LOW that FuseBase is actually a Trace customer. The citation is a Product Hunt review left by Kate Ramakaieva, who is a Marketing Specialist at FuseBase (confirmed on her PH profile) — that is peer-to-peer Product Hunt engagement between two startups, not a purchase signal, and the parent brief already flags it as the reviewer's own profile affiliation rather than a vendor claim.
