name: Skarbe (Skarbe, Inc.)
what_it_does: DEFUNCT — skarbe.com now serves a "Goodbye from Skarbe" wind-down notice; the company ceased operations around April 2026. While operating it was an AI sales assistant pitched as a CRM replacement for founder-led sales, branded around "Oskar, your AI assistant who never forgets." It connected to the user's email and calendar and ran in the background: auto-tracking deal conversations with no manual data entry, chasing cold leads, recording and summarizing calls, drafting follow-ups in the user's own voice, generating meeting prep briefs and prioritized next-step task lists, and nudging on overdue actions. Marketed as ~2 hours/day recovered. Reached 2,500+ users, supported 100+ languages, freemium trial model. Dual-HQ San Francisco, CA and Krakow, Poland, with Belarusian founders. Roadmap at the time of funding: automated lead qualification, a mobile app, and per-user personalized LLMs built on Mistral. Founders: Mikita Martynau (CEO, previously scaled PandaDoc from $10M to $100M revenue), Alex Talyuk (CTO, prior AI/CV/NLP work at SF startups), Ilya Korzun (COO and co-founder, originally the company's first angel investor — he is the person quoted in Trace's Product Hunt reference).
category: AI SDR / AI sales assistant (CRM-free sales automation for SMB and founder-led sales)
stage: pre-seed (wound down)
funding: $600K pre-seed announced 30 June 2025, led by FIRSTPICK, with Somersault Ventures and angels Andreas Mihalovits and Jeroen Van Ermen. That was the only round; total raised $600K. Some aggregators label it "Seed" rather than pre-seed — same round.
headcount_estimate: unknown — no reliable figure found. Consistent with a pre-seed team of under 10, and the company is now shut down, so any current number is zero.
yc_or_accelerator: FIRSTPICK (Baltic pre-seed accelerator/VC) led the round — not YC
sells_to: B2B SMB and prosumer — solo founders, indie startups and lean teams doing founder-led sales; explicitly positioned against Salesforce and HubSpot for people who "hate CRMs"
how_they_use_agents: The product was the agent. Oskar ran continuously over the user's inbox and calendar rather than waiting for prompts: parsing email threads and call recordings to extract deal state, maintaining a pipeline the human never had to update, deciding and surfacing the next action per deal, drafting outbound and follow-up copy in the user's voice, and building pre-meeting briefs from accumulated relationship history. The design premise was zero-input CRM — the agent observes and remembers instead of the human typing.
why_they_need_memory: Memory was literally the product promise — "an AI assistant who never forgets." Removing the CRM removes the structured database that normally stores deal state, so all longitudinal context (who was contacted, what was promised, objection history, relationship warmth, the user's individual writing voice) has to live in the agent's own persistent memory across months of email and calls. Their stated roadmap of per-user personalized LLMs on Mistral is the same need expressed as fine-tuning. This is the purest fit of the three for a company-brain/agent-memory vendor — and also a caution, since the company still failed.
confidence: high — funding, founders, founding year and the shutdown are all confirmed from multiple independent sources; only headcount is genuinely unknown

CLAIRE is its metadata-driven AI layer. The homepage claims 5,000+ enterprise customers, 80+ of the Fortune 100, and 130 trillion+ monthly cloud transactions. stage: Acquired — no longer independent. IPO'd on Nasdaq 1999, taken private 2015 by Permira + CPP Investments for ~$5.3B, re-IPO'd on NYSE (INFA) Oct 2021, and acquired by Salesforce (announced May 2025, ~$8B; completed Nov 2025).
funding: Not venture-stage. ~$5.3B take-private (Permira/CPPIB, 2015, with participation from Microsoft and Salesforce Ventures); ~$8B Salesforce acquisition closed Nov 2025. Revenue ~$1.64B in FY2024. Not verified against Crunchbase/PitchBook this session (search budget exhausted) — figures from Wikipedia and the company site.

sells_to: B2B enterprise (large regulated enterprises — Fortune 100 data/analytics and governance teams; CDO/CIO buyers)
how_they_use_agents: Two distinct things, which should not be conflated. (1) In their PRODUCT: Informatica positions IDMC as the trusted-data substrate underneath other people's AI agents — CLAIRE AI for metadata intelligence and copilot-style assistance, an MCP server to 'equip AI agents with trusted data,' and headless data management APIs so agents/agent frameworks can call governed data services. The pitch is infrastructure-for-agents rather than a named end-user agent product; I could not load a dedicated agentic-AI product page (404) to confirm specific named agents beyond CLAIRE. (2) As an Onyx logo, the plausible use is INTERNAL: a company-wide AI assistant over Confluence/Jira/Slack/Drive/support docs for a ~5,000-person distributed enterprise. Onyx describes itself as an open-source enterprise AI chat/search platform ('primary interface to AI'), which is an internal-knowledge deployment, not an embedded product component.
why_they_need_memory: ~5,000 employees across a highly technical, documentation-heavy product surface (hundreds of connectors, dozens of services, long-lived enterprise support cases), plus the disruption of being absorbed into Salesforce — institutional knowledge is scattered across wikis, tickets, and departing people. An assistant that answers the same questions repeatedly needs persistent org context: which service does what, which decisions were already made, who owns what. Their own product thesis ('agents are only as good as the governed data behind them') is essentially the enterprise-memory argument applied to structured data, so they are a philosophically aligned buyer.

Note: gap.com is the consumer storefront for the Gap brand; the corporate entity is Gap Inc. at gapinc.com, which is almost certainly what the logo represents.
category: Specialty apparel retail (B2C) — a pure end-user/IT buyer of AI tooling, not an AI vendor
stage: Public company (NYSE: GAP), 57 years old
funding: Not applicable — publicly traded since 1976, no venture funding. FY2025 revenue $15.4B, net income $816M. Market cap not verified this session.
headcount_estimate: ~82,000 employees (mostly retail store associates; corporate/tech headcount is a small fraction of this and I could not isolate it)
yc_or_accelerator: none
sells_to: Consumers (B2C retail). As a buyer of this category, the purchasing org is internal corporate IT / knowledge-management, not a product team.
how_they_use_agents: No agent appears in Gap's customer-facing product — they sell clothes. Gap Inc. has publicly talked about AI for merchandising, demand forecasting, personalization, and marketing content, but I could not confirm specifics from their site in this session and will not assert them. The Onyx relationship is almost certainly an INTERNAL enterprise-search/assistant deployment for corporate employees (merchandising, supply chain, HR, store ops) rather than anything embedded in a product. This makes Gap the clearest example in this set of the 'big non-tech enterprise buys a company brain' buyer profile — the value is answering employee questions over internal documents, not building agents.
why_they_need_memory: Four semi-autonomous brands under one corporate parent, ~82,000 employees, ~3,500 stores, and knowledge fragmented across merchandising systems, vendor/supply-chain docs, HR policy, store operations manuals, and brand-specific processes. High store-level turnover means institutional knowledge walks out constantly. A retrieval assistant without persistent memory re-answers the same policy and process questions forever; org-level memory (who owns which vendor, what the current markdown policy is, what was decided last season) is where the value would sit. This is inference from company shape, not from a stated Gap requirement.

name: ThoughtSpot
what_it_does: Analytics / business-intelligence platform, now marketed as an 'agentic analytics platform' — 'governed AI for analytics, everywhere work happens.' Originally search-driven self-service BI letting non-technical users query data directly; today the product centers on Spotter, an AI analyst agent, sitting on a governed semantic layer that defines business logic, joins, calendars, calculations, and row-level security before any analysis runs. Also ships Liveboards (interactive dashboards), automated insights, and embedded analytics for customers' own apps. Integrates with Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery/GCP, and AWS. Founded 2012 by Ajeet Singh and Amit Prakash; HQ Mountain View, CA. CEO Ketan Karkhanis since Sept 2024. Acquired Mode Analytics for ~$200M in 2023. Named customers on their site include Sephora, Booking.com, Cisco, Lyft, Brambles, Verisk, and Mattel.
category: AI/agentic analytics and BI software (dev-and-analyst-adjacent enterprise SaaS)
stage: Late-stage private, venture-backed — last disclosed round was Series F (Nov 2020). No IPO as of this research; no newer round confirmed in this session.
funding: ~$663M raised total across Series A–F; Series F was $100M in Nov 2020 at a reported $4.2B valuation. Investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures, General Catalyst, Sapphire Ventures, Silver Lake, and Snowflake Ventures. Reported $100M ARR in 2020. Any funding, valuation change, or IPO after 2020 is unverified — I could not run Crunchbase/TechCrunch searches this session, so treat the $4.2B as a stale 2020 mark, not a current one.
headcount_estimate: ~600 (Wikipedia figure; likely higher post-Mode acquisition — LinkedIn not checked this session, so treat as a floor)
yc_or_accelerator: none — traditional Sand Hill Road venture path (Lightspeed, Khosla led early)
sells_to: B2B enterprise, plus developers via embedded analytics. Buyers are data/analytics leaders (CDO, head of BI) at mid-market to large enterprises; end users are business teams.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the product now, not a feature. Spotter is an AI analyst agent that takes natural-language questions and — notably — does NOT do naive text-to-SQL: it 'translates questions into search tokens grounded in your governed semantic layer,' producing traceable, auditable queries. It does multi-step reasoning: decomposes the question, tests assumptions, checks results, reruns analysis, and recommends actions. It can act outside analytics too — create Jira tickets, update Salesforce opportunities, post to Slack, trigger workflows. Around it sits a family of agents: AgentSpot (multiplayer/shared agents built on company data), SpotterModel (semantic modeling), SpotterViz (dashboard generation), SpotterCode (AI-assisted coding), and customizable 'Spotter Analysts' per team. Separately, as an Onyx logo, their own internal use would be employee knowledge search. Flagging the nuance on is_ai_native: founded 2012, pre-LLM, as search-based BI — AI-forward from early on (SpotIQ), but not a post-2022 AI-native startup; the agentic layer is a 2024–2025 repositioning of a 14-year-old company.
why_they_need_memory: Two angles. (1) Product-adjacent: their entire architectural argument is that agents must be grounded in a governed semantic layer rather than guessing — a persistent, curated, shared context store is literally the thing they sell. Their Spotter page does not, however, describe per-user memory, feedback loops, or learning from usage history, so 'memory' in their product today means governed semantics, not accumulated experience. That gap is exactly what an agent-memory vendor would sell into. (2) Internal: a ~600–1,000-person company that absorbed Mode Analytics, changed CEO in 2024, and repositioned its entire product line in ~18 months has a lot of freshly stale internal documentation — the classic case for a company brain. Which of these motivated an Onyx deployment is unknown; the Onyx logo wall indicates internal use.

Ops-side: a ~1,100-person, heavily regulated fintech has policy, compliance, underwriting and support knowledge scattered across Slack, Notion, Jira, Zendesk and Salesforce; Onyx's pitch (secure, self-hostable, permission-aware retrieval) matches a fintech that cannot ship customer financial data to a generic chatbot. Post-Capital One, the integration itself creates a large knowledge-reconciliation problem.

Sells non-virtualized NVIDIA H100/Blackwell capacity with InfiniBand networking for training, plus a managed-inference layer called Nebius Token Factory, serverless AI, MLOps/DataOps/ModelOps tooling, and an agent stack (agentic search, AI orchestration, human validation). Named customers include Revolut, Shopify, Recraft and Sword Health. Reference NVIDIA Cloud Partner. Nebius sells: Token Factory (managed multi-model inference — the layer agents actually run on), Agentic Search (materially reinforced by the Tavily acquisition — Tavily is the search API a large share of LLM agent frameworks call for web grounding), AI Orchestration, and Human Validation (human-in-the-loop for agent output, adjacent to its Toloka stake). As a buyer: a company that went from ~$530M FY2025 revenue to ~$3B ARR in Q2 2026 while hiring hard across Amsterdam, Finland, Israel, Estonia and the US has an acute institutional-knowledge problem — runbooks, cluster/hardware configurations, incident history and customer capacity commitments changing weekly, plus a workforce partly inherited from a completely different company (Yandex). That is the archetypal case for retrieval over internal docs. As adjacency: Nebius' customers build agents on Token Factory and Tavily, and those agents need durable memory and grounding — meaning Nebius is simultaneously a customer of the category and infrastructure underneath it, which makes it a strategically interesting logo rather than just a revenue line.

stage: Private, family-owned for 115 years. Not a startup, never venture-backed, no outside investors.

how_they_use_agents: IMPORTANT CAVEAT — the only public evidence is Airia's own marketing. Airia's homepage lists Mars in a logo marquee under 'Used by leading security and AI transformation teams' and shows a card reading 'Mars: Governed AI across global brands / Mars centralizes model access, policy, and cost controls on Airia for product and operations teams worldwide.' There is no testimonial quote, no named Mars employee, and I independently confirmed the linked detail page airia.com/airia-in-action/mars/ returns HTTP 404. I found no first-party Mars confirmation of the relationship; mars.com's main site contains no AI or digital-transformation content at all. name: Trag

sells_to: Developers / engineering teams — bottom-up dev tools motion (GitHub PR integration, freemium + paid tiers, Product Hunt launch). B2B SMB / startup engineering orgs rather than enterprise.
how_they_use_agents: The core product IS the agent: an LLM reads every pull request with repo-wide context and reviews it against team-authored, plain-English rules, then posts actionable PR feedback like a senior engineer rather than a pattern-matching scanner. Agents also did the earlier refactor/migration automation. Trag's whole pitch — "automates tribal knowledge into deterministic rules" and repository-wide semantic context — is a memory problem stated as a product. Separately, as a ~5-person distributed startup (Yerevan/SF) they had no ops headcount, so a shared "company brain" that keeps tasks, people and models in sync substitutes for a coordination layer they couldn't staff. Caveat for the buyer-profile analysis: this is a lapsed data point — the company was absorbed in Aug 2025 and the testimonial predates that.

name: GodmodeHQ
url: https://godmodehq.com (site still up as an archive; banner reads "Godmode is sunsetting"; footer © The Money Company Limited)
what_it_does: GodmodeHQ was a London-based AI sales/GTM platform — an "AI SDR"/agentic outbound system. It scraped the web daily for buying-intent signals (hiring posts, funding news, tech-stack changes, blog/press activity), sourced and verified matching leads against your ICP, researched each account, then drafted and sent personalized email and LinkedIn outreach through connected accounts. The founder described it as a "reverse Google": instead of SEO results, it surfaced actual people with the specific need your product solves, deliberately capped at 50 emails + 25 LinkedIn invites per account per day (explicitly anti-blast). Later product lines: "Associates" (AI account executives, launched Nov 2024), user-buildable agents with tools/sources (Apollo, Salesforce, HubSpot, Gmail, Outlook, web search/scrape, document extraction), natural-language automations, publishable internal/external agents, AI-native lead-capture forms, and a unified inbox where a human reviewed and approved every agent action. Pricing was usage-based at ~$1 per lead sourced/researched/contacted ($250/250 leads, $500/500 leads, custom enterprise). Claimed 1,000+ teams and named customers/case studies including Paddle, Latonas, 403 Tech, Mission Cyber Group, First Degree Capital and Stellarup. IMPORTANT STATUS: SHUT DOWN. On 30 Apr 2025 founder Mert Deveci published "Godmode: Disabled" — after ~2 years they sunset the product, closed the company and returned capital to investors despite 3+ years of runway. Stated reasons: (1) they failed to crack enterprise sales — "replacing 50% of an AE's daily workflow created tension in our deal cycles; nobody likes feeling replaceable"; (2) they concluded it wouldn't become a venture-scale business. Access ended 1 May 2025. Mert Deveci is now building The Money Company (AI for accountants) plus Banker, Gora and CodeWindow, and lists himself as "building in stealth" / growth engineering at Neon.

funding: $2.6M pre-seed, reported Aug 2024 (Webrazzi, syndicated via Dealroom), from BITKRAFT Ventures, Delphi (Delphi Digital/Delphi Ventures) and Paribu Ventures, on top of an earlier angel round. A LinkedIn-sourced write-up says "backed by over $2.5M+ in venture funding," consistent with that figure. Treat $2.6M as reported-not-primary — GodmodeHQ never issued its own funding press release that I could find.

The shutdown post names the entire team: Mert Deveci (founder/CEO), Bertan Teberci (CTO), Gaston Che (frontend lead), Can Cotel (frontend & design engineer), Hussein Abou Eita (GTM). yc_or_accelerator: None found. Not YC. Directly VC-backed. Related entity: Troy Labs (Istanbul, founded 2022, 2-10 employees) — Mert Deveci is associated with it ("Troy Guild", a troylabs.io email appears in product screenshots); the Godmode site now sits under The Money Company Limited.
founded_year: 2023 (Dealroom: "founded by Mert Deveci in early 2023"; product launched April 2024; job posts as GodmodeHQ appear from Jan 2023)
sells_to: B2B SMB and mid-market sales/GTM teams — pricing tiers were explicitly framed as "businesses with up to $1M+ revenue," "$10M+," "$20M+." They tried and failed to move upmarket into enterprise, which is the reason they gave for shutting down.
how_they_use_agents: Agents were the entire product surface: (1) "AI Associates" — autonomous account executives that scoured the web nightly for intent signals, sourced and verified leads and drafted outreach, notifying the human each morning for approval; (2) user-built research agents wired to Apollo/Salesforce/HubSpot/Gmail/Outlook/web search/scrape/document extraction, invoked in natural language and publishable to coworkers or customers; (3) multi-step natural-language automations chaining research → summarize → draft → send; (4) an agent-configuration layer holding "full context of your business and your value propositions," formatting rules, purpose and a document knowledge base; (5) a review inbox where every proposed agent action (e.g. "Send email to Martin") required human accept-and-send.
why_they_need_memory: Their product only worked if agents carried persistent company context — ICP definition, value props, brand/formatting rules, knowledge-base documents, exclusion lists synced from the CRM, and the history of which prospects had already been touched. That is agent memory by another name, and they built a homegrown version of it ("agent settings," knowledge bases, rules). Internally, a 5-person team running an agent-heavy operation is exactly the profile that buys a cross-department "company brain" — Mert's Trace testimonial claims "2x the productivity across our entire department… a full month of work saved." Big caveat for the buyer analysis: GodmodeHQ shut down in April 2025, so this logo represents a founder-to-founder testimonial from a company that no longer exists, not a live paying account.

name: &Volume (also written "and Volume" / nVolume)
what_it_does: &Volume builds an AI risk-and-allocation layer for institutional digital-asset portfolios — "autopilot for risk management" / "risk management infrastructure for digital assets," self-described in the DeFAI (DeFi + AI) category. founded_year: 2024 (Startup Intros: founded 2024 in Edinburgh; Ilia Kraev says he founded nVolume/&Volume during his University of Edinburgh MSc project, MSc completed 2023 — so late 2023/2024 is the honest range)
sells_to: B2B, institutional finance — the site names family offices, asset managers and corporate treasuries. Prior positioning targeted crypto traders/prosumers, so they are mid-migration from prosumer to institutional. Founder is Edinburgh/Helsinki-based, ex-ICBC, BNP Paribas, UN; runs a quant fund as a hobby.
how_they_use_agents: Agents are the product. LLM/ML agents ingest live on-chain and exchange data, continuously score market/protocol/liquidity/counterparty risk, simulate scenarios, and either recommend (Co-Pilot) or autonomously execute rebalances and trades within user-defined risk limits (Autopilot). Their accelerator profile puts it bluntly: "&Volume builds AI agents that autonomously manage digital assets portfolios — protecting capital during crashes and capturing growth — while users keep full control." Separately, the Trace testimonial describes an internal/ops use: "1000+ of customer queries streamlined into a single autonomous flow, with results delivered to the right person" — i.e. an agent triaging and routing inbound customer queries to the correct human, which is a support/ops workflow, not their trading engine.
why_they_need_memory: Two distinct pulls. (1) Product-side: an autonomous agent that moves real capital must remember a client's risk limits, mandate, position history, past decisions and the reasoning behind them — and must be able to explain them after the fact. &Volume markets explainability explicitly ("risk can be measured, decisions can be explained"), which is a durable-memory-plus-audit-trail requirement, sharpened by operating for regulated institutional clients across the UK and Finland. (2) Ops-side: routing 1,000+ inbound customer queries to "the right person" requires the system to know the org — who owns what, what was answered before, which account a query belongs to. That is precisely the "company brain" pitch, and it is why a sub-15-person team spread across Edinburgh and Helsinki buys one instead of hiring a support/ops layer.

(1) Agents inside the product: BigID's homepage advertises an 'Agent for Stewardship' that automates 'data curation, validation, and enrichment at scale', and AI-driven classification across 100+ languages. (2) Governing OTHER people's agents — this is now the dominant theme in their 2026 news. Their site says BigID can 'detect when AI agents access sensitive data' and 'enforce permissions, monitor behavior, and flag unusual agentic activity before it leads to exposure.' Their 2026 press cadence is almost entirely agent-adjacent: 'BigID Extends Data Access Governance to AI Agents' (Mar 2026), 'Integrated AI Governance for Employee AI Use' (Mar 2026), 'AI Defense in an Agent-Driven Enterprise' (Apr 2026), 'The Rise of Non-Human Identities: Who Governs AI Access to Data' (May 2026), 'BigID Delivers the AI Sovereignty Standard' (Aug 2026), plus DSPM extended to markdown files 'in the age of vibe coding'. why_they_need_memory: A ~600-person security vendor with an unusually broad product surface (DSPM + DLP + privacy + AI governance + data catalog) and a very high documentation-to-headcount ratio: security research, regulatory frameworks (GDPR, CCPA, DORA, EU AI Act), connector/integration docs, and a heavy analyst/compliance content operation. Field, SE and support teams need grounded answers across that sprawl. Critically, as a security company selling permission-aware data control, they cannot use a knowledge tool that ignores ACLs — which is exactly Onyx's pitch (self-hostable, permission-aware, open source). They are effectively a reference buyer for the 'secure company brain' variant of this category.

Concretely: Agent Builder lets customers ship agents in a low-code canvas, model-agnostic (any third-party LLM or UiPath-curated models), with evaluation scoring before deployment and templates for ticket classification, document extraction, knowledge retrieval and content generation; Maestro orchestrates long-running processes across agents, robots and humans; Autopilot generates agent logic from prompts; Orchestrator schedules and monitors; the AI Trust Layer plus human-in-the-loop as a first-class workflow step handles governance. Separately, they are themselves an Onyx customer (verified: <div title="UiPath"> in Onyx's homepage marquee HTML).
why_they_need_memory: The most interesting data point in this set: a company that sells agent orchestration bought a third-party company-brain for its own internal knowledge. That tells you internal knowledge retrieval is treated as a distinct problem from the agent platform they ship — you build agents for customer workflows, you buy a brain for your own staff. Practically: ~4,000 employees across 100+ countries, a two-decade documentation legacy spanning the old RPA stack (Studio, Orchestrator, activity packs, thousands of KB articles) layered under an entirely new agentic stack, plus a 3M-strong developer community and forum. Support engineers and field teams must answer questions that span both eras, and the answers live in product docs, forums, Jira and Confluence. Their own filings stress governance and auditability, so a permission-aware, source-cited retrieval layer fits their control requirements.

name: Mission Inbox
what_it_does: Mission Inbox is dedicated email sending infrastructure focused on deliverability and inbox placement for high-volume senders. Rather than replacing a CRM or sequencer, it sits underneath them as the sending layer. Its differentiators: 'Isolated Cubes,' separate sending environments so sales, marketing, and transactional traffic cannot damage each other's reputation; dedicated IPs instead of shared pools; MI Shield, an AI-powered pre-send check on content, headers, DNS, and spam signals; and API, SMTP, and IMAP access plus webhooks, logs, and delivery analytics. Published pricing is transparent and low: Lite $50/mo (15 mailboxes, 5,000 sends), Scale $199/mo (30 mailboxes, 10,000 sends), Pro $99/mo for developers (5 domains, 100K sends), with $2 per extra domain and $1 per additional 1,000 sends. Marketing claims 50M+ emails processed monthly, a 98% inbox rate, and 8 redundancy layers across 3 continents. It positions explicitly against SendGrid, Mailgun, Resend, Gmail/Outlook, Mailforge, MailReef, Maildoso, and Hypertide, and integrates with HubSpot, Salesforce, Apollo, Instantly, Smartlead, Salesloft, Outreach, EmailBison, and PlusVibe. Named logos and case studies: Unit21, BloomTech, Practical Prospecting, Relay, AmpleMarket, Stream. Per LinkedIn the company rebranded and acquired CeyMail to move into transactional email, framing itself as 'mission control for every email your business sends.' Developer docs cover Go, Java, Node.js, PHP, Python, and Ruby. Note the site's own framing of the deliverability problem: '52% of business emails go unseen.'

A ~13-person team supporting agencies that each run 20+ client campaigns cannot scale that by memory — Practical Prospecting alone migrated 20+ client campaigns off three other platforms in a day. The team also publishes heavy SEO content (23+ blog posts, 9 comparison pages, 9 integration pages, industry pages) largely under a single author, plus a growing docs surface in six languages, which is a content operation that benefits from a shared knowledge base.
